en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Commentary on the Pāṭhika Chapter of the Dīgha Nikāya.
1. Commentary on the Pāṭhika Sutta: Commentary on the Story of Sunakkhatta. Regarding "Commentary on Unprecedented Words":
this refers to the commentary on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*) because it has not been previously taken up below; thus, it concerns what is unprecedented and new.
This is the commentary on the word, an exposition of its meaning; for it is said: "Having abandoned that which has come again and again.
Regarding the phrase "in the Malla country," whatever needs to be said there has already been stated according to the method explained above.
He dwelt in a grove endowed with shade and water because there was no monastery built in the vicinity of Anupiya. If he had not yet entered [the city], why is it said, "he entered"?
He said, “I shall enter,” and so forth; by this, he shows that figurative expressions (upacāra) are applied to what is yet to happen as if it were already past.
Now, illustrating that meaning through a simile, he says, “Just as...,” and so on. “This” refers to the thought, “It is indeed too early,” and so forth.
“Ativiya pago” means very early in the morning. Because of his modesty in covering his private parts...
And by his undertaking the going-forth as a wanderer, he was a clothed wanderer, not a naked wanderer.

2. Because of the Blessed One’s birth into a high family, his departure through the Great Renunciation, his practice of austerities not shared by others, his dwelling in seclusion, his being esteemed by the world, his great benefit to the world through his exhortations and instructions, and his crushing of the doctrines of others—

"Having great psychic power (mahiddhika), having great majesty (mahānubhāva)"—relying on such specific qualities of their own direct experience, even most followers of other sects, upon seeing the Blessed One, indeed display respect, reverence, and esteem; therefore it was said:
"Upon seeing the Blessed One, without being stiff with pride," and so forth. "By way of worldly convention" means by way of worldly usage.
"Cirassanti" means after a long time. They speak thus "ādīni" by way of conventional usage. "Tassa" refers to that wanderer of the Bhaggava clan.
"Gihisahāyo" means a companion from the time of being a householder. To show the manner in which he renounced, the words beginning with "paccakkhāmi" were spoken.

3. Regarding the word *uddissa*: it means "pointing out" by way of showing respect for the Teacher; this is the intended meaning here. To demonstrate this, he said, "The Blessed One is mine," and so forth.

When Sunakkhatta’s thought arose, "I renounce the Blessed One," and his speech was thus broken, from that very moment he had no further connection with the Blessed One, owing to his status as one who has left the Sakyan-son's fold (*asakyaputtiya*).
Because it is outside the teaching (*sāsana*). This, first of all, is the reasoning regarding the teaching here.
However, since this [reasoning] is not properly within the scope of others except for those skilled in the reasoning of the teaching, the Blessed One—having stated "Api nu... (But surely...
and so forth to show that he himself has no personal connection with it as something common to all—said to Sunakkhatta, "Who are you, and whom do you reject? Because...
This connection pertains to the mouth [the act of speaking], not to the offering of worship and so forth;

and since neither of these two exists here—namely, the state of being a petitioner nor the state of being one who is to be petitioned—the Blessed One said to Sunakkhatta, "Who are you, being, that you reject whom? Therefore, to demonstrate that point, it was said:
"Or a petitioner might reject the one who is petitioned. Or, a petitioner might reject the one who is petitioned.
This is the connection. You, however, are neither a petitioner, because you did not come into my presence saying, "Venerable sir, I shall live dedicated to the Blessed One";
nor are you one who has been asked, because I did not request it of you, saying, "Come, Sunakkhatta, live dedicated to me."
"Who is equal? means: among those who beg and are begged from, who indeed could be considered equal? "Whom? means:

whom among those very same beggars and those from whom they are begged do you reject me as being? "Empty men" means: men who are void because they lack any superhuman state (*uttarimanussadhamma*), such as the jhānas or the paths.
[Objection: But did not this Sunakkhatta produce mundane jhānas and certain higher knowledges (*abhiññā*)? [Response: Even so...
He gave rise to it; however, he fell away from his attainment at the very moment he conceived malice toward the Blessed One.
"Offense" (*aparādha*) refers to the arising of a defilement that serves as the cause for straying from right practice; thus it was said: "As great as your offense is, so great is your fault.
The phrase *yāvañca* is used to indicate the extent of a limit or boundary, as seen in such passages as "as far as by that Blessed One... and so forth.
"By you" (*teti*): by you. "This" (*idam*): this is merely a particle. "Offended" (*aparaddham*): having committed an offense.

This is what is meant: "O empty man, by you who say such things as 'Venerable Sir, I now renounce the Blessed One,' an offense has been committed to such an extent that there is no measure for that offense."
4. "Human qualities" (*manussadhamma*) refers to those qualities not to be practiced by humans except through the application of meditation (*bhāvanānuyoga*).
For since it succeeds merely through the mental resolve (*cittādhiṭṭhāna*) of humans, it stands as if it were a quality cultivated by them; thus it is so called.

Furthermore, the mention of "humans" here is because [this power] occurs most frequently among them. It is a miracle consisting of supernormal power (*iddhibhūta-pāṭihāriya*), not a miracle of mind-reading or instruction (*ādesanānusāsani-pāṭihāriya*).
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Made" means set in motion. "It goes forth" (*niyyāti*) means it emerges;
the sense is that it proceeds by way of emerging from the suffering of saṃsāra. For when the Dhamma goes forth, the person possessing it is said to "go forth.
However, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), it is shown that the prefix *ni-* is merely a particle and the meaning is simply "it goes" (*yāti*), hence [the word] "goes" (*gacchati*).
The meaning has been stated. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), it is a restatement by way of the locative case referring to the meaning already expressed as the primary subject;
thus, showing that the meaning here is "in that Dhamma they lead rightly to the destruction of suffering," he said: "when [the Dhamma] is leading [to the destruction of suffering]," and so forth.

5. It is known as the "foremost" (*agga*) because it is the highest; thus it is *aggañña*. "Description of the world" (*lokapaññatti*) means the making known of the world. "The foremost of the world" (*lokassa aggaṃ*)...
At the time of the world’s arising, it must be known and understood thus: "This is the summit of the world. "The boundary of the summit" means the initial boundary.

Having prattled on to this extent: "Venerable sir, from now on I shall no longer dwell under the Blessed One," and "For the Blessed One does not perform for me a superhuman feat of psychic power," and "No..."

Having thus prattled on at length with the words, "But, Bhante, the Blessed One teaches the origin of the world (aggañña)," it is said that he spoke this to demonstrate that the Blessed One was unable to perform the Teacher's duty through a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*) nor to explain the origin of the world.
Therefore, he said, "It is said that Sunakkhatta... and so forth. This is because there was no foundation for his position due to the subsequent words [of the Buddha].
"Without a foundation. For that very reason, "soundless," meaning without noise.
"For the purpose of seeing the danger" means for the purpose of seeing the danger pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). Therefore he said, "You will yourself incur censure.
However, the dangers pertaining to future lives (*samparāyika*) are manifold; showing these, Sunakkhatta—

"One should not believe" refers specifically to what pertains to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*). "By many reasons" means by the various modes of praise, such as "Thus indeed is the Blessed One, the Worthy One," and so forth.

Having spoken dispraise of those worthy of praise out of one's own foolishness, with the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) that "in this way, there will be no dispraise of me," [the Blessed One] has thus shown the danger in being a slanderer; furthermore, of him...
In order to make clear the reason for this statement, he said, "Thus indeed to you," and so forth; to show that, he said, "Then," and so forth.
For in this way, Sunakkhatta would not have even a brief opportunity to speak. "He departed" (apakkami) means that having risen from where he was standing, he withdrew.
"Departed" (apakkanto) means fallen away from the teaching. Therefore he said, "fallen" (cuto). "In this very manner" (evameva) refers to him as he was departing.

And he did not depart in such a manner that, upon the breakup of the body, he would be reborn in a state of deprivation; rather, he departed in exactly such a way that he would be reborn in a state of deprivation.
The commentary on the section concerning the Kora noble:

"By two phrases" means by two sentences, because they are introduced as a contrast and function as an exposition of both points for what follows. "By way of showing the connection" means by way of showing the connection known as *anusandhi* (the logical sequence).
Regarding the phrase *ekaṃ samayaṃ*, he says "at one time" (*ekasmiṃ samaye*) because the locative case is used here in the sense of a location. "Thūla" is the name of a district;

it received that name by way of the princes who resided there. He says "one who has undertaken the dog-vow" (*samādinnakukkuravato*) because this person possesses the dog-vow through its formal undertaking.
"And another" refers to [the practice] of the four-cornered [vow] alone.
"Wandering about, eating and consuming only after having done so, and discharging urine after lifting up the left foot"—such and other activities to be performed by dogs [are mentioned].
"Catur-koṇḍa" means moving or going on four limbs of the body;
one who possesses this is a *catur-koṇḍika*. Furthermore, because he [uses] four limbs of the body...
He moves with a clashing gait; therefore it is said, "clashing in four ways. For this very reason, he says, "the two knees," and so forth.
Or, *bhakkhasaṃ* means that which is to be eaten and that which is to be consumed. Therefore he says, "whatever kind of food there is, whether hard or soft.
Granted, eating indeed must be done with the mouth, but [this phrase] is intended to preclude placing food there by means of the hand.
To explain what "determination" (*avadhāraṇa*) is, he says: "without touching with the hand," which means without grasping. "Of beautiful form" (*sundararūpa*) means the state of being beautiful.
"Vata" is a particle used in the sense of aspiration, as in such expressions as "O, may I become a possessor [of this]" (*aho vatāhaṃ lābhī assa*).
Thus, his aspiration was: "A recluse indeed ought to be of such a nature; O, may I become like this!"
Therefore he said, “Thus indeed,” and so forth.
The particle *api* has the sense of reproach, as in such expressions as “even [if] one sprinkles, O Palaṇḍaka.
Regarding the Arahants and Buddhas, and the disciples of the Buddha, the view arose in him that “the Arahants are not those whose taints are exhausted. As it is said in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta:
“There are no superhuman states, no distinctions in noble knowledge and vision, for the ascetic Gotama.
The word “on the seventh day” (*sattamaṃ divasaṃ*) is used in the accusative case with the sense of the locative. “By alasaka” means by indigestion, a disease of the stomach.
Because his skin and flesh had become thin, he was like a withered leaf. “A clump of *bīraṇa* grass” refers to a thicket of *bīraṇa* grass.
“Matta” means that which has measure (*matta*); the meaning is “possessing a measure of food. Therefore he said, “moderate. “By measure, by measure” means by each respective measure.
By counting in units of one or two days, he remained without food, desiring to act contrary to the Blessed One’s word.
Even while in such a state, on the seventh day, seeing the food brought by his attendant, he cried out, “Shame! being unable to accept it.
With his heart drawn by craving for food, he ate that stomachful of food and passed away according to the very rule prescribed by the Blessed One.
Therefore it is said, “Then to him,” and so forth. “Even if... he were to think”: even if this naked ascetic (acela), having established the thought “Shame!
were to think, “I shall not eat even today,” then even while such a thought exists, because of the possession by a deity—
On that day... [and so on] ...he should do it. Why? Because the Tathāgatas speak without duplicity; their word is never false.
Since every place they go to becomes a courtyard, as they pull it along with them, every spot they traverse appears as an open courtyard extending to its surrounding borders.
"They" refers to the sectarians (titthiyā). "Having gone to the charnel ground itself" means...
Thinking, "We shall pass beyond the thicket of *bīraṇa* grass," they went on, yet after wandering about that area many times, they returned once more to that very same cemetery. 9.
"This" refers to this dead body. "Or he caused that very body to be cremated" means having resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhahitvā*) that body [to be burned].
Some say that he conversed with a *peta* who was already present. Or, having brought the Kora kṣatriya from the asura realm, he made him speak; or it may have been another *peta*.

What difference does it make here? However, because of the statement, "The domain of the Buddhas is inconceivable," it should be understood that the very body which had just been struck by Sunakkhatta rose up through the power of the Buddha and made that matter known.
However, the meaning has already been determined in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). For it will say later: "from the place where [it] was produced," and so forth.
10. *Vipāka* means fruit; the sense is "the production of the goal.
*Samānetabbāni* means they should be properly brought together; the sense is that they should be shown by being brought together according to their own forms. Of the miracles...
These should be understood as stated by the Blessed One in their successive order beginning with the first. However, some here say:

"There are six miracles: the manifestation of another's mind, the manifestation of the limit of one's lifespan, the manifestation of illness, the manifestation of rebirth, the manifestation of the casting off of the body, and the manifestation of the conversation with Sunakkhatta. If that [is the case], then for Sunakkhatta...
This was stated with reference to the manifestation of the mind; for if that were the case, it should have been said as "beings" along with the manifestation of their future appearance.

Alternatively, if it refers to the manifestation of the naked ascetic’s dying mind, that is already included by the statement "he will die on the seventh day," and thus should not be mentioned separately.
Therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained in the Commentary.
Commentary on the Naked Ascetic Koramaṭṭaka (Acelakaḷāramaṭṭakavatthu): 11.
"One with protruding teeth who has polished them" means one whose teeth have protruded and been polished.
It is said that before he became a naked ascetic, he wandered about having his teeth polished and his teeth exposed; therefore, they knew him as "Koramaṭṭaka. Whatever...
Giving to him, one honors him with the thought, "This ascetic is a person of noble character," and thus gives only what is foremost and best. Therefore it is said:

"He has attained the pinnacle of gain; he has attained the foremost gain. Many naked ascetics wander about surrounding him, and many wealthy householders endowed with great fortune approach and attend upon him from time to time. For this reason...
It is said: “He attained fame and an excellent retinue. Because they are to be fulfilled, the vows (*vata*) are called “steps” (*pada*).
Alternatively, they are “divisions of the vow” (*vata-koṭṭhāsa*) because they are not confused with one another. “Fully undertaken” (*samattāni*) means they were taken equally within oneself.

Regarding the word *puratthimena*, due to its connection with the suffix *-ena*, it is the accusative case in the phrase “Vesālī”; furthermore, since the suffix *-ena* is used in the sense of proximity, he says: “not far from Vesālī.”
12. By way of familiarity with the Teaching, he asked a question struck by the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*).
"He did not master it" means he did not understand it, nor did he accomplish it. Therefore, he said, "By the course of right knowledge," and so forth. Alternatively, *sampādana* means mastery.
Since mastery for one who has been questioned consists in answering correctly, he said, "Or else," and so forth, in order to show the absence of that [mastery]. By way of anger...
"His eyes reached a state of trembling," he said, thus: "having even rolled his trembling eyes. "Anger" (*kopa*) means wrath;
since that occurs by way of the mind's agitation, he said: "the mode of agitating. "Hatred" (*dosa*) means malice;
since that occurs by way of being corrupt toward the object, he said: "the mode of corruption. "The mode of dissatisfaction" (*atuṭṭhākāra*).
He manifested through bodily and vocal gestures the mode of occurrence that is the opposite of satisfaction and joy. Regarding the phrase *mā vata no*:
here, *mā* is a negation (*paṭikkhepo*), and *no* has the sense of "mine" (*mayhaṃ*); thus he said, "O, may it not be mine. Regarding the phrase *maṃ vata no*:
here, *no* means "doubt" (*saṃsayo*); thus he said, "Was it indeed mine? (*ahosi vata nu mama*).
14. Since the word *paridahita* refers to the wearing of clothes, he says, “*paridahito* means one who is clothed.
Because gain is caused by fame, the loss of gain is stated here as being due precisely to the loss of fame; thus it is said in the text, “deprived of fame.
Commentary on the Case of Acela Pāṭikaputta.
15. “I know all”—to speak and profess such omniscient knowledge is the "Doctrine of Knowledge" (*ñāṇavāda*);

it is with that Doctrine of Knowledge that [the Buddha] is associated. "Going beyond" means going beyond a limited area demarcated by a boundary to perform a miracle of psychic power (*iddhipāṭihāriya*). But what did this naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta think of himself?
“Does he not know the measure?”—No, he does not fail to know it. If that is so, why did he thunder an empty thunder?
Thinking, “In this way I shall become praised in the world,” he thumped his chest in hypocrisy. Therefore it is said: “The inhabitants of the city,” and so forth.
“Having set up” means having begun a contest of strength.

16. Because of a low disposition... [as before] ...it arose. For this has been said: "Beings who are inclined toward the low associate with, frequent, and attend upon beings who are likewise inclined toward the low.

Since such speech as has been described is caused by a corresponding state of mind, and that mind is caused by a corresponding state of view, therefore, after stating "without abandoning that speech," he shows how its non-abandoning occurs: "That..."
He said, "without abandoning the mind," and in order to show how that non-abandonment occurs, he said, "without relinquishing that view.
Alternatively, such speech is a great offense; the mind is a greater offense than that because it is the source from which it originates;
and the view is the greatest offense of all because it is the root of both.
Therefore, having shown this distinction because of their great blameworthiness, it should be understood that this sequence has been established.
Furthermore, in order to show how their abandonment occurs, the passage beginning with “I am not... is stated.

“Speaking thus, ‘I am not a Buddha’” means speaking straightforwardly, without guile, saying, “I am not a Buddha. Regarding the abandonment of the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*) and the view of phenomena (*dhammadiṭṭhi*):...

The same method applies here. Regarding the word *vipateyya* ("should fall"), he says "or it might split into seven pieces" because in the first alternative the prefix *vi-* is merely a particle (*upasaggamatta*), whereas in the second it has the sense of dispersal (*visaraṇattha*).
17. *Ekaṃsena* means "absolutely"; since an absolute statement is free from figurative expressions (*vacanapariyāya*), he says "without figurative expression" (*nippariyāyena*).
“Odhāritā” means determined, spoken after having fixed [the meaning]. “Vigatarūpena” means with its own nature departed.
Therefore he said, “with its own nature vanished,” meaning with its inherent nature removed by the power of supernormal success (*iddhi*).

Thus it was stated: “of itself,” and so forth. 18. It goes to two, thus it is “going-to-two” (*dvayagāminī*). To the question “What kind of two? he said, “with its own form,” and so forth. For this is the fault of a boil that must be thoroughly lanced.
19. Having been reborn in the Great Hell, Ajita the Licchavi general returned from there and wept in the presence of Pāṭikaputta the naked ascetic.
"Because of its non-existence" means because of the absence of the performance of miracles of the kind previously described.
However, the Blessed One indeed performed a corresponding miracle in order to inspire faith in the assembled assembly, as it is said:
“Having attained the fire element,” and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the discourse on the miracle of psychic power (iddhipāṭihāriya): 20.
Accumulation (nicaya) is the gathering or piling up of wealth and grain; one who is engaged in that is a “collector” (necayika), namely, a householder (gahapati).

Likewise for female lay followers and female householders. Because there is no limit to the number, saying "there are this many thousands of foot-soldiers," it is an immeasurable count even by the thousands.
"For that very reason" means that it is possible to grant release from bondage precisely because of such a vast assembly gathered on account of this [incident].
21. *Cittutrāsabhayaṃ*: fear that arises in the mode of terrifying the mind;
it is not the fear consisting of knowledge (*ñāṇabhaya*), nor is it the fear of an object (*ārammaṇabhaya*) described as "one fears from this. *Chambhitattaṃ*:
the state of the entire body being paralyzed by that very fear which terrifies the mind. *Lomahaṃso*: the bristling of the hair on the body due to that same fear and that paralysis.
The state of the body hairs being erect throughout the entire body refers to their being directed upwards like pegs on a wall;
thus it is said, "the upward-pointing nature of the body hairs.
Having searched along the perimeter, meaning having wandered around the edge of the wanderers' park while examining a hidden spot for his own place to sit, [he saw] a certain Sunakkhatta.
Or, for one like Sunakkhatta who has not abandoned his claim to omniscience, it is the natural law that his head shall split into seven pieces in the presence of the Teacher.
Therefore it was said: "May the fool not perish," and so forth.
22. *Saṃsappati* means that, unable to rise up like a young child on a stone slab, he writhes there due to his sinking down.

It wriggles here and there; therefore, he says, "it sinks. It moves about right there means that on that very stone, with its buttocks pressed down, it moves by way of shifting while seated, not by rising and walking on foot.
23. "Of ruined appearance" means one whose character is ruined through the loss of reputation and the loss of gain.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
25. “With yoke-fellows” means with oxen yoked to strong bulls. 26.
“Of him” refers to Jāliya; for he, together with the wanderer Maṇḍissa, approached the Blessed One.
"Having heard the Dhamma"—this occurred at a time prior to that, when he was not yet aware of the Blessed One’s qualities.
For this very reason, he said: "Let alone the miracle... [omission] ...there will be defeat. 27.
*Tiṇasīho* means a lion with a green color like grass. *Kāḷasīho* means a black-colored lion. *Paṇḍusīho* means a yellowish-white lion.
The lion is pale-colored. A *kesara*-lion is a white-colored lion, or a red-colored lion, one possessing a mane (*kesara*). Regarding the term "king of beasts" (*migarañño*):

although the word "beast" (*miga*) here is conventionally established for certain four-footed animals such as the *pasada* and the *kuruṅga*, it is stated here—"king of beasts means the king of all four-footed creatures"—to show that it is used in a sense common to all. Having come...
“Abode” (āsayo) means that which is settled upon; it is a dwelling place. “Lion’s roar” (sīhanādaṃ):
because of its endurance of dangers and its slaying of adversaries, it is the cry of the lord of beasts who has received the name “lion.
Furthermore, since that [roar] proceeds with a state of fearlessness toward anything whatsoever, it is called “the roar of the fearless. In this regard, in each respective case...

Because it is that which must be traversed and consumed by going into various directions, it is called "pasture" (*gocara*) in the sense of "fodder" (*ghāsa*); thus he said, "For the sake of pasture means for the sake of food.

"The best of the best" (*varaṃ varam*) refers to the fact that within the herds of deer—that is, among the multitudes of wild animals—one slaughters the best of the best, such as buffalo, wild boars, and so forth;
this is the construction of the phrase. Therefore he said, "the fat ones, the fat ones. For its quality of being "best" is intended precisely because of its state of being the very best of the best.
“Dependent on a brave nature” means dependent on a brave disposition; by that [it is meant].
For even by a brave nature, compassion is established toward weak creatures, thinking, “Why kill these feeble living beings? 28.
“Vighāsa” means unsightly food because it is the remains of what has been eaten by another; it is leavings. Thus he said.
“*Bhakkhitātirittamaṃsan*” means in that leavings; the meaning is “on account of the leavings.
“By the fault of *asmimāna*” means by way of the cause of the fault of *asmimāna*; the meaning is “on account of the sign of ‘I-making’ (*ahaṅkāra*)”.
To show how that *asmimāna* of his arose, the passage beginning with “*Tatrāyan*” was stated.
“*Segālakaṃyeva*” is also a reading, with the same meaning as stated above. “*Bheraṇḍakaṃyeva*” means exactly like the cry of the *bheraṇḍa* bird;
the *bheraṇḍa* is a certain two-faced bird, the sound of which is said to be extremely deformed and unpleasant. Therefore he said, “exactly an unpleasant and disagreeable sound.
Those who have gone well (*sugata*) by way of excellent and thorough practice in right conduct are the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddhā*).
They are called "the noble deeds of the Sugata" (*sugatāpadānāni*) because beings purify their mental continuums by means of them; these are the three trainings (*tisso sikkhā*).
Since they characterize those [beings] as "Sugatas" and serve as their instruction, it is therefore said: "in the characteristics of the Sugata," and so forth.
If these are both the characteristics and the teaching of the Sugata, how then was this Pāṭikaputta...?
Regarding that, [the question arises: "He lives by those trainings; what is his connection to them? To this, he says: "Of this," and so forth.

"We give to the Fully Enlightened Ones"—the intention is that they give with the perception (saññā) that they are giving to the Buddhas. By that, he... [lives]; it is not called "living" merely from having entered the lineage of the Sugatas.
Regarding the phrase "to the Tathāgata," etc., since a plural form is used for a singular entity, he says: "The Tathāgata," and so forth. A plural form is indeed used for one who is venerable.
Even though it is singular, it is expressed in the plural by means of a shift in grammatical number (*vacanavipallāsa*), as if using the plural form for the singular.
29. "Having scrutinized" (*samekkhitvā*) means having made equal, that is, having viewed with wrong view;
and since that viewing is itself just a conceiving (*maññanā*), he says "having conceived" (*maññitvā*). It was stated previously that even the scrutinizing mentioned there is indeed conceiving.
“*Amaññī* means ‘he conceived conceits again’”; by this, he shows the successive occurrence of his conceiving.
A *kotthu* (jackal) is so called because it cries out with a howling sound (*bheraṇḍakara-vaṃ*) and wails (*vikkosati*).
By this etymology—“a *byaggho* (tiger) is one who devours (*ghasati*) various living beings while causing them harm”—the term “*byaggho*” [also applies] to the king of beasts.
He said, "It might indeed be so": "'He conceives [himself] as a tiger' means he conceives [himself], 'I am a lion.

Although even a lion may be called a "tiger" according to the aforementioned etymological derivation, he said "or by a lion," etc., to show that the word "tiger" (byaggha) is conventionally established specifically for the king of beasts.
31. Because he was raised in a forest frequented by lions, it is said: "He grew up in a great forest, in a deserted forest. 34.
"The bonds of the defilements" refers to the bond of craving (*taṇhā*). For the bond of craving is firm, a strong bond, difficult to release.
As it is said: "Infatuated and enamored with jewels and earrings..."
The longing for children and wives—
this the wise call a firm bond,
which drags one down, is loose, yet difficult to release.

"By the fetters of the defilements" means by way of the ten kinds of fetters (*saṃyojana*). "The great abyss" refers to the four floods (*ogha*), which, like a vast expanse of water, are difficult to cross for those who have not accumulated the requisites of merit.
36. Commentary on the Exposition of the Designation of Primordiality (*Aggañña-paññatti-kathā-vaṇṇanā*):
Regarding this term, that which is to be known as "this is the foremost in the world" is *aggañña*; furthermore, it is the [origin] of the world...
He said, "The origin of the world, its course, and its lineage," meaning the "lineage of the conduct of the world's arising.
Since there is nothing superior to Perfect Enlightenment among all things to be known, he said, "I know up to the knowledge of omniscience," showing that as the ultimate limit.
By saying "my knowing," he relishes it through craving; by saying "I know," [he relishes it through conceit].
The construction is as follows: while adhering by way of views, one does not misapprehend by way of conceit, thinking, "I understand well; I understand rightly.
The phrase "paccattaññeva" (only for oneself) should be connected with both phrases beginning with "nibbuti viditā" (extinction known), thus:
"Extinction was produced only for oneself, and extinction was known only for oneself," by means of self-become knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*).
The meaning is that the extinction (nibbāna) which has been produced is known by oneself.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated, "by oneself in oneself," in order to show that the word "individually" (*paccattaṃ*) is repeated according to the method of recurrence, having taken on various case endings.

They are "those who have not known Nibbāna" because they have not attained Nibbāna due to practicing wrongly; for even the act of understanding occurs precisely through the attainment of that [Nibbāna].
It should be understood as follows: it proceeds by way of being desirable, thus it is *ayo* (gain), which is pleasure (*sukha*). Its opposite is *anayo* (loss), which is suffering (*dukkha*).
That very thing is called a calamity (*byasana*) because it is the ruin of welfare and happiness. 37. "Showing that":
the Blessed One also showed this by saying, "The followers of other sects perceive therein an essence. By way of sovereignty (*ādhipaccabhāvena*).
By way of its dominant characteristic (*ādhipacca-sabhāva*). That teacher’s doctrine by virtue of which a person is called a "teacher" is the "state of being a teacher" (*ācariyabhāva*);
thus he said, "the state of being a teacher, which is the teacher’s doctrine. "In this" means in the teacher’s doctrine.
"Thus having done" means for this reason. "It" refers to that teacher’s doctrine. It is called "the foremost" (*aggañña*) because it has the foremost as its object. By whom was it established?
In what manner was it formulated? To this he said: "By whom was it formulated, and how was it formulated? Regarding the *Brahmajāla*:

this refers to the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. For here he extends by reference (*atidisa*) the method explained in detail there; moreover, the text is identical in both that work and this one. 41.

It is called the "Teacher’s Tradition" (*ācariyaka*) because the corruption through play (*khiḍḍā-padosika*) exists as its root here. Therefore he said: "rooted in the corruption through play. The same principle applies here to the term "corruption through mental malice" (*manopadosika*).
47. Regarding the statement that the non-existence of the words by which one misrepresents is "by way of meaning," he says, "in the sense of being non-existent.
Since *tucchā* and *musā* are nominative singular forms used in the sense of the instrumental, he says, "by what is empty, by false speech.
Since the "inner core" of a statement is its unerring meaning, he says, "devoid of inner core" in the sense of the absence of that [meaning]. "They misrepresent" means...
"Overpowering and rubbing [them] together" means they revile them. "Perverted perception" means a perception that does not accord with reality (*ayāthāva*).
"The beautiful liberation" refers to the liberation described as "beautiful. "Color-kasiṇa" refers to color-kasiṇas such as deep blue, bright yellow, and so forth.
"All" means all of that which is beautiful, as well as the unattractive and the color-kasiṇa—all of it. "Not unattractive" means even the unattractive [is not seen].
"At that time, he does not perceive it as 'unattractive' (asubha), but rather perceives it as 'attractive' (subha)"; this is the meaning.

[This is] due to perversion, because of grasping what is not as it truly is, and because of speaking what is not as it truly is. 48. Since that wanderer, out of unremitting wrong grasping, did not wish to practice rightly, [he saw] one who was practicing rightly...
With the intention that "the ascetic Gotama and his bhikkhus might recognize me," he said, "Teach the Dhamma in such a way," and so forth;
therefore it was said: "It is fitting for me to [do] this... and so on. *Mamma* means a vital spot, a place that produces pain.
*Suṭṭhu* means carefully. Guard it in such a way that it does not perish.
"By means of habituation" means by means of the practice that leads to the destruction of the defilements (*kilesa*). The rest is easy to understand.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Pāṭhika-sutta*.
2. Commentary on the *Udumbarika-sutta*
Commentary on the Story of the Wanderer Nigrodha:
Regarding the phrase "of Udumbarikā," it is said that this is the genitive case used in relation to possession; thus he says, "in the wanderers' park belonging to Queen Udumbarikā.
Alternatively, there is the reading "Udumbarikāyaṃ," in which case this is the locative case used to denote location. This is the meaning here: [it means] "in the park of Udumbarikā."
The monastery established by Queen Udumbarikā is called "Udumbarikā"; it is [located] in that Udumbarikā. Therefore he said, "belonging to Queen Udumbarikā.

For since it was established by her, it belongs to her. Furthermore, in this context, due to the reading beginning with *varaṇa*, there is no appearance of a word that expresses the sense of "established" (*nibbatta*). "Sandhāna" means by way of joining together even those things that have been split apart.
“Sandhāna” is his name thus acquired. “Saṃvaṇṇito” means praised. “Iriyati” means proceeds.

“By noble knowledge” means by the supramundane knowledge that is noble because it is remote from the defilements. “By noble liberation” means by the supramundane liberation of the fruit, which is perfectly purified.
The word *divā* is synonymous with *dina*, just as it is with *divasa*.
Since the word *divā* is used here as a qualifier, it indicates a specific portion of the day; thus he said, "during the day of the day," and so forth.

Because the mind of one who has attained [meditation] is withdrawn from various objects, and because one possessing jhāna, through the attainment of seclusion, is free from social contact (*saṅgaṇikā*), [the mind becomes concentrated].

He is as if hidden away in solitude; therefore it is said, "from here and there... gone. They are called "mind-developing" (*manobhāvaniyā*) because they bring about the mind's expansion based on turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*); thus he says, "of those that increase the mind," and so forth.
The meaning is that [the mind] rises up, does not contract, and becomes unshrunken.

Regarding the phrase "as many as" (*yāvatā*), the meaning here is "as many as there are" (*yāvanto*); thus he says, "however many. The word *tesaṃ* is a genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).

And a specification must be made based on some particular distinction. To illustrate this distinction—that the Blessed One’s disciples, the lay followers (*upāsaka*), who reside in Rājagaha are endowed with certain specific qualities, and that this person is likewise endowed with them—he says: "However many... and so forth.
“Among them, he was an insider”—thus it is said. Therefore he says, “It is said that of the Blessed One,” and so forth.
(52) “Of them” means of those wanderers (*paribbājaka*). “By talk” means by frivolous chatter (*tiracchānakathā*). “By view” means by the manifestation of views.
“By appearance” means by their outward guise. “By conduct” means by their activity. “By behavior” means by the mutual conduct that ought to be practiced among one another.
"By dwelling" means by the manner of dwelling that should be practiced day and night. "By postures" means by the postures such as standing and so forth.
"Those belonging to other sects" (*aññatitthiyā*) refers to those associated with other religious orders because of their different mode of conduct.

"Having gathered together, having come together, forming a heap" means in the place where others are seated. "And those forests and forest-thickets" means forest-forest-thickets (*araññavanapatthāni*); therein, that which...
That which accomplishes the forest-dweller’s factor for those who dwell in the forest should be understood as “the forest.
“The jungle-thicket” (*vanapattha*) is a place beyond the village boundary where people do not frequent, where no plowing is done and no sowing is done. For it has been said:
“‘Jungle-thicket’ is a designation for remote lodgings,” and “‘Jungle-thicket’ is a designation for groves of trees.”
“‘Forest-dwelling places’ (vanapattha) is a designation for lodgings that are terrifying; ‘forest-dwelling places’ is a designation for lodgings that cause the hair to stand on end;
‘forest-dwelling places’ is a designation for lodgings that are remote; ‘forest-dwelling places’ is a designation for lodgings that are not frequented by people.
Therefore it was said: “Free from the vicinity of villages,” and so forth. “Remote” means secluded, very far away. Thus he said:
“‘Extremely distant,’ and so forth. ‘By the vicinity of the monastery’ means by the area surrounding the monastery.
‘Of people on the road’ means of people traveling along the path. ‘Of faint sound’ means having a thin sound due to the absence of loud or great noise.
‘Noise’ (*nigghosa*) is the sound produced when people come together and speak in one place; because its meaning is difficult to discern, [it is called so].”
Therefore it is said: “by a sound whose meaning is unmanifested. “Free from wind” means free from noise.

By the phrase “suitable for performing secret acts,” he clarifies that those places possess the characteristics of a forest (*arañña*), are secluded from people, and are secluded from the woods; likewise by the phrase “conducive to solitude.”

53. Regarding "by what" (*kenā*): since it is used both as a cause (*hetu*) and in connection with an accompaniment (*sahayoga*), it is called the instrumental case (*karaṇavacana*). Thus he says, "by what reason" (*kena kāraṇena*) and "together with which person" (*kena puggalena saddhim*).

For even a single grammatical designation (*vibhattiniddesa*) can illustrate multiple meanings, as is the case with the meanings of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), compounds (*pada*), and aggregations (*samāhāra*). "Conversing" (*saṃsandana*) means the joining of discourse through dialogue and conversation. "The state of proficiency in knowledge" (*ñāṇabyattabhāva*) refers to the state of being proficient in knowledge;
this occurs either by way of providing an answer to another's speech, or by way of providing a counter-response when another has spoken an answer.
He said, "It may be," meaning "by way of rejoinder and counter-rejoinder.

For when one refutes another's statement by means of a three-pronged method (*tipukkhalanaya*), and thereby brings about the state of being a genus (*jātibhāva*) for that other person's statement of refutation, it clarifies—that is, makes manifest—the proficiency of knowledge regarding the nature of such speech. "Lost in empty dwellings" means in dwellings that are empty houses.

"Lost, ruined, gone to non-existence. His wisdom would not be lost—that is, it would not fall into confusion due to the arising of various inspired responses when answering questions asked after being questioned and cross-questioned on this or that matter, nor would he be incapable of answering the questions posed.
"We shall hem him in" means we shall hem him in as if rendering him powerless; that hemming-in of the opponent is by means of a web of arguments.
"It is like a binding," he said, "we would bind [it]. To that end, he made the illustration of an empty jar;
in order to show that by way of contrast, it was said, "For a full jar," and so forth.
"Displaying his power" means manifesting his own power of knowledge, even though it was unreal. "Unmixed" means due to the absence of any confusion of birth.

“Unmixed. He said, “a lion with unmixed manes,” because if there were a mixing of different species, then just as a mule possesses the nature of a horse, a lion might likewise lack the strength of a lion. “Instantly” means at that very moment.
Regarding the phrase “the river named Sumāgadhā,” some say this, but showing that it is incorrect, he says, “the lotus pond named Sumāgadhā.”
Having said this, in order to show that its status as a lotus pond (*pokkharaṇī*) is mentioned in another sutta, the passage beginning with “on whose bank” was spoken.

It is called *moranivāpa* because it is the feeding-place (*nivāpa*) for peacocks (*morā*). For even when words have different grammatical bases (*byadhikaraṇa*), an external compound (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) certainly occurs, as in the case of “*urasiloma*” (hair on the chest).
Alternatively, *nivāpa* means that which is inhabited (*nivuttha*) there; thus, the feeding-place of peacocks is *moranivāpa*.
It is the place where offerings of food are given to peacocks. Therefore he said, “Where [there are] peacocks,” and so forth.

Since Nigrodha was one who preached self-mortification out of disgust for worldly life, and since he saw that in the Buddha’s teaching the monks—having abandoned the pursuit of self-torment—were dwelling having attained supreme consolation through the pursuit of meditation, he therefore asked:
“How indeed does the ascetic Gotama, without bodily mortification, [train] his disciples?”
Having conceived a doubt as to who this "Vinetī" might be, he questioned the Blessed One with the words, "Who indeed is he?

and so forth. That by which one breathes, and through which one becomes free from suspicion and apprehension, is called *assāsa*; thus he said, "having attained *assāsa* means having attained satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*) and joy (*somanassa*).
An *ajjhāsaya* is a superior, excellent disposition or reliance; thus he said, "being the supreme support. It is the primary, primordial [state].
The meaning is: the supreme conduct, the primary holy life, the supramundane path.
For it has been realized in that very same manner by all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples. Therefore he said: “The ancient... the noble path.
For the Blessed One spoke of it thus: “He saw the ancient path, the ancient highway. “Having fulfilled” means by way of the completion of its cultivation. “Having fulfilled” [is the term].
Alternatively, they say that "the underlying intention as the beginning of the holy life" (*ajjhāsayaṃ ādibrahmacariyaṃ*) is a textual supplement (*pāṭhaseso*) here.
Or rather, the construction here is: "Having attained consolation, they profess the underlying intention as the beginning of the holy life.
The Commentary on the Teaching of Asceticism and Disgust (*Tapojigucchāvādavaṇṇanā*).
55. Having been begun, it is interrupted and left unfinished; thus he said, "It remains as something not yet completed. 56.
The expression "loathing evil through energy" means that by means of energy which accomplishes a rigorous practice, one loathes evil by way of dispelling self-craving.
That which loathes is "loathing" (*jeguccha*); the state of being that is "loathsomeness" (*jegucchā*); excessive loathsomeness is *adhika-jeguccha*.
*Adhijegucchaṃ*: in that which is the supreme loathing of evil. *Tapaḥ* (asceticism) is that which heats (*tapati*) by means of an abundance of bodily fortitude;
it is the energy (*vīriya*) proceeding by way of the pursuit of self-mortification.

Through that [energy], there is a loathing of the evil characterized by an abundance of bodily fortitude; thus, both the loathing and the fading away [of defilements] are called "ascetic loathing" (*tapojigucchā*). Therefore, he said: "loathing of evil through energy. This is by way of dispelling craving for food, clothing, and lodgings.

The meaning is "the fading away of attachment to self. Regarding the various modes of conduct to be described below, such as the ascetic practices of the naked ascetics (acelaka) and so forth, "fulfillment" here means their purification when undertaken together, rather than the undertaking of them all without exception, because that is impossible;
thus he says, "fulfilled means purified. And their purification is [to be understood] by what is established in one's own system...
It is simply practicing according to the method. By way of the opposite, one's impurity should be understood.
57. “He does not speak even a single question”: this is said because he has not answered the first question asked by himself.
“One who relies on austerity” means one who lives having undertaken and practiced austerity consisting of the pursuit of self-mortification. “In the lion’s roar.”

In the commentary on the Sīhanāda Sutta. Since they should be understood there according to the method set forth in detail, they should also be understood here according to the method stated in that exposition of the meaning.
Commentary on the Defilements (Upakkilesa).
58. Having stated, “He undertakes it rightly,” he says, “He grasps it firmly,” to show that its right undertaking is indeed a firm grasp.
Having stated, “It should also be illustrated by one who lives according to the Dispensation,” the passage beginning with “For a certain person” is spoken to demonstrate that;
for pride of mind based merely on being a bearer of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), and the fulfillment of one’s intentions [thereby], are defilements of right practice.

This demonstrates that meaning; it should be understood that there is no similarity between those who possess the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) and the undertaking of austerities as previously described, even though both are non-leading to liberation.
“Of both kinds” refers to what was stated according to the distinction of defilements (*upakkilesa*), namely: “he is glad, his intention fulfilled,” and so forth.

"Of both kinds of ascetic," some say. However, since the meaning is also explained in the *Aṭṭhakathā* by way of those belonging to the Dispensation (*sāsana*), the meaning should be understood as "of both kinds of ascetic, namely, the outsider (*bāhiraka*) and the one belonging to the Dispensation.
For he will explain the commentary on the meaning in exactly that way further on. "To this extent" means: "Who else [besides me]..."

"Equal"—thus [there is] the arising of excessive conceit (*atimāna*) regarding one who is equal; and "enough with this much"—thus [there is] the arising of excessive conceit regarding one whose task is not yet finished. To that extent.
"Exalts" means he makes something superior. "Throws over" means he casts it above others; the meaning is that he holds it aloft.
"He draws down another" means he makes another inferior by drawing him down; "he casts down" means he throws downward, which is to say he treats with contempt.
"By creating the intoxication of conceit" means by the creation—that is, the production—of the intoxication known as conceit. "He becomes infatuated" means he falls into infatuation (*muccha*);
that state of falling into infatuation is a state of mind entangled by covetousness, adherence to rules and observances, and the bodily tie. In this regard:
And because there is a state of excessive attachment, he said, “clinging and obsessed. And since negligence here is simply negligence itself, he said, “he falls into negligence.

To show that one who merely purifies himself through the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) but does not apply himself to the meditation subject might proceed by way of self-exaltation and so forth due to that very purification through the ascetic practices, [the text] says “in the Dispensation,” and so on.
It has been said. Therefore he says: “The ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) itself...
receives [the requisites]. 59. “Those very same requisites”: obtained by having prepared them well and properly arranged them;

that is, obtained through the act of giving and the act of offering, having been carefully prepared with devotion and reverence. “Praising” means the proclamation of virtues. “Of him” refers to the ascetic (tapassin).
60. *Vodāsanti* means "dividing"; that is, it means "partitioning. However, since partitioning here is intended to be twofold, he says, "he falls into two parts.
He makes two portions according to what is pleasing and what is not pleasing. *Gedhajāto* means "one in whom greed has arisen.

Delusion (*mucchana*) occurs precisely through the loss of mindfulness, not while mindfulness is present; therefore, he says, "he will become agitated" (*samuṭṭhassati*). "Even a mere disadvantage" (*ādīnavamattampi*)...
He does not see even a slight danger in using [the requisites] with a state of greed and so forth. "Knowing the proper measure" means knowing the measure in using them.
"Even the mere use through reflection" means that he does not even practice using them after reflecting on them just once.
61. “Vicakkasaṇṭhānā” means having the shape of a very wide wheel. Because they consume everything, the teeth themselves are the “tooth-peak,” being like iron spikes.
“Apasādeti” means he encourages (pasādeti). “By way of the practice of nakedness, etc. means by way of the observance of nakedness and so forth.
“A life of austerity” means a life of austerity through the practice of effacement (sallekha).

62. "He performs austerity" means he practices the austerity characterized by the mental application of meditation; he acts as if he were practicing it. He descends to the walking path as if intent upon the practice of meditation. He sweeps the courtyard of the monastery as if fulfilling his duties and observances.
Alternatively, the reading is "ādassayamāno.
"Some fault" refers to some defect, whether physical or verbal. "A view" refers to a distorted perception.
"Disagreeable" means disagreeable because it is rejected by one's own established doctrine. "It is pleasing to me" means he says, "It is allowable to me.
"Should be approved" means it should be accepted as "this is so" because of its being correct, non-perverted, and real.
It should be rejoiced in as "well done, very well" because of its attractiveness to the ear.

63. One who has the habit of being angry is "wrathful" (*kodhana*). One who possesses resentment (*upanāha*)—which has the characteristic already described—is "resentful" (*upanāhī*). Since one who is thus constituted is possessed of that quality, it is said: "he is endowed with it. This same method applies to those following this as well.
However, there is this distinction: one who envies (*issati*) and is jealous (*usūyati*) is "envious" (*ussukī*).

Deceit (*saṭha*) is the concealing of non-existent virtues; one who possesses that is "deceitful" (*saṭha*). Guile (*māyā*) has the nature of concealing existing faults; one who possesses guile is "guileful" (*māyāvī*).
*Thaddha* (stiff) is characterized by the absence of prostration even toward those worthy of respect; one who possesses this is *thaddha*.
One who has the habit of conceiving of oneself as superior to those equal in virtues or as surpassing those superior to them, thereby treating them as inferior, is *atimānī* (conceited).

One who has evil—that is, base—desires consisting in the seeking of honor for non-existent virtues is *pāpiccho* (one of evil desires). One whose view (*diṭṭhi*) is wrong—that is, perverted—is *micchādiṭṭhiko* (one of wrong view).
“‘This alone is the truth, all else is vain’—because one is thus obsessed with oneself by means of this view, it is a ‘view’ (diṭṭhi).

Because one clings to that very [view], it is ‘clinging to one’s own view’ (sanditṭhiparāmāsi). In the Commentary, however, the meaning is stated according to the subject matter as: ‘One’s own view is the view itself.
It is called ‘holding fast’ (ādhāna) because it is held firmly; thus he says, ‘well-established and firm.’”
One who has the habit of relinquishing what was grasped is "one who relinquishes" (*paṭinissaggī*); by way of its opposite, one is "difficult to relinquish" (*duppaṭinissaggī*).
For this prefix *du-* has the sense of negation, as in "one of poor wisdom" (*duppañño*) and "one of bad character" (*dussīlo*).
[End of] the commentary on the section concerning the attainment of the pure sprout.
64. Here, Nigrodha, the phrase “an ascetic” indicates by way of a partial summary the preceding passage as it was recited.

Therefore he said, “Thus the Blessed One,” and so forth. “A doctrine already accepted” means a doctrine accepted such as: “The state of being naked and so forth is superior, and by that there is purification from saṃsāra.
“Austerity maintained” means that which has been undertaken and maintained through that very doctrine.

Regarding the ascetic practice beginning with nakedness (*acelaka-vatādi-tapaṃ*): by the statement “all is indeed defiled,” he shows that the intended meaning here is “the rough ascetic practitioner,” which refers to the hypothetical form mentioned in the commentary on the pure text where it says, “the application should be understood by way of both the one who practices austere penance and the one who maintains the ascetic virtues (*dhutaṅga*).
[This is stated] “for the purpose of showing the pure text.”
And by this [statement], he shows that only the canonical text (pāḷi) regarding the sectarians (titthiyā) is found here, but not their actual meaning.

"By way of the opposite of what was stated" means by way of the contrary of the stated meaning; the sense is "by way of its negation. Regarding the phrase "in that place," since the locative case has the sense of cause (hetu), he explains the meaning by using the instrumental case in the sense of cause, saying: "Thus, by that... and so forth.

"Exerting himself further" means that, being dissatisfied with the ascetic practices (dhuta-dhammas) as they were undertaken and not having yet completed his intention, he applies right effort by way of further application to meditation. "Beyond this" means beyond the manner just described.
Or, [it refers to] the state of being supreme or the state of being essential through austerity and self-disgust.

Not knowing what constitutes the state of being the "tip" or the state of being the "essence," and imagining that this very thing is its state of being the tip or its state of being the essence, he said, "They have reached the tip;
they have reached the essence. This concludes the commentary on the discussion regarding the attainment of the pure bark and so forth.
70. *Yamana* means restraint (*saṃyamana*); *yāma*. Because it consists of the non-performance of violence and so forth, it is fourfold;
thus it is the "fourfold restraint" (*cātuyāma*). That itself is the restraint (*saṃvara*). One who is restrained by that, with all doors guarded, is "restrained by the fourfold restraint.
Therefore he said: "Shut off by the fourfold restraint. Since "overstepping" means harming, he said: "He does not kill a living being. [This refers to] with a mind of greed...
Considering that they have been cultivated and fully developed, the "cultivated" refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*kāmaguṇa*).
And because this [state] is the very manifestation of those [pleasures], like the arising of a path, he said: "by the perception of them.
"This" refers to the bringing forward and the non-returning to the inferior; therefore he said: "the characteristic beginning with 'he brings it forward'."

"He brings toward" means he leads to superior understanding; therefore it says, "he increases further and further. Even a wheel-turning monarch performs such acts as salutation toward one who has gone forth;
thus, the state of going forth is supreme because of its association with distinguished qualities and its freedom from defects, which is why it is designated by the wise.
However, the state of a householder is inferior because it lacks both of those; hence it says, "for the sake of the inferior state of a householder."
71. *Tacappattā* means "having reached the bark"; the meaning is that she becomes like the bark. 74.
*Vasenā ti titthiyānaṃ* means "by way of the sectarians," that is, by way of the systems of the sectarians. *Nesaṃ* refers to the sectarians. *Taṃ* refers to the divine eye.

*Sīlasampadā* is the fourfold purity of virtue (*catupārisuddhisīla*) perfected in every aspect. *Tacasārasampattito* means "from the attainment of the essence of the 'bark' asceticism" (the ascetic practice of disgust).
"Visesabhāvaṃ" means "the specific nature.
"Not even the mere text of the Acelakas" means that there is not even the meaning contained within the text of the Acelakas; therefore, the sense is:
"we shall perish," that is, we shall be ruined. Alternatively, the syllable "a" is a mere particle, and "nassāma" means "we shall perish. "From where [could] a pure text [come]?"—how indeed?

Among us, there is the practice as it has come down in the pure textual tradition (*pāḷi*). This same method applies to the others as well. "Even by way of hearing" means that we do not know [it] even by the mere fact of its having reached the range of the ear.
75. Commentary on the Lamentation of Nigrodha.
"His" refers to the householder Sandhāna. "Harsh" means rough. "Insulting speech" means speech that should not be uttered.

Because when harsh speech directed toward someone is forgiven by that person, it becomes restored to its original state for the one who offered the forgiveness, therefore it was said: "This [fault] is in me," and so forth. 76.
He teaches the Dhamma for the sake of awakening, not for the sake of proclaiming his own status as a Buddha. "For the sake of debate" means...
It is for the purpose of the discourse that shatters the arguments of opponents. He teaches the Dhamma for the sake of subduing lust and the other defilements, not out of a desire for disciples.

"For the sake of crossing over the flood" means he teaches the Dhamma for the sake of crossing over the four floods, because his teaching brings about the complete crossing from this shore to the further shore.
He teaches the Dhamma for the sake of the final Nirvana of all defilements, because even by a mere trace of the teaching, the defilements remain untouched.
Commentary on the Conclusion of the Holy Life (Brahmacariyapariyosāna), etc.: 77.
"All this" refers to the entire discourse from the words "from seven years old" up to the phrase "seven days.
However, the intended meaning is that he was not deceitful, was free from guile, upright by nature, possessed of sharp wisdom, and one who understands through a brief instruction. For he—
"He will be able to attain arahantship in that very moment. "Crooked-crooked" means crooked, bent, and distorted by way of the crookedness of body and so forth.

When the Blessed One said, "I am not able to instruct one who is deceitful," he did not say this merely because of weariness, but rather because of that person's lack of capacity as a vessel for the Dhamma.
78. "By nature your teacher" means: he who was your natural teacher before this, let him alone now be your teacher by virtue of his former practice;
our intention is not that we wish to make you our resident pupils (*antevāsika*).
Our intention is not that we have need of instruction from you, but rather that we wish to make you understand the very principles of the Dhamma.
"By way of livelihood" means by way of subsistence. "Unwholesome" means having reached a particular category;
they have entered into those respective categories. "Associated with the distress of the defilements" means accompanied by the distress of the defilements because of being connected to them.
"Conducive to birth, aging, and death" means leading to birth, aging, and death. "Defiled" means that defilement exists therein, or it is directed toward defilement.
“Purification” (vodāna) is said to mean purity; because they serve as its conditions, they are called “purifying” (vodāniyā).

Being such, they purify beings; thus it is said, “they purify beings. The state of reaching the summit through the fulfillment and abundance of wisdom is to be desired only by way of the paths and fruits;
therefore it is said, “the path-wisdom... the abundance. Or else, both of these refer to the fulfillment and abundance.

For that which is its fulfillment is itself its expansion. "From that" means from the cause of abandoning the phenomena of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*) and the increase of the phenomena of purification (*vodānadhamma*).
79. "As by Māra"—this is not stated by way of illustration; rather, it is said to show that it is merely a statement of the fact that such a state exists.
To demonstrate this, "Māra, it is said," and so forth, was spoken. "Then" (*atha*) means after they had fallen into the possession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*) of Māra.
"He knew"—this is the construction. But why did the Blessed One not know it beforehand? Because he had not directed his attention [to them].
"Having warded off Māra" means having dispelled the obsession (pariyuṭṭhāna) created by Māra against them; for when there is a purpose, nothing is difficult for Buddhas to accomplish.
"He" refers to the cause for the arising of the path and its fruit. "Of them" refers to those wanderers.
*Touched* means touched by way of obsession (*pariyuṭṭhāna*). Regarding *yatra*, he says "in those" (*yesu*), taking it as a locative case used for specification (*niddhāraṇa*).

*Aññāṇatthaṃ* means for the purpose of thorough understanding (*ājānanatthaṃ*); here, the prefix *ā-* is merely an intensifier, thus he says "for the purpose of knowing" (*jānanatthaṃ*), meaning for the purpose of investigation (*vīmaṃsanatthaṃ*).
"The mind has not arisen" refers to the purpose of thorough understanding, thinking, "Let us first understand this Dhamma," [and thus] the holy life (*brahmacariyaṃ*)...
"Let us go forth"—even on a single day, not once did their minds arise [to do so].

But as for the expression "for seven days," what would that accomplish for them? The meaning is: "to fulfill the holy life for seven days," or "to fulfill [the period] of seven days by means of the holy life. "Breaking the opposing arguments" means crushing the opposing arguments.
"Exalting one's own doctrine" means the upholding of one's own doctrine. "By way of impression" means by way of the impression of the penetration of the Truths.
And the phrase "of these" is stated by way of the present treatise;

for it is a condition for the impression of others as well—namely, of gods and humans who hear [the teaching] either in the presence of the Blessed One or through tradition. As for that which has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning...
"That is indeed easy to understand.
This concludes the elucidation of the hidden meaning in the commentary on the Udumbarika Sutta.
3. Commentary on the Cakkavatti Sutta.

Commentary on the State of Having Oneself as Island and Refuge (Attadīpa-saraṇatā-vaṇṇanā) 80. "Utāna" means manifest; by its opposite, "anuttāna" means unmanifest, concealed, not extensive, and difficult to understand.
The commentary on words that are unmanifest is the "Commentary on Unmanifest Words" (Anuttānapadavaṇṇanā). [This concludes] the Commentary on Manifest Words.
The term is not explained in detail because there is no purpose for doing so. “Mātulā” is the name given to a certain tree according to its feminine gender;
because the city was built in the vicinity of that tree, the city itself came to be known as “Mātulā. Therefore it is said:
“In the city named Mātulā. “Not far” means not far from that city.

In this sutta, it is stated that while a discourse illustrating past history begins from the outset with the words, "Once upon a time, monks, there was a king named Daḷhanemi," a discourse specifically connected to future matters is also presented,
beginning with the words, "When human beings have a life span of two hundred and fifty years, their sons will have a life span of one hundred years."
“From the *Anāgatavaṃsadīpikā*, a discourse on the Suttantas.
For the illumination of future events is marvelous, and even therein, the description of the practice of a future Perfectly Enlightened One is most marvelous. “By a gathering” means by an assembly.
“The dining hall was unpleasant,” and so forth, is merely their own conjecture. “Unpleasant” means disagreeable.
"Even a slight offense committed against the Buddhas has a much heavier result than a slight act of merit," thus he said: "With the Buddhas...
it is equal. Therein: "there" means either in the vicinity of that city of Mātulā, or in that assembly.
Regarding the phrase "with oneself as an island": here, although one's own continuum is called "self" (attā) because it is not another, yet by virtue of being a seeker of welfare and happiness—
However, because it is not distinct from oneself, the Dhamma is intended here by the term “self. Therefore he said: “Self means the mundane and supramundane Dhamma.
An island (dīpa) is so called because water has gone away from it; it is a portion of land not overwhelmed by a flood.

But here, because it cannot be overwhelmed by the floods of sensual desire and so forth, it is like an island; thus they are “island-selves,” meaning those for whom the self is their island and their support.
Therefore he said, "One’s own self as an island," and so forth. And here, the state of being an island is the state of being a refuge; thus he said, "This is a synonym for that very thing.
It is a statement rejecting other refuges—that is, a statement rejecting the state of having anything else as a refuge.
For this is not merely a statement rejecting dwelling by making something else a refuge, but rather a statement rejecting the very nature of another being a refuge.

And because by the negation of that [one], the negation of the other is also established. Therefore he said, “For not...,” and so forth. Now, in order to prove this very point by means of another sutta, he says, “And this has also been stated,” and so forth.
If an ordinary self were intended here, how could it have the nature of being a refuge like a lamp?
Therefore, he asks, “But what kind of self is intended here? in order to show that the self here must be one of intentional meaning (*adhippāyika*).
“Self, indeed. The other [responds], showing the self as intended: “The Dhamma, both mundane and supramundane.
To show that the second section is taught as a synonym for the first section, it is said, “Therefore he said,” and so forth.
“In one’s own resort” means in a place that serves as the domain of the bhikkhus. Therefore he said, “in a place fit to wander. “One’s own” (sake) means how?

He said, "In the ancestral domain," because this [domain] is capable for the monks. It is called "in the ancestral domain" because it has come down from the father—the Perfectly Enlightened One—and because it was pointed out by him as "this is your sphere.
Regarding the word *carantaṃ*, he said, "This is the meaning," taking it in the accusative case in the sense of the genitive (*sāmī*);
the meaning is also "of those who wander," and thus, through a transposition of case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*), this [term] is used.

He shows this also by way of a permutation of terms (*vacanavipallāsa*). By the very fact that the Māra of defilements finds no opportunity, it should be understood that the other Māras likewise find no opportunity.
"This, however, is the meaning" refers to moving within one's proper domain (*gocare caraṇaṃ*); as for the basis (*vatthu*), it is presented by way of contrast.
It is a "bird-killer" (*sakuṇagghi*) because it kills birds; [it is] the *mahāsenasakuṇa* (the great-army bird). "Attained" (*ajjhappattā*) means attained by way of overcoming.
She approached [him], thinking: "This hawk will not be able to seize me. *Naṅgalakaṭṭhakaraṇa* means a place ploughed by a plough.
*Leḍḍuṭṭhāna* means a place where clods of earth have been thrown up. *Sake bale* means for the sake of her own strength.
*Apatthaddhā* means free from stiff arrogance, one whose arrogance has subsided. *Assaramānā* means calling out.
"A large clod" refers to a large clod resembling a sharp-pointed iron hammer, which had become dry at the spot where it was split by a plow.
"Having climbed up" means that, having entered beneath it and observed a suitable place for concealment, he stood there above it, pacing back and forth and not making a sound.
"Come now," and so forth, is a demonstration of his manner of remaining silent.
"Sannayha" means having balanced both wings by means of taking up the wind. "Paccupādī" means he entered.
"Tattheva" means right there on the clod where the quail had previously been standing. "Uraṃ" refers to his own chest. "Paccatāḷesī" means he struck it;
because he went with speed out of a fit of rage and struck it as he moved forward, he struck it while warding it off. "Ārammaṇaṃ" means...
[This refers to] the condition (*paccaya*).

Some say it means "the opportunity" (*avasara*). What is the connection (*anusandhi*) for this teaching that proceeds with the words "of the wholesome" (*kusalānam*)? It is simply according to the sequence [of the discourse].
For from the very beginning, by way of the discourse on oneself and the Dhamma, starting with "Monks, dwell as islands unto yourselves," both mundane and supramundane states were taught.

Those very things already included [in the previous category] are here included by the mention of "the wholesome" (*kusala*). Regarding the phrase "characterized by blamelessness" (*anavajja-lakkhaṇānaṃ*):

it means those whose intrinsic nature is the opposite of what is blameworthy (*avajja*). Some say it means "those whose intrinsic nature is free from blame. In that regard, in the first interpretation of the meaning, only those things subject to maturation (*vipākadhamma*) are included;
however, in the second, even those not subject to maturation are included. If this is so, how is it that they are to be undertaken and practiced?
However, this should not be viewed as meaning that "states whose nature is to ripen (vipākadhamma), such as virtue and so forth, must be maintained by formal undertaking.
Rather, "undertaking" (samādāna) should be understood simply as their proper acquisition within one's own continuum and their subsequent occurrence by way of conditions.
For states whose nature is to ripen, when properly instilled within the continuum of a being through specific conditions, constitute the excellence of life-span and other such attainments.
They say that [these states] serve as decisive supports (*upanissaya*) for the successive arising of increasingly superior wholesome qualities.

Regarding the phrase "merit increases" (*puññaṃ pavaḍḍhati*), he says "the fruit of merit increases" (*puññaphalaṃ vaḍḍhati*), explaining that this is a designation where the latter member of the compound has been dropped (i.e., *puñña-phala* is shortened to *puñña*).

Furthermore, the term "fruit of merit" is stated using a single-remainder collective compound (*ekadesasarūpekasesa*), meaning "merit and the fruit of merit" are both referred to as "fruit of merit. Thus he says: "successively..."
“Merit and the fruition of merit are also to be understood,” it is said.
The phrase beginning with “of mother and father” is merely an illustration; therefore, other such wholesome roots and decisive supports (upanissaya) should also be regarded as included.
“By way of affection” means by way of affection that serves as a decisive support, not by way of [affection] associated with the mind.

For there is no such thing as wholesome consciousness that is associated with affection (*sineha*). "A mind soft and gentle" means a mind that is exceedingly tender by way of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Just as it was said—"a mind soft and gentle toward mother and father"—to show the wholesome state leading to the round (*vaṭṭagāmikusalatā*) at its highest point, so too, to show the wholesome state leading to the turning away from the round (*vivaṭṭagāmikusalatā*) at its highest point, [it is said]:
It is said: “The four foundations of mindfulness... [and so on] ...the states conducive to enlightenment. Furthermore, other qualities such as generosity and virtue should be understood as follows:

those that serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) are the skillfulness leading to the round; those that serve as the decisive support for the cessation of the round (*vivaṭṭa*) are the skillfulness leading to cessation.
“The culmination” means reaching the summit and peak of the fruit-giving process due to its bringing about a distinction in the fruits; [this occurs] in the world of the devas.
And the conclusion is specified as "in the world of humans" (*manussaloke*) because this teaching has come down specifically according to the human world.
The construction is: "the attainment of the path, the fruit, and Nibbāna is the conclusion.
The result of the wholesome state leading to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭagāmika-kusala*) will be shown at the end of the sutta, beginning with: "Then, monks, King Saṅkha... and so forth.
The Commentary on the Story of King Daḷhanemi the Wheel-turning Monarch (81).
Herein, "here" refers to the place where this sutta teaching was begun with the words, "Bhikkhus, as to wholesome states...

This refers to the mention of "wholesome" states in a general sense, common to both those leading to the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and those leading to its cessation (*vivaṭṭa*). Therein, by way of the connection to wholesome states leading to the round of existence...
“Once upon a time, monks,” he began the teaching; and in beginning it, he did so by first indicating the mere subject matter being taught.
The words “monks” and so forth were spoken to show that he began after having briefly explained the matter to the monks who were receiving the Dhamma.
The intention is that although the Blessed One did not explain it in that [detailed] manner at the outset, he nonetheless explained it by way of its meaning.
82. *Īsakampīti* means even slightly. *Ovasakkantanti* means having moved back. *Nemābhimukhanti* means facing the portion of the rim.
They bound [it] in order to know whether the Wheel-treasure had moved back or not. *Tadetan’ti* refers to the shifting from the aforementioned place.
*Atibalavadose’ti* means when a very powerful misfortune has presented itself for the king.
"Appamatta" means not being negligent regarding the king’s command.
"Only as far as the single ocean's boundary" refers specifically to Jambudīpa;
for it stands surrounded by the Assakaṇṇa mountain to the north, thus having the single ocean as its limit. "By the power of merit" means...
By means of the power of merit that brings about the state of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti).
"Having done thus" means having donned the saffron-colored robes. "Well-performed karma" refers specifically to the ten courses of wholesome action (dasakusalakammapatha);
the detailed classification as "tenfold and twelvefold" will be explained later. "By fulfilling [it]" means having fulfilled it.
"By one who stands firm. "Faultless" (*niddosa*) means that faults which are the opposites of the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti-vatta*) have been removed.

"The duties of wheel-turning monarchs" refers to the conduct to be practiced by wheel-turning kings. For a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is applied to what is yet to be as if it were already present, just as it is said, "The Buddha went to Rājagaha.
Even though they have not yet attained the status of a wheel-turning monarch, they are practicing those duties; therefore, it is stated thus.
84. Regarding the commentary on the *Cakkavatti-ariyavatta*:
"That which does not allow one to act otherwise is the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*) for this; thus it is 'founded upon that' (*tadadhiṭṭhāna*).
By means of that mind founded upon it, "honoring" means performing with an attitude of reverence. Therefore he said, "Just as," and so forth. "Holding in high esteem" means...
Making it "heavy" by way of treating it with weightiness, like a stone parasol. For this very reason he said: "Because of the arising of reverence toward that.
"Honoring" means cherishing it as dear through the act of esteem. For this reason he said: "That very [person]," and so forth.
To show that for one who thus worships and pays respect, the aforementioned honors and so on come to pass, he said: "Referring to that," and so forth.
It is said: “By way of having arrived as one for whom the Dhamma is predominant.
By this, he shows that through the preeminence of the aforementioned Dhamma, it was carefully accumulated in each preceding state of existence.
“By performing all activities solely by means of the Dhamma”—by this, he shows the state of being inclined, leaning, and tending toward the aforementioned Dhamma in standing, sitting, and so forth.
