"Assā" means for the sake of protection, shielding, and guarding. Protecting others—that is, protecting another from misfortune pertaining to this present life and so forth—one protects oneself by means of that very same quality of patience and the like which accomplishes the welfare of others. "Mettacittatā" means by way of a mind of loving-kindness.
A covering is that which wards off cold, heat, and so forth, such as clothing, upper garments, houses, and the like. "Among those within" refers to one's own people.
Regarding "those who have become internal," this refers to one's children, wife, and other dependents.

By saying "establish them in the restraint of virtue" (*sīlasaṃvara*), he shows protection; by saying "give them clothing, perfumes, garlands, and so forth," he shows warding off (*āvaraṇa*); and by the other [phrase], he shows guarding (*gutti*).
By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "also by providing food and wages," [the inclusion of] the restraint of virtue is indicated.
It includes establishing [the Dhamma] and so forth. This same method applies to the inclusion of the word *pi* (and) in the subsequent instances as well.
"Negamas" are those whose residence (*nivāsa*) is in a market town (*nigama*); thus he said "inhabitants of market towns" and so on.
The ninefold pride-intoxication (*mānamada*) refers to the nine types of intoxication consisting of conceit (*māna*) that arise according to the pattern beginning with "I am superior."
*Mānamada* is so called because it occurs here in the manner of intoxication through pride (*māna*).

One who delights in beautiful bodily and verbal actions is *sūrata*; by lengthening the vowel *u*, its state is *soracca* (gentleness), which is the non-transgression of body and speech, or all good conduct of body and speech.
Alternatively, one who is well-restrained is *sorata*; its state is *soracca*, which is exactly as previously described.

"Good conduct. "Of lust and so forth" means of lust, hatred, delusion, conceit, and the rest. "By means of taming and so forth" means by means of taming (*damana*), subduing (*saman*), and causing final extinction (*parinibbāpana*).
"One's own self" means one's own mind; the sense is "one's own individual mind.

For in the case of lust and the other defilements, each stage—taming and so forth—is to be sought individually in the preliminary phase (*pubbabhāgiya*), because they are abandoned through the gateway of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*) all at once, as occurs at the moment of the Path (*maggakkhaṇa*).
"Alone by oneself" (*ekamattānaṃ*) means the self that is solitary and alone by virtue of seclusion. "From time to time" (*kāle kāle*) means at the times when one should approach them.

"Standing here" means standing in the place stated by way of conclusion as: "This, dear sir, is that. "The conduct" (*vattaṃ*) refers to the conduct of a noble wheel-turning monarch (*ariyacakkavattivattaṃ*).
"Should be brought together" means according to the enumeration given below as "tenfold" or "twelvefold."
And it should be made equal, showing it without deficiency or excess. "Of passion for what is not Dhamma" means passion for an inappropriate object.
"Of disproportionate greed" means greed that occurs with excessive intensity even toward an appropriate object.
Commentary on the Appearance of the Wheel-Treasure.
85. "While performing" means while performing the duties of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) in their entirety, not incompletely; thus he says, "while performing [them] having fulfilled [them].

To what extent, then, does his fulfillment occur? In this regard, for one who has performed the preliminary service, it is fulfilled at the minimum limit by twelve years, or by twenty-five, or by fifty years. And this—

They say that there is a distinction even in the desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*) according to whether it is sharp, medium, or dull, while for the other [the desire for existence], it is even greater than that.
Commentary on the Second Discourse on the Wheel-turning Monarch (*Cakkavatti*), etc.:

"According to his own opinion" means by way of his own desired mode, having bypassed the ancient tradition (*tanti*) and lineage (*paveṇi*) handed down through succession. Therefore he said, "ancient," and so forth.
“They do not swell” means they do not fill [the treasury], that is, they do not become prosperous. Therefore he said, “they do not increase.
Likewise he said, “in some places they are empty. In this context, they are called *amaccā* (ministers) because they conduct themselves together with (*amā*) the king in royal affairs;
those without whom the business of the state does not proceed. Having come down through succession, they belong to the king’s retinue.
They are courtiers. Therefore he said, "those who move within the assembly. Having been appointed to that position, they calculate the king’s income and expenditure according to their true state;
thus they are accountants (*gaṇaka*). Because they have attained a diversity of status due to their birth, family, learning, conduct, and so forth, they possess great measure (*matta*);
thus they are high officials (*mahāmatta*). Furthermore, since they are ministers of great power, he said, "high ministers" (*mahāmacca*). Those who [serve] the king...
Those who are established in the elephant corps and so forth are called "those belonging to the military units" (*anīkaṭṭha*); thus he says, "the elephant trainers and so on.

Those who live having consumed (*asita*) wisdom (*manta*) are "those who live by counsel" (*mantassājīvina*); the meaning is "those who live by intelligence" (*matisajīvā*), namely those who provide instruction in various royal affairs.
Therefore he says, "Counsel (*manta*) is said to be wisdom," and so forth.
Commentary on the Discourse on the Decline of Life Span, Beauty, and So Forth: 91.
"Because of powerful greed" means because of the powerful greed that has arisen thus: "In this world there are now many poor people;
if their wealth is not bestowed [upon me], my treasury will be exhausted."
“In successively higher planes” means in the successively higher sensual planes comprised within the five sense-sphere heavens (*kāmasagga*). The fruit of kamma is called the “summit”;
since that [fruit] here leads upwards, he said, “its summit is upwards. “Leading to heaven” (*sovaggika*) means either being connected with heaven or having heaven as its purpose.
“Of the ten distinctions” refers to the divine lifespan, beauty, fame, happiness, sovereignty, and the divine forms, and so forth.
Regarding the specific fruits: here, by the mention of "color" (*vaṇṇa*), one's own personal appearance is included; by the mention of "form" (*rūpa*), external forms as objects are included. 92.

"Well-restrained" means having properly prevented [the act] such that this person is unable to take what is not given with this body. "Rooted out" means destroyed at its very root by the taking of life. 96. Conduct (*caritta*) is behavior (*caraṇa*) driven by lust;
conduct itself is misconduct (*cāritta*). The intended meaning is sexual intercourse; however, because it is said "among the wives of others," he calls it "wrong conduct" (*micchācāra*).
100. *Paccanīkadiṭṭhi* (contrary view) is a view that is the opposite of right view, such as the [wrong] view that "there is no giving," and so forth.
101. [The term] "maternal aunt" and so on will be explained below by himself.

*Atibalavalobho* (excessively powerful greed) is an exceedingly strong, thick defilement by which one acts at the wrong time and in the wrong place. *Micchādhammo* (wrong nature) is false, inverted, and having a dissimilar basis.
It is a state of greed. Therefore he said, "of men," and so forth.
Its nature is that state of mind preceded by loving-kindness and compassion by which a person is called "filial toward his mother";
that aforementioned arising of consciousness and the action originated by it constitute filiality toward one's mother. Therefore he said, "toward the mother."

"This is the name for right practice. That which is a failure to practice rightly toward those who ought to be practiced toward rightly is also a fault, because it consists in the state of showing disrespect and so forth.
As for wrong practice, there is nothing at all that needs to be said; therefore, he says:

"Disrespect for mother consists both in the absence of such [right practice] and in its opposite. "Toward the elders in the family" means toward those who are senior in one's own family, such as one’s great uncles, paternal uncles, elder brothers, and so on.
103. Regarding the commentary on the "time of ten-year lifespan":
By the word "yaṃ" (which), the "time" (samaya) is touched upon; and since this is a nominative case used in the sense of the locative, he said, "yasmiṃ samaye" (at which time).
"Alaṃpatinī" means one who is sufficient for her husband. Because she is sufficient in the capacity of a wife, he said, "to give."
“Appropriate,” he said. “The finest flavors” means flavors that have become supreme by virtue of their sweetness and their medicinal quality.

“They will shine forth” means they will blaze up by way of being antidotes. Therefore he said, “There will not even be anything wholesome. “Oh, what a man!”—if even toward his mother and others he is such as this, what will he spare for anyone else? Oh, what a man of fiery majesty!

“As if toward a woman in the house” means as if toward a female slave or wife who has become a woman in his own household. “Intercourse” means a confusion of conduct, like that of a wife among one’s mother and the rest.
"Strong anger" (*balavakopa*) means anger that arises by way of a desire to kill. "Harbors ill-will" (*āghāteti*) means he strikes;

the meaning is that he afflicts the mind with his own hardness and harshness, for hatred has the function of burning its support. "Maliciously intends" (*byāpādeti*) means he destroys, because of the defilement of the mind and the agitation of the mind.
"Intense" (*tibba*) means sharp; however, this sharpness of his [is such] even when striking the body, [it affects] the object of affection.
It should be understood that even by skipping over [the intermediate periods], they are to be known through their occurrence; thus he said, "even while being beloved," and so forth.

"Kappa-vināsa" (the destruction of an eon) is simply "kappa" (an eon), with the omission of the latter member of the compound. An "antarakappa" (intermediate eon) is one that occurs within [a great eon].

Because this world possesses an eon consisting of the divisions of craving and so forth, it is called "kappa"; thus he said, "the destruction of the world occurring in the interval. This, then, is the antarakappa.

With reference to the inquiry as to how many kinds there are, how their arising occurs, and what is included within the "destiny" (gati), he says, "And it is called an intermediate aeon," and so forth.
"To those for whom greed was predominant" means while a generation characterized by an excess of greed was prevailing.
"They thought thus" refers to the recollection of former traditions as well as the attainment of a specific longevity for themselves.
A place dense with thickets of creepers and the like means a place that has become dense due to being covered by thickets of creepers and such.

Dense with trees means a place that has become dense because it is completely filled with trees. A river-ford difficult to cross means a place difficult to traverse on both this side and the far side of rivers with broken banks.
Therefore he said, "of rivers," and so forth. Uneven terrain among mountains means the space between mountains.
"On mountains" means on steep slopes or uneven places that are difficult to climb. "In common" means they will make them similar or equal by way of their continued life.
105. Commentary on the discourse regarding the increase of lifespan, beauty, and so forth:
"Extended" (*āyata*) means long or lasting for a long period of time. For the destruction of kinsmen through death is "extended" because it does not recur.
Because it can be obtained again through returning [to the precepts] by means of a formal undertaking, even due to fear of the king or other such causes.

"We might backslide" (*osakkeyyāma*) means we might retreat. Since even abstaining is in fact a relinquishing because its nature is that of renunciation, he said: "The meaning is 'we might abandon them'.
"Because of being nurtured in the womb of virtue" means that due to the virtue of the mother and father, there was growth in the womb which constitutes their constituent parts.

“Grown in the womb of virtue”—by this it is shown that, just as with temperature and nutriment, the continuity of a being receives a specific development by means of other external conditions as well.
Whatever else needs to be said on this point has already been stated in the *Brahmajāla-ṭīkā*.
“By the purification of the field” means by the purification of the object-base which serves as the foundation. But is not that specific development...
Would it not be the case that [the mind] arises as a mere continuity of form (*rūpa-santati*)? This is true;

however, when the continuity of form has been thus distinguished, the continuity of the immaterial (*arūpa-santati*) also becomes one that has received assistance, because its mode of existence is bound to that [form].

Just as when the physical body is supported by edible food (*kabaḷīkāra-āhāra*), the entire personal existence (*attabhāva*) is indeed said to be sustained; and just as, for example, [in the case of] a king...
Just as, by depending upon the specific merit of a wheel-turning monarch (cakkavatti), various unique qualities such as his jewel-woman arise—
occurring when that merit is present and not occurring when it is absent— so too, at that time,
by depending upon the aforementioned specific merit of the parents, the long life and purity of the fields of those children being born come to pass.

It should be understood that [this] occurs because, at that time, their wholesome volition arises in such a magnificent manner due to being fortified by spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), desire for the Dhamma (*dhammacchanda*), and so forth.
"In this" means in this human world; "therein" means among the classes of beings living while undertaking and practicing the aforementioned wholesome states.
"Right there" means in that very same class of beings. "By one's own perfection of virtue" (*attano va sīlasampattiyā*).
This has been stated because a phenomenon included within one's own continuity serves as a specific condition for that [result].
Furthermore, even here, it is not possible to deny the purification of the field (*khetta-visuddhi*).
"Parts" (*koṭṭhāsa*) refers to the eleven parts beginning with "a lifespan of forty years" and ending with "a lifespan of eighty thousand years."

"By taking what is not given, etc."—by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of the ten divisions of evil, beginning with [the destruction of] families and ending with the lack of respect for elders. 106.
"Craving arising in this way": this refers to the desire to consume, which occurs by way of inducing verbal transgression.
*Āsana* refers to the contraction of the body caused by an incapacity for physical activity; thus he said, "the state of being non-expansive," and so forth.
*Ghananivāsa* refers to the dense settlement of villages, market towns, and royal capitals—their existence not too far apart from one another.
*Nirantarapūrito* means filled as if without interval, due to the great number of beings who have flocked there.
Commentary on the Arising of the Buddha Metteyya: 107.
Although the teaching has previously been presented by way of increasing [lifespans], this, however, is not stated by way of increasing [lifespans].
If one asks why, he says: “For it is not,” and so forth. Buddhas do not arise during a time when the lifespan of sentient beings is increasing.
Because spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) is difficult to cultivate within *saṃsāra*. The time for the arising of a Buddha is thus only after that hundred thousand years have passed. 108.
It is called a "post" (*yūpa*) in the sense of being erected; here it is a "palace" (*pāsāda*), which is like a post because it possesses many stories, gables, upper chambers, and so forth.
By the phrase "by means of the king as the cause," he shows that the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause, [referring] to the excellence of his resolve and other such qualities.
Because he was endowed with great royal majesty and great renown, and because he delighted the great multitude through the four bases of sympathy, he became known as King Mahāpanāda.
In the *Jātaka*, that is, in the *Mahāpanāda-jātaka*, [the phrase] "In the past, that king named Panāda heard... refers to himself by way of another individual existence (*attabhāva*).
He describes it as if it were something else. For the Venerable Bhaddaji Thera, having shown the golden palace where he himself had formerly dwelt, spoke thus:
"Whose sacrificial post is golden" means that this sacrificial post—this palace—of whichever king is golden, made of gold.
"Sixteen spans high across" means it is sixteen arrow-lengths in width; however, it is half a *yojana* in height.
"Ubbhamāhu sahassadhā": they say that its height, the loftiness of this palace, was "sahassadhā," meaning it measured a thousand pillars;

furthermore, it was twenty-five *yojanas* in measure from its base. However, some here have lengthened the word to "āhu" for the sake of metrical ease in the verse, explaining the meaning as "ahu," which is "ahosi" (it was).
*Sahassakaṇḍo* means having a thousand tiers; there is also the reading *sahassakhaṇḍo*, which has the same meaning. *Satageṇḍu* means possessing many hundreds of turrets.
*Dhajālū* means endowed with banners—such as the spear-banner (*sattidhaja*) and the hero’s banner (*vīraṅgadhaja*)—which were fixed here and there upon the tops of the turrets and other parts.
*Haritāmaya* means made of refined gold (*cāmīkara-suvaṇṇa*). Some, however, explain *haritāmaya* as "inlaid with green gems."
They say: "Gandhabbas" means actors. "Six thousand sevenfold" means that six thousand gandhabbas danced in seven places within that palace for the sake of pleasing the king.
Even though they were dancing in this manner, it is said they were unable to make the king laugh. Then Sakka, the king of the gods, [summoned] a divine actor...
Having sent [the materials], he held a festival; then the king laughed. A village named Koṭigāma was built.

"The site" refers to the site of the Elder Bhaddaji. This has already been related in detail in the commentary on the Elder’s Verses (*Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā*). "Of the other" refers to the divine son Naḷakāra. "By the power" means by the sign of the power of merit (*puññānubhāva-nimitta*).
"Having given by way of a gift" means having directed that palace toward the door of giving by relinquishing his own proprietary claim over it.

"Having relinquished" means having given by way of mental renunciation, and then having relinquished by way of a detached abandonment through making [the gift] the property of those worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇeyya*).
"By this much" refers to the path of the teaching beginning with "In the past, monks...
and so on, up to the phrase "he will go forth."
Commentary on the Discourse on Increasing a Monk’s Life-Span, Complexion, and So Forth (110):

“This is for a monk in regard to life-span” means that when life-span is to be accomplished, this is what should be desired by a monk as the cause for long life. Therefore, he said: “This is the cause of longevity.
Because for one whose virtue is perfected, there arises non-regret, gladness, rapture, tranquility, happiness, concentration, knowledge of things as they truly are, and so forth.
Because the body is permeated by sublime forms arising from that [virtue], the element of beauty (vaṇṇadhātu) becomes serene in the physical frame, and a fair reputation spreads abroad;
thus he said, "For one who is virtuous," and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "joy and happiness born of seclusion, etc.," he includes the joy and happiness born of concentration, the bodily happiness not accompanied by joy, and the happiness of equanimity born of the purity of mindfulness.

It brings about non-repulsiveness for immeasurable beings because of its own state of being non-repulsive toward them. Its pervasiveness in all directions results from its expansion in all directions through the practice of bringing benefit and so forth in an immeasurable manner.
It is called "the power consisting of the fruit of arahantship" because, by virtue of its unshakable nature, it cannot be overcome by anything.
The word "in the world" (*loke*) is connected with both "even a single power" (*ekabalam pi*) and likewise with "hard to withstand, hard to attain" (*duppasahaṃ durabhisambhavam*).

These [terms] should also be connected [to this context]. For it is by means of those states included within the world (*loka-pariyāpanna*) that their power is difficult to overcome and difficult to attain, not by means of supramundane (*lokuttara*) states. "In this very [fruit]" means in this very fruit of arhatship; the sense is "for the sake of that.
"Supramundane merit as well" means both supramundane merit and the fruit of that merit increase until the destruction of the taints (*āsava-kkhaya*).

The construction is: "because of the undertaking of wholesome states leading to the turning away from the round. The intention is that they drank the drink of the Deathless by way of the attainment of the lower paths and fruits.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning) for the commentary on the *Cakkavatti Sutta*.
4. Commentary on the *Aggañña Sutta*.
The Commentary on the Vāseṭṭha-Bhāradvāja Sutta. 111. "In this" refers to the two phrases:
"in the Eastern Park (Pubbārāma)" and "in the Palace of Migāra’s Mother (Migāramātupāsāda). Within this context, one might ask: what is this Eastern Park?
How did it come to be called the Eastern Park? Who was Migāra’s Mother? And how did her palace come to be? These are the questions contained therein.
In the inquiry: this gradual discourse now being spoken is, from the beginning, a gradual discourse in brief.

Having seen the Blessed One Padumuttara appointing a certain laywoman to the position of chief attendant, and having conceived great reverence and esteem for that [act], she invited the Blessed One with that very matter foremost in her mind. "Of the son of Meṇḍaka... [and so forth].
[She became] the daughter of the merchant Meṇḍaka. She became a stream-enterer because she had performed such meritorious service.
He placed her in the position of a mother because of her excellence in virtue and conduct, and because she was worthy of veneration.

"Application" means that they reached a state of application (viniyoga) by way of absorption (appanā) in various places where absorption is to be attained. And [he was adorned] with others such as beryl, ruby, and emerald.
“Bhassati” means it descends. “A pure palace alone does not shine” means that a monastery consisting of a single, isolated palace does not look beautiful.
They call those dwellings which must be constructed by bringing out many projections “double-and-a-half houses.
Dwellings constructed by expanding in this way twice—having a central chamber with a walkway surrounding it on all sides—are called “double-and-a-half houses.”
“Cūḷapāsāda” means small palaces. The Uttaradevī Vihāra is the monastery built near the eastern gate of the city.

Because they did not adopt the sectarian marks (liṅga) of the heretics, they do not undergo the probationary period (parivāsa) for heretics. This is because they have not received full ordination (anupasampanna).
Because they have not committed any offense, they do not undergo probation for an offense (*āpattiparivāsa*). "Bhikkhubhāva" means full ordination (*upasampadā*).
"The Tevijja Sutta" means having heard the *Tevijja Sutta* in this *Dīghanikāya*.
113. "Walking about following" means they walked back and forth because they were unable to walk [independently], so as to inquire about the intended meaning and so forth.
Because it is impossible [to do otherwise]. "Of them" means of those two. Therefore he said, "more wise.
"The meaning" refers to the sense of existence (*bhavattha*). "Endowed with a noble family" means born into a highly exalted brahmin family that possesses a noble lineage.
"Brahmin families" refers to those brahmin families that are not afflicted by any loss or decline. Therefore he said, "endowed with wealth and so forth," and so on. These are the brahmins.
Having become arrogant, they revile them by striking at their birth and so forth, saying, "This outcaste has gone forth into the religious life," and so on.
"They speak abusively" means they speak after having treated them with contempt. "Suitable for oneself" means suitable for one's own disposition.
An abusive speech that proceeds intermittently, being broken up from time to time, is not called "complete" because of its fragmented nature.
By way of the opposite, it is called "complete"; thus he said, "In the interval," and so forth.
"Due to lack of support" means due to being without a foundation. "Shattered" means ruined.
"The other three castes" refers to the castes beginning with the Khattiyas as inferior. [Objection: Are not the Khattiyas indeed the most excellent caste, just as the Buddhas are?
"Are they arisen now only in a khattiya family? "This is true;
however, out of their own false pride and wrong grasp, they say, 'The brahmin alone is the best caste,' but that is merely their word.
They say, 'They are purified (sujjhanti),' meaning they become pure and do not incur blame or censure. Or rather, they are purified from the cycle of existence (saṃsāra)."

The remaining castes are not [Brahmins] because they are not born from semen and lack the mastery of mantras. They are "born from the mouth" (*mukhajā*) because they were born from the mouth of Brahmā, according to the words of the Vedas.

For that very reason, they are "born of Brahmā" (*brahmajā*), meaning they were produced from the Vedic word of Brahmā, the Great Brahmā. They are "created by Brahmā" (*brahmanimmitā*) because they were fashioned by him in both ways (from his mouth and from his mind).
They are "worthy of the inheritance of Brahmā" (*brahmadāyajjaṃ arahanti*) because they are entitled to the legacy of the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and so forth.
“Heirs of Brahmā. Regarding the word *samaṇaka* in the *Muṇḍaka Sutta*, the letter *ka* is used here in a sense of reproach;

thus he says, “they speak while censuring and loathing. *Ibba* means *sudda* (outcastes); however, because they are bound by the shackles of household life and are therefore more base, he says “householders.
*Kaṇha* means those of a dark nature. *Bandhu* in the sense of a bond; as for whose bond they are, he says “those who have become the kinsmen of Māra.”
“Born from the foot” (*pādāpaccā*) means those born from the foot [of Brahmā]. It is said that this is the doctrine of the Brahmins:
“Brahmins were born from the mouth of Brahmā, Khattiyas from his chest, Vessas from his thighs, and Suddas from his feet.
Since, at the time of the first aeon, there was no differentiation of the four castes and all beings were exactly alike, [the term is used].
But later, due to a difference in their application, it occurred; therefore it was said: “The ancients... not knowing.
“For the purpose of breaking up their adherence” means for the purpose of removing the adherence that had arisen thus: “Brahmins are the sons of Brahmā, his legitimate offspring born from his mouth.
“For the purpose of obtaining a son” means [thinking]: “In this way we shall clear our father’s debt.”
Having established themselves in their doctrine for the sake of obtaining a son—this, indeed, was the intention of those brahmins who followed the Dhamma.
"One whose flower has appeared" means one who has reached puberty;

for in women, from the time they reach maidenhood until the end of their final period of life, provided there is no obstruction, every eighth week during the third rotation known as the "womb-abode," a certain...
The red pustules, having formed, burst even before the flowers have been grasped; from that, blood flows out.
In this regard, there is the designation "season" and the designation "flower. "Nesaṃ" means "of these brahmins. "Saccavacanaṃ siyā" means:
if the statement beginning with "sons of Brahmā" were true, then [the mouth of] the brahmin women... [etc. ...would indeed be [the source], but this is not the case.
The Explanation of the Purity of the Four Castes (Catuvaṇṇasuddhivaṇṇanā) 115.
"The doctrine that severs the mouth" refers to the doctrine that severs the claim that "Brahmins were born from the mouth of Mahābrahmā.
"Incapable of noble state" means they bring about a lack of nobility. "Naturally black" means they are not pure by their very nature. "Dark" means...
“Defiled” means one who causes affliction; therefore he said, “the meaning is ‘suffering’. “The state of being white” means purity;
thus he said, “they are bright by virtue of being free from defilements (nikkilesabhāva). “White” means not defiled and not causing affliction; hence it was stated, “the meaning is ‘happiness’. 116.
Regarding the phrase “intermingled in both,” since it is expressed with a transposition of words, he said, “in both [categories] intermingled. “Becoming mixed” means...

“Sometimes dark states, sometimes bright states”—thus [it refers] to their being mixed within a single continuum and within one and the same individual existence (*attabhāva*), but not because they occur simultaneously.
By saying “in dark and bright states,” he indicates that the very states just mentioned are what are being referred to here; for those brahmins do not [recognize] those states...
They have transcended [the world], and that path by which they might transcend it does not exist for them; therefore it is said, "even while they are present.
They do not approve because of their state of speaking what is not according to reality. And "approval" means rejoicing intensely;
thus, in order to show the absence of that, it is said, "they do not rejoice, they do not praise. "Of the four castes..."
The genitive case is used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of connection (*sambandha*) in the phrase "of them" (*tesam*).
And those brahmins are not of such a kind, nor are they like that; for even in part they do not resemble an *arahant*, because there is no similarity between them and him.
Therefore, for that reason, wise people who speak according to reality [reject] the claim of those brahmins that "the brahmin caste alone is the best."
The Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddhas, do not permit [this].

Regarding the phrase "because of being far removed, etc.": here, he is an *arahant* because he has abandoned the defilements by being far removed from them; he is an *arahant* because he has slain the enemies that are the defilements;
he is an *arahant* because he has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra; he is an *arahant* because he is worthy of the requisites and so forth.
The meaning should be understood as follows: they are "arahants" (worthy ones) because of their worthiness in not performing evil deeds. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentaries.
"Because of the destruction of the taints" means because of the abandonment of all four taints without remainder. "The life of the holy life" refers to the life of the holy life of the Path.
He is one who has completed his dwelling because that dwelling has been finished, or he is one who has completed his dwelling because he has dwelt in the ten noble dwellings. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, there are these ten noble dwellings which the noble ones have dwelt in, do dwell in, or will dwell in.
What are the ten? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu has abandoned five factors and is possessed of six factors..."

“Having a single guard, four supports, having shaken off individual dogmatic views, with desires stilled, with intentions undisturbed, with bodily formations calmed, well-liberated in mind, and well-liberated in wisdom—these, monks, are the ten abodes of the noble ones.

Alternatively, it is called “dwelt” (*vusitaṃ*) because one dwells (*vussati*). It refers to the Noble Path and the Noble Fruit; [the term *ariyāvāsa*] is used here in the sense of wishing to express the excellence of possessing these.

The Arahant is called "one who has lived" (vusitavā). What is to be done (karaṇīya) refers to full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development, because these must absolutely be performed by those desiring to bring an end to suffering.
Since that [work] has been performed by means of the four paths, each with respect to the four truths, it is therefore said: "by the four...
one who has done what was to be done. They are like a burden in the sense of causing one to sink down.
The burdens, the defilements, and the aggregates. For it is said: "The five aggregates are indeed the burdens.
*Ohārito* means removed or cast off. *Saka-attho* means one's own goal; here, the letter *da-* is used for metrical or euphonic connection (*padasandhikaro*).

Granted that views and so forth are also indeed fetters, nevertheless, the sense of being "fettered to existence" (*bhava-saṃyojana*) is preeminent in the case of craving. As it is said: "Of beings hindered by ignorance..."
“...of the fetters of craving. Thus, in that very sutta, it is stated as the nature of the truth of origination; therefore it is said:
“The fetter of existence is called craving. “Liberated through perfect knowledge” means:
having known correctly—that is, having known exactly as it is, in accordance with reality, whatever is to be known—by means of the supreme path-wisdom which consists in knowing, one is liberated.
"In this world" means in this world of sentient beings. "In this selfhood" means in one's own personal existence;
"in another selfhood" means in the personal existence of another; the meaning is: in this world and in the other world.

(117) "Without interval" means without division. Therefore he said, "equal to their own family. "They follow after" means followers (*anuyantā*); those who are followers are indeed *ānuyantā*, meaning those who act in accordance with [the leader]. Therefore he said, "those who exercise power."

118. *Niviṭṭhā*: It is "settled" by way of entering into a matter worthy of belief. For that very reason, it is "firmly settled" (*abhiniviṭṭhā*) because of its excessive settling upon that [matter]. *Acalaṭṭhitā*: It stands in a state of immovability. *Yaṃ*:

That which is the speaking of a doctrine to be spoken without having investigated it, and the speaking of its meaning without having made it directly manifest—this is an impossibility, an impossibility because that [wrong view] was utterly eradicated right at the foot of the Bodhi tree. *Vicchindajananatthaṃ*: For the purpose of producing a severance.
The meaning is: "for the purpose of producing a breach in his faith in the Triple Gem, that is, for the sake of causing a change [in his state]. "He" refers to Māra.
"He was unable to utter a falsehood" means he did not dare to speak a lie in the presence of a Noble Disciple who had attained the fruit;
therefore, he confessed, "Yes, I am Māra. "On the stone-earth" means on the jewel-made stone-earth. "Sineru..."
The ground surrounding it was said to be made of the seven precious gems; some say it was made of gold.
In its breadth and height, it measured many thousands of yojanas and was exceedingly stable. "Why are you there? means for what reason are you there?
He snapped his fingers, saying, "Unable to stand," meaning unable to stand before a noble disciple (ariyasāvaka).
Being unable [to do so]. For this is the power of the attainment of the Noble Dhamma, such that even Māra himself, despite his great majesty, is unable to turn one back directly.

"The root of the path" (*maggamūla*) means the path itself is the root; of that [path]. Because of its having arisen, because of its having come into being. In the mental continuum established by that root of the path...
Having gained a foothold. Relying on the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, one born into the noble birth is said to be "born in dependence upon the Blessed One in the noble plane.
Regarding the phrase "dwelling in the breast," this is stated because [the Dhamma] originates from the breast of the Proclaimer of Dhamma;
or alternatively, it is "of the breast" (orasa) because it is of the noble lineage produced through effort in the breast. One born from the mouth is called "mouth-born" (mukhato jāto).

It has been said. For even in the case of a cause of a cause, there is a conventional expression similar to that for the cause itself, as in: "The meal was prepared by means of grass. Some, however, say:
"He is 'born from the mouth' because he was born by way of the gateway to liberation (vimokkhamukha)"; in this case too, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated.
According to the former sense, among the three connections—namely, being "born from the womb," "born from sweat," and "born from the mouth"—he is "born from the mouth."
Through this connection, the Blessed One’s status as a father is made manifest. By both of these meanings, it is precisely his status as the "Dhamma-born" that is illustrated.

The continuum of the aggregates (khandhasantāna) that proceeds subsequent to that [attainment], having become distinguished by the attainment of noble Dhamma (ariyadhamma), should be understood as "born from noble Dhamma";
or alternatively, all [such a continuum] is born depending upon and relying upon the noble Dhamma—the path and its fruition (maggaphala).
The continuity of the Dhamma should be understood as "born from the Noble Dhamma.
However, because those Noble Dharmas have not yet completed their function, it is said that they are "born from the Noble Dhamma" by way of merely being produced through the state of being noble.

Because they have completed their function, it is said that they are "fashioned" by way of the perfection of such production; hence, [the Buddha is described as] "born of the Dhamma, fashioned by the Dhamma."
It has been said. There is also a reading: “One who takes up the inheritance of the nine supramundane states is an heir to the Dhamma. Regarding the word *assa* (of him):
it refers to the statement previously mentioned as “I am the son of the Blessed One,” etc., and it is used while demonstrating its meaning—that is, while clarifying its underlying significance.

Because the Tathāgata possesses the nature of a Dhamma-body (*dhammakāyatā*) by virtue of being the locus for the aggregate of qualities such as virtue (*sīla*), which are not shared with others, there is nothing further that needs to be said; however, [this applies] to one who stands in the place of the Teacher.

In order to demonstrate the nature of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāyatā*), he himself raises the question, "Why is the Tathāgata called the Dhamma-body? and then answers that point with the words beginning, "For the Tathāgata...

Having reflected with his heart (*hadayena*)—that is, having thought with his mind for the sake of awakening the person to be trained who has approached him, thinking, "I shall teach this Dhamma to this person"—[he speaks] with his voice (*vācāya*).

"He brings forth" (*abhinīharati*) means that with a Brahma-voice, as sweet as the song of the *karavīka* bird, through the speech of teaching the True Dhamma, he brought forth and led toward the mental continuums of those to be trained the beneficial meaning according to their respective inclinations.
"By that" (*tena*) means by that reason, namely, by way of being thus devoted to the True Dhamma.

"His" (*assa*) refers to the Tathāgata. "Because of his being made of Dhamma" (*dhammamayattā*) means because of his being composed of Dhamma. Here, the Dhamma intended is in the sense of being supreme.

He says, “Having become Brahmā,” meaning that because he is the Dhamma-body (dhammakāya), he is the Brahmā-body (brahmakāya). Having abandoned all that is non-Dhamma without remainder, he has become Dhamma itself;
thus, he is “become Dhamma” (dhammabhūta). And since such a one, by his very nature, deserves to be called Dhamma itself, he says, “the essential nature of Dhamma” (dhammasabhāva).
119. *Seṭṭhacchedakavādaṃ*: the doctrine that cuts off the status of being "best," as stated in the words, "The brahmin alone is the best caste.

*Aparena pi nayena*: by another method than the aforementioned doctrine that cuts off the status of being best; namely, by the method of showing the ancient origin of the world. *Seṭṭhaccheda... pe... dassetuṃ*:
for he [the Buddha] also [said], "The brahmin alone is the best caste; other castes are inferior."

The meaning is: to show that this is called the "doctrine of the excision of excellence" because it cuts away the claim of superiority held by birth-brāhmaṇas, thereby disentangling them from the wrong view expressed as, "Brāhmaṇas are the sons of Brahmā, born from his breast and mouth, born of Brahmā.
"This state of being" (*itthabhāva*) refers to this particular mode, namely, the human condition; for a general designation applies specifically to a particular instance.
Or rather, this meaning should be understood as determined by way of the treatise (*pakaraṇa*).
"Produced by mind alone" means produced solely by the mind of access concentration (*upacāra-jhāna*), without external conditions.

That volition of access concentration by which they are produced there possesses a sublime distinction in its activity, such as the suppression of the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); therefore, it is equivalent to the fruit of absorption (*jhāna-phala*).
Regarding the distinction of its fruit, he said, “As if in the Brahma-world,” and so forth. As for the words “self-luminous” (*sayampabhā*):

because they dispel darkness there even without the light of the sun and other sources, shining by themselves, they are self-luminous; because they move in the atmosphere, that is, in space, they are sky-farers (*antalikkhacarā*);
and because their bodies and their places of movement lack the state of impurity found in other beings of the sense-sphere realm.
"Beautiful" (*subha*); "remaining as beautiful" (*subhaṭṭhāyin*)—this is how the meaning should be understood.
120. Regarding the description of the manifestation of the earth of flavor (*rasapathavī*):
"The entire world-system" (*sabbaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ*) means the complete hundred thousand million world-systems. "Leveling" (*samatanī*) means covering [them].
It spread out, but it remained established in that water; thus he said, "It was established. "Endowed with beauty" means possessed of excellent color.
"Free from flies and their eggs" means devoid of both flies and their eggs.
Even in the immediately preceding eon, there was only greed. Why? Because, through the long-standing habituation to greed, it was the very first [to arise].

"He acted accordingly" shows that he did so. "What indeed might this be?"—having conceived a doubt, thinking, "Its color and fragrance are known, but as for its taste, what could this possibly be?", he speaks.
"It stood" means it remained. This concludes the commentary on the manifestation of the moon, sun, and other celestial bodies.
121. Regarding the term *āluppakāraka*, since the word *āluppa* is here a synonym for *ālopa* (a mouthful), he says, "having made a mouthful.
Even regarding the moon and sun, which are directly perceived, worldly people experience delusion concerning their movement;

in order to dispel that, eight questions and answers beginning with "But who [makes] theirs... are taken up. Therein, "theirs" refers to the moon and the sun. "In what" (*kasmim*) means in what [place].
In this context, by the phrase "Who is above? the meaning "Who is below? is already expressed. Likewise, by the phrase "Who goes quickly?
the meaning "Who goes slowly? is also expressed. "Paths" (vīthiyo) refers to paths of travel.
"Together" (ekato) means they appear simultaneously at one moment. However, when the solar disc had set, the lunar disc became visible.
"Having known the inclination" means as if having known the preference.
"Both" refers to the interior and the exterior.
"Straight" refers to its length, breadth, and height. "Circular" refers to its circumference.
It moves straight and slowly when traveling with the sun on the new moon day, retreating little by little day after day;

yet on the full moon day, it retreats by half the path. It moves crosswise and swiftly, because at times within a single month it is seen to the south and at times to the north. This [phrase] "in two directions" refers to this.
This is stated by way of the majority. The stars indeed move in front of, behind, and alongside the moon.
"Their own place" means their own path of movement. They do not deviate because they proceed along their own respective tracks.
The swiftness of the sun’s direct motion is to be understood in relation to the motion of the moon. Its transverse motion is from the southern direction.
Travel from the northern direction to the southern direction is slow because it takes six months each way.
"He" refers to the sun. "On the Uposatha day of the dark fortnight" means having traveled together with the moon during the Uposatha of the dark fortnight, and thereafter.
"On the first day of the bright fortnight" means on the *pāṭipada* day of the bright fortnight. He proceeds by departing [from the moon] due to his own swift movement.
And because of its slow movement, it appears like a line in the western direction.

"Until the Uposatha day" means until the Uposatha day of the bright fortnight. "The moon increases gradually"—this is said because, due to the sun's light falling upon its upper part and the sun being at a great distance from below, [the moon] appears to increase day by day in succession.
This is said because, as one's own shadow diminishes, the region of the moon’s orb appears to increase gradually;
therefore, it is as if it increases by degrees. On the Uposatha day of the full moon, it becomes full;
the meaning is that it is seen with its orb completely full. It "runs and seizes" the moon.

Due to its slow movement and its own rapid movement. Regarding the phrase "gradually diminishing," the meaning should be understood according to the method stated for the phrase "gradually increasing" [in the previous section].
In that case, however, as the shadow diminishes, the disk appears as if it were increasing; here, as the shadow increases, the disk appears as if it were diminishing.
It is said that when the sun moves along a path where the rain-cloud deities (*vassavalāhaka-devaputta*),
scorched by the sun’s heat, do not emerge from their own celestial mansions (*vimāna*) and do not wander about engaged in play,
then the sun’s mansion descends below its usual course and moves; and by following its descent, the moon’s mansion also descends.
Because the sun moves having entered [that path], that path—due to the absence of water and its lack of suitability for goats—has acquired the conventional designation "Ajavīthī" (Goat-path).

Furthermore, when the sun travels along that path, the rain-cloud deities (*valāhaka-devaputta*), being free from the heat of the sun, frequently emerge from their own celestial mansions and, intent on play, wander here and there; at that time—
It is said that the sun’s celestial mansion (sūriyavimāna) moves after ascending above its natural path;
by the very act of ascending and moving above that, the moon’s celestial mansion (candavimāna) also ascends and moves above, because it shares the same course.

And this sharing of the same course is due to the fact that the mansion must be propelled by a circle of wind (vātamaṇḍala) moving in the same direction. Therefore, that path is called the "Nāga-path" (nāgavīthī) because of its abundance of water and its suitability for the Nāgas.

They have attained their common designation. When the sun rises neither too high nor too low, but moves along its natural path, then the rain-bearing clouds emerge from their celestial mansions at the proper time and according to their desire, and they move about in comfort;
because it rains at those times, there is seasonal harmony in the world, and by that seasonal harmony acting as a cause, that [harmony]...
The course of the moon and sun has acquired the designation “the cow-path” (*govīthī*) because it conforms to the path of cattle. Therefore, it is said: “the horse-path” (*ajavīthī*), and so forth.
Having thus answered the question, “How many paths do they have?,” he spoke the passage beginning with “the moon and sun” in order to answer the question, “How do they move?
Therein, “emerging from outside Sineru” means [moving] by way of the vicinity of Sineru.
Having performed a circumambulation and departing from that path of travel, they exit toward the Cakkavāḷa by moving transversely across themselves.

"They wander within" means that having thus emerged from Sineru moment by moment over six months by way of retreating, they reach the vicinity of the Cakkavāḷa; and from there as well, for six months, they retreat moment by moment.
Having emerged, they wander within as they reach the vicinity of Sineru.
Now, in order to explain in detail that very point which was stated briefly, the passage beginning with "by them" is spoken.
Those who go by way of the middle point between Sineru and the Cakkavāḷa, and by way of the middle point of Sineru itself, are said to "wander in the vicinity of Sineru."
It was said [of them], not that they were clinging to the upper galleries of Sineru. The same principle applies here to the phrase "wandering near the Cakkavāḷa. Regarding "in the middle":
it means by way of the straight middle path between Sineru and the Cakkavāḷa. The same principle also applies here to the phrase "in the middle of the Citramāsa month.
"All at once" means at one time, or by means of his own single simultaneous effort. "At midday" means when midday has arrived.

It is the time [of twilight]. For at that time, although the solar disc is rising, it is seen as only half-risen by one standing on this island (Jambudīpa), while for one standing in Uttarakuru it is seen as setting. Thus, the production of light occurs simultaneously across the three islands.
As for those star-forms which have conventional names such as Kattikā and so forth, they too are indeed just star-forms; thus it is said: “the remaining star-forms...”

"And *cā*" means the stars remaining after those designated as constellations (*nakkhatta*); that is the meaning. Both of these should be understood as celestial mansions (*vimāna*) where deities dwell.
Regarding the word *ratti*: it is called *ratti* because beings (*sattā*) "rest" (*tiyati*) or "cease" (*chijjati*) therein;
the meaning is the time when the noise of beings is stilled. It is so called because beings "rejoice" (*dibbanti*), "play" (*kīḷanti*), and "shine" (*jotanti*) therein.

*Divā*. It is called *māsa* because it measures (*minanto*) the lifespan of beings as if making an end to it. It is called *utu* because it causes (*vattetīti*) various activities to proceed (*arati*).
It is called *saṃvaccharo* because it proceeds (*vattetīti*) by revolving (*sarati*) as if speaking together (*saṅgamma vadanto*) of various beings and the occurrence of phenomena (*dhammappavatti*).
122. Avoidance is *vivajjo*; that itself is *vevajjaṃ*. The avoidance of color is *vaṇṇavevajjaṃ*, [referring to] the excellence of color.
The absence of that [beauty], however, is called "the state of being devoid of beauty" (*vaṇṇavevajjatā*). Therefore, it is said: "the state of being devoid of beauty.

"Of them" refers to those beings who possess beauty. "On account of excessive pride" means on account of pride based on one's own beauty by way of disparaging those who are ugly; the meaning is: "a cause for the inflation of pride. Its flavor is particularly intense.

"‘It exists’ (atthīti): this was said by her who had received the name Rasā. ‘They spoke in accordance’ (anubhāsiṃsu): they spoke out of compliance. ‘The discourse on the lineage of the world’s origin’ (lokuppattivaṃsakathā):

the discourse concerning the succession arising from the world’s origin; the meaning is the discourse on the tradition that arose in the beginning and has come down through the lineage. There is also a reading ‘anupatantī,’ which has the same meaning. This is the commentary on the manifestation of the earth-crust and so forth."
123. *Ediso hutvā* means having become like the *ahicchattaka* (the mushroom).

124. *Padālatā*: There is a creeper named “*padā*”; however, because it possesses excellent color, fragrance, and flavor, it is called “*bhaddalatā*” (the auspicious creeper). *Nāḷikā* means a reed-creeper. *Ahāyi* means it perished. 125. *Akaṭṭhapāko*:
That which ripens even in a place where no cultivation has been done; it grows spontaneously, just like wild rice (*nīvāra*).
The meaning is "that which has been produced. *Kaṇa* is also called *kuṇḍaka*. *Thusa* is the husk that remains enveloping the grain;
because of the absence of that, the rice is called "without *kaṇa*, without *thusa*. "Fully grown" (*paṭivirūḷha*) is a statement of the cause for its being ripe;
for it is ripe because it has fully grown. In whatever place the rice was gathered when it was ripe in the evening—
On the second day at dawn, that very spot remains filled with cooked rice; thus he said, "The place taken in the evening becomes cooked by morning," and so forth. As for "not being swept away":
even the spot where it was swept away appears, through the condition of their karma, as if not swept away at all—neither diminished nor incomplete—and not merely appearing so, but indeed...
He remains exactly as he has become.
Regarding the description of the manifestation of the female and male signs and so forth:
"In the time of being human" means that those who were previously human beings arise there now through the influence of their attachment.

This was stated because [the state] occurs; even for deities who remained in the female state in a previous birth, if the conditions for masculinity—such as dispassion toward that state and so forth—are absent, then at that time only the female characteristic manifests. Regarding the "conditions for masculinity":

these are the lack of independence from oneself, living in perpetual dependence on others, being dusty, slippery, and deceitful, the bearing of the womb, and having an inferior nature by way of one's original constitution.

The absence of heroic valor, the sense that one is "but a few people" and thus "despised," and so forth—preceded by such reflections on the disadvantages [of the female state]—is the revulsion toward the female state, thinking:
"Enough with this female state! For while remaining in the female state, it is impossible to experience the glory of a wheel-turning monarch, nor the glories of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā;
nor is it possible to attain the enlightenment of a Pacceka Buddha, nor even Perfect Enlightenment (Sammāsambodhi)."
“Because it is free from the aforementioned defects and because its intrinsic nature is supreme, this state called ‘manhood’ is the best and most excellent;
standing upon this, one is able to attain these successes”— thus, placing the aspiration preceded by such appreciation for the human state,
and “having a mind that inclines, leans, and tends toward that [state]”— in such ways, [one reflects] on the conditions for the human state.

Having fulfilled and increased [the practice] regarding the Dhamma. Without considering the manifest reality, nor the similar extensive harm pertaining to the present life and the future life, a person’s misconduct in sensual pleasures results solely in the fruit of the offense of expectation regarding women;
thus, the offense of expectation indeed brings about the state of womanhood. This is due to the inclination, tendency, and bias toward that [state], and because of the craving for it.
Regarding the phrase "by way of attaining the state of a sign," it is said: "A man, when obtaining a female existence, obtains it by depending on sexual misconduct.
The word *tadā* (then) refers to the aforementioned period of the first eon. *Pakatiyā* means by nature. *Mātugāmassa* refers to one who was a woman in a previous existence.
In the case of the word *purisassa* (of a man), the term *pakatiyā* should also be brought forward and connected here.
“Contemplating” means contemplating after having approached. It refers to those who look with a state of longing, such that lust arises for one another.
“Fever of lust” means the fever born of lust.
“Being carried away” means being led away once she has reached maturity.
Commentary on the Practice of Sexual Intercourse (Methunadhammasamācāravaṇṇanā) 127.
"Not even so much as a lump of cow dung was obtained" means they say this with the intention that the marriage ceremony itself was not properly obtained.
"Something to be drunk" (pātabyatā) refers to the state of having to drink something to be drunk—that is, the indulgence in that unrighteous practice out of defiled desire.
Having satisfied them exceedingly as if they were drinking, they attained the state of being fit for consumption;

or rather, they attained—that is, they approached—the state of being fit for drinking (*pātabyatā*). For this prefix *pā-* has the sense of "consumption," and the suffix *-tabba-* functions as an agentive;
thus, the meaning is that they consumed [it] according to their desire.
"Sannidhikāraka" means "making a store" (*sannidhiṃ kāraṃ*); he says "having made a store" (*sannidhiṃ katvā*), noting that the letter *ka* is merely for the purpose of increasing the word.
"Apadāna" means cutting off or breaking apart. "In each place" means in whichever individual place it was carried.
"Gumbagumba" means heap upon heap.
Commentary on the Division of Salivibhāga: 128.

“We shall establish boundaries” means we shall make a demarcation such as, “This portion of land belongs to so-and-so; this portion of land belongs to so-and-so. “Taking that as the foremost” means taking that as the beginning.
[End of] the Commentary on King Mahāsammata.

130. *Pakāsetabbaṃ* means it should be proclaimed by way of its fault (*dosa*). *Khipitabbaṃ* means it should be cast out. Therefore he said, "it should be removed" (*hāretabbaṃ*), meaning it should be extracted from the category of beings (*sattanikāya*).
*Nesaṃ* is a genitive case used for specification (*niddhāraṇe*).
131. *Akkharaṃ* means language (*nirutti*). For it is called "language" because it is to be spoken after having been determined upon by the great multitude.
Because it is firmly established in that very [object] and does not wander elsewhere, it is called a "syllable" (*akkhara*);

because it can be reckoned, it is a "concept" (*saṅkhā*); because it is conventionally designated, it is a "designation" (*samaññā*); because it makes things known, it is a "description" (*paññatti*);

and because it is a means of communication, it is "usage" (*vohāra*). "Arising" means occurring. "Not only the syllable" means not only the mere making of a designation. "The owner of the field" refers to that...
"Beings established after having taken possession of that region.
"By three classes" means by the three classes—khattiyas and so forth—distinguished by the three types of volitional formations (*saṅkhāra*).

They also say: "By the three householders: the khattiya followers, the brahmins, and the householders of the towns and the countryside. "Known as the foremost clan" means known as the preeminent family.
For the khattiya clan is the most excellent in the world, as it is said: “The khattiya is the best among those who rely on lineage.

However, by way of figurative identification (abhedopacāra), the syllable *akkhara*—which is also a synonym for *khattiya*—is likewise considered most excellent; thus it is stated in the Pāḷi: “by the foremost syllable.
Now, in order to show the meaning without resorting to figurative identification, it is said: “or at the head,” and so forth.
132. Regarding the description of the circle of brahmins (*brāhmaṇamaṇḍala*) and so forth:
in order to show that very state of non-violence (*anārambhabhāva*) by which those who have cast out unwholesome states are called "brahmins," the text says "without embers" (*vītaṅgārā*) and so on;
explaining the meaning of that, he says "having cooked" and so forth. "Tamenam" means...
He says, "These are those," because the exposition is by way of a transposition of the words.
"Forming" means making them mutually distinct through their mental nature, and forming them through the state of being like brahmins.

"Teaching" means explaining to others, referring to those who do not know how to compose such texts themselves. "Dwell" means they remain; the sense is that they sit down. Therefore he says, "they live."

“They waste their time” means they pass their days away. This is because it indicates that they have abandoned the practice of meditation, which is esteemed as inferior, and are instead intent upon books and such.
They have become “esteemed as superior” means they have become regarded as superior in this way: “The Veda-holders, the Sottiyas, the true Brāhmaṇas.

“Having undertaken the practice of sexual intercourse” means having entered into cohabitation as husband and wife, two by two. In the phrase “trading, farming, and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (ādi) includes occupations such as agriculture.
134. By "cruel conduct" (*luddācārakamma*) and "mean conduct" (*khuddācārakamma*): by cruel conduct such as harming others, and by mean conduct such as the work of a reed-worker or a woodcutter.
Regarding "quickly" (*suddaṃ*): here, *su-* is a particle in the sense of speed. *Dā-* is in the sense of reproach; thus it is said:
"They go quickly, very quickly, and contemptibly."
135. Showing that [the statement] was spoken by way of a reversal of time (*kālavipallāsa*), he said, "There indeed comes to be...
By this—that is, by the statement, "Vāseṭṭha, it is from these four circles that the circle of recluses (*samaṇamaṇḍala*) arises"—he demonstrates this matter:
namely, that which is called the circle of recluses... [and so on] ...that they attain purification.

"If, through these... [as before] ...there is rebirth, then, this being the case, would it not follow that these four circles alone are superior, while the circle of recluses is inferior because it is produced from them?

To show that this is not so, the words beginning with "these" are spoken. The circle of recluses follows [the others] because of its preeminence in qualities; for quality is the cause for the wise to follow.

It is not because of being a son of a good family, nor because of physical beauty, nor merely because of eloquence in speech. Therefore he said: “They follow only by way of the Dhamma, not by way of non-Dhamma.
And that Dhamma intended here is specifically the supramundane (lokuttara) one, by which one is purified from saṃsāra;

therefore, it should be understood that the term “the circle of recluses” refers specifically to the community of recluses belonging to the Dispensation. Thus he said: “For the circle of recluses,” and so forth.
Commentary on the Discussion of Bad Conduct, etc. 136.

"Karma undertaken through wrong view" refers to harmful and evil deeds such as violence, which are carried out under the guise of sacrificial rites and the like, according to such [Vedic] injunctions as: "Who is to be followed?
The goat, the fire, the sacrificial post, the animal. Regarding "the karma of one with wrong view": "This [person] has attained faith..."
[This refers to] the karma accompanied by wrong view that has proceeded [in the form of the thought]: “The path of the gods, by which those with sons go, free from sorrow,” and so forth.
“Taking it up” (*samādāna*) means its proceeding in such a manner, or the adoption of that view.
“One who does both” (*dvayakārī*) is one who performs both the wholesome and the unwholesome. Since these two do not proceed simultaneously, [the phrase] “at one time” is used.

Therefore, he says “at the proper time,” and so forth. There is no possibility of both results being given at a single moment, because there is no continuity of a sentient being associated with two minds at one and the same instant.

However, in order to show how the experience of pleasure and pain can occur for one who has performed both types of deeds, he says “but by which,” and so forth. “One who has become thus” means one whose constituent parts are deficient. For even both...
Wholesome and unwholesome kamma, once performed and accumulated, are inherently powerful; therefore, they manifest at the time of death.

Among these, the unwholesome is more powerful due to the acquisition of conditions. For specific conditions such as attachment and so forth are congenial only to the unwholesome, not to the wholesome.
Consequently, even though wholesome and unwholesome kamma may be equal in strength by virtue of having been performed and accumulated, [the unwholesome prevails].
Because it has obtained the opportunity to ripen through the acquisition of conditions, unwholesome karma is stronger than wholesome karma;
yet even when it has become thus, just as there is an occasion for wholesome karma that has also obtained the opportunity to give its result, so too, having encountered the necessary conditions,
it obstructs the wholesome karma that is about to grant rebirth and instead grants rebirth in the animal realm.

"Causes to be reborn. Regarding the phrase "the unwholesome is more powerful," one should explain the meaning according to the method already stated: "If the unwholesome is more powerful, it obstructs that wholesome [kamma]. Following that same principle: if among those [two], the wholesome is more powerful, it obstructs that unwholesome and causes rebirth in the human womb;
whereas the unwholesome is to be experienced in the course of existence (*pavattavedanīya*).
When it arises, it then makes one one-eyed, hunchbacked, or a cripple, or afflicted by diseases of the stomach and so forth.
It is with reference to this—that he experiences various kinds of suffering during the course of existence—that it was said: "He is a partaker of pleasure and pain.
In this regard, the analysis is as follows: among wholesome and unwholesome kamma of equal strength at the time of speaking, [the one that is performed] by way of repetition...
While being attended to, at the moment near death, if stronger wholesome impulsion-moments (*kusalajavana*) arise,
they ward off the unwholesome as it has appeared and, in the manner described, provide a wholesome rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
If, however, stronger unwholesome impulsion-moments arise, they ward off the wholesome as it has appeared and, in the very same manner, [provide an unwholesome rebirth-linking].
It gives rebirth-linking. For what reason? Because both types of kamma possess an equal strength and nature, and because they depend upon other conditions;
all this should be understood after careful investigation.
*Commentary on the Development of the Factors Conducive to Enlightenment* (Bodhipakkhiyabhāvanā-vaṇṇanā)

138. *Bodhi* is said to be right view of the path (*magga-sammā-diṭṭhi*), because one awakens (*bujjhati*) to the four noble truths by way of their intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) and their specific characteristics (*tassabhāva*).
Those factors such as mindfulness (*sati*), energy (*vīriya*), and so forth, which exist on the side of that [right view], are the "factors conducive to enlightenment" (*bodhipakkhiya*).
"In sequence" means according to the sequence of the teaching on the factors conducive to enlightenment. "Having followed the development" means...

Having reached the meditation that proceeds in successive stages, he said, "having practiced. It is possible to demonstrate the state of excellence of one whose taints are destroyed by means of the *nibbāna*-element with residue remaining;

however, this cannot be done by means of the other [the element without residue], because when that [residue] has completely entered the state of non-designation (*apaññatti*), it is no longer visible.
Thus it was said: "he attains final *nibbāna* by means of the *nibbāna* of the defilements (*kilesaparinibbāna*)."
"...attains final Nibbāna. "Having turned back" means having led him away from those four castes.
"That very same point" refers to the point already stated: "Only one whose taints are destroyed is the best among gods and humans.
"The doctrine that cuts off the status of being best" means the discourse that completely destroys the claim of birth-Brahmins to be the best. Having shown this...

"Having spoken. "Having turned back from the Suttanta" means having turned away from and extracted the *Aggañña Sutta*—which had previously proceeded by way of demonstrating mundane phenomena—with the words, "By following the cultivation of the seven factors conducive to enlightenment," and so forth, making it unconnected with that [preceding discourse].
"Reflecting" means attending to it. "Deliberating" means investigating the meaning from beginning to end.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Aggañña Sutta*.
5. The Commentary on the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*:
The Explanation of Sāriputta’s Lion’s Roar.
141. *Pāvāra*: that by which they cover or clothe the body is a *pāvāra*, meaning a garment (*vattha*). Alternatively, *pāvaraṇa* (covering) is a *pāvāra*.

These are synonymous terms for "garment" (*dussa*); thus, *dussa* itself is a *pāvāra*. One who possesses such a *pāvāra*—which exists for him in many varieties and numerous millions of types as his merchandise—is a *dussapāvārika*.
It is said that formerly, in his youth, he dealt exclusively in the merchandise of garments and *pāvāras*.
Having acquired much property, he engaged in trade; therefore, even though he stood in the position of a merchant prince (*seṭṭhi*), people perceived him only as a "ship's captain" (*pāvārika*).
In the word *Bhagavatī*, the particle *iti* has the sense of "beginning" or "manner"; by this, it includes the entire speech uttered by the Elder after having approached the Blessed One.
As for the question "Why did he speak thus?", it refers to the reason for speaking in that manner.
Why was the purpose answered as "for the sake of manifesting joy" after having asked [the question]?

Is this not like answering a *labuja* fruit when one has been asked about a mango? It should not be thought thus. For that arising of joy in the Elder toward the Blessed One at that time was stated as a determined form in its capacity as a cause;
therefore, he spoke thus—this very [joy] is what [was meant].

And because he employs such speech in the presence of the Blessed One by way of making known a form that has been determined, it is therefore answered as having the purpose of "making known the joy arisen in himself.
In that context—"therein"—refers to that making known of joy. "Well-dressed" means having changed his dwelling-garment while in the monastery. "Having folded" means having bound [the robe] together.
Having emerged from attainment, he began to recollect his own qualities by way of reviewing the bliss of that attainment, thinking, "Oh, how peaceful indeed is this noble abiding!
And having begun, he recollected them according to their respective specific distinctions within the general category of asceticism.
For instance, there is a specific distinction such as "the first jhāna" for that which was grasped in its generality as simply "concentration."
The specific classification of what was taken up generally as "wisdom" (paññā) is set forth by means of [terms] such as "knowledge of insight" (vipassanā-ñāṇa).

It is said that "only the knowledge of the divine eye (dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa) among the mundane supernormal powers (lokīyābhiññā) is mentioned [here] in order to show that for this Elder it is preeminent over the others";
however, the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) has also indeed been shown by way of its function in the passage beginning with "of more than a hundred thousand aeons."
Alternatively, it should be understood that the others are included here by way of their characteristic marks (*lakkhaṇa*).
Analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) is the knowledge pertaining to the distinctions of meaning, capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining those distinctions.
Likewise, [analytical knowledge of phenomena] is the knowledge capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the distinctions of phenomena (*dhamma*).
Knowledge that has reached analysis regarding phenomena (*dhamma*) is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached analysis regarding language (*nirutti*), which is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the distinctions of language, is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

Knowledge that has reached analysis regarding ingenuity (*paṭibhāna*), which is capable of discerning, clarifying, and defining the distinctions of ingenuity, is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*). This is the summary here.
The detailed exposition, however, is found in the *Visuddhimagga* and should be understood according to the method stated in its commentaries.

Knowledge that has reached the ultimate limit within the domain of a disciple is "disciple-perfection knowledge" (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*). Like omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), it extends to all knowable phenomena.
For this too has no separate preliminary practice; rather, it arises because the disciple-perfection has been perfectly fulfilled.

Its attainment occurs through the very attainment of the supreme path (*aggamagga*). The construction is: "He recollects the omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) of the Perfectly Enlightened Ones as far back as their sitting cross-legged.
The construction is: "He began to recollect the virtues based upon the Blessed One’s virtue (*sīla*). Because the virtues are manifold...
There is no simultaneous arrival of these [qualities] within the range of perception; and since that is the case, there must be recollection in an unexamined manner.
Therefore, the Elder, standing within his own domain, recollected them one after another in their specific forms.
And while recollecting, he first recollected virtue (*sīla*); showing this, he said, "By means of the Blessed One’s virtue," referring to virtue.
The meaning is "having undertaken. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.

Since the Elder here, after recollecting the qualities of the Blessed One one by one, subsequently recollected them by way of groups of four, five, and so on, he therefore stated "the four bases of psychic power" (iddhipāda);

and although the faculties (indriya) ought to have been mentioned next because they share the common characteristic of being the cultivation of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), he did not take them up, but rather [stated] "the four..."
The passage beginning with “the path” has been stated. The knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth (catuyoni) should be understood according to the method presented in the Mahāsīhanāda Sutta.
The four noble lineages (ariyavaṃsa) should be understood according to the method presented in the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta.
The factors of striving and so forth will appear in the Saṅgīti and Dasuttara Suttas. The six qualities conducive to harmony (cha sāraṇīya dhammā) [will appear] in the Parinibbāna Sutta.
These have indeed been explained. The eleven benefits of loving-kindness (*mettā*), such as sleeping in comfort and so forth, have been taught.

The twelve modes of the Wheel of Dhamma (*dhammacakka-ākāra*), which proceed by way of the three turnings regarding the Four Noble Truths—beginning with “This is the noble truth of suffering” and so forth—are found in the *Saṃyutta Nikāya* (5.1081), the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (15), and the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* (2.30).
Furthermore, there are the eight knowledges that occur in the paths and fruits, and the six unique knowledges (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*).
Thus there are fourteen kinds of Buddha-knowledge. The fifteen factors that ripen liberation should be taken from the commentary on the Meghiya Sutta.
The sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing is found in the Ānāpānassati Sutta. The eighteen qualities of a Buddha should be understood as follows:
the Blessed Buddha’s unimpeded knowledge regarding the past, regarding the future, and regarding the present.
The Blessed One’s knowledge is unimpeded. For a Buddha, a Blessed One, who possesses these three qualities, every bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge;
every verbal action and every mental action are preceded by knowledge and follow after knowledge.
For a Buddha, a Blessed One, who possesses these six qualities...
There is no decline in his zeal, no decline in his teaching of the Dhamma,
no decline in his energy, no decline in his concentration, no decline in his wisdom, and no decline in his liberation.
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these twelve qualities, there is no jesting, no shouting, no stumbling, and no [loss of mindfulness].
There is no impulsive state, there is no unoccupied mind, and there is no equanimity without reflection.
Regarding this, they say: "There is no *dava* (jesting)" means there is no activity with the intention of play;
"there is no *rava*" (clamor) means there is no hasty activity. Hasty activity is *dava*; doing something else while intending "I will do another thing" is *rava*.
"There is nothing untouched" means there is nothing not reached by his knowledge. "There is no hurrying" means there is no acting with haste.
"There is no unoccupied mind" means there is no purposeless mental activity. "There is no equanimity without reflection" means there is no ignorant equanimity.
However, some do not read "there is no deficiency in the teaching of the Dhamma," but instead read "there is no deficiency in zeal."
They recite: "There is no decline in energy, there is no decline in mindfulness (*sati*).

Regarding the eleven factors of dependent origination beginning with aging-and-death, the forty-four types of knowledge that proceed by way of applying the Four Noble Truths to each one are themselves the "bases of knowledge" (*ñāṇavatthu*), because they serve as the foundation for specific kinds of happiness. For it has been said:
"When, monks, a noble disciple understands aging-and-death thus, and understands the origin of aging-and-death thus..."
“He understands; thus he understands the cessation of aging and death, and thus he understands the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death,” and so forth.
Herein, “the origin of aging and death” is intended to mean birth. In the remaining terms, existence (*bhava*) and the others are to be understood accordingly.
Among the arising of wholesome states of consciousness, there are more than fifty wholesome phenomena, beginning with contact (*phassa*).
