The knowledge that "with birth as condition, there is aging-and-death"; the knowledge that "in the absence of birth, there is no aging-and-death";
the knowledge regarding the past time that "with birth as condition, there was aging-and-death" and "in the absence of birth, there was no aging-and-death";
and the knowledge regarding the future time that "with birth as condition, there will be aging-and-death" and "in the absence of birth, there will be no aging-and-death."

Knowledge: "Even this knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation"—this is knowledge.

Thus, by taking each of the eleven factors of dependent origination, beginning with aging-and-death, and applying [the formula] seven times to each, seventy-seven bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*) are to be understood. Therein, "even this" refers to the sixfold [knowledge].
Knowledge of review (*paccavekkhaṇañāṇa*) is stated by taking [the preceding knowledges] together as having the object of insight (*vipassanā*).
Knowledge of the stability of phenomena (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*) is the knowledge stated by condensing all six knowledges.

However, the "seeing" that occurs in the manner described by the phrase "subject to destruction," etc., is insight because it is the seeing of insight; it is merely the seeing of the subsequent insight (*paṭivipassanā*), and thus it is not considered a "factor" (*aṅga*).

They say this; however, since in the Pāḷi the factors are stated everywhere by way of knowledge, the meaning appears to be that the seventh knowledge is the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) expressed by the word "iti" as "the knowledge that [things] are subject to cessation.

For there is no connection such that even this "knowledge of the stability of phenomena" (dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa) is [also] called "knowledge," because of the inclusion of the term "knowledge" in this context.

Because the manifestation of knowledge is not intended here, there would also be the undesirable consequence that [the terms] "subject to destruction... subject to cessation" would be connected [to it].
Regarding the passage beginning "The twenty-four... the thunderbolt-knowledge," some first say:

"The Blessed One enters the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) twelve hundred thousand times ten million times each day, and he likewise enters the attainment of the fruit of arahantship exactly twelve hundred thousand times ten million times."

The knowledge that precedes and accompanies these attainments is called "the great thunderbolt-knowledge" (*mahāvajirajāṇa*) because it is unbreakable by opposing factors and because of its greatness.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Monks, two kinds of thoughts frequently occur to the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One: the thought of security and the thought of seclusion."
For the Blessed One’s thought of safety stands having fulfilled the attainment of great compassion, while his thought of seclusion stands having fulfilled the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.
Indeed, for Buddhas, the latency of the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) is light; they have reached the pinnacle of mastery over attainments.
Therefore, entering into and emerging from these attainments is accomplished in only a few thought-moments. [This applies to] the five fine-material-sphere attainments.
“The four formless attainments together with the four immeasurable attainments make ten;

adding the attainment of cessation and the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship, these twelve attainments the Blessed One enters each day, both before the meal and after the meal, a hundred thousand times ten million times. Thus is the knowledge that moves through the attainments to be entered.
Some say it is called "the great diamond-like knowledge" (*mahāvajirañāṇa*).
Others, however, say it is that knowledge which the Blessed One, on the day of his full enlightenment, during the last watch of the night—
having introduced his insight by way of dependent origination in reverse order starting from aging-and-death— began the direct contemplation of phenomena as they arise one after another.
Just as a man cutting through a vast, dense, and very difficult great forest might from time to time whet his axe on a sharpening stone so that it is well-sharpened,
even so, by entering the attainments— which are like sharpening stones—
from time to time in both forward and reverse order according to each factor of dependent origination, one should bring about the state of knowledge being sharp, clear, and brilliant.
“Reflecting upon it day after day, he attains attainments that yield fruits numbering in the hundreds of thousands, millions, and billions; it is with reference to this that it was said:
‘Relying on the twenty-four... [etc. ...the Great Vajira-knowledge. Is it not the case that there is no purpose for the Blessed One’s preliminary work (*parikamma*) in entering into attainments?
This is not an absolute rule. For instance, in the *Vedanā-paṭippassaddhi* and other such instances...

He attained the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) preceded by specific preliminary exercises (*parikamma*). However, others say: "There is no need for preliminary exercises in attaining mundane attainments; in attaining supramundane attainments, the corresponding preliminary exercise is indeed required.
Regarding the term "successive" (*aparamparā*), those for whom there is a teaching [of this] are "successive" (*aparampariya*) themselves. In the designation of the wholesome (*kusalapaññatti*):
"In the establishing of wholesome states. "Supreme" means the highest. "Standing upon the proximate cause" means standing upon the proximate cause of knowledge;
that is, being established in whatever prior proximate cause or prior application there may be.

"He has faith in its greatness" because, through the removal of opposing factors, faith—just like knowledge—attains a state of sharpness and intensity. "Than the remaining arahants" refers to the ordinary disciples (pakatisāvaka).
The eighty great elders are mentioned by name in the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* (Paramatthadīpanī). The four great elders are the elders Mahākassapa, Anuruddha, Mahākaccāna, and Mahākoṭṭhika.
Among those chief disciples as well, the elder Sāriputta was preeminent due to his excellence in wisdom.
Even more than the elder Sāriputta, a certain paccekabuddha possessed sharp and clear knowledge.
Because of the greatness of his resolve and because he has accumulated the equipment of knowledge. Although there are many qualities common to all Paccekabuddhas, it is said "But if...
and so forth to show that, even when they have gathered together in one place, some individual's knowledge might be distinguished by virtue of their previous practice regarding worldly objects.
"Only an omniscient Buddha (sabbaññubuddha) has faith in the qualities of a Buddha in their greatness."

This has been stated according to the sequence of the teaching as it appeared below. For Buddhas perceive the greatness of the Buddha-qualities through direct experience itself, not by way of mere faith.
Now, in order to clarify the aforementioned meaning by means of a simile, the passage beginning with "Just as if" (*seyyathāpi nāmā*) is commenced. It is profound...
"Shallow" is said for the purpose of knowing whether it is deep or shallow. "In the same way," and so forth, is the correlation of the object of comparison with the comparison as it has been shown.

Regarding the qualities of the Buddha, even the knowledge of ordinary worldly people, though its scope is limited, proceeds in a manner that does not proceed—that is, it functions by way of a nature that does not regress;
thus it is said, "It should be understood... one fathom... and so on. In that context, "known water" refers to...

It is like water known by its measure when it flows away. However, in the case of the Noble Ones (ariya), the knowledge that functions within their own domain proceeds precisely in the manner of its occurrence, according to their own penetration and according to their previous resolve (abhinīhāra), because its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) has not been overturned.

Demonstrating this, he said, "By the ten-fold bond," and so forth. In that regard, even for those who have penetrated the Truths, [the difference arises] by way of the specific prior application (pubbayoga) for the destruction of opposing factors.
In order to show that knowledge is preeminent and of great power, the Elder first presented the water ten fathoms deep as a simile for the knowledge of a stream-enterer;
then, he showed the similes of water distinguished by successively increasing multiples—ten times, twenty times, and eighty times—as being superior to that.
Now, if this is so, would it not follow that the qualities of a Buddha are limited and circumscribed? And by the Elder...
To show that one does not incur an offense by thinking, "I have distinguished and known them," he said, "In this regard, just as that man," and so forth.

Therein, "that man" refers to the man who stood after measuring the water in the great ocean at a distance of eighty-four thousand fathoms with a cord eighty-four thousand fathoms long; for he was taken as a simile for the Elder. By "following the nature of the Dhamma" (dhammanvayena)...
By means of inferential knowledge (*anumāṇañāṇa*). For that is called "conformity with the Dhamma" (*dhammanvaya*) because it proceeds by following a proven phenomenon;
likewise, it is called "inferential cognition" (*anvayabuddhi*) because one understands the meaning through the method of conformity;

and it is called "grasping the method" (*nayaggāha*) because it grasps the object of inference by way of an illustration according to the method already seen. Therefore, he said: "by conformity with the Dhamma," and so forth.
This sequence of the Dhamma does not belong to just anyone; rather, it belongs only to one such as the Chief Disciple.

Thus he said, "standing in the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple. If the Elder, having made a portion of the Buddha’s qualities directly manifest, grasped the rest by means of inference, would it not follow that, this being the case, the Buddha’s qualities have become limited and circumscribed?
Showing that this is not so, he said, "Infinite and immeasurable.
Having stated "he has faith," he spoke again—"For by the Elder... [etc. ...they are more numerous"—in order to clarify that very same point.
But how should this meaning be understood? To make this known through a simile that distinguishes the underlying intention, he said: "Just as..."
"How can one understand? and so forth was said because "some wise people here understand the meaning of what is spoken through a simile.
"Nine from this side and nine from that" means nine from this central point as far as the southern shore, and nine from this central point as far as the northern shore.
Now, in order to support the aforementioned meaning with a sutta, he recited the verse beginning with "The Buddha too."
"Like the great flood of the Yamaka-yugala Mahānadī": it is like the great flood of two great rivers that have become a pair by having come together as one.
"Having made it appropriate" means: having made appropriate—that is, suitable—the confidence (*pasāda*) which has arisen in me, having plunged into the qualities of the Buddha.
"No one else will be able to accept or receive it."

Because of not understanding things as they truly are. One is able to accept [the teaching] by means of correctly penetrating it according to its cause, its condition, its intrinsic nature, its function, and its fruit.

"Fullness" (pūratta) means the state of being filled. "At the time of trickling" means at the time of scattering, that is to say, at the time of falling. By the word "clear" (pasanna), the present existence of clarity is indicated.
By the phrase “one who has arisen faith,” the present state of faith is also indicated; thus he says, “the meaning is ‘I believe in this way. One who knows directly is an *abhiñña*;

one who possesses superior direct knowledge is a *bhiyyobhiñña*. That same term is stated as “*bhiyyobhiññatara*” (one who knows even more) by virtue of the desire for a word expressing an even greater excellence;
thus he says, “known more extensively. In the second interpretation, however, it means “he knows directly (*abhijānāti*).”
*Abhiññā* means superior wisdom (*abhivisiṭṭhā paññā*). One who has more *abhiññā* than that is *bhiyyobhiñño*.

By way of expressing an even greater excellence, he is called *bhiyyobhiññataro*. Since this excellence of his is produced by the further increase of *abhiññā*, it is said: "or one with more abundant higher knowledge" (*bhiyyatarābhiñño*). That by which one fully awakens is *sambodhi*:
the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) and the knowledge of the supreme path (*aggamaggañāṇa*). For [the latter] is the proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*) for the knowledge of omniscience.
The knowledge of the supreme path and the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) which has that knowledge of the supreme path as its proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) is called Sambodhi.
In this context, the first alternative is based on the aspect of striving (padhāna) for the vision of that goal, while the second alternative is based on the aspect of the proximate cause.
Why, then, is only the knowledge of the path of Arahatta mentioned here? Are not the lower path-knowledges of the Blessed One also [included]?

They proceed by way of the destruction of their respective opposites, together with their underlying tendencies (*savāsanā*). For the abandonment of the knowable obscurations (*ñeyyāvaraṇa*) is indeed the abandonment [of defilements] together with their underlying tendencies.
This is true; however, that [abandonment] is incomplete because the destruction of the opposites has not been fully accomplished. Therefore, he said, "or at the knowledge of the path of arahantship.
And here, it is shown that through the supreme path alone, the Noble Ones achieve the fulfillment of the threefold enlightenment (*bodhittaya*). Thus: "by the path of arahantship alone..."

The words beginning with “hī” have been stated. “Without exception” means leaving nothing out. “Are grasped” means they are grasped—that is, attained—by that which is grasped and attained through the path of arahantship.

“All” refers to everything that is to be attained by those [paths]. “By that” refers to the knowledge of the path of arahantship, which has full enlightenment as its proximate cause and omniscience as its foundation.
142. The excellence of the solid foods (*khādanīya*) is due to the power of their delicious taste; thus he said, "it comes sweetly. The excellence of the praise is due to its distinguished nature;
thus he said, "supreme" (*seṭṭha*). The excellence of the radiance is due to its vastness;
thus it was said, "abundant" (*vipula*). It belongs to a bull (*usabha*), hence it is *āsabhī*; however, here it means "like a bull," hence *āsabhī*. Therefore he said, "of a bull..."
“...in speech it is incomparable. To show by what quality it is similar to that [speech], it is said: “immovable and unshakable.

*Anussava* is tradition—that which has been heard from any source whatsoever. A lineage (*paveṇī*) is a succession of teachers who, having mastered the various branches of knowledge, communicate this or that meaning;
it is a tradition of teachers. Merely according to one’s own opinion: “thus, indeed...”
“It is said thus” (*itikira*) refers to hearsay. The “handing down of the Piṭaka” (*piṭakasampadāna*) is the grasping of the text of the Piṭaka through its own nature as a transmission.
“Reflection on the mode” (*ākāraparivitakka*) is the thorough investigation of the manner of the meanings as they have been heard.

“Acceptance after reflection upon views” (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*) is the endurance of contemplation through the view that “this is exactly so. [These arise] by means of scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*).

*Takka* (reasoning) is the act of reasoning by relying on a path of logic (*takka-magga*). *Naya-ggāha* (comprehension of the method) is the grasping of the method by relying on the rules of inference (*anumāna-vidhi*).
Because this Elder’s challenge was directed at the Blessed One while standing within the domain of a Buddha—a domain that is not his own—it is said:

"as if having penetrated it through direct knowledge (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*). It is called a *sīhanāda* (lion’s roar) because it is like a lion’s roar; its similarity to that consists in its resemblance to it.
Showing that he should be understood here as such by way of his preeminence, he said, "The lion’s roar," and so forth.
"Not faltering" means not becoming dull. "Not with broken spirit" means without wavering.
"For the purpose of eliciting a response" means to cause the opponent to provide an answer; for one who roars the lion’s roar is, in its true sense, capable of withstanding scrutiny.
In this context, it is called "cleansing the application" (*anuyoga*). And one who applies himself is said to have it cleansed. "To give" means to cleanse.

Some state that the meaning is "for the sake of giving," but that is incorrect; for it is not logical that he who roars the lion’s roar is the very same person who bestows the application therein. "Rubbing" (*nighaṃsana*) means grinding. "Heating" (*dhamamāna*) means warming.
And here, "tormenting" is spoken of by way of blowing on a bellows. "All those" refers to all those Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have passed away and ceased in the past; by this he shows:

regarding those Perfectly Enlightened Ones who existed in the past prior to your own resolution, while delimiting the phenomena within the range of a disciple’s knowledge—just as Māra and others did—...
"You might know the worldly mental activities of the Buddhas. But as for those Perfectly Enlightened Ones who have passed away beyond that—
whose path has been cut off, whose proliferation has ceased, whose cycle has been exhausted, and who have transcended all suffering—
how will you know the phenomena that lie beyond the scope of a disciple’s knowledge?"

Regarding the phrase "but of future Buddhas," the word *pana* (but/however) indicates a distinction. By this, it is shown that while knowledge might indeed have access to its own object in the case of the past—since the aggregates there once existed—it is asked, "How [can there be such access] in the case of the future, where nothing has yet arisen at all?
This is what the word clarifies. Therefore he said: "Even those of the future," and so forth. "[Known] by delimiting with the mind" means...

Why was it said [that the mind] does not extend beyond that? Is it not the case that the mind occurring during only the past and future seven days is the object of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa), and nothing beyond that?
This was not stated with reference to the function of the knowledge of others' minds; rather, it was stated with reference to the knowledge of past lives and the knowledge of future existences.
Therefore, there is no fault here.

He does not act in a place where it is already known because such a prohibition has already been established by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) itself, and because of the destruction of the bridge (*setughāta*).
But how is it that the Elder made only a categorical denial when both possibilities existed, rather than giving a qualified answer? To this he says: “The Elder, it is said,” and so forth.
It measures the further limit (*pāra*), thus it is a perfection (*pāramī*); that very thing is knowledge, thus it is “perfection-knowledge” (*pāramiñāṇa*).
“Sāvakapāramiñāṇe” means the knowledge of the perfections of disciples (sāvakapāramiñāṇa); [the question] regarding that.
This inquiry does not concern the knowledge of disciples that has reached the highest limit, but rather concerns omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa), the knowledge of omniscience.
Some, however, explain the meaning as “in the domain of the knowledge of the perfections of disciples. The same applies to the remaining phrases. “Able in virtue... pe ... in equanimity.

It is capable of knowing the causes comprised of virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation. For the virtue and other qualities of the Buddhas are the cause for the Buddhas' performance of Buddha-activities and for others’ knowing them as "Buddhas.
(143) Unlike inferential knowledge, it does not have doubt as its basis, but knows the knowable object according to its true nature as "this is this."
It is called *dhamma* because it upholds and determines; thus he says, "of the knowledge that is directly perceived (*paccakkha-ñāṇa*) of the *dhamma*.
It is called *anvaya* because it follows after; thus he says, "having followed the application" (*anuyoga*).

For it should be understood that the occurrence of inferential knowledge (*anumāna-ñāṇa*) follows an object established by direct perception; it is the inference of the unseen from the seen. Even when there is a knower of what is known...
Since knowledge is indeed understood in its actual meaning, it is said: "The knowledge of inference (anumāṇañāṇa) is understood as the grasping of the method (nayaggāho).

"Understood" (vidito) means pierced, obtained, or attained; such is the meaning. "Immeasurable" (appamāṇo) means unlimited because of its great range. Therefore he said: "It is boundless" (apariyanto).
"By that" (tena) means by virtue of its being boundless, or by that very boundless knowledge; by this alone, the Elder [grasps] whatever object is to be inferred.
This shows that he desires to know, and thus his inferential knowledge—unimpeded and free from attachment—operates regarding each respective point.
Therefore, he says, "By this," and so forth. In that context, "by this" means by this reason. It is called *uddhāpa* because it reaches up to the topmost part of the wall;
it refers to the base of the wall. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the gate-barriers, moats, and so on is intended.
It is to be understood thus: that which exists on the border is "borderland" (*paccantima*). The Elder showed himself by acting as a wise gatekeeper;
demonstrating this, he raised the objection: "Why did he say 'having a single door'?
He said "endowed with wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*) referring to that wisdom by virtue of which a person is called "wise."

*Veyyattiyaṃ* is proficiency, skillfulness, or cleverness in various duties that ought to be performed. *Medhā* is so called because it "measures" (*medhati*), meaning it destroys or dispels forgetfulness;
one who possesses this is *medhāvī*. That which has its arising in various instances (*ṭhāne ṭhāne*) is *ṭhānuppattikā*;
it is wisdom that arises from the specific circumstances. It is called *anupariyāya* because one proceeds along it by way of successive stages. That very thing...
*Patho* means a circumambulatory path, a road for walking all around the wall.
A *pākārasandhi* is a joint of the wall; it is a section of the wall where the bricks have fallen away.
As for that, it is so called at its minimum extent when even two bricks have disappeared; thus he says, "the place where two bricks have gone. *Chinnaṭṭhānaṃ* means a broken-off place.
"Broken and split in places" means a place that is torn; for that is called a "gap.
"Soiled" means stained. "Afflicting" means tormenting with the fever of the defilements (*kilesa-pariḷāha*). "Oppressing" means pressing down.
He said, "for wisdom that has not yet arisen to arise," because once wisdom has arisen, nothing can be done by the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*).

"Because they do not give. Therefore, it is because they fail to allow [the mind] to arise due to the impairment of its conditions. "With the mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness" means having properly established the mind through all fourfold modes of developing the foundations of mindfulness.
"Having developed according to their true nature" means having developed them by way of their non-perverted nature, so that their respective opposites are completely eradicated.

In the previous method, the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) were intended as mixed; therefore, to state it otherwise, the passage beginning with "But here...

was spoken. "Mixed" means they are mixed by way of serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the path (*magga*). Since it was stated previously in the passage beginning with "With minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness," one might take the foundations of mindfulness to be insight;
thus, [the text says] "having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are."
Because they are so stated, and because these factors included in the path possess the status of enlightenment factors (bojjhaṅga) in the primary sense,

and because when all of them have been fully attained by the Lord of the World, omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) is also necessarily attained— therefore, the Elder Mahāsiva said, "If 'the path' and 'omniscient knowledge' were taken as including the enlightenment factors,
it would constitute an excellent question," yet this was not how it was understood by the ancients.
This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). "Thus" (*iti*) is a reference to the manner already described. "The Elder" (*thero*) refers to the Elder Sāriputta.

"Therein" (*tattha*) means among those frontier cities and so forth. Nibbāna is like a city because it is to be approached by those seeking it, and because for those who have approached it, it is a place for attaining happiness free from danger.
Virtue (*sīla*) is like a rampart for those who have approached it.
Because it provides protection on all sides; because, like a circuitous path, shame (*hirī*) serves as the foundation for the rampart of virtue (*sīla*), for it is said:
“‘Circuitous path,’ bhikkhu, is a designation for shame. Because the Noble Path is like a gate, in that it is the direct way of entry into the city of Nibbāna.
And because the General of the Dhamma (*dhammasenāpati*) is like a wise gatekeeper, in that he examines those beings who have entered and are entering the city of Nibbāna.
*Dinno* means "given"; *sodhito* means "cleansed.
(144) *Nipphattidassanatthaṃ* means for the purpose of showing accomplishment; it means for the purpose of showing attainment.
Regarding the phrase "the ninety-five heretics," since the Elder was previously a wanderer (*paribbājaka*) and was wandering in search of Nibbāna even before that, those various...
Having approached the heretics, he asked about Nibbāna; they did not satisfy his mind, and it was with reference to this that it was said.
Those heretics have already been mentioned above. "Right there" means while the teaching was being given to that very nephew.
Like one eating a meal provided by another, the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*) came into his hands.
He performed and attained it. "Successively higher" (*uttaruttara*) means higher and higher because of surpassing and transcending each preceding stage;
for that very reason, because it has been brought to a state of excellence, it is "successively more refined" (*paṇītapaṇīta*).

Alternatively, "successively higher" means one after another. "More refined" means more excellent and most excellent—this is the meaning. "Dark" (*kaṇha*) means black, the nature of defilement (*saṃkilesadhamma*).

The bright [states] are pure and have the nature of purification. "Having made them with their opposites" means having made both, in their respective order, together with their opposites by way of showing the relationship between that which is to be abandoned and that which abandons.
Having set aside the dark by way of the teaching, such as "This is a dark state; this is its abandoner," and having brought forth the bright, such as "This is a bright state; by this..."
"Having thus warded off the white, [one should ward off] the black. "With exertion" means with activity by virtue of its capacity to produce a fruit;
therefore he said, "with result" (*savipāka*). The meaning is "having the nature of ripening.
"In that Dhamma taught" means: in that Dhamma taught by you according to the method stated, [the Blessed One [discerned] a certain portion of the Dhamma].

[He spoke] having known and penetrated the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*). For when that knowledge is stated, the knowledge of the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths is established even without being explicitly mentioned.
The phrase “in the Dhammas of the Four Noble Truths” is a demonstration of the manner in which it is stated in the ancient commentary (*porāṇaṭṭhakathā*).
However, the opposing view (*vipakkha*) will follow later. “In this” refers to the expression “he reached a conclusion regarding the Dhammas.”
*Therasallāpo* means a discourse on the determination [of the Dhamma] similar to the discussion among the elders (*thera*). *Kāḷavallavāsī* means a resident of the Kāḷavalla monastery.
*Idāni* means at this present time, at the moment of speaking such words as "Now, venerable sir.

*Imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne* refers to this passage, namely "he reached a conclusion regarding the teachings" (*dhammesu niṭṭhaṃ agama*), or to this thorough reflection (*yoniso parivitakka*) which serves as the cause for reaching that conclusion. "In this..."

But why is it said, "he has reached the final conclusion regarding the qualities of the Buddha"? Is it not the case that the Elder had already reached the final conclusion regarding the qualities of the Buddha at the very time he attained the knowledge of the disciple’s perfections (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*)? This is true; however, it was stated in this way because [that realization] has now become manifest.
"All" refers to everything stated by the Venerable Suma, beginning with "regarding the phenomena of the Four Noble Truths. In [the state of] Arhatship...
Regarding the phrase "he has reached the ultimate" (*niṭṭhaṅgato*), the questions and answers should be understood here according to the same method already stated.

Although the General of the Dhamma (*Dhammasenāpati*) already knew even prior to this that "the knowledge of the perfections of a disciple (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*) has been attained by me," he has now reached the ultimate in that knowledge because,
by way of grasping the underlying principle (*nayaggāha*), he has encompassed the countless and immeasurable varieties of the Buddha-qualities and thereby accomplished his task.
Showing this, he said: “The Elder Mahāsīva... [omitted] ...in the qualities (dhammesu), having reached the culmination in the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection (sāvakapāramiñāṇa).

However, the Buddha-qualities have come down by way of method; knowing them as they truly are through grasping that method, because he has reached the culmination in the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection by way of knowing them exactly as they are, it is precisely the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection that belongs to him, both by way of its successive arising and by way of the great multiplicity of duties to be developed through each of those stages.
And it was stated with the plural term “in the teachings” (*dhammesu*).

Because the Elder, by way of grasping the Buddha-qualities—which are infinite, immeasurable, and have no other object—according to their underlying principles, developed an especially eminent confidence in the Blessed One, he said:
“To an even greater degree,” and so forth. Having said, “It is well-expounded,” in order to demonstrate that very quality of being well-expounded, he said: “The path that leads out.”
It has been said. For the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma is to be understood through the accomplishment of that purpose for which it was taught.
It "leads out" (*niyyāti*) for the sake of the fruit, meaning that because its maturation is immediate, it proceeds by producing its fruit immediately upon its own arising.

Alternatively, it is "leading out" (*niyyānika*) because it leads out from the prison of the round of existence, or because it has the habit of leading out (*niyyāna-sīla*). It is capable of crushing lust, hatred, and delusion.
Here too, the connection is established by supplying the words, "He shows:
'I am confident in the Blessed One. By the word "crookedness and so forth" (*vaṅkādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes being warped, bent, and other defects in practice.

The Blessed One [taught] to you the excellence of the Buddha, the excellence of the Dhamma, and the excellent practice of the Saṅgha, through the knowledge of the disciple’s perfection attained by reaching a definitive conclusion regarding the teachings.
Showing that because he had reached the ultimate goal, [the Dhamma] had become perfectly clear and manifest to him, the Elder said: "The Dhamma has been well-proclaimed by the Blessed One;
the Saṅgha has practiced it well. This concludes the commentary on the teaching of wholesome states.
145. *Anuttarabhāvo* means the state of being supreme. That quality by which the Blessed One is unsurpassed is the state of being unsurpassed;
that is *anuttariya*. Since there is nothing whatsoever superior even to that quality, it is said:
"That teaching of yours declares itself to be unsurpassed. *Kusalesu dhammesu* means for the sake of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).
For this locative case is used in the sense of a cause; therefore, the meaning is that the Blessed One alone is unsurpassed even by reason of his teaching of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*).
"Showing the ground" means showing the objective field (*visaya*), for wholesome states are the objective field of the teaching of wholesome states.
"In the stated phrase" refers either to the sentence thus stated, namely, "in wholesome states," or to the category of states thus stated.
Why is it said, “in five ways”? Should not *kusala* also be intended in the sense of being skillful, as in such passages as, “You are skilled in the parts and sub-parts of the chariot,” and so forth?
This is true; however, that sense of skillfulness is already included within the sense of being produced through proficiency (*kosallasambhūta*), and thus it is not taken separately.
As it is said in the *Jātaka*: “Is it well with you, sir? Is it free from ailment with you?”
Because it has been included [in the scriptures], it is said: “Having reached the method of the Jātakas, it is appropriate that ‘wholesome’ (kusala) be understood in the sense of health.

In such passages from the Suttas as, “What do you think, householders, are these states wholesome or unwholesome, blameworthy or blameless?”—it is those very states described as “wholesome” that are described as “blameless”;
thus he says, “according to the method of the Suttantas.”
“Having attained [it], it is fit to be called ‘wholesome’ (kusala) in the sense of being blameless. In the Abhidhamma, wisdom (paññā) is stated to be “skill” (kosalla);

thus, for the wholesome state caused by wise attention (yonisomanasikāra), the meaning of “skill” is the sense of being well-composed, and the sense of “free from distress” (niddaratha) is established because it indicates the absence of affliction.

Furthermore, the sense of “having a pleasant result” (sukhavipāka) is established by the Abhidhamma method, since after stating, “Because of having performed and accumulated what is wholesome,” it points out a desirable ripening (vipāka).

He said: “The Abhidhamma... [etc. ...in the sense of result. In the *Bāhitika Sutta*, while the Master of the Dharma (Dhammabhaṇḍāgārika) was extolling the Blessed One’s bodily conduct and so forth, he spoke of wholesome bodily conduct to King Pasenadi, saying: “That bodily conduct which, O Great King, is blameless.
For there is no kamma for the Blessed One that results in pleasure; it is entirely free from all that is blameworthy.

In other contexts, bodily conduct and so forth are called "wholesome" (*kusala*); however, here, in the phrase "among wholesome states," the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhammā*) are called "wholesome.

Since these—when associated with serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the Path—are invariably productive of a pleasant result, the word *kusala* signifies "blamelessness" (*anavajja*) by virtue of being free from fault. Thus he says: "But in this case... should be understood."

And by doing so, this statement—"But the foundation of mindfulness of the fruit is not intended here"—is justified, since it is understood as referring only to that which possesses a ripening result (*savipāka*).

The phrase "in fourteen ways" and so forth should be understood according to the method explained in the *Satipaṭṭhāna* [Sutta]. "In the sense of exertion" refers to the side of the wholesome (*kusalapakkha*).
By way of its nature as grasping. "By way of function" means by way of functions such as the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states.

For that very reason, it has a fourfold nature. "In the sense of succeeding" means by way of its nature as bringing about success. Among the bases of success (*iddhipāda*), desire and the others have distinguished natures, while the others do not;
furthermore, the distinction among those [others] consists in their being preceded by desire and so forth. Therefore, he said: "They have different natures by way of desire and the rest."
"By way of the intrinsic nature of resolution and so forth" means by way of the specific characteristics of serenity, resolution, and so on.
"In the sense of supporting" means by way of being a support for the associated states. "In the sense of unshakability" means by way of an intrinsic nature that cannot be shaken by opposing factors.

"By way of its specific characteristic" means by way of the intrinsic nature of resolution and so forth. "In the sense of leading out" means from the side of defilement and from the prison of the round of existence.

And [it is so] in the sense of conclusion. "By way of establishing and so forth" means by way of their own intrinsic nature, which consists of establishing, investigating phenomena, exertion, endearment, tranquilization, concentration, and equanimity.

"By way of cause" means by way of being the cause that brings about Nibbāna. "By way of seeing and so forth" means by way of their own intrinsic nature, which consists of seeing, directing the mind, embracing, arousing, purifying, exertion, establishing, and concentrating.
The purpose of showing the conclusion of the Dispensation is as follows: the Dispensation, in its ultimate sense, consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiya-dhammā*).
In this context, those [qualities] accompanied by serenity and insight constitute the beginning of the Dispensation; those included within the Path constitute the middle;
and those consisting of the Fruit constitute the end—it is for the purpose of demonstrating this. Therefore he said, "Of the Dispensation," and so forth.
Furthermore, the phrase "This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed" is the conclusion of the teaching as it was undertaken. It refers to the very meaning already stated.
Furthermore, the concluding statement has been spoken. "That teaching" refers to the mode of teaching regarding wholesome states, the method of teaching, and that which is to be taught;
he fully knows—that is, he knows with distinguished knowledge—entirely, completely, and without remainder.
Because he knows it entirely without remainder, there is nothing further above or beyond that is to be directly known. "From this" means by the Blessed One.
Regarding "through direct knowledge": there is no other phenomenon in the ultimate sense or person by way of designation that the Blessed One does not know;
this does not exist and is not found, because everything has been directly known by you [the Buddhas] correctly.
There is no one superior to the Blessed One in the direct realization of wholesome phenomena and in his teaching.

Commentary on the Teaching on the Designation of the Bases (Āyatanapaṇṇatti): 146. Regarding the "establishment of the bases" (*āyatanapaññāpanā*): this refers to the bases of the eye and so forth, and of visible forms and so forth;
[the teaching] concerning their internal and external classification, their homogeneous classification, their origination, their passing away, their nutriment, and their disadvantage.
The meaning is: "and as a teaching on escape.
Regarding the commentary on the teaching on the descent into the womb (gabbhāvakkanti):
"In the descents into the womb" means in the descents, that is, the entries, into the mother's womb by way of being conceived in a womb. In the womb...
Or [regarding] the descents into the mother’s womb. "Enters" is said because, by way of conditions, one who is being reborn there is as if entering;
thus it is stated. "Abides" means it proceeds through the persistence of the continuity (*santāna*);
and since one who has become such is as if dwelling there, he says "dwells. This is the first descent into the womb for ordinary worldly humans.

The first [type of] descent into the womb is presented here by way of teaching for the majority of people. The application should be understood in the same way for the phrases "the second descent into the womb," and so forth.
*Alameva* means "it is indeed appropriate."
"They are unable to shake it" means that he is stating precisely that such winds do not arise at all. "The rest" refers again to the textual passage beginning with "This is unsurpassed.
148. Commentary on the Description of the Modes of Direct Address (*ādesanā-vidhā-ādesanā*):
They are called "direct addresses" (*ādesanā*) because by means of them one directly addresses (*ādisati*) another's mind; these are the signs as they appear, and so forth. These very [signs]...
Because they exist in a state where their forms are not intermingled with one another, they are "modes of direct knowledge" (*ādesanavidhā*) or "parts of direct knowledge" (*ādesanābhāga*);

[the phrase] refers to those modes of direct knowledge. Therefore he said: "In the divisions of direct knowledge" (*ādesanakoṭṭhāsesu*). "By means of a sign that has arrived" (*āgatanimittena*) means: by means of a sign that has come to both the person for whom one predicts and to oneself;
for it is because the demonstration of the method of predicting gain, loss, and so forth—having reached its mark—is occurring that one says, "This very thing will happen."

This has been stated. However, in the Pāli text, only the examination of another’s mind and so forth is found in the passage beginning with “Is your mind thus?”; this should be understood as being given merely as an illustration.

For the subject matter is presented specifically to clarify the meaning already expressed by the words “this will be such-and-such. The sign of going (*gatanimitta*) means the sign of movement. The sign of standing (*ṭhitanimitta*)...
"Name" refers to the sign of one's own presence nearby, or the sign to be grasped by means of another person's going or staying.
It is [known] by hearing the sound of people who know others' minds, or of others who speak after having known the mind of another through hearing;
and of yakkhas, pisācas, and so forth—namely, the hiṅkāra-yakkhas, the ear-pisācas and other pisācas, as well as the kumbhaṇḍas, nāgas, and so on.
"By way of the diffusion of thought" means by way of the thought that proceeds with a diffusive nature. "Arisen" means arisen from that [thought].
"Of those who prattle on" means of those who speak improperly or variously because they do not understand some matter.
In the phrase "of those who are asleep, heedless, etc.," the word "etc. includes those whose minds are overwhelmed by feeling and so forth. (From the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*)

However, because it is stated that "for one who is thinking, 'I will say this' or 'I will say thus,' a sound called the 'vibration of thought' (vitakkavipphārasadda) arises," it is understood that for those who are awake,
remaining in their natural state, and not speaking, the sound of the vibration of thought occasionally arises—
what is called "muttering mantras" (mantajappo) in the world. Regarding which, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, there is the quality of being imperceptible by the auditory faculty (*asotaviññeyyatā*).
Thus it was said. With reference to such [speech], the teacher Ānanda stated:

"It is said in the Sutta that one hears with the divine ear a subtle sound produced by the movement of the tongue, palate, and so forth, and arising from the vocal volition (vitakka), and then reports it.
However, speech possessing the aforementioned characteristics is not excessively subtle; it falls within the range of one's own fleshly ear when situated in its immediate vicinity.
"It goes" can indeed be known. "Of that" means of that person.
"By way of that" means by way of that thought. Thus, it should be understood that this method of direct address has also come down by way of the knowledge of others' minds (cetopariyañāṇa).
Some, however, state the meaning as "by way of that sound," but that is incorrect; for by the grasping of a sound...
The consciousness that arouses it is what is grasped; and by following the apprehension of the sound, it is the meaning itself that is grasped, not the consciousness.

By this very fact, the explanation offered by some—who say, "that which one thinks about" means "the object which one thinks about," and "by way of that" means "by way of that object"—is also refuted.

They are called mental formations (*manosaṅkhārā*) because they are formed by the mind; these are feeling and perception. "Directed" means placed and established through the state of striving, by way of removing previous hindrances.
Therefore he said, "the mental formations are well-established. He said, "he will cause it to proceed," because the very act of thinking a thought is its arising.
"He understands" is stated by way of showing the connection with the words previously mentioned.

"Brings": by means of arrival, that is, by way of the arrival at the stage of jhāna; by means of the prior stage, that is, by the commencement of insight (vipassanā) which is the entire preliminary stage of the path.
Both of these refer to one who has personally attained jhāna and has realized the path, and who, seeing another practicing for that purpose, thinks:
"This person, practicing in this manner, will certainly attain jhāna and [realize] the path."

This was said to show that one knows by means of inference, without direct higher knowledge (*abhiññā*), [thinking], "He will attain it. Therefore he said, "One knows by way of its arrival," and so forth.

The word "immediately" refers to the time of emergence; for at that time, by the very act of understanding the thought-processes that have arisen, there is the understanding of the specific qualities of the jhāna, such as whether it is conducive to decline (*hānabhāgiya*) and so on.

But does this knowledge of others’ minds (cetopariyañāṇa), which knows another’s mind by discerning it, know the minds of all beings without distinction because of its nature as a supernormal power (iddhi)? Showing that it does not, he said, “In that regard,” and so forth.
“Not those of the noble ones”: it does not know the supramundane mind (lokuttaracitta) by which they became known as noble ones, because that has not been penetrated (appaṭividdha).
Just as an ordinary person does not know the supramundane consciousness of any of the Noble Ones because it has not been penetrated,
so too a lower Noble One does not know the supramundane consciousness of a higher one for that very same reason— it has not been penetrated.
Furthermore, just as a higher Noble One does not enter the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) of a lower one, why then would he [not know] his supramundane consciousness?
With reference to the objection that [the higher one] does not know [the lower], he says: “But the higher one knows the lower,” the intention being that it has been penetrated.
Having stated that “the higher one does not enter the lower attainment,” he provides the reason for this with the words “For of those,” and so forth.
“Of those” refers to the noble ones (*ariya*). Each successive lower attainment is characterized by a subsiding due to the reaching of a different plane (*bhūmantara*).
Therefore he said, “It is only rebirth there,” meaning not birth in a higher plane.

There might occasionally be an error regarding what is known through signs and so forth, but not regarding what is known through the knowledge of direct higher power (abhiññā-ñāṇa); thus he said, “There is no... [omission] ...no error.
“The Blessed One knew that,” etc., is the remainder.
Commentary on the Teaching on the Attainment of Vision (Dassanasamāpattidesanāvaṇṇanā):
149. In the *Brahmajāla*, that is, in the commentary on the *Brahmajāla Sutta*. This designation is by means of the elision of the latter member of the compound.
"Ardor" (*ātappa*) is energy; it overcomes indolence and the entire side of defilement. Here, only wholesome energy is intended.
Because of the proximity of other terms such as "diligence" (*appamāda*). "To be exerted" means by way of exertion; the sense is: striving with effort directed toward cultivation (*bhāvanā*).

"To be devoted to" means by way of devotion. Since such terms are intended for the agent who performs them frequently and are thus desired [as objects], the other terms should be understood as having the agentive function (*kattusādhana*), just like the term "ardor" (*ātappa*). One does not neglect in one's practice.
"By this" means diligence (*appamāda*), which is the non-forgetting of mindfulness (*sati*). "Right attention" (*sammāmanasikāra*) means that by this one attends rightly;

it is an occurrence of a wholesome state of consciousness (*kusalacittuppāda*) proceeding in such a manner. He speaks thus specifically regarding the application to development (*bhāvanānuyoga*). According to the sequence of the teaching, it is first called the "attainment of seeing" (*dassanasamāpatti*), because it is an attainment occurring by way of the correct seeing of the loathsome aspect within the physical body (*karajakāya*).

"By way of the direct method alone" means that because it is supported by the attainment of the vision of the characteristics already mentioned, and because it consists of the path and fruit of vision,
the first fruit of recluseship is the attainment of vision without any indirect method.
"Having passed beyond skin, flesh, and blood, he contemplates the bone" means that without contemplating those [other parts], he contemplates the bone itself.
He reviews it. Regarding the attainment of the first jhāna based on the divine eye with a skeleton as its object:
according to the method already stated, this is the attainment of the first jhāna supported by the divine eye, having a skeleton as its object.
For a bhikkhu who, having produced the fourth jhāna in the light-kasiṇa and made that the basis, has attained the knowledge of the divine eye, [perceives] a skeleton in a conscious body...
Having grasped [the object], one produces the first jhāna there by means of attention to the repulsive;
this attainment of the first jhāna is the second "attainment of seeing. Therefore it was said: "Bone, bone," and so forth.
As for the attention to the thirty-two aspects mentioned here in the Pāli, that is stated by way of purifying the path. In that regard:
Or, for one who has already gained proficiency, the contemplation of the bones succeeds with ease according to the method already described.

For this very reason, the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrases "this very [contemplation]" and "and having transcended" is used in the sense of conjunction. "That jhāna" refers to the first jhāna as previously stated.
"This" refers to this attainment of the fruit of once-returning (*sakadāgāmiphala*). It is "excellent" because it leads to the vision of the Four Noble Truths.
Without a figurative sense, the second attainment of vision is primary. It occurs up to the third path; thus it is said:
"The fourth attainment of vision is spoken of by way of one whose taints are destroyed.

In the text, the word *ca* (and) in the phrase *purisassa ca* (and of a man) is used in a distributive sense; therefore, it refers specifically to what is being stated as distinct from the two aforementioned attainments.
This illuminates its specific distinction. Because it flows without interruption and is thus similar to a stream, consciousness itself is called the "stream of consciousness" (*viññāṇasota*).
This consciousness, having received the immediately preceding condition from what precedes it, proceeds by becoming the immediately preceding condition for what follows;
this is its similarity to a stream due to its having entered the stream. Therefore, it is described as being in the state of that which is to be known.
And here, consciousness is indeed one; therefore, it is said in the commentary: “The stream of consciousness is consciousness itself.
By both parts means by the near part (*orabhāga*) and the far part (*parabhāga*). For this world is its near part and the other world is its far part;
it is connected by way of these two. Hence he said: “Established in this world,” and so forth. Of consciousness...

Since there is no stability for anything that breaks up moment by moment, it is said "by way of desire and lust" because, through the influence of craving, that [body] is called "established. For this has been said:
"Bhikkhus, if there is lust for physical food, if there is delight, if there is craving, it is established..."
There consciousness has grown. Wherever consciousness is established and has grown... [as before] ...there is the production of renewed existence in the future, and so forth.

"Kamma" refers to wholesome and unwholesome action; this is a term used in the instrumental sense (*upayoga-vacana*). They approach by means of kamma, thus it is called "kamma-bhava" (existence as kamma).

"Approaching" means consciousness (*viññāṇa*); for the formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*), accompanied by whatever karma it possesses, proceeds only after having approached the very state of that [karma].
"Established here" is said because of its approaching the state of karma performed and accumulated here.
"Drawing along the karmic existence" refers to the karmic consciousness (*kamma-viññāṇa*) drawing along the karma associated with itself.
Having obtained rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*), it draws [the being] toward that [new existence] by producing rebirth-linking.
Precisely because of that capacity for producing rebirth-linking, it is said to be "established in the next world" by establishing its own fruit there. However, some say:

"The formative consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) that is incapable of giving its result in the future is 'established in this world'; but that which is capable of giving it is [established] in the next world."
When they say, "It is established," that is merely their own opinion, because it has been stated [in the texts] as "uninterrupted on both sides.
And as for what they say, "It is established in the other world," that is indeed already established in this world;
for without its being established in this world, its establishment in the other world is not possible. This applies to both those in training (sekha) and worldlings (puthujjana).
“Knowledge of the penetration of minds” (*cetopariyañāṇa*) is the knowledge that delimits the minds of both those in training (*sekkha*) and worldlings (*puthujjana*).
This is stated because it demonstrates the state of being established by way of desire and lust for the mind that is to be delimited.
The meaning of the fourth attainment of vision should be understood by way of the negation of what was stated regarding the third attainment of vision.

Because the meaning of the first two attainments was previously stated by way of serenity (*samatha*), the phrase beginning with "Furthermore" (*apicā*) is spoken now in order to show it by way of insight (*vipassanā*). For the meaning already stated is liable to be removed if it remains motionless;

indeed, when another aspect of the meaning is being shown, the passage is said to have "moved. Regarding the phrase "another method": here, it refers to the state of the first jhāna as the first attainment of vision.

There is nothing new here. Regarding the statement, "The second jhāna is the second," they say that "the second attainment of vision is the second jhāna obtained by means of the skeleton-color kasiṇa," and the third jhāna is likewise obtained in that same way.

However, as for the state of being an "attainment of vision," it refers to a bhikkhu who, having produced the fourth jhāna upon the light-kasiṇa and making that the basis, has attained the divine eye.
Having offered [the bone] and grasped a conscious bone, one generates the first three jhānas there by way of the color-kasina (vaṇṇakasiṇa).
For him, the third jhāna is the third attainment of vision by way of the divine-eye knowledge (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*), which serves as the basis.
The fourth jhāna is the fourth fine-material-sphere jhāna; having generated that, it becomes the foundation (*pādaka*).
Having thus attained the knowledge of the divine eye, that fourth jhāna is the fourth attainment of vision.

Here too, it should be understood that for trainees (sekkha) and worldlings (puthujjana), the third attainment of vision occurs through the delimitation of the mind, while for an Arahant, the fourth attainment of vision occurs through the delimitation of the consciousness. For this is the explanation of the meaning according to the text.

One should reconcile [the terms]. Regarding the phrases "first path" and so forth: the first path, which is based on the first jhāna having a skeleton as its object, is the first attainment of vision (*dassanasamāpatti*).
The second path, which is based on the second jhāna having a skeleton as its object, is the second attainment of vision.
The third and fourth paths, which are accompanied by knowledge of others' minds and are based on the fourth jhāna, are the third and fourth attainments of vision.
Furthermore, the discernment of a person (*puruṣa*) in this context should be understood by way of non-delusion.
150. *Puggalapaṇṇattīsūti*: "In the designations of persons" means in the making known of persons. [They are distinguished] from one another without confusion by way of their specific qualities.
Regarding the designations: "by way of worldly convention" means by way of worldly consensus (*lokasammuti*).
For this is a worldly convention, namely: "a being," "a person," and so forth. One is called a "being" (*satta*) because of being attached (*satta*) and clinging to form and the other aggregates.

One is called a "person" (*puggala*) because of filling (*pūraṇa*) and falling away (*galana*) from each respective class of beings, and because of falling through death. One is called a "man" (*nara*) because of leading (*nayana*) the continuity [of existence]. Of the personal existence...

A "person" (poso) is so called because of nourishing (posana). This is stated by way of illustrating this common designation (sādhāraṇa-paññatti), namely, "All this is the person," and not by way of the specific designation intended here [in the Abhidhamma].
Therefore, "among worldly designations" means among those designations pertaining to the world of beings (sattaloka).
It is "unsurpassed" because that designation is not shared with anything else.

Regarding the phrase "by two parts," this plural form is used in the sense of cause (*kāraṇa*) and also in the sense of separation (*nissakka*); furthermore, this meaning should be understood through repetition (*āvutti*) and so forth.
Thus he said, "of the formless attainments," and so on. By this, the doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷanāga is presented as follows:

"Because he is liberated by the liberation of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vimokkha*) through attainment, and by the liberation of eradication (*samuccheda-vimokkha*) through the Path, he is 'liberated in both ways' (*ubhatobhāga-vimutta*). [And] from the mental body...
The doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka Mahādhammarakkhita proceeds thus: "He is 'liberated in both ways' because he is liberated from the form-body (rūpakāya) as well [as from the mental aggregates].

The doctrine of the Elder Tipiṭaka Cūḷābhaya proceeds thus: "He is 'liberated in both ways' because he is liberated once through the liberation by suppression (vikkhambhana-vimokkha) via meditative attainment, and liberated once through the liberation by eradication (samuccheda-vimokkha) via the Path."
It should be understood that the compilation of these three Theravāda traditions has been made together here.

"Liberated" (*vimutto*) means liberated from defilements; or, the meaning is liberated from the two bodies by means of the suppression and eradication of defilements. In the phrase "of the formless attainments" (*arūpasamāpattīnaṃ*), the genitive case is used for specification.
"Non-returners who have attained Arahantship" is stated with reference to their former state; for [they are not yet Arahants].

One who has attained Arahatship is called a Non-returner (anāgāmī). "The text" refers to the *Puggalapaññatti-pāḷi*. "Having touched the eight liberations with the body" means having attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) by means of the co-nascent mental body (*nāmakāya*).

"And when he has seen with wisdom, his taints are utterly destroyed" refers to the conditioned phenomena through the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*) and the four truths through the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*).
Having seen [the Truths], the four taints (āsava) become completely exhausted. "Having seen" means by reason of seeing. For it is not by means of wisdom that they see the taints;
rather, because they are exhausted for the sake of seeing, it is said, "having seen, they are exhausted.
This is stated because their exhaustion is dependent upon seeing, and thus seeing is described as the preliminary action for the destruction of the taints.
One who is "liberated by wisdom" (*paññāvimutta*) is so called because they are specifically liberated by wisdom, due to the complete exhaustion of the taints (*āsava*) without remainder.

This is by way of excluding the eight liberations (*aṭṭhavimokkha*), and not by way of excluding the fine-material jhānas (*rūpajjhāna*) which constitute a portion of them. For it is established that even if a portion of the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*) is absent, there is no exclusion from the eight liberations;
for if even one of the immaterial-sphere jhānas were present, he would be "liberated in both ways" (*ubhatobhāgavimutta*).
"It is called [one] liberated by wisdom, not one liberated by wisdom.
"He realizes the limit of what has been touched" (*phuṭṭhantaṃ sacchikaroti*): "the limit of what has been touched" (*phuṭṭhanto*) means the end of what has been touched;

the intention is that it refers to the time immediately following the immaterial jhānas (*arūpajjhāna*). This is the accusative case used in the sense of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*), meaning precisely at the time immediately after what has been touched.
That which is to be realized has been realized by means of the method for realization; this is what is meant. Therefore, it says, "He [possesses] the contact of jhāna," and so forth.
"Some taints" refers to those taints to be abandoned by the three lower paths.

For one who is liberated from the material body and from a portion of the mental body by the immaterial jhāna through the liberation of suppression, by him the liberation known as cessation is observed and made manifest.
It is as if it were realized, yet it is not realized by means of the body. However, when certain taints have been exhausted by making cessation the object, it becomes realized by that [body];
therefore, because he realizes with the mental body (nāmakāya) the cessation to be realized exactly as it was perceived, he is called a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhī).
But he is not called "liberated" because some taints have not yet been fully destroyed.
“Attained the vision” (diṭṭhantaṃ patto) means that he has attained what follows immediately after the knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which is designated as “seeing.

There is also a reading, “Because it was seen, it was attained” (diṭṭhattā patto); by this, he illuminates the attainment of cessation through the view consisting of the seeing of the Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, he said, “Formations are suffering,” and so forth, starting from the first fruit up to the highest path.
Regarding the phrase "one attained to view," he said: "This one also, like the body-witness, is sixfold.
He understands as it really is: "This is suffering; this much is suffering; there is no suffering beyond this.
Because he understands this according to its true nature, and while understanding it, [he understands] the five aggregates of clinging—excluding craving—as the "truth of suffering."
He understands. Furthermore, since this craving arises from here as suffering, he understands, in accordance with reality, that "this is the origin of suffering.

Since both this suffering and its origin cease, are stilled, and reach non-occurrence upon attaining Nibbāna, he understands, in accordance with reality, that "this is the cessation of suffering. The Noble...
However, the Eightfold Path goes toward that cessation of suffering; therefore, one understands it as it really is: "This is the practice leading to the cessation of suffering.
Up to this point, the determination of the truths at different moments has been shown.
Now, in order to show them at a single moment, it is said: "Proclaimed by the Tathāgata," and so forth. "Proclaimed by the Tathāgata" means...
The Tathāgata has penetrated, known, and made manifest [them] at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). "Dhammas" refers to the Dhammas of the Four Noble Truths.
"Well-seen" (*vodiṭṭhā*) means they are clearly seen. "Well-practiced" (*vocaritā*) means well-conducted; the meaning is that by means of them, his wisdom has been thoroughly exercised.
Such a person as this is called one who has "attained through vision" (*diṭṭhippatto*).
"Released through faith" means released by way of believing; by this he shows that even for one who is not released in every respect, there is a state of being released by mere faith.
Alternatively, "released through faith" (*saddhā-vimutta*) has the meaning of "resolutely intent through faith.

"In the same manner as stated" means in the same manner as stated regarding the body-witness (*kāyasakkhin*). "But not as in the case of one who has attained vision" means as in the case of one who has attained vision (*diṭṭhippatto*).
The meaning is: "The taints are utterly exhausted; he is not liberated by faith alone. But is there any difference between them regarding the abandonment of defilements?
There is none. Then why does one liberated by faith (saddhāvimutta) not reach the level of one who has attained through view (diṭṭhippatta)? It is due to the difference in their progress.
For one who has attained through view is able, while suppressing defilements during the course of progress, to do so without difficulty and without fatigue.
To suppress [the defilements], one liberated by faith suppresses them with difficulty and exertion; therefore, he does not reach the level of one who has attained through vision.
Thus he said, "Among these," and so forth.
That which bears and holds fast to the object as it truly is is *dhamma*; that is, wisdom (*paññā*). "Preceded by wisdom" means having wisdom as its primary factor.
"Paññāvāhī" means it carries wisdom; the meaning is that it causes wisdom to proceed with excellence. Alternatively, "paññā vāheti" means wisdom carries this person;
the meaning is that it leads him toward Nibbāna. This same method applies to the description of the *saddhānusārī* (follower by faith) as well.
Therefore, because it is stated in the *Visuddhimagga*, the meaning here should be understood according to the method explained there in the *Visuddhimagga* and its commentaries.
Commentary on the Teaching on Exertion (Padhānadesanāvaṇṇanā) 151.

“By way of exertion” means by way of application to development (*bhāvanānuyoga*). The seven factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*) are called “exertions” because they must be exerted upon and developed by virtue of their being based on seclusion (*viveka*), etc.
Commentary on the Teaching on the Way (*Paṭipadādesanāvaṇṇanā*)

152. "For one who arouses concentration with difficulty and toil" means: for one who, having suppressed the defilements during the preliminary stage while coming [to the path], arouses supramundane concentration while being exhausted by hardship, suffering, volitional effort, and exertion.
"One who realizes that state slowly" means: when the defilements have been suppressed, one remains for a long time in the service of insight (vipassanā).
The meaning is: for one who, having dwelt in that state known as supramundane concentration, realizes it slowly and gradually—meaning one who penetrates it, witnesses it, and attains it.
"This is called" refers to that which arises in this manner;

because of the difficulty of the practice for suppressing the defilements, and because of the slowness of the wisdom resulting from the preparatory period of insight (vipassanā-parivāsa), at the time of the Path...
Even the wisdom that arises in a single moment of consciousness is called "the painful way with sluggish direct knowledge" by way of its mode of arrival.
The meaning in the three subsequent sections should also be understood according to this same method.
[End of] the commentary on the teaching concerning the conduct of speech and so forth.
153. *Bhassasamācāre* means in verbal conduct. *Ṭhito* means speaking without interruption that which has been commenced.
Therefore he said: "speaking without cutting off the course of the discourse.
*Musāvādūpasañhitaṃ* means accompanied by false speech occurring here and there. *Vibhūti* is called separation; that which is connected with this is *vebhūtika*.
That itself is divisive speech (*pesuñña*). Therefore, he said: "speech that causes division.

It is called "born of contention" (*sārambhajā*) because it arises from contention, which is characterized by the desire for superiority. To show the manner of its occurrence, he said: "You are immoral," and so forth. External talk is unpleasant;
even if it is pleasant, because it brings about mental distress in another, he shows that it belongs to the side of seeking superiority through contention.
He spoke the words beginning with “*Tuyhan*” (to you). “Proceeding as a discourse on distraction” means occurring by way of a discourse on distraction.
“Having placed victory before oneself” means having prioritized one’s own victory. The construction is: “he does not speak anything at all.
“*Mantā*” is said to be wisdom (*paññā*), taking it to mean the act of deliberating or knowing. This word “*manta*” is a particle (*nipāta*) synonymous with “*mantetvā*” (having deliberated).
He said, "Having investigated. "Only a fitting discourse" means a discourse that is appropriate for oneself and for the listener.

"Fit to be treasured in the heart" means it should be established in the mind because it is the cause for obtaining the attainment of meaning, the excellence of phrasing, and the knowledge of the meaning (*atthaveda*), and so forth;
the sense is that it should be attended to as a basis for liberation (*vimuttāyatana*). Even though it is complete in all its parts...
Speech spoken at an improper time and to an unworthy recipient, like [speech] spoken to an unfit vessel, does not bring about its purpose;

thus he said, "at the proper and opportune time. And in order to show that this well-spoken speech, endowed with these four factors, brings great power and great benefit to sentient beings by leading them to the perfect awakening to truth, he said, "When spoken in this way," and so forth.
Regarding "virtue and conduct" (*sīlācāra*): it refers both to virtue and conduct, that is, to purified virtue and purified mental conduct.

"Established" (*ṭhito*) means being firmly grounded. He says "one who speaks truth" (*saccakatho*) because truth exists for him; this same method applies here to the term "faithful" (*saddho*) as well.
Therefore, he says "endowed with faith. But one might ask: "Has truth not already been mentioned below? Why was it stated [again]?
For while truth was spoken below when describing verbal conduct, here, in speaking of virtue by way of the rejection of its opposite,
truth is spoken in its own essential form (*sarūpena*) in order to show that virtue as perfected.

Although this is a different topic within a discourse that is person-centered (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), nevertheless, having already spoken of truth, to speak of truth immediately thereafter constitutes a redundancy (*punarutta*).
Thinking, "May there be no occasion for another to reproach me," one desires to provide a rebuttal to that point and asks, "Why is this stated again here?
[The answer is: Truthfulness of speech was already explained below by way of demonstrating well-spoken words endowed with four factors.
Here, it is stated—"In this way, virtue is thoroughly purified"—in order to show [virtue] even down to... [and so forth]. However, regarding this present matter:

One should present the *Rāhulovāda Sutta*, which proceeds according to the method beginning: “Thus, Rāhula, meager indeed is the asceticism of those who have no sense of shame regarding deliberate lying,” and so forth.
He said, “in the six sense-faculties,” etc., because one has “guarded doors”—that is, doors closed by the bolt of mindfulness (*sati*).
One who knows the proper measure in food is called "one who knows moderation in food" (*bhojane mattaññū*) by way of seeking, receiving, consuming, and relinquishing.
"Evenly" (*samaṃ*) means without unevenness. For even conduct (*samacāritā*) consists in abandoning bodily unevenness and so forth, and fulfilling bodily evenness.
Regarding the phrase "in sitting" (*nisajjāya*), the word *iti* here has the sense of "etcetera"; by this, [the passage] beginning with "he purifies the mind of obstructive states" is included.
He embraces [the practice]. For the application of vigilance (*jāgariyānuyoga*) through meditation is the purification of the mind, not merely the dispelling of sleep.

"Free from sloth" (*nittandi*) means one who has abandoned lethargy and drowsiness (*thinamiddha*). However, since that state of being free from sloth becomes manifest upon the disappearance of physical languor, it is said:
"devoid of physical languor. By the phrase "aroused in energy" (*āraddhavīriyo*), both types of the arousal of energy are included.
In order to demonstrate that by analyzing it, it was said: "By bodily energy, too," and so forth. "Socializing" (*saṅgaṇikā*) means dwelling in a group or living together;
however, since that can also occur through the defilements (*kilesas*), in order to distinguish it from that, it was said:

"socializing in a group" (*gaṇasaṅgaṇikā*). It is socializing with a group, thus "socializing in a group. "By way of the basis for exertion" means by way of the cause for attaining a distinction not yet attained.
"One who dwells alone" means not only by way of physical solitude. "The company of defilements" refers to a state of mind accompanied by defilements.
"In whatever way" means either by way of insight (*vipassanā*) or by way of reflective discernment (*paṭisaṅkhāna*). Contemplation directed toward the object occurs by way of serenity (*samatha*);
contemplation directed toward the characteristics [of phenomena] occurs by way of insight (*vipassanā*).
“Of beautiful eloquence” (*kalyāṇapaṭibhāno*) means one whose eloquence is beautiful. However, since it is intended that his perfection of eloquence be accompanied by skill in speech, he says:
“and endowed with the art of expression... etc. For “eloquence” (*paṭibhāna*) is called both knowledge and the manifesting of words through that knowledge.
In this context, one whose eloquence is joined with what is meaningful and joined with reason is “one of joined eloquence” (*yuttapaṭibhāno*).
Because he is unable to answer quickly immediately after being questioned, his ready wit is lost; thus he is "one whose ready wit is lost" (*mutta-paṭibhāno*).
However, in this context, "one whose ready wit is lost" is intended to mean one whose speech is incoherent; it is with this intention that it is said:
"A bhikkhu established in the practice of virtue does not have ready wit. "Capable of going" refers to [the ability to travel] for the sake of hearing the Dhamma not yet heard.

“Capable of going”: capable of proceeding. “Capable of retaining”: because it is accompanied by exceptional mindfulness and energy, it is capable of retaining the Dhamma exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was mastered.
“Mutī” is a name for inferential wisdom (*anumāna-paññā*) because of its nature of investigating and inferring.
“By three phrases”: by the three phrases, “possessed of gati, possessed of dhiti, possessed of muti. “Below”: below.

“In ‘one who has aroused energy’”—this refers to the place where that was stated. “Here”—this refers to the place where it was said, “one who is steadfast. It has already been stated that energy was included as a subordinate quality below;
this is the meaning intended. “Below”—in the passage “devoted to the practice of wakefulness, a meditator,” it is insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) that is spoken of.

“Here”—in the passage “one who is steadfast, one who is wise,” it is the wisdom of grasping the Buddha’s word that is spoken of, because it illustrates the wisdom of skill in the sequence of actions and their results, and so forth.

Just as sensual desire for objects (*vatthukāma*) is experienced according to its occurrence, so too is sensual desire as defilement (*kilesakāma*); thus it is said: "one who is not greedy for sensual desires as objects or as defilements.
154. Commentary on the Instruction, the Method, and the Teaching:

"By means of one's own skillful attention" (*attano upāyamanasikārena*) means by means of the initial attention and the attention of cultivation (*bhāvanāmanasikāra*) that have arisen within oneself. "One who is practicing" (*paṭipajjamāno*) means one who is practicing for the sake of purification (*visuddhi*).
155. *Kilesavimuttiñāṇe* means in the knowledge of the abandoning of defilements. 156. *Pariyādiyamāno* means grasping by delimiting;

it refers to one who, being unable to delimit [the entire past], recollects only the pure aggregates along with name and clan. To explain this very meaning, the passage beginning with "For one... was stated.
He is able to encompass it. The meaning is that what was stated—“I was there, with such a name,” and so forth—was spoken by way of one who is unable [to encompass it].
And “of one who is unable” means of one who is unable to ascend; however, in descending, his knowledge has become firm.
Therefore he said, “recalling only the pure aggregates,” and so forth. This refers to the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. He did not perceive it.
