Because their knowledge is blunted by adherence to views (*diṭṭhābhinivesa*). Therefore he said, "because they are followers of speculative views" (*diṭṭhigatika*). "Position" (*ṭhāna*) means remaining fixed on one side.
"Certainty" (*niyama*) means a restriction of argument, a state of having a fixed doctrine. Therefore he said, "having taken this," and so forth. 157.
"By way of counting in groups" (*piṇḍagaṇanāya*) means not counting as "one, two," and so on, but rather by way of grouping through the production of collective terms and the like.
By way of counting. "By way of uninterrupted counting" means counting by way of an unbroken sequence, abandoning sequential counting;

it is counting by lumping together into one everything that is to be counted, such as "there are so many leaves on this tree" or "there are so many *āḷhaka* measures of water in this reservoir. For sequential counting is interrupted from time to time.
"It is a cessation of the process. Furthermore, this counting is called "mental counting" because it must be performed by the mind alone, without regard for hearing [the words].
Thus he says, "by mental counting. This demonstrates only the counting of the aggregate (*piṇḍagaṇana*), not the counting of individual divisions.
It cannot be counted by others because there is no one else who could count it. Showing that the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*) has been fulfilled:
Since there is no fulfillment of that [perfection] without the fulfillment of the others, he said, "because of the fulfillment of the ten perfections.
Therefore, he said, "because of the thorough penetration of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). The Elder demonstrates this by showing that it is just this much [that was fulfilled].
As for what is stated in the Canon—that "he recollects with its aspects and its particulars"—that refers merely to his recollection.
This was said with a specific intention (*sandhāya*), for the limitation of life by counting years and so forth is not its province.
(158) It is "supreme" (*anuttara*) only for you, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones (*sammāsambuddha*), because it is not shared by others.
Now, in order to show that this teaching lacks any internal division—like gold that has been melted down—it is said: "The Buddhas of the past, too," and so forth.
"By this reason as well" means by way of being unsurpassed and by way of being exactly identical to other Buddhas.

(159) They are "with taints" (*sāsava*) because they have entered the state of being objects for the taints (*āsava*). They are "adherences" (*upādhi*) because they are adhered to after having approached;

they are "imputations of faults. They are "with adherences" (*saupādhika*) because they are accompanied by adherences. For in the case of non-noble supernormal power (*anariya-iddhi*), some [beings] are subjected to reproach due to the fault of their own mind.
They give; this matter can be illustrated by the *Kevaṭṭa Sutta*. It is not called "noble" (*ariya*) because it possesses a nature subject to taints (*sāsavabhāva*).

It is faultless (*niddosa*) because it is to be practiced by those free from faults—the *khīṇāsava*s—and because it does not occur together with faults. For that very reason, it is beyond reproach (*anupārambhā*).
It is called "noble power" (*ariyiddhi*) because it is the psychic power (*iddhi*) of the noble ones (*ariya*).
"Perceiving the unrepulsive" means perceiving what is desirable, with the mind proceeding in a desirable manner. "Repulsive" means disagreeable, undesirable.
"Perception of elements" means the perception that "these are elements. "Brings to bear" means he applies or directs [the mind].

"Toward an undesirable object" means toward an undesirable object consisting of a sentient being. Or, "he pervades with loving-kindness" means while bringing forth loving-kindness, which is the wish for their welfare.

It pervades that [object] everywhere. "Or he applies it by way of elements" means either by reflecting on the specific nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*) he applies it by way of elements, or he causes the attention directed toward the elements (*dhātumanasikāra*) to occur there through reflection.

Regarding beings who are not repulsive, such as relatives and friends, by reflecting on their true nature as phenomena—which, through the perception of impermanence (*aniccasaññā*), are of a different nature [from oneself]—[he contemplates] "hair and so forth..."
He pervades the perception of foulness and exercises attention to foulness, thinking, "This is merely a heap of impurities.

Regarding "equanimity with respect to the sixfold [sense] base": it is called "equanimity with respect to the sixfold base" because it occurs at the six doors with the characteristic of not abandoning its naturally pure state amidst the presentation of the six desirable and undesirable objects; it is equanimity as the middle state (*tatramajjhattupekkhā*).
"That teaching" refers to that mode of teaching and method of instruction regarding the two types of supernormal powers (*iddhividha*).

"Entirely" means completely, without remainder, and in its fullness; he knows it with preeminent knowledge. For one who knows it entirely through higher knowledge (*abhijānato*), there is nothing further beyond that to be known through higher knowledge.
"From this" means from what has been known by the Blessed One. No other phenomenon exists in the sense of ultimate reality (*paramattha*) [that remains unknown].

Or, by way of designation, there is no such person who could say, "The Blessed One does not know this," nor is such a thing found, because you have all correctly understood everything through direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).

Regarding the two types of supernormal power—the act of knowing and the teaching—there is none superior to the Blessed One. In the phrase "by this too," the word "too" (*pi*) does not merely serve to aggregate the meaning already stated.

Furthermore, the meaning of the collective sense of what has not yet been stated should also be understood. For even by the passage beginning with "Venerable Sir," the demonstration of the Blessed One’s qualities is an elucidation of the cause for that very same faith (*pasāda*).
Otherwise, it would be merely a description of the Teacher’s qualities and so forth.

160. Previously, the qualities of the Buddha were shown by way of the statement beginning with “This, venerable sir, is unsurpassed”; this other mode, beginning with “That which, venerable sir...,” is now commenced. Therefore, he says: “By another aspect as well.
Because they have faith in the perfect enlightenment of the Buddhas, these sons of noble family who possess distinguished faith are called Bodhisattvas, or Mahābodhisattvas.

This is the intended meaning (*adhippāya*). For they, from the time of their great resolution (*mahābhinīhāra*) onwards, have been attached and clinging to Great Enlightenment through the attainment of a state of certainty, such that they cannot be led away by anyone.
Consequently, their faith (*saddhā*) toward it can never be altered;
by this very fact, it should be understood that even their karma and its fruit are shown to be incapable of being altered by faith. Therefore (*tasmā*), because...

Due to the desire for an expression of excellence (*atisayavacanecchā*) and through the proximity of other words such as "that has been attained by the Blessed One," this phrase "by a faithful son of good family" refers to a distinguished object;

therefore [it is so stated]. Because the attainment of all the qualities of a Buddha is rooted in the realization of supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*), it is said that "there are nine supramundane states.
In the compound terms such as "by one who has aroused energy" (*āraddhavīriyena*), [the meanings of] "energy" (*vīriya*), "fortitude" (*thāma*), and so forth [are intended].
These are the component words. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the term *parakkama* (exertion) is included, but not the term *dhorayha* (burden-bearer).
For the latter is not a synonym for energy (*vīriya*), but rather a designation for one who possesses energy. Indeed, a *dhorayha* is so called because he is "yoked to the burden.
Therefore, it is said: "by a Great Being capable of bearing that burden. "With energy exerted" means with unremitting energy.
"By means of *thiravīriya*" means by means of energy that has attained firmness through the application of extraordinary effort (*ussoḷhī*).
"By means of incomparable burdens" means by means of burdens not shared with others; for the Lords of the World endure what others cannot endure.

All that mass of qualities of the Buddhas, consisting of inconceivable and immeasurable varieties—namely, the perfections (*pāramitā*), the Buddha-qualities (*buddhaguṇa*), and the beings to be trained (*veneyyasatta*)—because this triad belongs to all Buddhas alike.
It is exactly the same; therefore he said, “The past and the future... [etc. ...is deficient; it does not exist.

“Devotion to the pursuit of sensual pleasure” means engaging in devotion while being attached to sensual pleasure. “Who knows that there is a ‘next world’?”—here the intention is that one holds such a view as:
“Who is within the range of the senses? This is merely an object of the senses. “Pleasurable” means desirable.
"Bringing happiness. "To a female wanderer" means to a young female ascetic wanderer (*tāpasaparibbājikā*).
"Gentle" means delicate. "Hairy" means possessing the soft hair of youth. "With her hair tied in a topknot" means having bound her hair into a topknot (*moḷi*).
"Sporting" means making herself an object of pleasure, or causing the sense faculties to move about there. "Wretched" means utterly defiled.
It is the Dhamma of foolish village-dwellers. It is called *puthujjanika* because it belongs to *puthujjanas* (ordinary worldlings).
To show how it receives the designation "belonging to *puthujjanas*," he said, "it is to be practiced by *puthujjanas*.

Alternatively, it is "ignoble" (*anariya*) because it is practiced by ignoble persons. Since the meaning of "noble" (*ariya*) is "faultless," it is therefore stated that "the ignoble is not faultless."
"Connected with what is unbeneficial" (*anatthasaṃyutta*) means connected with various and extensive misfortunes pertaining to the present life, the future life, and so forth.

"Devotion to self-mortification" (*attakilamathānuyoga*) means the practice of one's own mortification and exhaustion. "Dukkha" is that which has suffering (*dukkha*) as its characteristic; "dukkhama" is that which has suffering as its object.
Regarding "higher mental states" (*ābhicetasika*): "abhiceto" refers to an excellent, purified mind, or "adhicitta"; in that [state]...
"Born of higher consciousness" (*ābhicetasika*) means belonging to higher consciousness or dependent upon higher consciousness.

"Abidings in happiness in this very life" (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*) means abidings in happiness in the present life; "present life" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the directly perceived personal existence (*attabhāva*). The meaning is: "belonging to those who are abidings in happiness therein.
This is a designation for the fine-material-sphere (*rūpāvacara*) jhānas. For indeed, having entered those [jhānas], the meditators seated here in this very...
They experience the bliss of renunciation, which is undefiled within their own person; therefore, they are called "abidings in happiness in this very life.
They are described as "abidings in happiness in this very life" because they are accompanied by joy and because they are associated with the subtle bliss of supramundane fruition.
Together with the path, the jhāna that serves as the basis for insight (vipassanā) is described: "Cunda, there are these four indulgences in pleasure..."

By the passage beginning with "for the sake of utter disenchantment," the attainment of fruition belonging to the fourth jhāna is described as a dwelling in happiness in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra*).
The meaning is that the four fine-material-sphere jhānas are called "jhānas of dwelling in happiness in this very life.
"One who obtains at will" means one who obtains according to his desire, obtaining them by virtue of his own wish at whatever moment he so desires.
The meaning is: "one who is capable of attaining. Therefore he said, "one who obtains according to his wish.
"One who obtains without difficulty" means one who is capable of attaining because opposing states have been completely eradicated simply through ease.

"One who obtains without trouble" means one who obtains what is not difficult—that is, what is abundant—and is capable of emerging exactly according to the predetermined limit. For some indeed are merely obtainers [of the attainment].
Yet he is not able to enter it at any desired moment. Another is able to enter it in that way, but suppresses the obstructive factors only with difficulty.
Another enters it in that way and suppresses the obstructive factors without any difficulty, yet he is unable to emerge at the predetermined limit, like a waterwheel.
But the Blessed One, because he has completely severed all impediments and has rightly attained mastery,
is able to accomplish all this perfectly.
This concludes the commentary on the manner of granting the inquiry.
161. "In a ten-thousandfold world-system" means in a ten-thousandfold world-system that stands surrounding this world-system together with it.
For, taking them as one by way of being a single field of birth (*jātikhetta*), it is said, "of a single world-system.
That such a number constitutes a single field of birth should be understood through the nature of things (*dhammatā*). "By way of inclusion" means...
Some say that the birth-field (*jātikhetta*) of all Buddhas is exactly that much [in extent], and that the realization of the Dhamma (*dhammābhisamaya*) belongs only to the deities dwelling therein.

Others hold that the birth-field is the area capable of being brought under a common application through such events as the shaking of the earth and the approach of the deities of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*).

The field of authority (*āṇākhetta*) is the area where the exercise of authority proceeds by the mere power of his word. The field of knowledge (*ñāṇakhetta*) is that which has become the objective range of a Buddha’s wisdom.

"Place" (*ṭhāna*) means the field of the objective domain (*visaya-khetta*). The mention of only the six [types of] "descending" (*okkamana*) and so forth is merely illustrative, because its shaking is also obtained at times such as the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*).
The "field of command" (*āṇā-khetta*) is that which partially contracts and expands;
it is where the command prevails through the head-honored acceptance by the deities dwelling there, and that indeed belongs solely to the Buddhas.
It is by his majesty alone, not by way of intention. However, because of the statement, “As far as he might wish,” his command would indeed continue even beyond that.

As for the phrase “they do not arise,” it exists; for when the Blessed One, standing in this world-system, said, “I have no teacher, there is none equal to me,” he was speaking from the standpoint of this very sutta: “But what, friend Sāriputta, exists at present?”
When asked, "Is there another ascetic or brahmin equal to the Blessed One in perfect enlightenment? he would say, "No, venerable sir.

Then, in order to demonstrate the reason for this, the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta) presented this sutta: "It is impossible, it is out of the question, that in a single world-system there should be two Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones. Thus did the General of the Dhamma speak.
The intention is that, with the exception of this world-system which has become a Buddha-field, it is stated that there is no arising elsewhere.
"Together" (*ekato*) means simultaneously; the meaning is "at one time. But how is that time delimited?
Showing that it extends from the moment of taking rebirth-linking in his final existence until his Parinibbāna through the elements, he says: "There, at the seat of enlightenment," and so forth.
"From the time he sat down" is stated in reverse chronological order. The demarcation of the field was already established, [the thought being]:
"This is the birth-field of the Buddhas. But by whom was it demarcated? By the Bodhisatta while he was still arising [in that existence].
"From the time of his final passing away" means from the time of his final nirvana in the element of nirvana without remainder. "In the interval between these two" refers to his final existence.

Within this interval, delimited by these two events—the Bodhisatta’s taking of rebirth-linking and his final Nirvana through the elements (dhātuparinibbāna)—the commentary on the account of the disappearance of the Tipiṭaka states, "It was not prevented," and in order to show the reason for that, it says, "For three... and so forth. [This refers to] the disappearance of the practice.
Because the Dispensation has declined, the arising of another [Dispensation] finds its opportunity. "The way" (*paṭipadā*) refers to the preliminary way that brings about penetration (*paṭivedha*).
Having stated that "learning is the measure," the passage beginning with "just as" was spoken to show this matter by taking the Bodhisatta as an illustration.
It should be understood that this is given as a lowly example; for it is the stability of the Dhamma that leads to liberation.
By demonstrating this, he shows the dhamma that does not lead to liberation.
"When the matrix has disappeared" means when the matrix of the textual tradition of the training rules (sikkhāpada-pāḷi), which proceeds by way of the formula beginning "Whosoever, monks...

has disappeared. Regarding the Pātimokkha, which is reckoned as the recitation of the origins (nidāna-uddesa), and regarding the formal acts of going forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā), the Dispensation...
It endures. Just as going-forth and full ordination exist only while the Pātimokkha is maintained, so too do both of these exist only when the Pātimokkha exists;
for in the absence of both, there is an absence of the Pātimokkha. Therefore, because these two are the causes for the endurance of the Dispensation, it was said:
"When the Pātimokkha, going-forth, and full ordination endure, the Dispensation endures. Because...
Or rather, because the *pātimokkha* depends on full ordination (*upasampadā*), and full ordination depends on going forth (*pabbajjā*), and since these two— going forth and full ordination—
are established through the establishment of that [the *pātimokkha*], the Teaching (*sāsana*) endures as long as the *pātimokkha* endures.
"Declined" means that the final two types of penetration and the two types of moral discipline have been combined into one, and from that point onward, it has perished.

The meaning is that after the final penetration, the teaching of penetration is said to be destroyed; and after the final breach of the moral discipline, the teaching of practice is said to be destroyed.
This is the commentary on the disappearance of the Dispensation (*sāsana-antaradhāna*).
By this it is certainly said that "the scripture is the measure for the stability of the Dispensation";
yet, since the scripture has practice as its cause, in the absence of practice it becomes groundless, like penetration [of the Truth].

Therefore, having shown that the disappearance of practice is the specific cause for the decline of the Dispensation, he states that this decline of the Dispensation culminates in the Parinibbāna of the relics.

To demonstrate this, it was said: “There are three kinds of parinibbāna,” and so forth. It should be understood that the gathering together of the relics and so on occurs solely through the resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of the Buddhas.
“Those” refers to the rays. “Compassion” (*kāruñña*) means the compassion felt for those lamenting.
The gathering together in one place at the site of the Great Bodhi Throne of the relics that were scattered throughout Jambudīpa, other continents, and the worlds of the devas, nāgas, and brahmās;

The emission of rays, the arising of the fire element therein, and their becoming a single mass—all this should be understood as occurring solely through the power of the Teacher’s resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"Because it would not be wonderful" means that there would be the fault of a lack of wonder even when both [the Teacher and the disciple] were arising [together]. As for "those called Buddhas":
"Just as gold split down the middle is uniform, so too their teaching is of a single flavor";
thus he says, "And because there is no distinction in the teaching," by which he establishes its lack of wonder.
By the phrase "because of the absence of dispute," he shows that two [such teachings] do not arise together for the sake of avoiding dispute.
"In that regard" means in the *Milindapañha*. "A single enumeration" (*ekuddesa*) means one, uniform, undivided enumeration. The same method applies to the remaining terms as well.
"It retains only one Buddha" (*ekabuddhadhāraṇī*):

by this he shows that such is the nature of these qualities of a Buddha, that this world-system is incapable of retaining a second set of Buddha-qualities. For [these qualities] are produced by specific conditions...

The specific nature of phenomena cannot be prevented. Having stated, "One should not hold [to them]," he spoke the words beginning with "it would move" (*caleyya*) in order to clarify that very non-holding through various synonyms.
Therein, "it would move" (*caleyya*) means it would quiver; "it would shake" (*kampeyya*) means it would tremble;
"it would incline" (*nameyya*) means it would lean to one side; "it would bend down" (*oṇameyya*) means it would sink; "it would bend away" (*vinameyya*)...
It would bend here and there in various ways. "It would be scattered" means it would be dispersed like a handful of chaff by the wind.
"It would be blown away" means it would perish. "It would be destroyed" means it would become utterly shattered. And being in such a state, it would not remain anywhere;
thus he said, "it would not reach a place of stability."
Now, showing an illustration for that, he said, "Just as, O Great King," and so forth.
Therein, *samupādikā* means that which goes or proceeds equally upward; the sense is that it moves level upon the water.
*Vaṇṇena* means by its shape. *Pamāṇena* means by its height. *Kisathūlena* means by its state of being thin or thick; the sense is by its circumference (*pariṇāha*).
*Dvinnampi* means "of both" (*dvepi*) or "the bodily weight of both.
*Chādentan* means pleasing, causing a relish to arise. *Tandīkato* means rendered sluggish by that food.
*Anoṇamitadaṇḍajāto* means having become like one whose staff cannot be bent because of the inability to bend over due to eating until full. *Sakim bhutto va* means "having eaten but once."

"One might die immediately after eating even a single *vaḍḍhitaka*. [The questioner asks] with the intention that the earth can indeed stand by means of the Dhamma, but if it were to shake even once because of an excessive burden of the Dhamma, it would be destroyed. Furthermore, the Elder [says]:
"In this world, what is called a 'jewel' (*ratana*) is that which sustains a household and is esteemed by the world; yet, due to its own heavy nature, it causes the breaking of a cart."

The cause that has become an excessive burden is thus seen; and likewise, the Dhamma—sustaining its possessor with specific benefits and happiness—is esteemed by the wise as being of a weighty nature due to its profundity and immeasurability, and thus becomes an excessive burden that is the cause for the shaking of the earth.
Demonstrating this, he said, "In this case, O Great King, there were two carts," and so forth; by this very [statement], [he shows] the Tathāgata’s...
It should be understood that the cause for the shaking of the earth was described from the time of the Bodhisatta’s descent into his mother’s womb onwards.
"Of one" means from one; the meaning is: having taken a jewel from a certain cart, from that cart.
"Recited" means uttered; the meaning is spoken.
"Foremost" (agga) means foremost among all sentient beings.

"Natural disposition" (sabhāvapakati) means a natural state that is intrinsic and beyond description. "Due to the greatness of the causes" (kāraṇamahantattā) means by virtue of the magnitude of the causes;
for the Buddha-qualities are produced through the great causes known as the perfections (pāramī), which are the qualities that constitute Buddhahood.
This has been said: The earth and other such things are vast objects, and great entities such as Sakka are each unique within their own respective domains;
likewise, the Perfectly Enlightened One is also great and unique within his own domain. And what is his domain?
It is the plane of Buddhahood, or as much as there is to be known. Thus, "the Blessed One is like space, with an infinite domain, and he alone."
By saying, "It is thus," he demonstrates that there is no other Buddha in other world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*) besides the world-system mentioned as "in one world-system. His own declaration,
which was set forth with the words "In my presence," etc., because it possesses unerring meaning, produces confidence in the Teacher.
He said, "The practice of the Dhamma... the way of practice," because for one who practices correctly, it gradually leads even to the supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma).
He said, "the discourse itself," because following after a discourse, its subsequent occurrence, is "discourse-following" (vādānupāta).
This is the commentary on the marvelous and wonderful.

162. He was named Udāyī; however, because of his large body, the Elder was known as Mahā-Udāyī, on whose account the use of a border for the sitting cloth was permitted in the Vinaya. "Five colors" means five kinds, distinguished by the *khuddika* (small) and other types.
His body was so extensively pervaded by sublime matter produced by rapture that he is described as "one whose body is suffused with uninterrupted rapture"; it is for this very reason that...

In another sense, it is also said to have the characteristic of pervading. Since the word *appa-* here has the meaning of "absence," as in expressions such as *appakasirena* ("without difficulty"), he says:

"Fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*) means freedom from craving (*nittaṇhatā*). "In three ways" means by way of the modes of according with what is obtained, according to one's strength, and according to what is appropriate.
"Does not not speak" means that he certainly speaks. "For the sake of robes and so forth" refers to speech employed for the purpose of procuring robes and other requisites.
He does not speak. "According to the person to be guided" means according to the individual who is to be led. He speaks [thinking], "In this way, this person will enter into the Vinaya.
Verses such as "I am the conqueror of all, the knower of all" and discourses such as "Bhikkhus, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers" are also included.

163. *Abhikkhaṇaṃ* means frequently. Because it is free from verses (*niggāthaka*) and because it proceeds by way of questions and answers, it is called "Veyyākaraṇa" (Exposition). All the rest is easily understood.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning in the Commentary on the *Sampasādanīya Sutta*.
6. The Commentary on the *Pāsādika Sutta*:
An Account of the Death of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta.
164. Those who know the method of piercing by hitting the target of a *lakkha* without missing are called "piercers" (*vedhaññā*). Therefore, it says, "trained in the bow.
"For the purpose of learning a craft" means for the purpose of learning crafts such as archery.
It is called a "long palace" because it was built according to a medium measurement, suitable for the range of an arrow's flight.
“Of short duration” (*sampati-kālaṃ kataṃ*) means made for a brief time. “Divided” (*dvedhikajātā*) means having become divided, having developed a split.
“Split” (*dvejjhajātā*) means having reached a state of duality. “Quarreling” (*bhaṇḍanaṃ*): that by which they quarrel and revile one another is a quarrel;

it is a hostile state of mind. “That” refers to the quarrel. “Proclamation” (*paññatti*): the established rule [stating], “This bathing and so forth must not be done. “Dhamma and Vinaya” (*dhammavinayaṃ*).
The word *pāvacanaṃ* means the established doctrine (*siddhanta*). "Piercing with the arrows of their mouths" [is explained as follows]:

"Coherent" (*sahitaṃ*) refers to my own speech being coherent, well-connected, linked in its preceding and succeeding parts, consistent with the meaning, and consistent with reason. Therefore, he said, "coherent with the goal" (*atthasaṃhitaṃ*).
"Practiced" (*adhiciṇṇaṃ*) means habitually practiced. "Reversed" (*viparāvattaṃ*) means turned back by way of demonstrating contradiction; it is "reversed."
The meaning is "corrupted. Therefore he said: "Having come upon my argument, which has long been well-mastered through the passage of time, turn back from it.
The meaning is: "Go there and wander about seeking [the answer]; train yourself. If you are able, untie right now the knot of fault that I have just tied.
"Death itself" means death by way of mutual slaughter. "These of Nāṭaputta" refers to these [views].
The Nāṭaputtiyas; however, since they were his pupils, he said "among the resident disciples" (*antevāsikesu*). *Paṭivāna* is the turning back from a previous practice;
those whose nature (*rūpa*) or intrinsic character (*sabhāva*) is that [turning back] are "those of the nature of turning back" (*paṭivānarūpā*).
Therefore he said, "of the nature of turning back. *Kathana* is the explaining of the meaning. *Pavedana* is the making known by bringing forward reasons and examples. Therefore he said:
“*Duppaveditaṃ* means *duviññāpitaṃ*. It does not lead to tranquility; thus it is *anupasama-saṃvattanaṃ*.
That very thing is *anupasama-saṃvattanikaṃ*; [it refers] to that. Because it stands as a cause for being established after having been raised up, it is a *thūpaṃ* (a monument);
he says “*bhinnathūpe*,” meaning “with a broken foundation. Or alternatively, *thūpaṃ* should be understood as the state of the Dhamma’s leading out [to liberation].
It is "elevated" (*samussita*) in the sense of surpassing other states within the system of the Nigaṇṭha.
Although it was considered "unbroken" by some, it is actually broken and ruined, being entirely non-existent in every respect; thus it is "a heap that has collapsed.

That very state of deliverance (*niyyānabhāva*), which is the refuge for those desiring to be freed from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*), is absent here; therefore, it is "without a refuge" (*appaṭisaraṇo*). In that [system]...
"In a ruined stupa, without a refuge"—this is how the meaning should be understood here.
"Taking the teacher as the authority" means having become like a teacher’s closed fist, he became the standard of measure.
"In various ways" means in diverse manners. 165. "They behaved in that very same way" refers to their conduct in a former existence. "Sāmākā" refers to the *sāmāka* grain.

Having said, "By whom his preceptor [was ordained]," in order to show in detail how the Venerable Cunda had the Dhamma-treasurer as his preceptor, it was said, "It is said that at the time of the Buddha," and so forth. In this context, "at the time of the Buddha" is a statement of fact (*bhūtakathana*);
it is not a qualification. For indeed, the General of the Dhamma passed away even before the Teacher’s final *parinibbāna*.
Commentary on the Offering of the Jewel of the Dhamma:
“He gave him a co-resident” means that having made him his co-resident, he gave him [to the Buddha].
“The root of the discourse” means the cause for the Dhamma discourse to be received from the presence of the Blessed One. “He causes to arise” means...
"He raises up" means he lifts [them] out from the mire of poverty; this is the intended meaning. "They resound" means they sound perfectly.
Having performed three rounds for each single stroke, there are nine rounds by day and nine rounds by night.
He goes specifically to attend upon [the Buddha], by way of attending upon the Buddha; however, he also goes from time to time for purposes such as asking questions.

And as he went along during the day... [as before] ...he proceeded. Because it extracts the meaning of the matter desired to be known, the question itself is the "extraction of the question" (*pañhuddhāra*);
taking hold of that very thing, he proceeded due to his own great wisdom and because of his tirelessness in the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma.
[End of] the commentary on the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by one who is not a Fully Enlightened Buddha.
166. Even when that matter has been announced, he is the master; in order to show his status as master, [the Blessed One] said:
"He alone knows its beginning, middle, and end. "Evaṃ" (Thus) is an acceptance of the statement.
For the Blessed One, accepting the gift of discourse brought by the Elder Cunda, said "Evaṃ. "Evaṃ" refers to the poorly proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya.
This refers to the grasping of the activity of dwelling in a state of dualism and so forth among the disciples.
Because... [as before] ...it becomes manifest, since the meaning intended for those of lesser capacity (*neyya*) reaches a state of clarity through the method of contrast (*byatireka*).
Alternatively, because... [as before] ...it becomes manifest through the seeing of the danger (*ādīnava*) in faults and the benefit (*ānisaṃsa*) in the qualities that are their opposites.
"Because of reaching a state of dissolution. "Having stepped aside" (*vokkamma*) means having moved away. This expression is also due to the elision of repetition (*āmeḍita*);
it is as if it were said "having stepped aside, having stepped aside," by which the meaning "from time to time during that stepping aside" is obtained.
Thus he said, "not continuously," and so forth. "Practice in accordance with the Dhamma, etc. refers to the Dhamma of the sublime liberation taught by that Teacher.
“Not practicing in accordance with the Dhamma,” and so forth. By the word “and so forth” (ādi), those modes of conduct contrary to propriety mentioned in the Pāḷi are included.

Regarding the phrase “even human status,” by the particle “even” (pi), the inclusion of such factors as “the absence of analytical wisdom,” “non-adherence to faults,” and “not being dogmatic in one’s views” should be understood.
By the words “in that very way,” the various modes [of practice] are shown in their respective order.

Although it is said that [the person] has renounced [wrong practice], nevertheless, just as the manner of practicing is prescribed by delimiting it with the phrase "let him practice thus," so too is it done by the phrase "let him practice in this way"; this is stated as a demonstration of its meaning.
Because of having been incited [to it], he generates demerit through wrong practice.

167. It is called a *ñāya* (method) because by means of it one knows the Dhamma of liberation (*muttidhamma*). The practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhamma*) spoken by that Teacher is the *ñāyappaṭipanna* (one who has entered upon the method).
Since he is considered the cause for the attainment of that Dhamma of liberation, it is therefore said: "one who has entered upon the cause" (*kāraṇappaṭipanna*).
"He will bring to completion" (*nipphādessati*) means he will accomplish it; it is said that he will reach success (*siddhi*).
It exists. "Producing suffering" means that it produces suffering both now and in the future. One exerts effort because of having entered upon a wrong practice.
[This concludes] the commentary on the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Fully Enlightened One, etc.
168. "Leads out" (niyyāti) means it proceeds; or rather, the meaning is that it conduces to (saṃvattati).

170. Here, in order to show the absolute support for a disciple’s right practice, the Teacher’s state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One and the well-expounded nature of the Dhamma are praised; thus it is said, "having shown praise for the clansman who has practiced rightly.
For in this way, while this teaching had arisen as a portion dealing with defilement (saṃkilesabhāgiya), it now proceeds as a portion dealing with purification (vodānabhāgiya).

The progression [of the teaching] has been illustrated according to its connection. "With meaning unawakened" means with meaning undisclosed; the sense is that they have not been led to the ultimate meaning, which is the penetration of the fourth truth.
In the text, the word "of him" (*assa*) should be construed with the two words "disciples" (*sāvakā*) and "in the true Dhamma" (*saddhamme*), as in:
"the disciples of this Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*), in his true Dhamma. It was composed with all-inclusive phrases; of everything...
It has been brought together in one place by means of words that summarize the meaning of the teaching. Therefore he said: "The meaning is that it has not been made a comprehensive summary.

Alternatively, it is called *saṅgahapadakataṃ* because the Brahma-faring (*brahmacariya*) consists of words that are to be summarized by way of their connection between what precedes and what follows.
By contrast with that, it is "not made into a summary of words" (*na ca saṅgahapadakatam*).

The construction [of the term *sappāṭihīra*] is as follows: *paṭihāra* is the removal of lust and the other defilements, or the warding off from the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*) for those who practice according to the instruction, and the leading toward Nibbāna. By changing the vowel *ā* to *i*, that same word becomes *paṭihīra*;
*paṭihīra* itself is *pāṭihīra*. That which is "with *pāṭihīra*" is *sappāṭihīra*. Likewise, it is *sappāṭihīra* because of its being well-proclaimed (*suppavedita*).
"Made" means made with wonder-inspiring power (*sappāṭihirakata*). However, such [teaching] is connected to the escape from the round of existence (*vaṭṭa*) and has escape as its purpose;
therefore, it is called "leading out" (*niyyānika*). "From the world of the gods" means starting from the world of the gods, beginning from the classes of form-sphere deities (*rūpī-devanikāya*).
"Well-expounded" means thoroughly expounded. "As far as gods and humans" means by as many as there are among gods and humans.
Having completely pervaded both gods and humans, it is well-expounded. It is called *anutāpo* because it leads to remorse;
furthermore, because it acts as if it itself were producing remorse, it is said: "it produces remorse" (*anutāpakaro*). 172.

*Thiro* means stable in nature, unshakable by anything; the aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth belonging to those beyond training (*asekha*) are the qualities that constitute stability.
173. "Secure from the bonds" means because of being unafflicted by the bonds. "Of the True Dhamma" means of this True Dhamma; "his" means of this Teacher. 174.

Those called "lay followers practicing the holy life" (*brahmacārino*) are specifically non-returners (*anāgāmin*). Since stream-enterers (*sotāpanna*) and once-returners (*sakadāgāmin*) are also similar in this regard, it is said: "Noble disciples living the holy life. 176.
"Endowed with all causes" means endowed with as many causes as there are that constitute being "endowed."
"Endowed with causes" means possessed of, attained, approached, fulfilled, or provided with them. "This very Dhamma" refers to this very Dhamma of the Teaching (*sāsana*).
It was employed regarding matters that do not lead to liberation, in order to demonstrate his own proficiency in wisdom through a mere drop of water.
The statement beginning with "Udako sudaṃ... was spoken by the Blessed One to show how his own omniscience applies enigmatic speech to the meaning that leads to liberation;
in order to demonstrate this, he said "So kira... and so forth.
This concludes the commentary on the Dhamma to be recited and related matters.
177. *Saṅgamma samāgamma*: by way of coming together in that very place for those who are already present there, and by way of gathering from other locations through being summoned.
Therefore he said, "having come together, having gathered. *Atthena atthaṃ*:
the meaning occurring in one part of the text together with the meaning occurring here and there in other parts. *Byañjanena byañjanaṃ*: [the phrasing with the phrasing].
The same principle applies here as well. "By those who bring together" means by those who make it uniform, or by those who bring in a simile.
"Should be recited" means it should be properly sung—that is, spoken—and since that recitation is the path of oral transmission (*vācanāmagg*), he says "should be taught. 178.
"Of that which has been spoken by him" refers to both the meaning and the phrasing of what was spoken by that bhikkhu. [This concerns] the improper grasping and implanting of the meaning.
In order to show how they are, it is said: "The four foundations of mindfulness," and so forth.

It is the object that is taken as the "foundation of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhāna), not mindfulness alone that is the "foundation of mindfulness. The term "foundations of mindfulness" (satipaṭṭhānāni) is applied to that meaning;
it is not [the case that] "foundations of mindfulness" [is the term]. "More appropriate" (upapannatara) means more fitting. "More closely adhering" (allīnatarāni) means more firmly attached.
*Yā ceva* is stated with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*), or by the elision of a case ending (*vibhattilopa*). Again, *yā ceva* is a designation using the same change of gender.
*Neva ussādetabbo* means "not to be exalted," because it was spoken [in that way] having been omitted.
*Na apasādetabbo* means "not to be disparaged," for the sake of avoiding dispute. *Dhāraṇatthaṃ* means for the purpose of supporting or for the purpose of discerning.
181. "Endowed with meaning" means endowed with an unerring meaning; it stands having approached and acknowledged that "this is the meaning herein.
And one who is such is called its "awakened knower"; thus he says, "the knower of the meaning.
"Praise this bhikkhu in this way" means, according to the method already stated, [praise] that Dhamma-preacher bhikkhu in such a manner as: "Friends, we have gained much," and so forth.
“Praise him. In order to demonstrate his state of being worthy of praise, the passage beginning with “For he” was spoken.
He is called “the Buddha” because he performs the function of a Teacher regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures, and because he is perfectly established therein.
By the words “It is a gain for us,” and so forth, the Teacher, manifesting his state of being dear and venerable to the bhikkhus, [spoke] of himself...
"He established him in his proper place" is what was said.
182. Regarding the commentary on the reasons for permitting requisites and so forth:
"Even more excellent than that" refers to the previous praise bestowed upon a bhikkhu who has practiced rightly, beginning with the words "here..."

Furthermore, after the teaching had proceeded with the words, "But, Cunda, there is a Teacher who is a perfectly enlightened Buddha," and so forth, the teaching was further expanded above that with the words, "Here, Cunda, a Teacher arose in the world," and so forth.
Expanding the teaching even further and more specifically, he said, "The causes and conditions," and so on.
In this context, "causes and conditions" (*paccaya-hetu*) means the cause conducive to conditions. Those that arise...
The "taints" (*āsava*) are the taints of sensual desire and so forth that arise due to both the cause of seeking conditions and the cause of enjoying them.

Regarding those taints pertaining to the present life, [the Sutta says]: "Here, monks, a noble disciple, having abandoned wrong livelihood, makes his living by right livelihood"; and: "Here, monks, a monk, reflecting wisely on his robe..."
And by teaching right practice through such passages as, "He practices," the Blessed One is said to teach the Dhamma for the sake of warding off [obstacles].
Regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures, he says: "If anyone among you grasps the meaning or the phrasing of the Pāḷi incorrectly, he should neither be exalted nor disparaged;
rather, he should be thoroughly instructed for the purpose of attending to that very same meaning. Thus, regarding the Dhamma of the scriptures...

The Blessed One, directing the bhikkhus toward right practice while they were practicing wrongly, is said to teach the Dhamma for the sake of warding off those taints (*āsava*) pertaining to future lives that arise on account of quarreling.
"So that they do not enter" means so that those taints do not descend into the continuum of one's own mind. "For the sake of warding them off by destroying the root" means as follows:

There is a destruction of the root; thus, by way of the destruction of the root, there is abandoning. "That" refers to the robe. Just as the robe is permitted only for the purpose of this [necessity], so too are alms-food and the rest.
This is the commentary on the pursuit of pleasure and so forth.

183. *Sukhitaṃ* means that which has experienced pleasure. *Pīṇitaṃ* means nourished and well-satisfied. Since one who is in such a state possesses a stout body, it is therefore said, "he makes [the body] stout.
186. *Naṭṭhitasabhāvā* means having an unstable nature. The intention is that because their speech is unstable, their very nature is also unstable.
Therefore he said, "We have no tongue," and so forth. Granted, [it was said] "with five eyes."

It has been said; however, by way of including what was not previously mentioned, the four kinds of eyes are to be understood. For omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*) is called the "all-around eye" (*samantacakkhu*).
Or else, it is called "by one who knows" (*jānatā*) with reference to its occurrence in the mode of knowing all knowable phenomena.
It is called "by one who sees" (*passatā*) with reference to its occurrence in the mode of seeing them directly, as if they were the fruit of the palm in one's hand. This [term] is called *nema*.
"A place in the earth not entered by pillars and so forth" means "not entered into deep ground. "Well-planted" means having been dug into the earth and properly established.

"In him"—that is, in one whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*). "Not overstepping, immovable, and unshakable," because for those whose taints are destroyed, overstepping is the destruction of the bridge. "The stream-enterers and so forth"—here, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the once-returners, non-returners, and arahants are included].
Regarding those who have attained the fruit of non-returning, they are incapable [of falling back] in all nine places, just like those whose taints are destroyed.
However, as for stream-enterers and once-returners, they cannot be said to be "incapable in the third and fifth places"; rather, they are indeed incapable in the other seven places.
[End of] Commentary on the Exposition of the Questions.

187. "In the guise of a householder" means with the marks of a householder. The intention is that one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), even if he has attained Arahantship while in the guise of a householder, does not remain [in that state], because of the absence of a secluded place.
"By way of him" means by way of one who has attained Arahantship while remaining in the state of a terrestrial deity. "This question" refers to: "He is incapable of transgressing nine points."
This question arises because the other [qualities] are established as a matter of course by virtue of his renunciation or his parinibbāna, which render him incapable [of falling away].
If this is so, why is the term "bhikkhu" mentioned? He says: "Because his faults have been destroyed," and so forth. "Without limit" means without boundary;
he says "vast" to indicate that this [knowledge] is very extensive. For the vastness of knowledge should be understood from the vastness of the knowable.
By this, it is shown that even that which is called "indeterminate" (apariccheda) is, in fact, determinate for the Teacher’s knowledge.
For it has been said: "The knowable is bounded by knowledge. "Non-designation in the future" means the non-designation of knowledge regarding a future object.
Why was the word "as if" (viya) included in the phrase "having made it as if directly perceived"?
Is it not the case that all the knowledge of the Buddhas occurs by making its own object directly manifest (*paccakkha*), since they possess a single measure of cognition?
This is true; however, the term "axle" (*akkha*) refers to the sense-faculties such as the eye.

That which functions in relation to that axle is consciousness dependent on the eye and so forth, and its object is conventionally established in the world as "directly manifest" (*paccakkha*). It is with this as an illustration [that the following is said].
He said, "as if making it directly perceptible," not because the Blessed One’s knowledge functions in a manner that is not directly perceptible. For they say thus:
"The manifestation is made manifest, with an untroubled mind;..."
"Knowledge of the past and future will abide as direct perception.
By "that which is established elsewhere" is meant that which functions within another domain. "Should be brought together" means it should be explained by making things equal;
however, since explaining is called "making known," the sense expressed is "should be made known. "Such as that" means constant.
It occurs continuously. There is no such thing as "knowledge" [without a specific mode], because it is impossible for knowledge to arise without adverting (āvajjana).
Furthermore, if knowledge were to proceed in only a single mode, there could be no comprehension of an object that possesses various modes.

Even if such comprehension were possible, it would be a comprehension of the object in its unexamined form; consequently, knowledge and the knowable would be indistinguishable from one another. For indeed...
An object that has not been understood through discernment as “this is for you” is said to be merely known;
therefore, such statements as “whether walking or standing” are nothing more than talk for the foolish. Thus he said: “Just as the foolish and unskilled imagine.

“Following after mindfulness” (satānusāri) means knowledge that proceeds by way of following after mindfulness. Thus he said: “associated with the recollection of past lives” (pubbenivāsānussatisampayuttaka).

“He sent forth knowledge” means he set knowledge in motion. Because the obscuration of the knowable has been completely abandoned in every respect, the meaning is simply that unimpeded and unobstructed knowledge goes forth and proceeds.
According to the statement, “Awakening (bodhi) is called the knowledge in the four paths,” awakening is the knowledge of the four paths;
therefore, it is the reviewing knowledge that arises from having attained that [awakening].
It is said: "Knowledge born of enlightenment arises. Knowledge born of enlightenment is the knowledge of the four paths produced at the foot of the Bodhi tree;

and that indeed arises for the Tathāgata with reference to the future, directed toward the non-occurrence of that [further becoming], because through its arising there is no further existence in the future.
How does the Tathāgata possess the vision of knowledge that transcends the future?
Does he "make it known"? Since the past period is vast, there is no contradiction in the fact that his knowledge and vision extends beyond it and makes it known therein.
However, the sectarians, not knowing this matter as it truly is, merely make manifest their own ignorance by asking, "What is this?
How is this? Therefore, [the Blessed One spoke] regarding the occurrence of phenomena included within one's own continuum...
Having in mind [this], it was said: "Knowledge and vision directed toward something else," and so forth.

However, if it were being stated with reference to the other [kind of knowledge], then for such a purpose, the Blessed One would have proclaimed a knowledge and vision that transcends even the future time;
thus, [the former] is not connected with the goal. This is the meaning here, as he said: "Neither for the sake of this world nor for the sake of the next world..."
“Or dependent on [something]. However, that which brings harm to sentient beings because it is connected with what is unbeneficial—in such cases, the Tathāgata has destroyed the bridge [to it].
By the phrase “similar to the Bhārata War or the abduction of Sītā,” he demonstrates that for the most part the subject matter of that discourse is not based on fact.
“With a cause” means having a cause by way of an indicative reason (*ñāpaka-hetu*). Furthermore, that cause is established by means of an illustration (*nidassana*).
"Making that his reason" means having made it a reason by way of that [statement].

For just as a *hetu* (reason) is so called because it establishes the meaning admitted [in the proposition], so too an illustration (*nidassana*) is that which establishes [the point]. "Only at the appropriate time for those who are fit" means only at the time when those who are fit have reached [the opportunity].

This refers specifically to the application [of the teaching] for those who are to be converted (*veneyya*) and are suitable for that discourse; or else, it refers to the discourse having arrived at a point where it brings benefit.
The meaning is that he speaks at the very time [it is appropriate].
By the phrase "because of speaking thus and so" (*tathā tatheva gadanato*), he shows that this is an analysis of the term "Tathāgata" through the elision of a reduplicated word (*āmeḍita*).

And the intention of the phrase "thus and so" (*tathā tatheva*) is that it refers both to what accords with the true nature of the Dhamma and its meaning, and to what accords with the inclinations of those to be trained (*veneyya*).
“Seen” (*diṭṭha*) refers to the sense-sphere of visible form (*rūpāyatana*) because it is that which is seen.
By this, everything that has been seen, is being seen, will be seen, or might be seen when conditions coincide—all that is taken as “seen,” since no distinction of time is intended.

The same method applies to “heard” (*suta*) and the others as well. “Heard” (*suta*) refers to the sense-sphere of sound (*saddāyatana*) because it is that which is heard. “Sensed” (*muta*) [refers to the object] together with its support...
It is to be grasped by reaching and attaining it oneself through the sense-faculties such as the nose. Therefore he said, "because it is to be grasped after being reached.

"To be cognized" (viññātaṃ) means that which is to be known; however, since that which is to be known is distinct from what is seen and so forth, he said, "the sphere of phenomena such as pleasure and pain.
"Attained" (pattaṃ) means attained in whatever way, having come into one's hand or been acquired. Therefore he said, "or having sought..."
"Or without having sought it. "Sought" means that which was sought for the purpose of obtaining;
whether that [object] has been obtained or not yet obtained, in either case it is indeed "sought. Therefore he said, "whether obtained or not obtained.
By these two phrases, both types of what is obtained and both types of what is sought have been indicated; thus, in those respective ways, it was fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
It shows [this]. "Wandered over by the mind" means wandered over by the mind alone, without having brought about physical contact;
the meaning is "reflected upon. "Yellow," and so forth—the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes all the classifications of visible objects (rūpārammaṇa), such as red, white, and the rest.

"Joyful in mind" (sumano) means joyful through passion (rāga), through greed (lobha), or through faith (saddhā) and so on. "Dejected in mind" (dummano) means [dejected] through thoughts of ill-will (byāpādavitakka).
Or one is "dejected" by way of thoughts of cruelty (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*). "Neutral" (*majjhatta*) means being neutral either by way of ignorance (*aññāṇa*) or by way of knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
This same method applies everywhere. In each instance, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), there are included:

the sound of a conch and the sound of a drum; the scent of leaves and the scent of flowers; the taste of leaves and the taste of fruits; the clung-to (*upādinna*) and the not-clung-to (*anupādinna*); neutral feeling (*majjhatta-vedanā*); and wholesome kamma (*kusala-kamma*).
The inclusion of such terms as "unwholesome kamma" (akusalakamma) should be understood in this way.
"Not reached" (appatta) means not attained by knowledge; the meaning is "not known. Therefore he said: "not realized by knowledge" (ñāṇena asacchikata).

"Because it has been gone to in that very way" (tatheva gatattā) means because it has been known and fully awakened to (abhisambuddha) in that very way. By the word "gone" (gata), there is the same meaning as "awakened" (buddha).
Meaning: Grammarians state that "roots have the sense of motion (gati), yet they come to have the sense of understanding (buddhi).
Commentary on the Section on the Indeterminate (Abyākata):
Having stated, "Having spoken of the incomparable," [the text] shows that there is no one who is even equal, let alone superior.
It is said, “the unsurpassed state. Furthermore, to show that this incomparability and unsurpassedness abide having fulfilled omniscience, it is said, “omniscience.

To show that this omniscience became manifest in the world through the state of being a Wheel-Turning Monarch of the True Dhamma, it is said, “having declared his status as a King of Dhamma. Likewise, by virtue of his omniscience...
And showing how the Teacher proceeds regarding these perversions of speculative views (*diṭṭhigatavipallāsa*), he says “Now,” and so forth.
Therein, “lion’s roar” means a roar of fearlessness, a supreme roar. For this is a supreme roar, namely, the demonstration that a question which is to be set aside is indeed to be set aside.
And its state of being set aside is established in the Canon itself by the passage beginning with “For it is not...,” and so on.
He is called a *tathāgata* because he has come (*āgata*) to this state (*itthatta*) in the same manner as one must come through the accumulation of karma and defilements;
thus he is a "being" (*satta*). Indeed, he is called a "being" because he is attached (*satta*) or clinging to form and the other aggregates.
Furthermore, "this state" (*itthatta*) should be understood as the personal existence (*attabhāva*) that has been attained and is thus directly manifest.
By the phrase “it is not conducive to welfare,” he reveals that the opponent’s doctrine is a useless prattle by demonstrating its failure in both respects.
Furthermore, since it is equally devoid of benefit for both worlds, someone might suspect that it could nonetheless be “oriented toward liberation”;
therefore, to dispel that suspicion, he says, “and it is not conducive to the Dhamma. Thus he said.

“It is not based on the nine supramundane states. Even if that [teaching] does not itself lead to the turning away from existence (*vivaṭṭa*), one might still suspect that it serves as a basis for turning away;
therefore, in order to dispel that suspicion, the words “not fundamental to the holy life” (*na ādibrahmacariyaka*) and so forth were spoken. 190.
Granted, craving (*taṇhā*) too should be declared as “suffering” (*dukkha*) because its intrinsic nature is suffering; however, by virtue of being the source [of suffering], it...
"Therefore, it should be treated separately" means "setting aside craving. For this reason, he said, "It is the producer of that very suffering," and so forth.
But is not ignorance and the rest also the origin of suffering? True, they are the origin;

however, because it is the cause for the diversity of karma and because it serves as a specific condition for the arising of suffering, craving possesses the sense of "origin" to a superior degree. Therefore, it alone is described in that manner in the Suttas.
Thus it was said. Therefore he stated: “Craving has been declared as the origin of suffering. “The non-occurrence of both” means the cause for the non-occurrence of suffering and its origin.

“The full understanding of suffering,” and so forth, is a demonstration of the function of the Path; by this, it should be understood that the purpose of cultivating the Path is also shown by implication.
For the direct realization through full understanding and the others do not occur without the direct realization through cultivation.

They arise thus: The establishment of the truths, by virtue of being a practice of heedfulness and because it serves as a sign for the fame of one’s noble reputation and so forth, brings about worldly benefit in this life to a preeminent degree;

yet, as long as the state of knowledge has not reached its sharp and clear perfection, it does not lead to the attainment of the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma), but rather results in success and prosperity within various fortunate realms of existence (sampatti-bhava).
It is said that "this is dependent upon the welfare of this world and the world beyond.
"Dependent upon the ninefold supramundane dhamma" means it proceeds by depending on all nine types of supramundane dhamma, because they constitute the means for its attainment.
Since the holy life (*brahmacariya*) of the Dispensation is lived for the sake of the full awakening to the Truths and not for any other purpose, therefore this is the "definition of the Truths."
“It is called ‘the first foundation’ because it is to be taken up in the mind first.
191. Regarding the commentary on the view based on the past:
“That has indeed been explained by me”—that has indeed been explained by me in that manner; for what ought to be explained, I have not left unexplained.
By means of the completeness of his declaration that "it does not exist," he reveals the Buddha’s perfect enlightenment through the excellence of his own teaching of the Dhamma.
Therefore it is said: "roaring the lion's roar. Views that have arisen previously serve as the support for views that arise subsequently;
thus it is said: "views themselves are the resort of views. "Diṭṭhigatikā" means "those belonging to the destinations of views."
The meaning is: "the manifestation of views. "This very view is the truth" means that the view that "the self and the world are eternal" is indeed the truth—efficacious and non-perverted.
"The speech of others is vain" means that the speech of other recluses and brahmins, such as "the self and the world are not eternal," is vain, empty, and false.
"Not made by oneself" means "not self-made"; thus he said, "not self-made," the intention being that it occurs according to one's own desire.
Regarding the phrase "There indeed is," the word *kho* here functions as a particle of inquiry; the meaning is "Is there, indeed?
Thus he said, "Indeed, friend, this is said," and so forth. "Friend, that which is called by you 'the self and the world are eternal'..."
"This exists, indeed; this is not non-existent. Therefore, because it is merely a matter of words, I do not approve of those who say of him, "Only this is true;
everything else is false. In this way, both the meaning and the construction of the passage should be understood.
Furthermore, whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated in the *Brahmajāla-ṭīkā*.

"By way of the description of views" means: by way of describing a view—namely, "thus has this view arisen"—in accordance with reality through its origin, its passing away, its gratification, its danger, and the escape from it.

By means of equal knowledge that functions without perversion, I do not see anything at all as equal to it. "Supreme description" means the description of those phenomena that are to be directly known.
Not knowing this, outsiders cling to mere conceptual designations of views; and not knowing them as mere designations, they obstinately grasp at them and speak of them with dogmatic adherence.
And herein, that which is called "conceptual designation of views" is the manifestation of how views are grasped by those who hold to views;
and regarding that, there is no one whatsoever superior to the Blessed One.
Some say: "This matter—that there is no one equal to him—is indeed already clarified in the *Brahmajāla Sutta*.

However, when it is stated as 'the supreme designation' (*adhipaññatti*), it is to be understood that its cultivation serves as a cause for world-weariness (*nibbidā*). It is by virtue of this [supreme designation] that the Blessed One, proclaiming his unsurpassed state, let out the lion’s roar:
'I do not see anyone who is my equal. In the *Aṭṭhakathā*, however...

Regarding what was said, “‘By way of designation’ and ‘by way of higher designation’—these two are one in meaning,” and regarding what was further stated, “But here, in the phrase ‘by way of designation,’ both designation and higher designation are intended;
and in the phrase ‘by way of higher designation,’ both are likewise intended,” it is understood that the Blessed One uttered this lion’s roar by way of both. Both.

The statement that "the *peta* is identical in meaning" is said with reference to the commonality of their status as designations (*paññatti*), not because of an absence of difference. Therefore, he says, "For, from the point of view of difference," and so forth.
"Designation of the aggregates" (*khandha-paññatti*) refers to the making known, the showing, the manifesting, the establishing, and the setting down of the aggregates as "aggregates.
For in passages where it is said, "He explains, he shows, he makes known, he establishes," the term used is "making known" (*paññāpanā*).
"Designation" (paññatti) means seeing, revealing, or making known; in passages such as "the bed and chair are well-designated," it means placing or setting down.
Here, both meanings are applicable.
Commentary on the Abandoning of Reliance on Views.

196. "For the purpose of abandoning" means for the purpose of ultimate relinquishment. Because by that abandonment all bases of views are correctly transcended and surpassed, he said, "It is a synonym for 'for the sake of transcending.
Not only were the foundations of mindfulness mentioned, but they were also established within the mental continuum of those to be trained.
Having stated "taught" (*desitā*) in order to show this, he said "laid down" (*paññattā*) because it was so spoken; thus he says: "Taught means told; laid down means established.
Now, in order to show that the teaching on the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) brings about the absolute abandonment of the bases for views, he said:
"By the development of the foundations of mindfulness," and so forth. Therein, by the phrase "by the development of the foundations of mindfulness":

He shows that their abandonment occurs precisely through their cultivation (*bhāvanā*), whereas the teaching is stated as such because it serves as a necessary support (*upanissaya*) for that cultivation. All else is easily understood.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) on the commentary to the *Pāsādika-sutta*.
7. Commentary on the *Lakkhaṇa Sutta*:
Explanation of the Thirty-two Marks of a Great Man 199.

One who is great because of the greatness of his qualities, such as his initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), is a "Great Man" (*mahāpurisa*). He is characterized by these [marks]; thus they are called "marks" (*lakkhaṇa*).
The marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇāni*). They manifest and reveal that Great Man; thus they are called the "manifestations of a Great Man" (*mahāpurisabyañjanāni*).
A Great Man is inferred or measured by means of these; thus they are called the "signs of a Great Man" (*mahāpurisanimittāni*).
Therefore he said: "This... [etc. ...the causes. 200. "They bear" means they bear the recitation of the marks; by that, they know the marks according to their actual form, not...
But he shows it by way of its origin. Therefore he says, “And yet not,” and so forth;
by this he shows that this exposition of the causes of the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa) is unique and not shared by others. When he asks, “Why does he say this?
he is asking for the reason for the origin of the sutta as previously stated. The Teacher, having replied, “Because it is appropriate to the occasion (aṭṭhuppatti),” [proceeds] with that very same...
In order to show the origin of the discourse in detail, he said, "But that... and so forth. "Sabbapāliphulla" means blossomed with flowers on every side.
For the very blooming of a flower is its completion. "Like the Pāricchattaka [tree]"—they say this having merely accepted what was obtained by oral tradition.
"Uppajjati" means it is obtained; the sense is that it is produced.
"By which karma" means by which wholesome karma (*kusala-kamma*). "Which is produced" refers to whichever characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*) is produced.

"For the purpose of showing" means for the purpose of showing each respective wholesome karma in terms of its essential nature, its function, its specific mode of occurrence, its conditions, and its specific fruit;
it is precisely for this reason that the cause for not enumerating the characteristics taught in their sequential order is clarified.
The cause has been illuminated because this [explanation] proceeds by way of showing the cause for characteristics that share a common cause all together.
"Evamāha" means he spoke in this manner, by way of these various expressions beginning with, "Even the non-Buddhist seers maintain [this].
This concludes the commentary on the characteristic of the well-placed soles of the feet.
201. Regarding the phrase “purimaṃ jātinti,” they say that this is the accusative case used in the sense of the locative, meaning “in a previous birth.

Alternatively, because of the statement “standing in the continuity of the aggregates (khandha-santāna) inhabited previously,” it is the accusative case used in the sense of continuous connection (accantasamyoga).
For wherever in a birth the Great Being begins to perform meritorious deeds, from the moment he begins—
In that regard, he is exclusively devoted to meritorious deeds. Therefore, he said, "firmly resolved," and so forth. The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well.

The aggregates (*khandhā*) that have been inhabited are called "birth" (*jāti*), because there is no birth apart from the aggregates, and because the characteristic of arising—which is a transformation—is not applicable here [to a separate entity].
"By way of being born" means by way of the process of being born. By the word "thus" (*tathā*), [he refers back to] "previously..."

He connects this phrase with “those who have dwelt [in the aggregates]. “By way of existence” means by way of being produced through conditions. “By way of having dwelt” means by way of the state of having resided.

“In the sense of a dwelling place” means by way of the state of being inhabited; for the meaning of *niketa* (abode) is the meaning of residence (*nivāsa*). “Therein” refers to the world of the devas and so forth.
By the word “and so forth,” he includes certain realms of animal birth. It is not easy.

Because the heavenly realm is exclusively happy, while the miserable realms are exclusively painful, and because of the abundance of suffering, an opportunity for the performance of meritorious deeds is not easily obtained due to the rarity of the convergence of requisite conditions;
furthermore, when such merit does arise, it is neither sublime nor extensive.
Therefore, one must acknowledge the distinction of the field according to the destination of rebirth, as in the case of "giving to an animal."

For it is said: "Having given to one who observes the precepts, a hundredfold reward for the gift may be expected; having given to an immoral worldling, a thousandfold reward for the gift may be expected.

Furthermore, because there is an abundance of happiness in the human realm, the opportunity for performing meritorious deeds is easily found, and for the most part, the convergence of necessary conditions is readily available. As for the suffering that exists therein—
That which arises also specifically serves as a decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the performance of merit; thus, "faith has suffering as its proximate cause.
For instance, when a sword is being fashioned with a hammer, its constant heating in fire or its moistening with water is not a specific condition for its capacity to perform the act of cutting;
rather, it is the moistening with water *after* having been heated, through their combined application, that is so.

That is its specific condition. Likewise, for the continuity of a being, the state of possessing exclusively suffering, the abundance of suffering, the state of possessing exclusive happiness, and the abundance of happiness are not specific conditions for the capacity to perform meritorious deeds;
rather, when there is the common application toward the scorching of suffering and the cultivation of subtlety, meritorious action finds its supporting condition.
Because of its capacity, it is possible; being so, the meritorious deed arising thereby possesses great radiance, great expansion, and is capable of cutting through opposing factors.
Therefore, the human state is a specific condition for the performance of meritorious deeds.
Hence it was said: "In that regard, it is not easy [for all]; it is easy only for one who has become a human being."
Now, what is the meaning of the word *manussabhūtassa* (“of one who has become human”) here? Because of the abundance of mind (*manassa ussannatāya*), they are called “humans” (*manussā*).

The meaning is that their minds have been accumulated through qualities such as courage, mindfulness, and fitness for the holy life (*brahmacariya*), and thus their mental states possess exalted virtues. Who, then, are they? They are the specific class of beings dwelling in Jambudīpa. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Bhikkhus, by three grounds do the humans of Jambudīpa surpass the humans of Uttarakuru and the gods of the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. By which three? They are courageous, they are mindful, and there is the living of the holy life here.”
"For indeed, Buddhas, Blessed Ones, Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, Great Disciples, Wheel-turning Monarchs, and other beings of great power arise right there.

Because they possess similar forms and so forth, people dwelling on the other great continents were likewise recognized simply as 'human beings,' along with those dwelling on the small islands," say some. Others, however, [say...]
They say: "Because of the abundance of a mind accompanied by greed and so forth, as well as by non-greed and so forth, there are humans.
For among those beings who belong to the human species, greed and the like, as well as non-greed and the like, are particularly abundant.

Through the abundance of greed and the like, they fulfill the path to the states of loss; through the abundance of non-greed and the like, they fulfill the path to the happy destinies and the path leading to Nibbāna. Therefore..."

"Because of the abundance of a mind accompanied by greed and so forth, as well as non-greed and so forth, those distinguished beings who dwell on the four continents are called 'human' (manussa) along with those who dwell on the small island.
However, the worldlings say, "They are humans because they are the descendants of Manu.
Manu is the name for the being of the first eon, the originator of worldly conventions, who ordained what is beneficial and harmful for sentient beings.

By virtue of directing beings toward what is to be done and what is not to be done, he occupies the position of a father; he who is called "Mahāsammata" in the Dispensation—our own Great Bodhisatta—is so designated.

Beings who abide by his direct and indirect instructions and admonitions are called "human beings" (*manussa*) and "descendants of Manu" (*mānusa*) because they are like his children. For that very reason, they are also called "Mānavas" and "Manujas."
And they are so designated. "Of one who has become human" means having been born among humans, or having attained the human state;

this method is stated with reference to the common worldling. However, in the case of the Great Bodhisattvas, because their mental continuity has been properly conditioned through the practice of wholesome states starting from the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*), for them—

In order to show that wholesome kamma is indeed weightier for those reborn in a happy destination (sugati) as well as for those reborn in a miserable destination (duggati) arising from themselves, it was said:
“Or rather, this is not the reason,” and so forth.
“In such a body” means in a body such as that of an elephant and so on. Kamma performed while remaining [in such a state] cannot be easily illustrated.

Because it is not well-known in the world. It is easy to illustrate by saying, "In such a country, in such a city, a king named so-and-so, having been a brahmin, performed this wholesome deed," because it is thus easily understood.
"Firm grasping" means one who grasps without laxity, one whose grasp has reached strength. "Unwavering grasping" means one who grasps without fluctuation; therein, by nothing whatsoever...
"Unshakeable. "It recoils" means it contracts, or it turns away through a sense of loathing.
"It spreads out" means it becomes extensive and reaches fullness.
"This of yours is like the great ocean": this flood of water is indeed like the great ocean.
“Giving” (*dāna*) is that by which one gives; it is the volition of relinquishment (*pariccāga-cetanā*).
“By way of giving” means giving by way of relinquishing the object to be given after having made it ready.

“By way of sharing” means sharing—that is, the act of distributing that very same thing with others—and the volition proceeding in such a manner. “In the undertaking of virtue” means [the undertaking] of virtue in a proper manner...
The meaning is that it occurs in taking up or grasping. Showing that by way of the time of its occurrence, he says, "at the time of filling.
One who is beneficial to a mother is *matteyyo*; however, he says "motherly duty" (*matteyyatā*) to refer to that quality of Dhamma by virtue of which one is called "motherly.
The same method applies to "fatherly duty" (*petteyyatā*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in this or that [instance]":
"Among others who are distinguished from one another, those which are described as wholesome by virtue of their wholesomeness are called 'wholesome'"; thus he says "in such cases.
"In superior wholesome states" means in those wholesome states that are more distinguished; however, that state of being more distinguished occurs in relation to each preceding stage.
To show that it is the most excellent wholesome state among these which is intended here according to the principle of reaching the peak, [he says]:

It is said: “There are wholesome states, there are exceedingly wholesome states,” and so forth.
