One might ask: “Are not the wholesome states that constitute the equipment of knowledge included within the perfection of wisdom (paññāpāramī) called ‘wholesome’ in the primary sense because they are conditions for the attainment of omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa)?

Why then are these [other] states, which consist of the equipment of merit (puññasambhāra) and produce the marks of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa), described in that same way? [The answer is: Because they belong to the mental continuum of all Great Bodhisattvas...
This is because the perfections (*pāramī*) serve as the conditions for the attainment of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).

Indeed, from the time of the Great Resolve (*mahābhinīhāra*) onwards, whatever merit the Great Being performs, he dedicates it all solely for the realization of Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).

Thus, there are four types of practice: practice with its requisites (*sasambhārābyāsa*), practice over a long period of time (*dīghakālābyāsa*), uninterrupted practice (*nirantarābyāsa*), and careful practice (*sakkaccābyāsa*).
Through repeated practice, connected with the fulfillment of the four foundations, they gradually culminate in the state of great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
By the word "even once" (*sakimpi*), the particle *pi* includes even that which has been performed many times but is interspersed with dissimilar actions.

"By frequent performance" means by way of cultivation (*bahulīkāra*). "Accumulated" (*upacita*) means increased further and further. "Massed together" (*piṇḍīkata*) means made into a heap. "Heaped up" (*rāsīkata*) means...

It is made by way of being a mass (*rāsi*). For wholesome kamma, when it occurs many times and has thus acquired a state of cultivation within the continuum, becomes as if consolidated and as if formed into a mass.

Because it acts collectively with respect to its result, the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*) would become too narrow and the peak of existence (*bhavagga*) too low, if that matter were to exist—this is the intended meaning. "By way of vastness" means:

Because of its greatness. Furthermore, because that kamma—being embraced by loving-kindness, compassion, mindfulness, and clear comprehension—is raised up far beyond [ordinary deeds] and is a phenomenon that establishes a measure, it deserves to be called "immeasurable" (*appamāṇa*) due to its being devoid of measure; therefore, it is said, "because of its immeasurability.
It "overcomes" means it stands having surpassed [other states] through the loftiness of its fruit. In terms of meaning, [it refers to] the most excellent among the excellent.
Thinking that this is merely the acquisition of enjoyments, he said, "He receives an excess.

"Attains" means he finds; the meaning is that even as he is being born, he is already endowed with it. Because they touch not by a single part, but by all parts, since they touch with every portion, it is said, "with soles of feet touching in their entirety" (*sabbāvantehi pādatalehī*). Just as when [the foot] is placed down...

All the areas of the soles of the feet act together because they are level and even due to their lack of depression; the same applies to the lifting [of the feet]. Thus it is said: "He touches evenly;

he lifts evenly. Now, in order to demonstrate the majesty of this mark of a Great Man by way of explaining the natural result (nissandaphala) obtained through its attainment, the passage beginning with "Even if... was stated.
In this context, "hell" (*naraka*) refers to a pit; he enters it because of his attainment of evenness.

Regarding the phrase "the place where one should stand with the mark of the wheel," this is said because the mark of the wheel also stands by way of contact upon that portion of ground which the sole of the foot touches.
Furthermore, its standing in such a manner is due precisely to the quality of having well-placed feet (*suppatiṭṭhitapādatā*); thus, it is [included] under the quality of having well-placed feet.
In the praise of his majesty, one should not wonder, "What is the purpose of bringing in another characteristic?

By "the splendor of virtue" (*sīlatejena*) is meant the radiance of virtue; by "the splendor of merit" (*puññatejena*) is meant the radiance of the wholesome; by "the splendor of the Dhamma" (*dhammatejena*) is meant the radiance of knowledge.
By all three terms, the qualities of the Blessed One who has become a Buddha are grasped; by the phrase "of the ten perfections," the qualities that produce Buddhahood are grasped.

202. Like the great ocean, it is a boundary because of its sovereignty over all lands. By the three phrases "without barrenness" (*akhila*), "signless" (*animitta*), and "thornless" (*akaṇṭaka*), the very absence of theft is expressed;
thus he says "free from robbers," and so forth. In the sense of harsh contact, "barrennesses" (*khila*) refers to their state of being painful contacts through friction.
In the sense of being a condition for calamity, "signs" (*nimitta*) refers to their being causes of misfortune.
By the words beginning with “entirely,” the absence of thieves who wander alone is stated;
however, by the word “without a scar” (*nirabbuda*), it is shown that the absence of thieves who wander in groups is stated—hence the phrase “in groups, in groups.
“Unobstructable” means not to be hindered by anyone, unresistible, and not to be dragged from one’s place. “Adverse” means undesirable.
"One who exists as an adversary" (*paccatthika*) refers to an enemy who does not manifest hostility in an overt manner.
"One who is hostile and unfriendly" (*paccāmitta*) refers to an enemy who manifests hostility in an overt manner.
They were unable to suppress him; on the contrary, they themselves met with ruin and calamity, and they even proclaimed their status as his disciples.

Regarding the passage beginning with “Kamma,” *kamma* refers to the accumulation of merit conducive to the [thirty-two] marks, which was performed and accumulated for the sake of attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, he said, “for more than a hundred thousand eons,” and so forth.

*Kammasarikkhaka* (the counterpart to the deed) refers to that which is appropriate for the state of being firmly established and unshakable by anyone at the time of performing that very same accumulation of merit.
The state of being a sign that indicates the characteristic known as "well-placed feet" (suppaṭṭhitapādatā) is its quality of not being obstructed by others;
this state of being a sign belongs to that very characteristic itself, which is why it is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:
"What is called 'concordant with karma'... [is] a mark of a Great Man (mahāpurisalakkhaṇa). The characteristic is the firm stability of the feet during standing and walking.

[This is] the name. The placing of the feet evenly upon the ground, the touching of the soles of the feet with all parts [of their surface], and the lifting up in exactly the same way—therefore, because his feet are well-settled with all parts even, he is called *suppatiṭṭhitapāda*;
the state of being such is called the characteristic of *suppatiṭṭhitapādatā*. It is by the very fact of touching the ground well and evenly that...
For their firm establishment therein is established as that which is called "conformity with karma" (*kamma-sarikkhaka*).
"Characteristic benefit" (*lakkhaṇānisansa*) means the source of obtaining the marks, that is to say, the beneficial fruit of the karma conducive to the marks.
As for the outflow-result (*nissanda-phala*), it has already been explained below.
203. "In the classification of action and so forth" means in the divisions designated as action, similarity to action, time-characteristic, characteristic, and benefit.
This was stated with reference to the composition of the verses; however, the intended meaning is that there is nothing new in the sense.

"The ancient elders" refers to the teachers of the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathācariyā*). "Verses of commentary" (*vaṇṇanāgāthā*) means verses of praise (*thomanāgāthā*), which take up the very same matter already stated and express it by way of praise.
Because it was set in motion. Later on, the "Elders" (therā) came together by means of committing the Canon (pāḷi) and the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā) to writing;
these were the Great Elders who, having transcribed the Three Pitakas along with their Commentaries into books, ensured that the True Dhamma would endure for a long time.

"One who grasps each single word" (ekapadiko) refers to one who takes up each individual word in such passages as "he was firm in his undertaking. "The extraction of the meaning" (atthuddhāro) refers to...
It should be understood that this is an "extraction of the meaning" (*atthuddhāra*) because it extracts [the sense] by way of verse composition for the purpose of easily grasping that meaning;
it is a demonstration of the nature of investigating that meaning by taking words as they appear in the Canon (*pāḷi*) and arranging them in verse form,
but it is not intended as a rejection of the fact that [the text] was established by the Keeper of the Dhamma Treasury (*dhammabhaṇḍāgārika*).

In order to show the great assistance that truthfulness of speech provides to wholesome states (kusaladhamma) and the extreme blameworthiness of its opposite, false speech, the author speaks immediately thereafter of the wholesome courses of action (kusalakammapatha-dhamma).
Even while doing so, he extracts truthfulness from that list and discusses it separately;
for it is more appropriate that the wholesome courses of action themselves be referred to as "wholesome states" (dhamma) when they are mentioned in close proximity to the term "truth" (sacca).
It is said: "Dhamma refers to the dhammas of the ten courses of wholesome action.

Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood according to the maxim of the ox and the calf (*gobalībadda*-nyāya). Regarding "the taming of the faculties," this means restraint of the faculties.

Since the mention of the courses of wholesome action already includes its prohibitive morality (*vāritta-sīla*), the term "restraint" (*saṃyama*) was employed specifically to indicate that the other [positive] morality (*cāritta-sīla*) is also included; thus, "restrains" refers to the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃyama*).
It has been said. That by virtue of which a person is called "pure" is that purity (*soceyya*), namely, good conduct of body and so forth.
Although this was already stated for the purpose of showing this very classification, it is stated again;

or else, the mention of "purity" is for the purpose of including even the higher human states such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) by means of the term "purity of mind. It is "become a dwelling-place" (*ālayabhūta*).
It is that which serves as the foundation for serenity (samatha) and insight (vipassanā). Regarding the "Uposatha rite":
it is the meritorious deed to be undertaken and practiced by undertaking the vows on the Uposatha day; here, "Uposatha" is used according to the principle of association.

Some say, "For non-violence" means "for the non-harming of beings," but that is already included by the mention of virtue (sīla). Therefore, "for non-violence" means "for compassion" (karuṇā). By the very inclusion of non-violence...

And here, by way of the common characteristic of the "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*), all four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*) are included in their access stage (*upacārāvatthā*) according to the method of "taking the characteristic" (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*).

"Entirely" means without remainder, completely full. Thus, because the characteristic is comprised within a state of existence belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), only those wholesome sense-sphere phenomena conducive to that [characteristic]—consisting of bodily good conduct and so forth, which form the equipment of merit (*puññasambhāra*) through the inclusion of the perfections (*pāramitā*)—[are intended].
They are indeed divided twelvefold; in this verse, they are shown by way of a tenfold grouping beginning with "truth" (*sacce*). This same method applies to the remaining characteristics as well.

The word *aṃnubhī* is stated with the nasalized vowel *aṃ* for the sake of metrical ease (*gāthāsukhatthaṃ*). Those who explain the syllables (*byañjana*) or the characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) are called *veyañjanikā*.
"That which is to be suppressed" means that which is to be warded off by him—that is, by the Great Man (*mahāpurisa*).
Or [it refers] to that mark of a Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa*). And here, by way of the term "mark," the equipment of merit conducive to that [mark] is meant.
Commentary on the Mark of the Wheel on the Soles of the Feet (204):
"Fear" means terror; it is twofold, occurring in the mode of being startled and in the mode of being terrified.
He said: "The fear of agitation and the fear of terror. To show these two fears by way of analysis, the passage beginning with "Therein" was stated.

"Dispelled" means that just as thieves and the like do not commit plundering, binding, and so forth against another, and what has been done is restored to its original state through restitution and the like;
and just as fierce elephants and the like are avoided from afar.
They are "removed" in such a way that, when they remain in their respective places without being avoided, there is no overcoming [of them].
"He carries beyond" means he transcends. "That place" refers to that place fraught with danger (*sāsaṅka-ṭṭhāna*).

"Of those unable" is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative; the meaning is "unable. Alternatively, "of those unable" is a genitive used in the sense of disregard. "Together with his retinue."

"With its retinue" (*saparivāraṃ*). In this context, when one gives some object of charity and, as part of that retinue, gives other objects of charity as well, then that merit consisting of giving (*dānamaya-puñña*) of his is said to be "with its retinue.
To demonstrate this matter in detail, it was said: "In this regard, food," and so forth. In that passage, just as with the object of charity...
Showing that the retinue of that gift of food and likewise its careful preparation were accompanied by joy, he spoke the passage beginning with “Then...
The construction is: “Having given rice porridge, she gave [the other items]. This same method applies to what follows as well.

“She wound the thread for the robe” means she made the sewing-thread for the robe by winding it in double strands, triple strands, and so forth. “Dye” refers to the substances for dyeing, such as *alli* and others.
"Like withered leaves" means foliage that has turned pale yellow upon the arrival of autumn.
"The lower ones" refers to the four [types of food], beginning with boiled rice. By the mention of "grass mats" (*nisada*), grass mats made of young shoots (*nisadapota*) are also included.
"Chinese flour" is Sindhu red powder. "Koja" refers to coverings such as *uddaloma* (hair with the tips upward) and *ekantaloma* (hair on one side). "With well-divided intervals" means...
"With well-distinguished intervals": by this he shows that the positions of the parts of the wheel are clearly defined.

He says, "kings who have been consecrated," because only those kṣatriyas who have received the royal consecration (*abhiṣeka*) are able to delight the brahmins and others within their own realm through the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgrahavastu*) due to their sovereign power, and not others. [The phrase] "villages, market towns, and so forth, as obtained from the king" refers to...

Those who enjoy [wealth] by virtue of their sovereignty are "enjoyers" (*bhojaka*); those who possess such enjoyment, or who are engaged therein, are "possessors of wealth" (*bhogika*), and it is they who are called "those with wealth" (*bhogiya*).
"Giving with its retinue" means giving with its retinue in the manner already described.
"May he know" refers to the mark of the wheel produced with the intention, as it were, that "may the world together with its devas know."
The similarity to the kamma has been shown by way of the characteristic itself. If that were so, there would be only a triad, not a tetrad;
therefore, the state of being an indicative sign for the wheel-characteristic due to its having a great retinue is called "similarity to kamma. For this very reason, he said:
"It was produced so that one might know it together with its retinue..."; and he will further say: "It is the sign for long life."
Likewise, it is said: "That characteristic exists as an indicator of that meaning. Furthermore, the outflow-result (nissandaphala) should be understood as the overcoming of opposites.
For this very reason, it is said in the verse: "The crusher of enemies" (sattumaddano). 205. Regarding the word "etam" (this):

this refers to the speech consisting of the composition of the verses; since that speech is in fact the verses themselves in meaning, he says: "These verses are called 'explanations of that meaning' (tadatthaparidīpanā)."

“Puratthā” means “previously,” even as it is said in the word “pure. Since the Great Man did not practice in only one past birth, nor in just a few births, but rather practiced in exactly that same way in each preceding and more remote birth, therefore, in order to show his practice therein, it is said:
“Pure puratthā” (formerly, previously). And for this present birth as well, by way of the past time, it is said: “purepuratthā.”
Since it is possible to say [something more], he said "of this [life]" and so forth, in order to provide a qualification by stating "in previous births.
Some say that this is a statement rejecting the karma performed in the Tusita heaven in a former birth;
however, that is merely their own opinion, because no such karma was performed there. "Apanūdana" means one who removes. "Adhimutta" means one who is intent or devoted.

"By meritorious karma" means by meritorious karma such as giving and so forth. "If it were thus" means: if each single characteristic were produced by merely a hundredfold amount of meritorious karma, that being the case.
"They did not approve" means that the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā did not approve of the production of the characteristics by merely a hundredfold amount of meritorious karma.
To the question, "But how did they approve? he says: "But in the case of infinite [merits]," and so forth.
"Each single deed" means each individual prior deed such as giving and so forth. "Having made each one a hundredfold" means:
however many beings there are in infinite world-systems, all those [beings] have each performed meritorious deeds such as giving a hundred times;
from among those, each single meritorious deed was made a hundredfold by the Mahāsatta—this is what is intended by the term "hundredfold. Therefore, here...
The word *sata* is a synonym for "many" (*bahubhāva*), not a term denoting a specific number, as shown in such instances as "a hundred [many] gods and humans" (*satagghi sataṃ devamanussā*).
Therefore, he said: "Therefore, they accepted this meaning: 'one who possesses a hundred marks of merit' (*satapuññalakkhaṇo*).
[End of] the commentary on the three marks beginning with long heels (*āyatapaṇhitā*).
206. *Sarasacuti* (natural death) is the natural death of a being born after having lived for as long as its lifespan.

*Antovaṅkapādatā* (inwardly curved feet) is due to the inward curvature of the soles of the feet, like that of a drawn bow-staff. *Bahivaṅkapādatā* (outwardly curved feet) is due to the outward curvature [of the soles].
*Ukkuṭikapādatā* (hunchbacked feet) is due to the concavity in the middle of the soles. *Khañjanakā* (lame) refers to those who limp on their toes.
*Aggakoṇḍā*: those with a protrusion at the tip [of the toes]. *Paṇhikoṇḍā*: those with a protrusion at the region of the heels, due to the area of the heels being raised.

*Unnatakāyā*: with an elevated body, meaning by way of not being bent down, with a well-raised physique. *Muṭṭhikatahatthā*: those with hands made into fists for the purpose of grasping weapons and the like. *Phaṇahatthakā*: those with hands whose fingers are interlocked with one another.
"This is the correspondence of action here" refers to this among the characteristics of these three.
In this context, the state of being a sign indicative of the Tathāgata’s long life consists of these three marks: long heels, long fingers, and a body straight like that of Brahmā;
their similarity to the corresponding action is to be understood here. As for the outflow-result (*nissandaphala*), however, it should be seen as freedom from obstacles and so forth.
Even fear arising from the sign of an object that ought to be feared is caused by self-attachment; [such fear] does not arise in one who has abandoned attachment.
Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of that," he says: "Just as I have fear of death, my life is dear to me.
"By well-performed" means by wholesome kamma well-done and accumulated.

"Having passed away" means having passed away from the heavenly realm. "With well-formed limbs, with beautiful arms," and so forth—these are the qualities of the parts of the body [described] by these characteristics.

These were spoken in order to show that [the factors] are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*). "For the sake of maintenance" means for the sake of the continued existence of the personal existence (*attabhāva*) over a long period of time.
Therefore he said, "for the sake of long life. "From there" means from the state of having maintained [the body] after becoming a wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*).

"Attained mastery" means having attained both mastery over the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and so forth, as well as mastery over the mind (*cetovasibhāva*); [this refers to] how, through the development of supernormal power (*iddhi*), one develops the bases of supernormal power (*iddhipāda*).
The meaning is: "He sustains [himself] for a longer time"—this is the construction. 208.
Regarding the description of the characteristic of the seven kinds of delicacies (*sattussadatā*):
"Those in which flavor has arisen are *rasitāni*, that is, those possessing great flavor (*mahārasāni*). Therefore he said, "of those endowed with flavor. "Such as flour-based snacks and so forth."
"Cakes, *sakkhali*, sweetmeats (*modaka*), and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), plantains and other such fruits are included.
"Flour-milk-porridge" (*piṭṭhapāyasa*) is milk-porridge that must be cooked after adding flour. By the word "and so forth," similar kinds of soft foods, rice-gruel, and so on, are included.

Here, "resemblance to the action" (*kammasarikkhaka*) refers to the state of being an indicative sign for the attainment of excellent food, which is a characteristic of a tree frequented by birds. Following this method, one should determine and apply the "resemblance to the action" regarding each respective characteristic.

209. "The Supreme Giver of the Finest Tastes": the Supreme One, the Lord of the World, is the giver of the finest and most excellent tastes to all beings. "Of the supreme and finest tastes" means the most excellent tastes even among those that are already excellent.
"Indicative of food such as hard and soft edibles" means it indicates the obtaining of such things as hard and soft food.
It is called "conducive to gain" because it is the fruit of karma conducive to gain.
He speaks by way of metaphorical designation (*kāraṇūpacārena*).

Or, "indicating its meaning" means it indicates the meaning consisting in his being a giver of excellent food. Regarding the phrase "he attains that," he says "he attains that" (*taṃ adhigacchatī*), explaining that here the vowel *ā* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).
In the word "supremely a gainer" (*lābhiruttama*), the letter *r* serves to facilitate the euphonic junction (*padasandhi*) of the words.

Commentary on the Characteristics of Hands, Feet, and so forth: 210. *Pabbajitaparikkhāraṃ*: the requisites of one who has gone forth, such as the bowl and robes; *gihiparikkhāraṃ*: the requisites of a householder, such as clothing, weapons, vehicles, and beds.
*Sabbanti*: all assistance. *Makkhetvā nāseti*: having stood in a state of greed (*makkhibhāva*), he destroys it by smearing it over, as if with oil. *Makkheti*: he smears.

It is as if one were to anoint [the body] with oil heated a hundred times. "By discourse that increases welfare" means by discourse that brings benefit. Here, the mention of "discourse" is merely illustrative;
bodily activity that brings benefit to others is also "beneficial conduct" (*atthacariyā*). However, in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, beneficial conduct is described solely in terms of vocal activity.
"By equality" means by establishing [others] in a similar state or an equal position; and this establishment of them in an equal position—

Making oneself like [the other], sharing the same enjoyment through happiness, and sharing the same enjoyment with that person when one’s own happiness arises or when his suffering arises—this is what is meant by the phrase “by way of having the same pleasure and pain.

And since that state of having the same pleasure and pain becomes manifest through sitting together and so forth, he said “on a single seat,” etc., to demonstrate it. For it is not possible to share enjoyment [in this sense] otherwise.
Because of his inferior birth, he is difficult to manage. If one does not act accordingly, he becomes angry because of his superior wealth; therefore, he is hard to deal with.

Indeed, due to his lowly status by birth, he does not desire to share even a single possession. And due to his lowly status in terms of wealth, he becomes angry if one does not act accordingly. "By both" means by birth and wealth.
Even one who is equal is easy to manage, precisely because of that state of equality with the other.
Because he does not expect to share in the same enjoyment [of requisites], and because there is no anger toward one who does not do so.

Even when some food is not being given, or when some act of conciliation is not being performed, he does not look upon it with an evil mind because of his virtuous nature. For that very reason, even the sharing of use...
[as before] ...occurs. "Of such a kind" means: if he is a householder, he is equal in both respects; if he is one who has gone forth, [he is equal in the latter].
The intended meaning is "possessing virtue.
"They are well-integrated" means they are indeed thoroughly integrated due to the state of firm devotion; therefore, he said, "they do not break apart.
"The act of integration through giving and so forth" refers to wholesome action that proceeds by way of gathering others through the various modes such as giving.

211. By one who is not despised, not treated with contempt, and held in esteem. "Pamoda" means laughter; as for the phrase "not by lack of joy," here that very [joy] is expressed by means of a double negation.
And because its nature is one of elation (*odagya*), it is not "depressed" (*dīna*); and because it is associated with the Dhamma, it is not "concealed" (*gabbhita*).
Thus he says: "The meaning is 'not by one who is depressed, nor by one who is concealed. The construction is: "by the quality of not excluding sentient beings."
“Atiruciraṃ” means exceedingly beautiful; he says “supāsādikaṃ” because it brings confidence to those who behold it.
“Suṭṭhu chekaṃ” means extremely beautiful. “Vidhātabbo” means capable of being arranged or displayed.
“Piyavādī” means one who speaks kindly, just as in the term “sabbavidū. “Sukhameva sukhataṃ” means happiness itself, that state of happiness. And the Dhamma...
"And in accordance with the Dhamma" means both the supramundane Dhamma and the preliminary practices (pubbabhāga-dhamma) that are suitable for it.
Regarding the description of the characteristics such as the upturned feet and so forth:
by the phrase "conducive to welfare," discourse on the Dhamma based on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) is indicated; therefore, he says, "based on the welfare of this world and the next world."

“Connected with the Dhamma” (dhammūpasaṃhita) means dependent on turning away from the round of existence (vivaṭṭa-nissita); therefore, the ten courses of wholesome kamma should be understood as having turning away as their support.

“He demonstrated” (nidaṃsesi) means he showed them; he made those states manifest by bringing them before his very eyes. “A discourse that demonstrates” (nidaṃsanakathā) is a discourse that makes things clear.
It is “foremost” (agga) in the sense of being the eldest; “best” (seṭṭha) in the sense of being praiseworthy; “preeminent” (pāmokkha) in the sense of being at the head.

In the sense of being supreme through striving (*padhāna*), it is "excellent" (*uttama*); because it is to be chosen in various ways by those seeking welfare and happiness, and because it is most delightful (*pavaroti*), it is "pre-eminent" (*pavara*).

Thus, although words such as "foremost" (*agga*) and so forth express distinct nuances of meaning, he said they are "all synonyms" because there is no difference in their essential meaning (*bhāvattha*).
They are "leading upwards" (*uddhaṅgamanīyā*) because they cause those who hear them to proceed higher and higher toward distinction. Having reckoned (*saṅkhāya*)...
Because his heels are established even below [the level of] the back of the feet, he is "one whose heels are below" (*adhosaṅkhapāda*).
"Heel" (*saṅkha*) is a name for the ankles. 213. "The sacrifice of the gift of Dhamma" (*dhammadānayañña*) means the sacrifice known as the gift of Dhamma.

"Well-established" means perfectly established. The meaning is that they remain hidden and unperceivable in the region of the shank, four finger-breadths above the back of the foot, according to the natural measure of a finger.
214. Commentary on the *eṇijaṅgha* (antelope-shank) mark:
"Craft" (*sippa*) is that which serves as the cause of livelihood for beings and is given the name "craft" in the sense of being something to be learned.

The way of livelihood (*ājīvavidhi*). It should be understood as "knowledge" (*vijjā*) in the sense of being something to be known for the sake of one's livelihood and for the sake of benefiting sentient beings; thus it refers to the sciences of spells (*manta*), medicine, and so forth.
They "move" (*caranti*) by means of it toward a happy destination (*sugati*) and proceed to happiness; thus it is called "conduct" (*caraṇa*).

The knowledge that one is the owner of one’s own karma (*kammassakatāñāṇa*) is referred to as "karma" (*kamma*) through the elision of the latter part of the compound; hence he says: "Karma is the wisdom that knows one is the owner of one’s own karma. "And those very [things]" refers to the elephants and so forth mentioned previously.
And so forth. "The seven treasures" refers to the seven treasures beginning with pearls.
By the word *ca* (and), there is the inclusion of such things as clothing and bedding that serve as the king's personal requisites. "Worthy of the king" means suitable for the king’s enjoyment.
"Of all" is a collective reference to everything mentioned previously, starting with "worthy of a king. These are called the assemblies of the Buddhas.

It is said that "the four assemblies constitute the divisions of recluses" because they are those who have stilled evil both partially and completely, and who have practiced for the sake of suchness (*tathattha*).
"Teaching crafts and so forth" means the instruction in crafts; for even in the Canon, under the heading of "teaching" (*vācana*), instruction is intended.
It has been shown. "Squatting posture" (*ukkuṭikāsanam*) means sitting in a squatting position while performing various services.
"Messenger on foot" (*jaṅghapesanikā*) refers to being sent from house to house or village to village, exhausting one's legs for the sake of a specific purpose.
It is as if it were written and then dropped, because its nature is incomplete. "Coiled upward in succession" means starting from the region of the ankles up to...
Because the accumulation of flesh has gradually increased all around from the region of the knees, [the calves] have risen up in succession and are well-rounded.
"The mark of the eni-deer shanks" means the mark of shanks resembling those of the eni deer merely by way of their configuration.
Regarding the phrase "yatupaghātāya," the letter *ta* here serves as a sandhi-conjunction; it is stated thus by means of the elision of the nasal vowel (*anunāsika*).
“Yaṃ,” and so forth. Because it was stated that “the body hair points upward and the skin is delicate,” the challenger asked, “But can one characteristic be produced by another deed?

The Teacher replied, “It is not produced. When the challenger then asked, “If that is so, why is another characteristic mentioned here?”—anticipating this very objection—the Teacher said: “Yaṃ... (That which... [and so on].

"But it arises... [and so on]... "it is stated here," he said. In that context, "but what arises" refers to whatever characteristic is produced by the karma that brings about the characteristic currently being described. "That is a secondary mark" means that such a characteristic is called a characteristic concordant with the characteristic currently being described.
Therefore, for that reason, in this discourse on the characteristic of the shanks like those of an antelope (*eṇijaṅghalakkhaṇa*)—
“With hair standing upright and delicate skin” is stated as another mark.
216. [The commentary on the mark of] delicate skin:
One is a *samaṇa* (ascetic) by virtue of having stilled evil, not merely by the act of going forth. One is a *brāhmaṇa* (brahmin) by virtue of having banished evil, not merely by birth.
Because he grasps great matters, his wisdom is great; thus he is "one of great wisdom" (*mahāpañño*).
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well, which is why it is said: "The meaning is 'endowed with great wisdom and so forth.
As for "diversity" (*nānatta*): this is the diversity, this the variety, of those qualities such as great wisdom by virtue of which the Blessed One is celebrated as "one of great wisdom" and so on.
The greatness of any particular immaterial phenomenon (arūpadhamma) is to be understood through the accomplishment of its function;
thus, demonstrating that accomplishment of its function, he said: "She is of great wisdom because she grasps the great aggregate of virtue," and so forth.
In this context, [greatness is to be understood] by way of greatness of cause, greatness of condition, greatness of support, and greatness of classification.
The greatness of the aggregate of virtue (sīlakkhandha) should be understood by way of the greatness of its task, the greatness of its fruit, and the greatness of its benefit.
In this context, the causes are non-greed and so forth. The conditions are shame, fear of wrongdoing, faith, mindfulness, energy, and so forth.

The support consists of the fixed destiny toward the enlightenment of disciples, the enlightenment of paccekabuddhas, or perfect full enlightenment, as well as the distinguished individuals who possess these destinies. The classification is as follows:

The classification consists of right conduct (*cāritta*), restraint (*vāritta*), and so forth. The function (*kicca*) is the destruction of opposing factors by means of its constituent parts (*tadaṅga*) and other methods. The benefit (*ānisansa*) is being dear and agreeable, and so on.
This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, should be understood according to the method presented in the *Visuddhimagga*, the *Ākaṅkheyya Sutta*, and other such texts.
In this same manner, the greatness of the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*) and the others should also be understood by expanding upon them as appropriate.

Furthermore, because the scope of the "right and wrong places" (*ṭhānāṭhāna*) is vast, it should be understood according to the method presented in the *Bahudhātuka Sutta*. The "abidings and attainments" (*vihārasamāpatti*) should be understood by way of the extraction of the aggregate of concentration (*samādhikkhandha*).
The "Noble Truths" (*ariyasacca*) encompass the entirety of the Dispensation; they should be understood according to the method presented in the *Saccavibhaṅga* and its commentary.
The "foundations of mindfulness" (*satipaṭṭhāna*), etc., are to be understood from the *Satipaṭṭhāna Vibhaṅga* and other such texts.

And according to the method set forth in their commentaries: because the fruits of recluseship (sāmaññaphala) bring about great welfare, great happiness, great benefit, and great security from bondage (yogakkhema);

and because they are peaceful, sublime, subtle, beyond the sphere of mere reasoning, and to be personally realized by the wise; and because the higher knowledges (abhiññā) possess a great accumulation of requisites, a great range of objects, a great function, a great majesty, and a great production.
And its greatness should be understood from the accomplishment of the greatness of Nibbāna, such as the intoxication-subduing quality.
Regarding the term *puthupaññā* (wide wisdom), the meaning here should also be understood according to the method already stated. However, this is the distinction:
knowledge proceeds toward the various aggregates, [discerning] "this is called the aggregate of form... pe... this is called the aggregate of consciousness," thus regarding the five [aggregates].
Knowledge proceeds in dependence upon the differentiation of the aggregates. Regarding those as well: "The aggregate of form is of one kind;
the aggregate of form is of eleven kinds. The aggregate of feeling is of one kind; the aggregate of feeling is of many kinds. The aggregate of perception is of one kind.
The aggregate of mental formations is of one kind. The aggregate of consciousness is of one kind."
"the aggregate of consciousness is of many kinds"—thus knowledge proceeds by way of the differentiation of each aggregate according to its divisions such as the past and so forth.
Likewise, it proceeds by way of the diversity of the sense bases (*āyatana*), thus: "This is called the eye base... [and so on] ...this is called the mental-object base.
Among these, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), while two belong to the four planes. Thus, knowledge proceeds in dependence upon the diversity of the bases.
Knowledge proceeds. Regarding "in various elements": "This is called the eye-element... [and so on]... this is called the mind-consciousness-element.
Therein, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara), and two elements belong to four planes. Thus knowledge proceeds regarding various elements;
this is stated by way of the clung-to (upādinnaka) elements, for even in the case of Paccekabuddhas and two [types of Buddhas],...
Regarding the primary disciples, knowledge proceeds with respect to such differences among the elements subject to grasping (*upādinnaka-dhātu*), yet this is only in part, not in their entirety.
However, regarding the elements not subject to grasping (*anupādinnaka-dhātu*), they know only their characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, but not their differences.
Only for the omniscient Buddhas [is there knowledge] such as: "Because of the abundance of this element of name (*nāma-dhātu*), of this tree..."
One stalk is white; this one is black, this one is smooth, this one has thick bark, this one has thin bark.
The leaf of this one is of such a kind in terms of color, shape, and so forth. The flower of this one is blue, this one is yellow, red, or white;
it is fragrant or foul-smelling. The fruit is small, large, long, round, or well-shaped.
“Badly shaped, smooth, rough, fragrant, foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, sour,
pungent, astringent; a thorn that is sharp, not sharp, straight, crooked, black, blue, or white”—
thus knowledge proceeds in dependence on the diversity of elements.
“In various dependent originations” means in the variously classified factors of dependent origination, distinguished as internal and external;
for each individual factor, such as ignorance (*avijjā*), is designated as “dependent origination. Thus it is said in the *Saṅkhāra Piṭaka*:
“Twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations. “In various voidnesses and non-apprehensions” means in various intrinsic natures that are devoid of permanence, essence, and so forth.
In modes that are empty in nature, and therefore by their very essence unapprehendable as woman, man, self, or what belongs to a self;

the letter *ma* here is used for the purpose of euphonic conjunction (*padasandhi*). "In various meanings" means in the various kinds of meanings that constitute the object of the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), such as the conditionally arisen and so forth.
"In phenomena" means in those things that constitute the object of the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), such as the conditions and so forth.
“In various kinds of phenomena”: in the various etymological explanations (*niruttī*) consisting of words that determine the meaning and nature of those very same phenomena.

“In inspired insights (*paṭibhāna*)”: in the various types of knowledge—such as the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*)—which, being objects [of cognition], receive the name “inspired insights” because they arise and present themselves in such and such ways, with the thought, “These knowledges illuminate this meaning.
This is as in the passage beginning, “In the various and manifold aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*), etc.”
The multiplicity of virtue has already been stated; as for the others, their multiplicity is self-evident because they are easily understood according to the method already explained.
However, since Nibbāna is non-differentiated and singular, its multiplicity must be understood by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Thus he said, "having transcended the states shared with worldlings," whereby its multiplicity is illustrated through such expressions as "the intoxication of pride" and so forth.
Having thus shown the greatness and diversity of wisdom by way of its objects, it is now said, "What is laughing wisdom (*hāsapaññā*)?

and so forth, in order to show its quality of laughter by way of associated states, its quality of impulsion (*javana*) by way of the mode of occurrence, and its sharpness and other qualities by way of function.
In this context, "abounding in laughter" means abounding in joy (*pīti*). The remaining terms refer to that same [joy].

Synonyms: "He fulfills virtue" means that, being joyful and exceedingly elated, he fulfills virtue in its entirety, setting aside the restraint of the faculties because that has been treated separately.

For wisdom accompanied by rapture and joy proceeds as if blooming and expanding upon the object through a sense of delight; it does not proceed in this way when accompanied by equanimity. Again, "the aggregate of virtue"...
He spoke of the noble aggregate of virtue (*ariya-sīlakkhandha*). The same method applies to the "aggregate of concentration" (*samādhikkhandha*) and so forth.

That which quickly impels all that form as impermanent—that which proceeds with great speed toward the material phenomena as "impermanent"—is like a thunderbolt released by Indra, due to the preponderance of previous volitional formations and the remoteness of opposing factors.

The meaning is that *javanapaññā* (impulsive wisdom) is so called because, without missing or failing the characteristic, it penetrates the characteristic of impermanence in the aggregate of form with speed.

The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. Having thus shown impulsive wisdom by way of insight having the characteristics as its object, the passage beginning with "form" is stated in order to show it by way of powerful insight. Therein:
"In the sense of destruction" means because of its nature of destruction, since it breaks up right where it arises.

"In the sense of fear" means because of its state of being terrifying. "In the sense of corelessness" means because of its state of being without core, due to its lack of a core of self and its lack of a core of permanence and so forth.
"Having weighed" means having weighed with the wisdom of insight (*vipassanā-paññā*), which functions as a scale. "Having scrutinized" means...
"Having scrutinized by means of that very same scrutiny; having analyzed" means having made it manifest according to its true nature and having made it directly present.

"Having made it clear" means having made it evident. "In the cessation of form" means by way of being inclined, leaning, and tending toward *nibbāna*, which is the cause for the cessation of the aggregate of form.
Now, in order to show impulsion-wisdom (*javanapaññā*) by way of insight (*vipassanā*) that has reached its culmination:
Again, "form," and so forth, was stated. Some say, "by way of insight leading to emergence.
The sharpness of knowledge is to be understood specifically through the abandonment of its opposites.

Having stated, "Sharp wisdom is that which quickly cuts off defilements," he spoke the passage beginning with "arisen sensual thought" in order to show those defilements by way of their classification.
"One of sharp wisdom becomes one of swift direct knowledge, and his practice does not waver"—thus it is said:
"The four noble paths are attained in a single sitting," and so forth.
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, conditioned, dependently arisen, and subject to destruction."
The penetration of the truths succeeds through seeing things as they truly are—namely, that all conditioned phenomena are subject to decay, fading away, and cessation—and not otherwise.
To show, by way of its cause, the nature of penetrative wisdom (*nibbedhika-paññā*), it is said: "He is full of urgency regarding all conditioned formations," and so forth.
In this context, "full of urgency" means a constant sense of spiritual agitation (*saṃvega*) toward all conditioned formations, according to the method already described.
"Abounding in trepidation" means having a mind that is frequently terrified toward all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) by way of the trepidation born of knowledge;

by this, he speaks of the contemplation of danger (*ādīnavānupassanā*). Furthermore, by the phrase "abounding in disenchantment," he speaks of the contemplation of dispassion (*nibbidānupassanā*), and by "abounding in aversion," etc., he describes its successive arising.
"Outward-facing" means having the face of knowledge directed toward *nibbāna*, which lies outside of all conditioned phenomena.
Likewise, it is one for whom the doors of liberation have proceeded. "Nibbedha" means penetration;
that which possesses this is "nibbedhikā," or alternatively, that by which one penetrates is "nibbedhikā. That very wisdom is "nibbedhika-paññā" (penetrative wisdom).
Furthermore, whatever has not been analyzed here in terms of its meaning is easily understood, both because the method has been stated below and because the sense is plain.
217. Regarding the phrase "honoring one who has gone forth": here, in order to show what kind of person one must honor so as to obtain wisdom, it is said, "a wise person who has gone forth.
Furthermore, "honoring" (upāsana) here is intended in the sense of attending upon (upaṭṭhāna), not merely by sitting near;
thus he says, "one who has attended upon" (payirupāsitā). "Welfare" (attha) means benefit. "Having made [him] internal" (abbhantaraṃ karitvā) means...
Having made it internal. Therefore he said, "conducive to welfare" (*atthayutta*). This is a neuter noun in the locative case;

the meaning is "having made it associated with benefit. Alternatively, the word *antara* is a synonym for "mind," as in such passages as "in whom there are no corruptions within" (*yassantarato na santi kopā*).
Therefore, "a different welfare" (*atthantara*) means "an inclination toward welfare" (*hitajjhāsaya*).
"By one who has gone for the sake of attainment" means by one who proceeds for the sake of attainment; the sense is "conducive to attainment.

"Skilled in both arising and the sign" means proficient in the method of arising and the method of the sign. And here, under the heading of proficiency in arising and the sign, he demonstrates skill in characteristics (*lakkhaṇa-kosalla*) itself.
Alternatively, [it refers to] the production of the remaining characteristics of the Buddhas.
The arising of wheel-turning monarchs is inferred from the signs that are the benefits they are to obtain;
the meaning is that they are skilled and proficient by way of inferring both that arising and those signs.
"Having known, he will see" means he will see having known through knowledge (ñāṇa), not through visual consciousness (cakkhuviññāṇa); this is the intended sense.
“In the instructions on what is beneficial” (*atthānusāsanīsu*) means: in the instructions concerning things that are beneficial.
Since the practice of beings toward what is beneficial is preceded by the avoidance of what is harmful, it follows that the harmful must also be delimited and understood;
thus it is said, “the knowledges that discern what is beneficial and what is harmful,” which is why it is stated that “skill regarding loss, just like skill regarding gain, is to be desired.”
218. Regarding the description of the characteristic of golden complexion:

in order to show that one is "free from anger through the power of reflection (*paṭisaṅkhānabala*) and the subduing of anger, and not through the power of meditation (*bhāvanābala*)," it was said, "not by the path of non-returning," and so forth.
Thus, being "under the control of freedom from anger" means, like the young brahmin Magha, not falling under the sway of anger.
"Because he has gone beyond. "He did not become resentful" means he did not become resentful by way of anger.
For what is intended here is that resentment which, by way of anger, becomes the condition for enmity (*upanāha*) toward an object that serves as the basis for the arising of anger;
it is not [resentment] by way of greed. Therefore he said, "Like a crooked thorn," and so forth. For that [thorn], wherever it catches, agitates that very place.

...clings in this way. "There and there" means in each respective vital spot (*mamma*). A "vital spot" (*mamma*) is a place that causes pain even at the mere touch [of a weapon]. "Arising first" means having arisen previously.
Ill-will (*byāpāda*) is stronger than that because, through the habituation of the mind, it causes the mind to become corrupted.
Hostility (*patitthiyana*) is stronger than that because, through its excessive habituation, it persists even while in the state of that ill-will.
It is more powerful because it establishes itself through the attainment of strength by way of being an adversary.

Regarding "fine bedspreads and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) should be understood as including excellent food and other such things, since even the gift of food is a cause for the perfection of complexion.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, when a donor gives food to recipients... [etc.]..."
“He gives life, he gives beauty,” and likewise he will say, “or by the gift of material goods.
219. *Ti adāsi*: “*Deva*” means a cloud, or specifically Pajjunna. “*Varatara*” means more excellent.

Because it is a state different from the condition of renunciation (*pabbajjā*), it is called “non-renunciation” (*apabbajjā*), which is the state of a householder. “*Acchādenti*” means they cover; that is, they conceal their private parts with these [garments].
Coverings and undergarments; that is, those coverings, as well as other garments such as woolen blankets (*kojava*) and the like, and the finest upper robes.
"Destruction" means the destruction of performed karma before it has ripened.
Commentary on the characteristic of the male organ being concealed by a sheath.

220. *Samānetā* means one who brings together properly, one who causes them to assemble. It can be performed by one established in royalty, because success is achieved only for one who has many attendants.
"There is no one who acts" is connected [to the previous phrase] as "concealing the fault," or alternatively, it refers to "performing the act of concealing a fault.
Is not the act of concealing a fault indeed blameworthy? True, it is blameworthy when done with a defiled mind.
Regarding "one who conceals": this refers to an action performed by way of avoiding harm arising for another through a mind that is not defiled.
By the phrase "by one providing for relatives," it is shown that this deed proceeds by way of conduct for the benefit of those known.
221. *Amittatāpanā* means having the nature of tormenting enemies; the meaning is that they are of such a character whether or not they actually torment their enemies.

For indeed, there are no such things as "enemies" for the sons of a Wheel-turning Monarch (*cakkavatti*); whoever might exist [among them], all the kṣatriyas and others become followers of them solely through the power of the wheel.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the characteristics such as being well-rounded (222):
*Samaṃ* means equal. One knows it to be equal—that is, identical—to whatever quality is recognized in the world; for that reason, therein...
One practices in the other by means of the very method of practice. "He knows for himself" means that, being independent of others, he knows by himself.
Or, "he knows the person" means that he knows each respective person as they truly are, [discerning] "this one is superior, this one is middling, this one is inferior.
"He knows the distinction between persons" means the distinction existing in each respective person.
He knows, whereby he becomes one who practices appropriately by giving gifts and performing services as befits each occasion. Therefore it is said:

"This person is worthy of this," and so forth. "In the sense of obtaining success" means in the sense of causing the attainment of successes pertaining to the present life and so on. "The act of equal gathering" means the act of gathering each individual after having understood them equally and according to their respective needs.

223. *Tulayitvā* means having weighed; *paṭivicinitvā* means having investigated. *Nipuṇā* means from skillful application; *atinipuṇā* means exceedingly skillful. That skillfulness of theirs is subtle wisdom (*saṇhasukhumā paññā*), hence he says "subtle wisdom.
224. *Khemakāmo* means one who desires safety, one who desires freedom from calamity.
Knowledge of the ownership of kamma brings about the growth of beings and provides all forms of success; therefore he says, "by wisdom, that is, by the wisdom of the ownership of kamma."
"Completely fulfilled" (*samantaparipūrāni*) means fulfilled on all sides, in every respect; for that very reason, they are "unimpaired" (*ahīnāni*) and "not deficient" (*anūnāni*).

"By wealth and so forth" means by wealth, grain, and the like. (225) "Confidence through conviction" (*okappanasaddhā*) is the faith of believing after having leaped upon and plunged into the object worthy of faith.

That same [faith], because it proceeds by way of deepening confidence even toward objects that inspire serene trust, is "confidence through serenity" (*pasādasaddhā*). "By hearing the scriptures" (*pariyattisavanena*)...
By means of hearing the *pariyatti* (the scriptures) which brings about the welfare and happiness of beings.

It is stated thus because retention, mastery, and so forth are rooted in that [hearing]. "Of these" refers to faith and the other [faculties]. "Sahānadhammo" means that which has the nature of decline (*hānadhamma*);

"asahānadhammo" means that which does not have the nature of decline; the state of being such is "asahānadhammatā," meaning the quality of having a nature that is not subject to decline. This is the sense.
Commentary on the Characteristic of Reaching the Tip of the Tongue (Rasaggasaggitālakkhaṇa) 226.

Even a meal the size of a sesame seed: "It pervades everywhere" means that as it remembers all the nutrient-carrying channels (*rasāharaṇī*), it pervades the entire body by its own nature. "Flowing evenly" means they proceed without being uneven, but straight.
"The action that produces health" means the action that brings about a state of non-disease and non-harm for sentient beings. [This refers to] taste, which is divided into sweet and so forth.
They are called *rasaggasā* because they swallow (*gasati*) or carry away (*harati*) [flavors], or because they themselves swallow, devour, and cause that [flavor] to enter within.

The "summit of those that swallow flavors" (*rasaggasaggā*) refers to the foremost among those that swallow flavors; since these exist therein, they are called *rasaggasaggī*. That itself is the characteristic.

For indeed, even when the underlying object (*vatthu*) is not distinct, a conventional expression (*vohāra*) is employed as if it were distinct for the purpose of making known the specific qualities residing therein.

For example, as in the expression “the body of a stone statue” (*silāputtakassa sarīram*). Alternatively, the characteristic known as “having the finest taste” is the characteristic of having the finest taste (*rasaggasaggilakkhaṇam*).

227. Since the word *vadha* also has the sense of “afflicting,” as in “having struck himself again and again, he weeps,” it was stated as “by killing and striking” (*māraṇavadhena*) for the purpose of distinguishing it from that; the meaning is “by striking consisting of killing. [In this context,] the sense of afflicting...
The word *vadha* (killing) has this meaning: by means of slaying and by means of oppression. *Ubbādhanāya* means by means of pressing down repeatedly after having cast [the person] into a prison.
Therefore he said: "by means of entering a prison. [This concludes] the commentary on the characteristics such as the deep-blue eyes.
228. *Visaṭanti*: having made it distorted by way of being angry. Therefore he said, “Like a crab,” and so forth.
*Visācī* means a distorted appearance; the sense is that it is crooked. Therefore he said, “With the corner of a squinting eye,” meaning by the casting of a sidelong glance.
*Viceyya pekkhitā* means looking not straight ahead, but having directed the movement of the gaze and then looked. Therefore he said:

“Whoever, having become angry,” and so forth. “The other” refers to the one who is angry. “Does not look” means that having become angry, he does not look at that person as they walk in front of him, nor when behind his back.
“Astray” (viteyya) means crookedly or sideways; the meaning is that he has transgressed the manner of looking appropriate for wise people.
Looking straight ahead, without looking askance, belongs only to one whose mind is upright and not a vessel for those evil qualities that produce crookedness.
He says, "Having become straight-minded, looking straight," because the connection is made by supplying the words, "and how he looks straight.
"Pasaṭa" means properly spread out by way of being opened wide. "Vipula" and "vitthata" are synonyms for that same state.
One whose seeing or looking is dear and to be cherished is called "piyadassano."
"Kāṇa" means one who looks with the eyes not closed. "Kākakkhi" means one with squinting eyes. "Vaṅkakkhi" means one who looks askance.
"Āvilakkhi" means one whose range of vision is turbid or confused. It is five-colored by way of the colors blue, yellow, red, white, and black.
Among these, the yellow and red colors are due to the streaks located within the white circle (the iris), while the blue, white, and black colors are due to their respective circles.
[These qualities] are to be understood. Some say: "‘Transparency’ (pasāda), however, is said with reference to the clear appearance of those colors.
But the meaning of "five-colored transparency" is that it is accompanied by the aforementioned five colors, or that the transparency is adorned by them.

"Those which produce excellence of the eyes" refers to the perfection of the eye, such as: "The state of having five-colored transparency, the capacity to see what is concealed or distant," and so forth.
The causes. "Appointed in the science of marks" means engaged in the science of marks, being highly skilled.
Regarding the description of the mark of the turbaned head (230):
"Foremost" here refers to being preeminent, the state of being the eldest and best, and being one whom the multitude should follow; thus he said, "the leader of the group," and so forth.

“Foremost-ness” (*pubbaṅgamatā*) means the action of one who is foremost. For that action of good bodily conduct and so forth by virtue of which the Great Man became a leader for the many people—that action is intended here as “foremost-ness,” not the state of being a leader itself.
Therefore he said: “In this context, ‘action’ is what is meant by ‘foremost-ness. “With head filled with rapture and gladness” means with rapture (*pīti*) and gladness (*pāmojja*).
And having a perfectly formed head, he generally wanders about possessing a mind associated with knowledge accompanied by joy.
"A Great Man" (Mahāpurisa) means one born of the nature of a Great Man.
Regarding "of many people" (bahujana), he says "of many people" (bahujanassa) because the accusative case is used here in the sense of the genitive. In the sense of "enjoying,"...

*Paṭibhoga* means an object of enjoyment; it is *paṭibhogiyā* because it is beneficial for that [enjoyment]. Sentient beings who perform services, such as providing the necessary requisites after knowing the appropriate place and time, are those who "bring forth" (*abhiharanti*), meaning they speak of [the service].
Because they counteract (*paṭiharaṇa*) various services and cause them to proceed (*pavattana-karaṇa*), they are *paṭihāra*, meaning a servant;
the state of being such a one is *paṭihāraka*. Thus he said, "the state of being a servant" (*veyyāvaccakarabhāva*).
"Visava" means one who possesses mastery (vasa); he who has such mastery over his desires is called "visavī. Thus it is said: "one who has attained mastery" (*ciṇṇavasī*). 232.
Regarding the description of the characteristics such as having a single hair to each pore:
"It proceeds in accordance" (*upavattati*) means that it functions by approaching a state of conformity. Therefore, it is said: "it follows the underlying intention" (*ajjhāsayaṃ anuvattati*).
The characteristic of single hairs: this is the characteristic of having a single hair in each individual pore. Regarding "by single hairs":
on the bodies of others, even in a single pore, many hairs arise; such is not the case for the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, by those hairs that have arisen individually in each pore, coiled, curved, and turned to the right, [the body] is covered.
It is said that his body is like [that of a lion] in the passage, "He has limbs covered with individual hairs.
234. Regarding the description of the forty minor marks and so forth:
"An assembly that cannot be divided" means an assembly that cannot be split by others through any form of persuasion, or by demonstrating logical arguments.
"By way of non-slanderous speech": the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative; it refers to wholesome action that is the opposite of slander.
One who has such slanderous speech is "a slanderer"; [the phrase refers to] that person who is a slanderer.
"Incomplete" means not complete by virtue of being deficient by forty [verses]. "Sparse" means having gaps.
Commentary on the Characteristics of the Large Tongue, etc. (236).

"One whose speech is acceptable" means one whose words are to be accepted due to being treated with respect and reverence; it refers to one whose words are to be taken as "this is so," and whose instruction is received with the head bowed in assent.
"With a bound tongue" means a tongue that is obstructed by veins and other structures such that it cannot be turned back easily. "With a hidden tongue" means...

Due to an abundance of *rasa* (tissue), the tongue resembles a hidden cheek. "Double-tongued" (*dvijivha*) means that by virtue of its power of transformation (*kappa*), the tongue becomes two-fold at the tip.
"Stammering" (*mammana*) refers to speech where the palate is not properly formed. Sound is broken and takes on a fractured form through qualities such as being harsh, rough, or grating.
Alternatively, they are "broken-voiced" (*chinnassara*) due to a voice that proceeds in interrupted fragments; or they are "fractured-voiced" (*bhinnassara*) due to its manifold forms.

Or they have a "crow-voice" because their voice is unpleasant like that of a crow. "Sweet" means desirable; it is so called because the physical basis [of the voice] is thoroughly purified by the fruit of kamma.
"Affectionate" means producing joy, or that which is to be loved. 237.
"Because it is associated with abuse" means being connected with abuse, or accompanied by the grounds for abuse. "Causing affliction" is said in the sense of causing irritation.
It brings affliction to others. It is called "crushing the multitude" because it crushes many people, or because it causes their destruction.
Alternatively, here the prefix *a-* has the sense of intensification (*vuddhi*), as in such expressions as "the qualities of one beyond training" (*asekkhā dhammā*);
therefore, the meaning should be understood here as "uttering speech that is exceedingly intense and harsh. And regarding "he did not speak," here [it means] he did not fail to speak...
The designation [of the word *vācā*] is by means of the elision of the final vowel (*saralopa*). "Well-composed" (*susaṃhita*) means well-connected. But by what is it well-composed?
Since the word "sweet" (*madhura*) was stated immediately after, it is understood to mean "by sweetness.

But what is its sweetness? He says: "well-endowed with affection" (*suṭṭhu pemasaṃhita*). As for the word *vācā*, since its object is a plurality of things used [for speaking], he says "speeches" (*vācāyo*).
And that state of having various objects of application for her [the voice] should be understood as being in grammatical apposition with the phrase "leading to the heart.

Regarding the reading "pleasing to the ear" (*kaṇṇasukhaṃ*), the words beginning with "just as" (*yathā*) were stated to show that this is a neuter designation used in the sense of the abstract noun (*bhāva*).

He said "was experienced" (*vedayittha*) to indicate that this is a description using a shift in tense (*kālavipallāsa*), meaning "let it be experienced" (*vedayatha*). "Brahmā’s voice" (*brahmassaratan*) means the excellence of the voice.
Or it is like the sweetness of the voice of Brahmā. "Of many, much" (*bahūnaṃ bahuṃ*) is to be construed as: "much well-spoken [speech] of many people. 238.
Commentary on the Lion-Jaw Characteristic: *Appadhaṃsiko* means "indestructible.

This designation is made by changing the letter *y* to *k*, just as in the expression "states that lead out" (*niyyānikā dhammā*). "From quality" (*guṇato*) means from the quality attained by oneself. "From position" (*ṭhānato*) means from the particular place in which it is situated.

"Palāpakathā" means talk that is frivolous chatter (*samphappalāpa*). "Those with sunken jaws" have jaws that are shriveled and withered on one side or both sides. "Those with crooked jaws" have jaws that are curved and distorted on one side. "Those with protruding jaws" have jaws that hang down toward the front. 239.
"Those of scattered speech" refers to those who engage in frivolous chatter; by contrast, the Great Bodhisattvas are "those of unscattered speech.
Since speech itself is called the "path" (*byāppatha*) because it is the means for attaining its intended meaning, he said: "unscattered... path of speech."
“...should be. Regarding “by twos, by twos,” this is not a reduplicated expression because the terms do not share a common grammatical referent (*asamānādhikaraṇato*);

rather, it is said “by twos, by twos” to show the doubling [of the number] by two, as in “by four. Therefore, since “those consisting of two pairs” refers to those consisting of four, he says “of four-footed [animals].
“Of such a nature” means that, according to the method already stated, it is unassailable by anyone.
By virtue of his qualities, he is of such a nature.
240. Commentary on the characteristics of even teeth and so forth:

Because of his pure morality and conduct, those persons who are completely—on all sides or in every way—pure constitute his retinue; thus, he is one "with a completely pure retinue" (*parisuddhaparivāra*).
241. "He abandoned" (*pahāsi*) means he relinquished by way of substitution (*tadaṅga-vasena*) and by way of suppression (*vikkhambhana-vasena*).
"Tāvatiṃsa" refers to those whose city or town is the triple heaven; they are the Tāvatiṃsa gods. The best among them is the lord of the triple heaven, Indra.
By that lord of the triple heaven—thus it is said, "by Sakka. It is called "lapana" because one speaks or talks with it; thus, it is the mouth.
He said: "The face-born are called 'lapanajas'. They are *sukkā* (white) because of their excellent whiteness;
they are *suci* (pure) because they are not even slightly defiled; they are *sobhanā* (beautiful) because of their beautiful shape, and because they are well-cultivated through insight (*vipassanā*).
Granted, a particular region that serves as a dwelling place for people—that is, human beings—is called a "province" (*janapada*).
Furthermore, since the entire region designated as the four great continents together with their surrounding retinues is intended in that way, it is said:
"the country delimited by the Cakkavāḷa. But is it not the case that the aforementioned region is delimited by the ocean, and not delimited by the Cakkavāḷa mountain?
That region is indeed also delimited by the Cakkavāḷa; therefore, it was stated in that manner. Or alternatively, those things dependent on the ocean are also dependent on the base of the Cakkavāḷa.
And for those beings, it serves as their respective foundation; encompassing them all, he said, "delimited by the world-sphere" (*cakkavāḷaparicchinna*).
Regarding the phrase "delimited by the world-sphere," the meaning here should be understood as "delimited by the world-sphere.
"Of him" refers to that wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*). Again, "of him" refers to that country. Regarding the term "the happiness of many people" (*bahujanasukha*): here...
He says "the many people" (*bahujana*) because the plural ending of the singular has been elided.
To show the method by which they practice for the welfare and happiness of others, it is said, "having become equal in pleasure and pain.
"Free from evil" (*vigatapāpa*) means one whose unwholesome states have been washed away through total eradication. "Affliction" (*daratha*) refers to physical and mental feverish distress.
In this context, since mental fever has already been expressed by the phrase "free from evil" (*vigatapāpo*), he says "free from bodily distress and fatigue" (*vigatakāyikadarathakilamatho*).
Lust and the other [defilements] are called "stains" (*malā*) because they cause the continuum in which they arise to become soiled.

They are called "barren wastes" (*khilā*) because of their nature as refuse. Because they specifically cause great harm to sentient beings, hatred is called "the bane" (*kalī*); thus it is said, "and of the bane of hatred."
"Panūdehi" means by those who carry away [defilements] from one's own continuum through the process of uprooting; that is to say, by those who abandon them. The rest is easily understood.

And herein, because all the characteristics have as their cause the accumulation of merit within the continuum of a Great Man, that entire meritorious deed is the cause for every characteristic, since the fruit possesses such distinguished form.
For a cause that is not distinct in form cannot serve as a condition for a result that is distinct in its intrinsic nature;

therefore, this teaching proceeds by demonstrating, in their specific distinctions, which particular meritorious deed is the specific cause for each respective characteristic. In this regard, just as such-and-such meritorious deed, consisting of bodily good conduct and so forth, [is the cause] for having well-planted feet...

The reason has been stated; however, one cannot say that the same reason applies to "having a head like a turban," because the former was stated as the cause for "well-placed feet" (suppaṭṭhitapādatā) characterized by firmness of undertaking, while the latter was stated as being characterized by precedence.
Likewise, whatever is the cause for "long heels" (āyatapaṇhitā), that same [cause] does not apply to "long fingers" (dīghaṅgulitā) or "Brahma-like straightness of body" (brahmujugattatā).
And this is because the cause possesses a distinct nature, for a cause that is not distinct in its own form cannot serve as a condition for a result that has a distinct intrinsic nature.

In this regard, just as when various faculties such as the eye arise from a single action (*kamma*), a distinction in the action must be admitted—either by way of a difference in state or a difference in capacity; for an action in one state [cannot produce results in another].
The cause of the eye is the very same as the cause of the ear and so forth, or it possesses an undifferentiated capacity;

therefore, the craving for sensual pleasure (kāmataṇhā) previously produced—which constitutes the aspiration for a personal existence consisting of the five bases—becomes a condition by way of its specific nature through the influence of conditions, acting as the means for accomplishing the capacity of karma to produce a fruit of a specific nature. Thus, even though it is one...

Just as [a seed] appears to assume various forms by virtue of its capacity to produce many kinds of fruits, so too here there is no contradiction in saying that "even a single wholesome deed performed as abstention from taking life produces all three characteristics, such as long heels and the rest. Therefore it was said: "That [deed] of his..."
"Because of having performed such karma... [as previously stated] ...he acquires these three marks of a Great Man. However, there is no need to speak of their arising through various distinct karmas;
rather, the singular designation "of that karma" (*tassa kammassa*) found in the Pāli should be understood as being used in a general sense.
And by doing so, the expression "the mark of a hundred merits" (*satapuññalakkhaṇa*) is justified.
“The same method applies to such passages as ‘He acquires these two marks of a Great Man,’ and so forth.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) for the commentary on the *Lakkhaṇa Sutta*. 8.
Commentary on the *Siṅgāla Sutta*.”
Nidāna-vaṇṇanā 242.
The connection is made by bringing forward the phrase "enclosed by a rampart.

"Furnished with gate-towers and watchtowers" means it was provided both with gate-palaces and with watchtowers established here and there upon the top of the rampart. Because it was enclosed by bamboo [fences],...
It has a blue appearance because it is densely covered with trees bearing flowers and fruits.
It is delightful due to its excellence of shade and water, as well as the excellence of its terrain.
"In the guise of a crow" means in the form of a *kalandaka* (woodpecker). "Bait" means food. "That" refers to the pleasure grove.

The phrase “kho pana” is merely a poetic ornament; therefore, the explanatory statement “at that time” (tena samayena) is appropriate. “Gahapati Mahāsāla” means one who is a householder (gahapati) and possesses great wealth (mahāsāra);
this designation is formed by changing the letter *ra* to *la*. He was a householder who had attained great prosperity through his wealth.
The passage beginning with “But his son was faithless” and so forth constitutes the introduction to the discourse (suttanikkhepa), arising from a specific occasion (aṭṭhuppattika).
This was undertaken to show the origin of the matter (*aṭṭhuppatti*). He is "without faith" (*assaddho*) due to the absence of conviction in the fruit of kamma.
He is "unconfident" (*appasanno*) due to the absence of serene confidence (*pasāda*) in the Triple Gem. "He spoke thus" means he says it in the manner now being described.

The intention is that this is the final word spoken out of a desire for his welfare, which is to be remembered for as long as life lasts. "Various directions" (*puthudisā*) means individual directions; since those are many, he says "many directions" (*bahudisā*).
243. Regarding the passage beginning with “He has not yet entered,” what is to be said has already been stated below. “Not only now” means not at this very time.

To the question “What then? he says: “Even at the time of dawn,” and so forth. “The discipline for householders” (*gihivinaya*) refers to the entire system of training for householders—that is, for those living in the home—including the conduct and the observances (*vatta*) of householders, such as “A householder should behave in this way. It is the complete [code] for the conduct and observances of householders.
Because it is stated with specific distinction in this sutta. "In that very way" means he saw exactly as it was seen by the Buddha-eye.
He stood there having taken up the practice of paying homage as something to be performed according to his duty. This concludes the commentary on the six directions and so forth.
244. Upon hearing these words, he reflected, being urged on by the power of the Buddha, by the cause of his own right aspiration, and by the force of his merit.
"It is said that those are not they" means: "It is said that those six directions—the east and so forth—which are now being honored by me, are not [the true ones].
He states that "nipātamattaṃ" (a mere particle) signifies its lack of meaning. "Pucchāpadaṃ" means a word of inquiry.
When the Blessed One was asked by the householder’s son about the six directions that should be honored, he did not explain them at the outset due to his skill in teaching;

rather, in order to first make him a fit vessel for the practice, and to provide instruction on what is to be avoided and what is to be cultivated, he began his discourse with the words, "Insofar as, householder’s son... and so forth.
In this context, "defilements that are karma" means defilements that have become karma. "They are defiled" means they remain as if soiled or stained;
the meaning is that they are tormented. "Therefore" refers to the fact that [killing] is a cause for such defilement.

Although the drinking of liquor is to be avoided by lay followers because it constitutes one of the five precepts, it is mentioned after the taking of life and so forth because it serves as a gateway to the states of misery (apāya).
It was with this intention that it was said “four,” and not “five. Others say: “Because it does not exist as a separate course of action (kammappatha). [The opponent replies:

“Even the drinking of fermented liquor (*surā*) has appeared as a separate course of action because of such statements as: ‘Bhikkhus, the drinking of fermented and distilled liquors (*surā-meraya-pāna*), when indulged in, developed, and cultivated, leads to hell,’ and so forth.
For likewise, being a deed of misconduct (*duccarita-kamma*), it acts as a drag on the back of one going to a state of misery.”
