Some say they are "fixed," according to whose opinion there would be eleven courses of action (kamma-patha).

Therefore, their inclusion within the aforementioned courses of action should be understood as being by way of being contributory factors and sharing the same nature; thus, it is well said: "Because they do not exist as separate courses of action.
As for drinking fermented liquor, because it is a gateway to the loss of wealth and a state of ruin, he spoke of it as being "four" [in its consequences].
It is called a *ṭhāna* (basis) because the fruit stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein, owing to its dependence upon that; thus he says, "by bases" means "by causes.

They fall away (*apenti*), or they go away (*apagacchanti*) from these, or they cause one to fall away (*apeti*); hence they are *apāyā*. The gates or doors to the states of loss (*apāya*) are the *apāyamukhāni*.
The same method applies here for the term *vināsamukhāni* (gates of destruction).
Although it was previously stated in general terms as “of a noble disciple,” it is specifically the one established on the first stage who conforms to the method about to be explained;
therefore, it is said, “he is that stream-enterer. The word *pāpaka* is a synonym for the inferior; thus it is said, “by those base ones.

Alternatively, they are called *pāpaka* because they cause one to reach (*pāpenti*) the suffering of the states of misery (*apāya*) and the suffering of cyclic existence (*vaṭṭa*); [therefore] “by those base ones.”
"Covering the six directions" means: since beings are seen in those various parts, they are designated as "directions";
thus, he covers and shields them so that there is no opening for himself toward them.
"For the purpose of overcoming" means for the purpose of mastering. For whoever [overcomes] the harm pertaining to the present life and the future life...
One overcomes by means of avoidance; for that very reason, one accomplishes both purposes.
Such a person is said to be practicing for victory in both worlds, because of the subduing of adversaries and the accomplishment of one’s own welfare. Therefore he said, "This world... and so forth.
The five enmities, beginning with the taking of life, are called *vera* (enmities) because they cause the flow of enmity. "Has been undertaken" means it has been successfully accomplished.
This accomplishment occurs through fame and renown here among beings by way of pleasing their minds and by way of producing an absence of enmity;

thus he said, "both satisfied and accomplished. Again, "five enmities" refers to five fruits of enmity, using the elision of the latter member of the compound (*uttarapadalopa*). "Of which one? means "of which [person]?
Because it is associated with defilements, it is called a "defilement"; because of its connection with that, he speaks of what resembles it.
As in the cases of “the first jhāna with rapture and happiness” and “a blue cloth.

And here, association should be understood as being due to their belonging to the same category (*tadekaṭṭhatā*), not because they arise simultaneously (*ekuppādāditā*). By taking it in this way, the defilement of the kamma of killing by means of views, conceit, greed, and so forth, is established;
likewise, the defilement of sexual misconduct by means of hatred and so forth. Therefore, he said: “It is indeed defilement,” and so on.
Furthermore, by virtue of the meaning already stated previously, the sequence of their defilements (kilesapariyāya) can indeed be found even in the presence [of these texts].
"Only for the purpose of illustrating this" means that it is only for the purpose of illustrating the meaning expressed by the passage beginning with "Now, as for killing living beings.
If this is so, why was it stated again? He says: "For the sake of composing verses"; the intention is that the Blessed One spoke in verse-form for the sake of easy comprehension of that meaning.
Commentary on the Four Bases, etc. (Catuṭhānādivaṇṇanā) 246.

Regarding the question, "Why does this summary statement proceed with the words 'he performs evil karma'?"—this was stated as "The Blessed One [said this]," etc., in response to an objection concerning what is included within the text.
For while the summary was formulated by way of the bright side (the wholesome), it is also [to be understood] by way of the dark side (the unwholesome).
The exposition has begun. Regarding the "doer": it is the doer of evil karma who becomes manifest;

for just as one who acts does indeed commit evil, so too does one who does not act [manifest as its opposite]. Skill in teaching here consists in explaining the practice of purifying qualities preceded by the avoidance of defiling qualities.
Demonstrating first the doer, he said: "Release the left, [take] the right..."
"Take it! For in this way, while showing the thirty-eight auspicious signs, the Blessed One, after saying "Non-association with fools," said "And association with the wise.
Regarding "into a wrong course through desire": here, he says "into a wrong course through desire and affection," showing that the vowel *a* is elided by way of euphonic combination (*sandhi*).
He says "by desire" (*chandena*), indicating that the ablative case is used in the sense of a cause.
In this context, the word *chanda* refers to craving (*taṇhā*), not to wholesome desire (*kusalacchanda*) and so forth; thus he says, "by affection" (*pemena*).

"In subsequent phrases" refers to sentences such as "going to a state of hatred" (*dosāgatiṃ gacchanto*). By the phrase "the same method applies," he extends [this explanation] to the explanatory statements such as "by hatred, by anger" (*dosena kopena*).
"A friend" (*mitto*) means a firm friend; the meaning is "an associate" (*sambhatto*). "One seen" (*sandiṭṭho*) means a companion merely by having been seen.
"By way of natural turbulence" means by way of turbulence that arises naturally; the meaning is "by way of opposition that persists for a long time.
For this very reason, he said: "or by way of anger arisen at that moment.

Having spoken something improper or groundless, one who relies on resorting to what is uneven—such as thieves and the like, or by undertaking and practicing uneven bodily misconduct and so forth—is "dependent on the uneven."

He does not go toward wrong courses such as *chandāgati* (going by desire) because all four types of going to wrong courses have been abandoned by means of the Path. "Going to wrong courses" (*agatigamana*) should be understood as unwholesome mental states that proceed in such a way as to lead to the states of misery (*apāya*);

they are so called because one goes to a wrong destination (*agati*) by means of them. "Fame" (*yasa*) is that which is praised; it is the sound of praise. It is "fame" because one is surrounded by attendants in the capacity of those who precede and follow;
thus he says, "both fame consisting of praise and fame consisting of a retinue. "Is declining" (*parihāyati*) refers to whatever [was previously possessed] to whatever extent.
It is obtained; thereafter it diminishes and goes to complete exhaustion.
247. Commentary on the Six Ways of Losing [Merit]:
*Pūvasurā* (cake-liquor) is that which is made by putting cakes into a vessel, adding the appropriate water, and kneading them together. The same applies to the remaining types of liquor.
"Kiṇṇa," however, refers to the seed of that liquor; having added those which are also called "surā-moḍaka" (liquor-ferments), it is made "kiṇṇa-pakkhitta" (with ferment added).

That which is mixed with various ingredients such as harītakī and sāsapā is "sambhāra-saṃyutta" (joined with ingredients). The long-aged juice of flowers such as madhuka, tāla, and coconut is "puppha-āsava" (flower-liquor).
The juice of fruits such as panasa is "phala-āsava" (fruit-liquor). The juice of grapes is "madhu-āsava" (honey-liquor). The juice of sugarcane is...
Gulāsava (molasses liquor). The juice of various ingredients such as *harītaka*, *āmalaka*, *kaṭuka*, *bhaṇḍa*, and so forth, which has been aged for a long time and is mixed with those ingredients.
"All that" means all ten kinds. It is called "intoxicant" (*majja*) because it intoxicates one who drinks it by virtue of its capacity to cause intoxication.

"The basis for negligence consisting of fermented liquor, distilled liquor, and intoxicants" (*surā-meraya-majja-pamādaṭṭhāna*) [is a *karmadhāraya* compound]: it is the basis for negligence (*pamādaṭṭhāna*) that consists of fermented liquor, distilled liquor, and intoxicants (*surā-meraya-majje*). "Addiction" (*yoga*) means attachment (*anu-anu-yoga*).
It is the state of being endowed with that again and again. Therefore he said, "repeated performance," meaning its occurrence in succession.

Wealth that has already arisen declines because of the ruin caused by addiction to drink. And wealth that has not yet arisen does not arise because one who is negligent lacks a guide in his undertakings.
"Of wealth" (bhogānaṃ) refers to those things which have received the name "wealth" (bhoga) in the sense of being something to be enjoyed.
Regarding the "strands of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇānaṃ*). The meaning of the term "gateway to the states of loss" (*apāyamukha*) has already been explained above.

"At an improper time" (*avelāya*) means at an unsuitable time; that is, when there is no protection for one's property and so forth while wandering about. "Wandering in the streets" (*visikhāsu cāriyā*) means roaming through the thoroughfares.
"Festivals" (*samajjā*) refers to a great public gathering where dances and other performances are staged; it is for the purpose of seeing such things that one goes there.
"Going about by way of delighting" means approaching and frequenting social gatherings. Regarding "by way of seeing dancing and so forth":

it should be understood that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) has been elided [from *dassanādi*], meaning "by way of seeing dancing and the like. Alternatively, hearing is included under "seeing" by way of the grammatical principle of "residual inclusion of dissimilar items" (*virūpekasesanaya*).
Or else, because the five sense-consciousnesses have the nature of looking toward their objects, the act of hearing is also subsumed under the category of "seeing."
It is stated simply as “by way of seeing. Here, mental laziness is not the cause; thus, it is stated as “bodily laziness.
“Exertion in what is appropriate” means being devoted to that [practice] due to its excellence.
The commentary on the six dangers of fermented liquor and spirits, etc.
248. "To be seen by oneself" means visible (*sandiṭṭha*). That which is visible is itself "visible-in-the-present" (*sandiṭṭhika*);

however, this designation is made in the feminine gender due to its dependence on the word *dhana-jāni*. He said, "existing in this world," meaning that the sense here is "pertaining to the present life" (*diṭṭhadhammika*).
Alternatively, they are "visible-in-the-present" because they are to be seen equally or correctly; the meaning is that they exist at the same time as one's life. [They are] "increasers of quarrels."
Because one does not see the danger in quarreling with a friend. It is a "field" (*khetta*) because it is a place of origin.
Alternatively, "source" (*āyatana*) means a cause or a mine. They attain ill-repute in the next world because they produce karma that leads to ill-repute.
Or, "exposure" (*kopīna*) refers to secret deeds that should not be done, which become public. And those intoxicated by liquor... previously.
Having wandered about concealing such a deed committed by themselves while sober, they reveal and make manifest even their enemies when intoxicated;
therefore, because that liquor reveals that private part (*kopīna*), it is called "that which reveals the private part" (*kopīnanidaṃsanī*).
This is how the meaning should be understood here. The phrase "wisdom regarding one's own actions as one's own property" (*kammassakatāpaññā*) should be regarded as a mere illustration.

For it can be understood that "whatever worldly wisdom there is, it indeed weakens. Thus, in order to establish this point by way of contrast, the passage beginning with "But as for path-wisdom" was stated.

By the phrase "it does not even enter within the mouth," he indicates that the weakening of path-wisdom caused by liquor is something difficult to remove. Is it not so, then, that by [this statement regarding] liquor...
Is it not the case that the obstruction of the capacity to weaken that wisdom is unchallenged, because the Noble Ones are challenged only when they are not already engaged?
This is not so, because it has been stated that this meaning implies: "They do not even have constant engagement; how much less the performance of a task?
However, if there were ever an engagement of it by way of imagining an impossible situation (*aṭṭhānaparikappa*), even then—
It is not at all able to weaken that [wisdom] even slightly, because it is firmly established by having completely removed its opposite.
Therefore he said: "But it is not able to make the wisdom of the path weak.
And here, by means of the term "the path," it should be understood that what is shown is the inability to bring about weakness in any of the mundane or supramundane wisdom of the Noble Ones.
That by which one goes is a "pada" (footstep); it is the cause.

249. For him who wanders at improper times, his self is unguarded, unprotected from its own inherent nature, and even from the approach of those things to be avoided because they have not been avoided.
Therefore he said, "Wandering at an improper time," and so forth. By the word "pi" (also) in the phrase "thorns, etc.," pits and the like are included.
He embraces them. By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even by an enemy," thieves and others are included.
Regarding the term "sons and wives": since the mention of "sons" here includes daughters as well, he says "sons and daughters.

"A longing for what is outside" means having made a longing for something external to the fixed objects within the house, by way of sensual desire. "In regard to evil deeds committed by others" means in regard to those committed by others.
Regarding evil deeds: he is suspected because of wandering here and there at improper times; it takes root because it is seen by others in whatever place the theft occurred;

and it cannot be described, meaning one is unable to describe it by delimiting it as "this much suffering" or "this much mental distress. All of that [is found] in a person who wanders at the wrong time.
It must be brought and placed upon him. How so? Because there is no other person of such a kind who might be suspected [of being a robber].

"Thus" (iti) means in this way. "He" (so) refers to the one who wanders at improper times. "Surrounded" (purakkhato) means he moves about having placed those who suspect him of being above them, in front of himself. 250.
"The dancing of actors, dancers, and so forth" (naṭanāṭakādinaccaṃ) refers to the performance of dancing and dramatic acts by actors and dancers. By the word "and so forth" (ādi),...

It includes everything that remains. Having stated, "In this regard, one must go there," the passage beginning with "Of that" was spoken to show how, by going there, there is the non-arising of wealth not yet arisen and the destruction of that which has already arisen.

*Gīta* refers to what pertains to melody (*sara*), what pertains to composition (*pakaraṇa*), what pertains to rhythm (*tāḷa*), and what pertains to instrumental accompaniment (*apadhāna*)—as prescribed in the treatises on music (*gandhabbasattha*).

All other types of singing should also be understood in this way. "Instrumental music" (*vādita*) refers to the playing of the lute, flute, drum, and so forth. "Narratives" (*akkhāna*) refers to stories such as the Battle of the Bhāratas and the Abduction of Sītā.

"Hand-clapping" (*pāṇissara*) refers to the clashing of bronze cymbals; some also call it "hand-striking" (*pāṇitāḷa*). "The kumbha-thūna" refers to the sound of a square-shaped wooden drum; some say it is the sound of a "box-drum" (*kuṭabheri*).
By the phrase "the same method applies," he extends the meaning already stated regarding dance—beginning with "In what place? and so on—to singing and the other arts.
251. He conquers by defeating the gambler. Against the defeated man, who is like a mere plaything, he engenders and arouses enmity and hostility for the sake of victory.
To demonstrate this production of enmity, it is said: “I have won,” and so forth.
A “conqueror” (jinoti) is one who is victorious through the loss of wealth incurred by the defeat in gambling. Therefore, he said: “Being defeated by another,” and so forth.
"He grieves over wealth" means he laments with reference to that wealth. "In a place of legal decision" means in any place where a legal dispute is being decided.
"Of one questioned as a witness" means of one who has been questioned in his capacity as a witness. "A gambler" means a dice-player.
"A cheat" means one addicted to the vices of gambling. "You too, indeed, are a son of good family" means you are a son of noble birth.
The intention is: "We no longer see you as such, O son of a clansman.

"One who is cut and broken" means one whose moral shame (*hirī*) and fear of wrongdoing (*ottappa*) are severed; the meaning is that he is shameless and lacks dread of blame. "For his sake" means for the purpose of him.
"Unwanted" means not desired. She will have to be supported because she will be perpetually empty and hollow due to her defeat in gambling.
Commentary on the Six Dangers of Bad Friendship (Pāpamittatā): 252. *Akkhadhuttā* means gamblers at dice;
those who, for the sake of dice, bring about the destruction of their wealth. *Itthisoṇḍā* means those intoxicated by women;
those who, for the sake of sexual enjoyment with women, become feverish with passion. Likewise, those intoxicated by food and so forth are to be understood in the same way. *Pipāsā* means thirst.
There is a craving for liquor that arises higher and higher; therefore, it is called "drunkenness" (*pānasoṇḍā*). Those such as the *nekatika* have already been explained below.
They are called "friends" (*mittā*) because they are the basis for the arising of friendship.

"Therefore" means because of [association with] evil friends. 253. "Business" (*kammanta*) means work; just as a thread itself is called a "thread-end" (*suttanta*), so too work itself is called "business" (*kammanta*). That...
When it is said, "I am going to do [it]," the term *kammanta* means that work (*kamma*) reaches its completion (*niṭṭhāna*) within it; thus, it is a place for performing work (*kammakaraṇaṭṭhāna*).
When it is said, "I am going there," [the meaning is] that.
Regarding *pannasakhā*: they are called *pannasakhā* because they proceed to drink liquor (*sura*) by means of leaves (*panne*). Therefore he said, "This is precisely the meaning."
“*Sammiyasammiyo*” means one who possesses the word *sammiya-sammiya*; thus he said, “speaking as ‘a true friend, a true friend.
“He becomes a companion” means he acts like a companion. “Seeks only an opening” means he searches for a flaw, desiring to do him harm.
“The provocation of enmity” means the instigation and persistence of enmity toward oneself by others; thus he said, “an abundance of enmity.”
"Anattha" means that harm being done to others exists here; its state is "anatthatā. Thus it is said, "the state of causing harm" (*anatthakāritā*).
For one who causes harm to others is, in actual fact, a causer of harm to himself; therefore, "anatthatā" refers to the causing of harm to both. An *ariya* is called a living being (*satta*);
one who is base (*kucchin*) is an *ariya* in the sense of being miserly (*kadariya*). Of which phenomenon...
By virtue of that, he is called "miserly" (kadariya); that state is miserliness (kadariyatā), which is stinginess (macchariya).
However, with reference to its being difficult to relinquish, it is said: "It is extreme miserliness, a state of rigid stinginess.
And because he is unable to rise up from his unchanging nature, while taking on debt he is said to "plunge into debt" even as he sinks down. When the sun has not yet risen...
Thus, not undertaking his work, he is one whose nature is to remain inactive during the night.
"Wealth" (*attha*) means riches. "Pass away" (*atikkamanti*) means they depart. Alternatively, "wealth" (*attha*) means duties.
"Pass away" (*atikkamanti*) means they have passed their [proper] time; even the passing of those [duties] is, in meaning, the passing of wealth itself. By this line of reasoning...
By this means—that is, by the method of discourse beginning with “From which, householder’s son,” etc.—which is a way of attaining welfare.
“So much action” refers to the fourteen kinds of evil action thus described: the four defilements of action, the four ways of going to ruin, and the six doors of loss for wealth.
Commentary on the Counterfeit Friend (Mittapatirūpaka) 254.
"Disadvantage" refers to such things as the loss of wealth, incrimination by others, embarrassment in the midst of an assembly, and death in confusion—
these being disadvantages pertaining to the present life— and the affliction of miserable rebirths, as well as short lifespan and frequent illness even in happy realms.
Excessive poverty, lack of food and drink—such is the kind of misfortune that arises.
"Whatever fears" refers to whatever fears are found in the world, such as the fear of self-reproach, the fear of reproach by others, the fear of punishment, and so forth.
"Calamities" means obstacles. "Afflictions" refers to those things that arise repeatedly, as if in close contact with the body.
"Calamities. "Aññadatthu" is a particle used in the sense of "exclusively," as in the expression "Aññadatthudaso" (one who sees exclusively);
thus it is said, "ekamsena" (exclusively). Whatever is fit to be grasped, he carries away; he simply seizes it. One whose action has speech alone as its highest point is "vacīparamo.
Therefore, he says, "by mere words alone," and so forth. "Anuppiya" means flattery.
Or that which is called "pleasure" (*ruci*): he becomes a companion in those various causes of ruin, such as the drinking of liquor and so forth, through which wealth perishes and vanishes.
(Verse 255) He is only a taker and not a giver; to demonstrate his state of being exclusively a taker, [the text] says "of a companion," and so forth.
It has been said: having given some small thing—whatever limited object such as flowers or fruit—one hopes for much, desiring many costly items such as pairs of garments.
Having become like a slave, performing various services for a friend, how could one be called a non-friend?
To this he says, "This," and so forth. [He refers to] him for whose sake one performs service.
He associates with him for the purpose of avoiding misfortune and to demonstrate his own friendship. "For the sake of benefit" means for the sake of increase;
this is the distinction between these two. 256.

"On another day" means on the following day. "Has not come" means he did not arrive. "Exhausted" [is said] because [the gift] was given to such a person and to so-and-so. "In the gathering of grain" means when the collection of grain to be prepared from the harvest has been made.

257. When it is said, "Let us do whatever [deeds] such as giving," he gives his consent by saying, "Very well, friend, let us do so. By stating, "The same principle applies even to wholesome deeds," he extends this rule by way of analogy.
Is it not the case that one who consents in this manner is indeed a friend, and not a non-friend or a counterfeit friend?
This is merely a demonstration of one who speaks agreeably. Or rather, [it refers to] the companion [who considers] the place and time... in that [situation].

Or, when someone says, "Let us do it," without perceiving the contradiction or other faults that would arise from doing so, and another person who knows this speaks agreeably, saying, "Very well, friend, let us do it," it is with reference to such a person that it is said, "He approves of his goodness. Therefore it was said:
"The same principle applies even in the case of what is good."
259. Having understood that these are merely semblances of friends and not true friends.
260. *Suhadamitta-vaṇṇanā*:
"With beautiful hearts" means having auspicious minds by virtue of the presence of affection.

261. Regarding the phrase "protects the heedless": since protection at such a time when something inappropriate has been done through negligence is already included by the statement "it is a refuge for one who is afraid," the passage beginning with "having drunk liquor" is stated to show a different method of protecting the heedless.
Even going outside [is not safe] for one who has not established protection within the house.
“Belonging to the side of negligence” means it is stated that “a companion has gone outside. “Removing fear” means warding off fear.
Because it is the cause of enjoyment, wealth is called “enjoyment” by way of metaphorical designation (*phalūpacāra*).
“In matters of duty and business” refers to when minor or major tasks have arisen that must be performed.
262. “A discourse fit to be concealed” (*nigūhituṃ yuttakathaṃ*): it is a discourse fit to be concealed, that is, fit to be covered up;
or, it is a discourse for which concealment is appropriate—namely, one’s own deed. “He guards it” means he covers it by not revealing it.
By the word “even” (*api*) in the phrase “even his life,” he shows: “How much more so other possessed objects? (*kimaṅgaṃ pana aññaṃ pariggahitavatthuṃ*).
"263. *Passantesu passantesu*: by this reduplicated expression, he indicates the repeated commission of evil even while being restrained.
For one who commits it again and again must be especially restrained from evil. *Saraṇesu*: "Be steadfast in the refuges," meaning practice having made them firm;
or, "be steadfast in the refuges" by way of the status of a lay follower (*upāsaka*). *Nipuṇam*..."

Gently. "The reason" refers to that which is joined with such factors as the ownership of one's actions (kammassakatā) and so forth. "This action" refers to this wholesome action consisting of giving and the like.

Although the word "action" is spoken in a general sense, its status as wholesome is made manifest by its proximity to the other phrase "they are reborn in heaven," just as the possession of qualities such as faith, moral shame, moral dread, and non-greed is manifested. Faith and the others...
For these qualities are the path leading to heaven. As it is said:
"Faith, moral shame, and wholesome generosity—these qualities are followed by the virtuous."
"For they call this the divine path;
by means of this one goes to the world of the gods.
(264) "Bhava" has the meaning of a state that increases prosperity; by way of its opposite, he said "abhava" (non-becoming). Thus: "By non-becoming..."
“...for lack of growth. *Pārijuñña* means loss or ruin. *Anattamano hoti* means he is not pleased; this is because of his state of compassion.
He thinks of that non-existence (*abhava*) as if it had fallen upon himself. Now, to show that existence (*bhava*) in its true nature, the passage beginning with “*tathārūpaṃ*” is stated.
*Virūpo* means hideous. *Na pāsādiko* is a synonym for the same thing. *Sujāto* means—
He is of a beautiful nature, perfected in birth.
"Jalanti jalanto" means blazing. "Aggīva" means like a mass of fire. "Bhāsati" means he shines.
Because the Blessed One spoke thus—"blazing, he shines like fire"—in order to show his distinguished radiance and his manifest presence in the world.
Therefore, when the fire shines with particular intensity and is visible even to those standing at a distance from where it is situated,
the passage beginning with "At night" was spoken in order to clarify that matter by way of its visibility and other such qualities.
By the phrase "moving like a bee," he shows that his gathering of wealth is righteous and consistent with proper conduct.
He said, “Even oneself,” and so forth. “While making a heap” means while acting so that one’s collection of wealth, grain, and other possessions remains gathered together in a mass;
likewise for one who exerts effort in such conduct. “The measure of a wheel” means the measure of a chariot wheel.
“Accumulation” means growth and further increase. Some read, “Possessions go toward accumulation.”

"Having struck together" (*samāhatvā*) means having brought together. The word *alaṃ* illuminates the sense of "suitability" in such passages as "It is sufficient (*alaṃ*) to become disenchanted with all conditioned things; it is sufficient to become dispassionate," and so on;
however, in such passages as "the distinction of noble knowledge and vision that is sufficient (*alamariyañāṇadassanavisesa*)," it signifies "adequacy.

Since the word *atta*—as in "one who has wrapped himself" (*yo veṭhitatto*) and so on—is a synonym for "intrinsic nature" (*sabhāva*), he said "of suitable intrinsic nature" (*yuttasabhāvo*) and so forth, demonstrating all of this.
“Saṇṭhapeti” means to establish correctly; the meaning is to cause [them] to proceed rightly.
“Vibhajanto” means dividing his own wealth into four parts according to the method thus described.

Because of that division, he binds friends; he ties them fast through the sixteen kinds of good friendship by not failing to digest [the practice of] loving-kindness. Therefore he said: “Unbreakable...”
"...sets aside. But how does one "bind friends" by dividing wealth into four parts according to the method described?
To this he says, "For one who... and so forth. Therefore the Blessed One said, "Giving, he binds friends.

"He would enjoy" means he would utilize or employ [the wealth]; the sense is that he would use it for the purpose of giving to ascetics, brahmins, the poor, those in need, and so on, as well as for the sake of the deities dwelling therein.
The employment [of wealth] for the sake of offerings to deities (*petabali*) and as wages for barbers and others is also indeed "use" (*upayoga*).
For it will be said: "But regarding these," and so forth. "Income" (*āya*) should be desired as four times the amount of the minimum expenditure;
otherwise, expenditure would not continue by way of non-interruption, and one would be unable to store, lend, or distribute what has not been accumulated. Thus it is said: "With two [parts], work..."
"one should employ it. "Having deposited" means having buried; the sense is that one has placed it underground.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "due to kings, etc.," it includes fire, water, thieves, famine, and so forth. By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "barbers, etc.," it includes potters, dyers, and others.
Commentary on the Chapter on Covering the Six Directions.

"By four reasons" means by the four reasons beginning with "going according to one's will. "Having abandoned the unwholesome" means having abandoned both the unwholesome referred to as "the four defilements of action" and the unwholesomeness of going to a bad destination.

"By six reasons" means by the six reasons consisting of the perception of danger in drinking intoxicants and so forth. [This refers to] the sixfold [unwholesome conduct] divided into addiction to drinking intoxicants and the rest.
Having avoided the gateway to the ruin and the gateway to the destruction of enjoyments; "sixteen friends" means:
having cultivated and frequented sixteen kinds of virtuous friends—four by way of being helpful and so forth, and four each according to their specific duties such as guarding against negligence;
and because of living righteously by abandoning wrong livelihoods such as trade in weapons and the like, and conducting oneself according to the proper method (*ñāya*).
He lives by a right livelihood. "Worthy of homage" means they should always be honored because of their helpfulness and their virtues, and one should conduct oneself toward them with humility.
The meaning of the word *disā* has already been explained above.
"Fear of coming [to harm]" refers to the misfortune that arises there from practicing wrongly or not practicing correctly; for it is from this that they fear.

This is called "fear. In order to show the reason why mother, father, and so forth are designated as being in the eastern direction and so on, it is said, "because of their former beneficence," and so forth;
by this, he shows that they possess the status of the eastern direction and so on due to a similarity in function.
For indeed, mother and father are seen to occupy the position of the eastern direction with respect to their children precisely because of their state of being benefactors.

The eastern direction is so called because it is the direction from which one comes. Teachers are the southern direction for a pupil because they are worthy of offerings (*dakṣiṇā*) by virtue of being like the south—due to their skill in discerning what is beneficial and what is harmful, and according to the method already stated.

In this same manner, the meaning of "the western direction" and so forth should be understood as appropriate. Because of the great abundance of suffering in the household life, those various specific duties...
It is said, "for the purpose of overcoming suffering as it arises," and thus it is stated: "he crosses over those various specific sufferings.
Since servants and laborers generally remain in the presence of their master by way of attending upon his feet and performing duties appropriate thereto, it is therefore stated:
"by way of being established at the base of the feet. By means of qualities...

"By means of qualities that bring about higher states" means by means of being established in the state of standing above, that is, being firmly established on the path to heaven and the path to liberation.

267. "Supported" (bhatō) means nourished; however, to show that this nourishment was carried out by them from the time of birth onwards through the provision of conditions for happiness and the removal of conditions for suffering, it is said: "having given suck," and so forth.
“Jaggitō” means maintained. “Tē” refers to mother and father.
Because protecting the fields and other property belonging to mother and father—without letting them perish—is the cause for their continued existence through successive generations, it is said:
“By protecting that, one indeed establishes the family lineage. Regarding the phrase “from an unrighteous lineage”: by way of family, locality, and so forth...
"Having found a man equal to oneself, one should bind him by the neck, the hand, or take away his signet ring"—from such an unrighteous tradition as this.
"Having taken away" means having removed [that charge] and having caused that accusation to be relinquished.
For it is precisely by separating them from that charge that their parents may become the inheritors of their lineage in the future. In the righteous lineage...
"Establishing" means setting down [the lineage] in a righteous clan and a righteous tradition through abstinence from violence and so forth.
"Without interrupting the distribution of tickets for meals and so forth" means without discontinuing the giving of ticket-meals and other such provisions.
Regarding the phrase "I am fulfilling my inheritance": herein, one is said to be fulfilling the inheritance only while existing in a state worthy of receiving that inheritance.
It is the one [who has performed the duty] who "practices" (paṭipajjati), not the other; therefore, in order to show that meaning, the words beginning with “mother and father” were spoken.
“To the child” means to the son. “Having reached the legal decision” means having recourse to the legal decision as it has come down thus:
“the giving away of the son. “I am practicing my inheritance” was said; this “I am practicing my inheritance” is the fourth instance of speaking.
It has been stated. "Of them" means of the mother and father. "Starting from the third day" means starting from the third day after the day of death.

What is called "prevention of evil" pertains to the future. For even regarding an object already attained, prevention can only occur when the transgression is yet to come, not while it is currently taking place.
However, an evil deed that has already been committed can only be remedied by mere censure; thus he said: "Even if done..."
“They blame,” it is said. “They settle” means they establish [them]. It is said that mothers and fathers of the aforementioned type teach only blameless crafts;
thus it says, “the crafts of arithmetic, calculation, and so forth. “By means of beauty and so forth”—by the word “and so forth,” one includes wealth, retinue, and the like.
“Suitable” means appropriate.

"Constant time" (*niccabhūto samayo*) refers to the period of frequent practice. For this word *nicca* has the sense of "frequent," as in such expressions as "constantly laughing" (*niccapahaṃsito*) and "constantly joyful" (*niccapahaṭṭho*).
"Time" (*samaya*) is simply the appropriate and fitting occasion; thus, "time for giving" (*kālasamaya*) means the very moment when it is suitable.

By the phrase "rising up again and again" (*uṭṭhāya samuṭṭhāya*), he shows that they were constantly engaged and devoted to giving. "Placing the crest-jewel" (*sikhāṭhapana*) refers to the time of childhood.
When sons and daughters reach the time of youth, there is the danger of marriage—of giving them away in wedlock or taking them in marriage.

One should guard [the sense-doors] so that this danger does not come; thus, changing the grammatical case from the nominative "puratthimā disā" (the eastern direction) to the instrumental, the construction is applied as "by the eastern direction" [meaning, by guarding the eastern direction]. To show both how that danger might come and how it might not come:

“‘If indeed’ and so forth was said. ‘Those who have practiced wrongly’ means that sons would be practicing wrongly by both failing to act according to the correct practice—such as [the thought] ‘I will support those who supported me’—and by failing to refrain from its opposite, which is wrong practice.
‘This fear’ refers to ‘the fear of being censured by the wise for being unworthy of one’s mother and father,’ and ‘the fear of the opponent’s argument.”

In such ways as these, [fear] might come upon one's children. Regarding the phrase "not suitable for children," the word "of children" (*puttānaṃ*) should be brought over and connected here as well, in this manner: "this fear might come upon children.
For it is considered that from the very time parents become capable of giving instructions and admonitions to their children, those [admonitions] ought indeed to be given to them.

It has been stated thus. For this teaching is given with reference to children: for both those who have practiced rightly, there is no fear whatsoever arising from themselves or from their parents, because they have practiced rightly.

Precisely because they have practiced in this way, [the offense] remains concealed, owing to the fact that the hospitality (paṭisanthāra) which ought to be performed therein has been properly rendered.
“Khemā” means free from calamity. For calamities that arise through the non-performance of the aforementioned right practice do not occur through its performance.

The meaning of the passage beginning with “Not indeed to you,” which was spoken by the Blessed One at that time but was not included in the Saṅgīti, should be understood as having come down through oral tradition. Therefore he said: “The Blessed One said this to Siṅgālaka. Here, the word “hi” (for/indeed) [indicates the reason].
This is for the purpose of emphasis. For instance, by saying "nothing else," it excludes anything other than that.
268. By the very mention of rising upon seeing the teacher from afar, acts of courtesy such as going out to meet him are established even without being explicitly stated;
showing this, he says, "having gone out to meet him," and so forth. "By attendance" means by waiting upon. "By going to attend three times" means...
"By approaching at the three times—morning, midday, and evening—for the purpose of attendance.
However, as for approaching for the purpose of learning a craft, since that approach is included within attendance by way of its specific motive, he said: "Learning a craft...
[etc.]... occurs. A desire to hear is *sussūsā*; furthermore, that is preceded by respect and reverence toward the teacher and the training to be learned.
One should desire [to hear] with the thought: "Surely, by training in this craft, I shall obtain such a quality as this.
And such hearing is preceded by faith; therefore it is said, "by hearing with faith.
To show the same point by way of contrast, it is said: "Without faith... one does not attain. Therefore, its meaning is as follows:
It should be understood by way of the opposite of what was stated above. With reference to this, it was said: "the remaining minor services.
To show that analysis in its entirety, it was said: "by a resident pupil," and so forth.
In the phrase "attending upon, etc.," the word "etc. includes such things as preparing a seat and fanning. "The duty of a resident pupil" refers to that which must be performed by a resident pupil.
The duty to behave correctly toward the teacher. "By receiving the craft" means by the careful mastery of the craft's manual;
for through its thorough mastery, the practical application according to that manual is also properly mastered. Therefore he said, "Having grasped a little," and so forth.

“They train those who are ill-trained”: here, the training in conduct (*ācāra-vinaya*) is intended. However, the training in instructing in a craft (*sippa-sikkhāpana-vinaya*) is included by the very phrase “making them grasp what is well-grasped,” as stated in “In this way you should sit,” and so forth.

For teachers do not train their pupils only in matters pertaining to the present life (*diṭṭhadhammika*), but also in matters pertaining to the future life (*samparāyika*); thus he said, “evil friends.”

“...should be avoided. Regarding the learning of a craft, he says, “having them learn by demonstrating the technique,” because the purpose of learning a craft is solely for the sake of accomplishing its practical application.
“Among friends and relatives” means among one’s own friends and relatives.
“They prepare [it]” means they prepare it by way of grasping it as their own possession, thinking, “This is our pupil,” and so forth. Thus, regarding oneself—
They provide for them by means of demonstrating what has been acquired, and by means of enumerating his virtues through such terms as “one who is learned” (*bahussuta*).
They provide protection in all directions by establishing him in the state of one who belongs to the four quarters (*cātuddisa*), since this accomplishes his state of living happily everywhere.
Therefore he said, “One who has mastered a craft,” and so forth. For the protection of beings is twofold: [protection of the body and protection of the mind].
[This is] by warding off internal dangers and by warding off external dangers. Therein, the internal danger consists of hunger, thirst, and so forth;
it is warded off by the accomplishment of gain, because through that [gain] one provides the appropriate protection. The external danger has its cause in thieves, non-human beings, and so forth;
it is warded off by the accomplishment of knowledge (vijjā), because through that [knowledge] one provides the appropriate protection.
Therefore it was said: “In whatever direction,” and so forth.
Previously, by the passage beginning “Having mastered a craft,” the protection of the directions through the arising of gain by means of teaching a craft was shown;
now, by the passage beginning “Or whatever [craft] he has mastered,” it is shown by way of praising his virtues through the successful accomplishment of that mastered craft.
“Also by taking [it]” means for the purpose of obtaining gain; this is the distinction between these alternatives.
“The rest” refers to what has come down in the Pāḷi, beginning with “it is concealed,” and what has come down in the Aṭṭhakathā, beginning with “and having spoken thus.
“In this” means in this second section on directions. “Precisely by the former method” means by the very method stated previously in the first section on directions.

269. "Honoring" (sammānanā) means esteem; however, since that [esteem] is characterized by acting for others' welfare and characterized by giving, and is already included within the fourth and fifth bases of sympathy, it is stated here as "speaking with words of esteem" in order to show its characteristic of affectionate speech.
"Lack of disrespect" (avimānanā) means the absence of disrespect; it is the non-performance of disrespect. Therefore he said: "Just as..."
“Slaves, laborers, and so forth,” and so on. For when women are treated with contempt by their husbands, their entire retinue likewise treats them with contempt.
“Attending upon” means attending upon the sense faculties. One is said to “transgress against her” because one behaves toward one’s own wife by treating her with disdain and disregarding her.
Regarding the phrase “by relinquishing authority”: here, the kind of relinquishment of authority that is appropriate for a wife—
Showing this, he said, "entrusted in the house where the meal is prepared.
For even work such as farming or trade that must be managed while staying at home is not the burden of a noble woman, but rather the burden of the husband;
however, the property brought from there must be placed by her after having been well-guarded. They think, "All authority is indeed called 'entrusted' (vissaṭṭha)."
The intention [is as follows]: Women are not satisfied even by obtaining costly and abundant ornaments as they would be by obtaining a son;
therefore, to satisfy them, he speaks of "the giving of ornaments" with the words, "according to his own means.
As for the "tasks to be performed by a wife," these refer to the manner of preparing food and so forth; thus he says, "the times for cooking rice-gruel and boiled rice," and so on.

The members of the household are constantly supported by the mistress of the house through appropriate honors and kind words, as well as by gifts of food and so forth, by sending delicacies from elsewhere or presents arising right there, and by sending beloved articles on festive days and the like; thus it is said: "Here..."
“Retinue” means... [as before] ... “relatives. Wealth brought in refers to wealth that has been introduced from the outside into the house.
First, a housewife must possess skill in providing food and be diligently engaged in that task;
after that, she must be concerned with the duties and non-duties dependent on her husband; and after that, with the duties to be performed for her children and retinue.
He said: “In the preparation of rice gruel, meals, and so forth,” and so on.

Having stated “without negligence,” he spoke the words beginning with “Just as” in order to clarify that very lack of negligence through both negative (vyatireka) and positive (anvaya) illustrations. “Here” means in this third section on directions.

“Precisely in the manner previously stated” means in the manner stated in the first section on directions. Thus, although the Blessed One designated “the western direction as wife and children,” etc., [he proceeded as follows].
He sent her off toward the western direction as if she were his daughter, not as his son. Why?
For children are indeed favored and shown compassion by their mother’s care during their childhood;

however, when they have reached the age of discretion, the method by which they too must then be cared for is described in the first section on the directions, beginning with the words, "She restrains them from evil."

"Since it has already been shown, what further purpose is served by this answer?"—the answer is that whatever needs to be said regarding the bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), such as giving and so forth, has already been stated above.
270. In order to skip over the first four points and reveal only the fifth point, the passage beginning with "by non-deceitfulness" (*avisaṃvādanatāya*) was spoken.
Therein, "of whichever name he takes up" refers to a companion [he addresses] because of his state of need for a particular object.
He speaks his name. Regarding the phrase "without deceiving": here, non-deception is twofold—by speech and by action.
To show both of these, the words "this too" and so forth are stated.

Furthermore, the expression "by giving" should be regarded as merely illustrative, since gathering [people] by means of the other bases of sympathy is also possible through non-deception, and because that is what ought to be desired.
Furthermore, *aparapajā* refers to later generations (*pacchimā pajā*), or to those who arise one after another (*aparāparaṃ uppannā*).

To show both aspects—namely, cherishing (*mamāyanā*) and performing acts of honor (*sakkārakiriyā*)—it is said, "cherishing them" (*kelāyantī*), and so forth. "Cherishing them" means they treat them as their own. 271.
"By arranging their work according to their strength" means that for the slaves and laborers, [she provides] according to their strength, in accordance with their respective capacities.
“By the management and supervision of those works” means by having them performed; thus he said, “by young men,” and so forth.
“By the provision of food and wages” means by the granting of appropriate food and wages to each respective slave or laborer.
For this very reason he said, “this is the son of a lowly man,” and so forth. Regarding “medicines, etc.,” the word “etc. includes suitable food, clothing, dwellings, and so on.
He gathers them together. He says, "in wonderful sweet flavors," because the very state of being pleasant is the marvelous quality of flavors.
"Of them" refers to the slaves and laborers. "By letting loose" means by releasing them from their work.

"Knowing the time" means knowing the time, such as whether it is "the remainder of the forenoon" or "the remainder of half the forenoon. Any great festival is called a *chaṇa*. The *Kattika* festival...
The "Phagguna festival" refers to a great festival characterized by a specific lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*).
Since rising early and retiring late have already been described in the *Mahāsudassana Sutta*, they are not mentioned here.
Regarding the term "those who take what is given," this is a restrictive statement because of the emphasis placed on the preceding word; thus, it excludes [others] by way of that restriction.
In order to show this, it is said: "without having taken anything by theft. Therefore he says: "of one who takes only what has been given by the owners.
By the two negations in the phrase "not being resentful, thinking 'we receive nothing,'" he shows that they obtained what was rightfully theirs to receive.
However, the phrase "not being resentful, thinking 'what is the use of this work having been done? is a demonstration of the cause for their state of joyful heart.
Because of the distancing from opposing factors. Showing a contented heart is also a demonstration of the cause for performing deeds well.

"Fame" (*kitti*) itself is the "praise" (*vaṇṇa*); thus, it is "fame-praise. They carry that fame-praise—that is, the discourse on virtues—[to various places]; they bring it to this or that direction, hence they are "bearers of fame-praise" (*kittivaṇṇaharā*).
For "fame" (*kitti*) is so called because it is to be praised in such and such ways; it is virtue. The "praise" (*vaṇṇa*) is the description or speaking of those [virtues].
This is their praise. Therefore, he said: “They bring forth talk of virtues.
(272) Those bodily actions and so forth for which loving-kindness (*mettā*) exists as the cause are called *mettāni*.

To show how and in what manner these arise, the passage beginning with “Therein” (*tattha*) was stated. Regarding the phrases “going to the monastery” (*vihāragamana*) and so forth, [the term] “a mind of loving-kindness” (*mettacittaṃ*)...

The phrase “having established” should be brought forward and connected [to the context]. Regarding the term “unbarred door”: here, “door” refers to the disposition of non-greed, because it is the gateway for giving.
When that [disposition] exists, there is a desire to give whatever object is to be given; this is what is meant by being “unbarred.
For a clansman living in a house is one whose door is unbarred even when the physical gate of the house is closed; otherwise, he would be one whose door is barred even when it is open.

"At the door of the house" means "the door is not closed. Therefore it was said, "there," and so forth. "Even while dwelling [there]" is an elliptical expression meaning "even after opening [the door].

The same principle applies here to the phrase "even after closing [the door]. The term "to those possessing virtue" is stated for the purpose of demonstrating the purification of the offering from the perspective of the recipient.

Even regarding the field of compassion, there is indeed the state of having an unclosed door through giving. By the phrase "only when existing," the statement that what is non-existent does not exist is indicated.
He shows that it must be desired just like a reply to a question, because it produces gentleness of mind in the wise who seek [the Dhamma].
The phrase "to be consumed before the meal" is stated because the term "edible" (āmisa) is conventionally established only for things that are temporary (yāvakālika).
The phrase "all beings" demonstrates the excellence of the aspiration of those recluses and brahmins, as it illustrates their absence of partiality.
Because the development of loving-kindness can also be obtained through partial pervasion.

Regarding that desire for the increase of wholesome qualities on the part of those supporters which leads them to enter their homes in such a manner, it was said: "Even as they enter, they truly show compassion with a virtuous mind.
The purification of what has been heard means elucidating its meaning exactly as it is.
"By dispelling doubt, they purify": thus it is said, "having explained the meaning, they remove uncertainty.
As for "hearing," it refers to the Dhamma; for if one does not practice correctly, hearing is rendered useless.
Therefore, "cleansing what has been heard" means causing one to practice correctly; thus it is said, "or causing them to practice for the sake of suchness."
273. *Alamatta* means having the nature of being capable; and since that, in its actual sense, is simply "capable," it is stated as "capable of dwelling in a household.
*Disānamassanaṭṭhāne* means in the cause for paying homage, which is designated as the manifestation of the aforementioned directions.
The construction is: "Having become wise, skillful, and clever, one gains fame. Because of his association with gentle qualities, he is "gentle"; "gentle quality" refers to...
In this context, showing that there is subtle and skillful wisdom (*sukhumanipuṇapaññā*) and gentle speech, it is said: "by speaking... [etc. ...or by speaking.

Regarding the phrase "by the state of honoring the directions" (*disānamassanaṭṭhānena*): that knowledge by which one, proceeding according to the method described, honors the six directions as they have been stated is the "state of honoring the directions";
by means of that, one is "possessed of ready wit" (*paṭibhānavā*). For by that [knowledge], through the application of various duties as they arise, [one is so called].
One who practices here is called "eloquent" (*paṭibhānavā*). "Humble in conduct" (*nivātavutti*) means one whose nature is to be deferential.
"Not stubborn" (*atthaddho*) means not rigid; that is, devoid of rigidity characterized by the inflation of the mind.

"Endowed with initiative and energy" (*uṭṭhānavīriyasampanno*) means possessed of physical energy. "By way of continuous performance" (*nirantarakaraṇavasena*) refers to that which has been undertaken...

By way of constant practice in action. "Wisdom arising from the occasion" (ṭhānuppattiyā paññā) means wisdom that arises immediately, at that very moment, when a particular purposeful task presents itself.

"One who provides support" (saṅgahakaro) means one who gathers beings together as is appropriate. "One who creates friendship" (mittakaro) means one who produces the state of being a friend; furthermore, that...
In terms of its meaning, one who seeks friends is called "one who searches for friends" (*mittagavesano*).
One who knows the speech spoken [by others] is called "grateful" (*vadaññū*); thus it is said, "he knows the words spoken by one who has previously acted [for him].
Now, in order to show that very same point—which was stated briefly—in detail, the passage beginning with "of a companion" (*sahāyakassa*) was spoken. Regarding how it occurred previously...

Having demonstrated generosity (*vadaññutā*) through verbal knowledge, he now says "apica" and so forth in order to demonstrate generosity even through verbal knowledge that does not proceed by means of observing external signs.
With the words "yena yena vā pana," etc., he shows the etymological meaning of the word *vadaññū* as one who makes known.
He says "netā" because he brings the intended meaning directly before one's eyes. Therefore, he said:
“He who leads by means of wisdom, demonstrating this or that meaning. The connection is made by bringing in the phrase “he leads this or that meaning. He leads again and again;
thus it is “he leads repeatedly,” which is to be construed by bringing in the words “this or that meaning.

“In this or that” refers to those individuals who are to be gathered by means of the various forms of gathering, such as giving and so forth. “By means of the axle-pin” means by means of that which is fixed upon the head of the axle.
*Āṇiyā*: "Yāyato" means while going. "Puttakāraṇā" means for the sake of a son; for it is honor or worship that ought to be performed by a son, caused by a son.
"Upayogavacane" means in the sense of the accusative case. "Vuccatī" means it is spoken; thus, it is the meaning.

Or, when the accusative case is to be expressed, it is called "paccatta," which is the nominative case. "Sammā pekkhantī" means they look upon [it] exactly as it ought to be done. "Pasaṃsanīyā" means worthy of praise.
They are to be praised. The intention is that these [persons] exist there as individuals who should be supported, acting toward them as is appropriate.
274. “Thus the Blessed One,” etc., is the conclusion. “Whatever direction” means whatever direction characterized by mother, father, and so forth, such as the eastern direction and others.
“One should revere” means one should pay homage. This refers to the question of the householder’s son beginning with, “But how, indeed? etc.
Because the teaching was undertaken by way of [specific] questions, it is said, "having stood upon the questions.
There is nothing left unsaid, because the practice of heedfulness regarding the duties to be performed by householders has been explained without exception.

For, by the very fact that the practice to be observed toward parents and others—and the manner in which they themselves should act toward them—has been explained without remainder, the procedure to be followed toward kings and others is also effectively explained by implication.
The "training for householders" (*gihivinaya*) is so called because householders are disciplined by it and they approach the discipline through it.
"According to the instruction" means according to the way the Teacher has instructed here regarding the conduct of a householder; thus, in that manner, without violating it.

For one who practices in this way, "only growth is to be expected" means that only growth—in terms of the welfare pertaining to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal—is to be desired, as it is certain to occur.
The Elucidation of the Meaning Obscured in the Commentary on the *Siṅgāla-sutta*.
9. Commentary on the *Āṭānāṭiya-sutta*:
Explanation of the First Recitation Section.
Regarding the phrase “having established protection in the four quarters,” this was spoken with reference to the protection established in the four directions at two locations;
to show both of these, the passage beginning with “of the asura army” was stated.
For, through their own diligence in their respective duties and for their own protection, they established this guard over those two locations in the four directions.
For that establishment of a guard by Sakka, Lord of the Devas, in the four directions around the celestial city for the purpose of repelling the army of the asuras,

was his own non-negligence regarding his duty. But that establishment of a guard in the four directions when they approached the presence of the Blessed One was his non-negligence regarding the protection he had already provided.
Therefore it was said: “For the purpose of warding off the asura army,” and so forth. In the Pāḷi, the term *catuddisaṃ* is used in the accusative case with the sense of the locative;
thus, showing that meaning by way of the locative, he said “in the four directions.
“Having established a guard” means that Vessavaṇa and the other four Great Kings, having established a guard—that is, protection—in the directions each was respectively to protect, did so properly.

"Having stationed," meaning having stationed a host of forces such as the army of *yakkhas*. "Having established a guard," meaning having established a protective barrier capable of repelling adversaries.
Thus, by these three phrases, in their respective order, there is a threefold protection:
inside the gate of the celestial city, near the gate, and outside the gate—namely, the stationing of the guardians of the quarters.
Or rather, the state of being established through protection is illuminated. Therefore he said: “Having thus [acted] for Sakka... pe ... having done so.

Regarding the phrase “with reference to seven Buddhas,” the reason for the obstruction with reference to those very seven Buddhas should be understood according to the method stated in the *Mahāpadāna-ṭīkā*.
“The command of the Dhamma” means the command consisting of the Dhamma; the meaning is the Teacher’s Wheel of the Dhamma (*dhammacakka*). “From the assembly...”
"...external existence, non-participation," and so forth—thinking, "We shall perform such and such an act of exclusion.
*Sāvana* means the proclamation three times in succession to all four assemblies;

just as Sakka, lord of the gods, establishes a guard in the four directions for the purpose of warding off the army of the asuras, so too do the Great Kings [establish guards] in such specific matters.
They establish their own protection; for even these [beings] find it there to be full of danger and fear. Therefore it is said, “even for themselves,” and so forth.
*Abhikkanta* means “transcended” (*atikkanta*), the sense being “gone beyond”; thus he says, “it is seen in the sense of destruction. For this very reason, it is stated immediately after:
“the first watch has passed” (*nikkhanto paṭhamo yāmo*). *Abhikkantatara* means “more exceedingly lovely. And such a thing is beautiful.
"He is called Bhaddaka" means "he is seen as beautiful.
"Ko" refers to who among the devas, nāgas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so forth. "Me" means mine. "Pādāni" means the feet.
"Iddhiyā" means by means of this such-like divine power (*iddhi*). "By glory" (*yasasā*) means by such a retinue and by such a distinction. They shine.
"Shining forth. "With a lovely appearance" means with an exceedingly lovely, desirable, and beautiful complexion. "With color" refers to the radiance of the body's hue.
"Illuminating all directions" means shining upon the ten directions like the moon and like the sun, making them one mass of light and one expanse of radiance;
such is the meaning of the verse. "Beautiful" means having a sublime form, a perfected form. "In rejoicing" [means...]
Regarding *sampahaṃsane*: "In this context" refers to the phrase "when the night has advanced. "By that" means because it is a synonym for destruction (*khaya*).
"In the sense-field of visible forms (*rūpāyatana*), etc."—by the word "etc.," the inclusion of phonemes (*akkhara*) and so forth should be understood.
"Golden-colored" means "having golden skin"; thus he said "of the skin. For it is likewise stated: "His skin resembles gold. They are "accumulated" (*saññūḷha*).

"Connected. "Praise" (*vaṇṇa*) means the description of qualities; thus he says "by way of eulogy," which means by way of laudation. "In the section on clans" (*kulavagge*) refers to the divisions of clans such as the Khattiyas and so forth.
Therein, "complexion" (*vaṇṇa*) is the skin in the sense of that which is to be praised, as in the passage beginning "clear and translucent";
it is praise in the sense of describing; and it is eulogy in the sense of extolling. [This is] from the non-confusion of one with the other.
*Vaṇṇa* (complexion/class) is so called because it is to be described (*vaṇṇitabba*) and set aside (*ṭhapetabba*), referring to the group of families such as the Khattiyas.

It is *vaṇṇa* because by means of it one is described (*vaṇṇīyati*) or made known; thus it is a descriptive cause. It is *vaṇṇa* because it appears through its state of being thick, thin, and so forth; thus it is shape (*saṇṭhāna*).
It is *vaṇṇa* because it is to be described and measured as "large," "small," or "medium"; thus it is measurement (*pamāṇa*). It is described...
"It is revealed by the eye" means "color"; thus should the application of the word *vaṇṇa* be understood in its respective meanings as "the sphere of visible form" (*rūpāyatana*).
This refers to the word *vaṇṇa*. It should be understood as referring to the skin, because when the sphere of visible form is being apprehended, it must be apprehended by way of the skin.
Others, however, say: "But the element of color residing in the skin itself is what is grasped here by the term 'color' in the phrase 'of golden color.'"
"Entirely and perfectly" (*kevalaparipuṇṇa*) means "perfectly complete without leaving even a single part behind"; thus he said, "the meaning is 'without remainder'.
In the word *kevalakappa*, the term *kappa* is a particle used merely for metrical completion; its meaning is simply "entirely" (*kevala*).
Since the word *kevala* signifies "abundance," he said, "the meaning is 'for the most part' (*yebhuyyatā*). However, some [explain] "slightly... [and so on].
"They are not incomplete, but complete," they say. This being so, the meaning of the word *kevala* would simply be "without remainder" (*anavasesa*).
However, the word *kappa* has been added to the phrase for metrical expansion, as in "complete indeed, completely complete" (*kevalameva kevalakappa*).
Alternatively, "completely complete" means they are fit to be conceived or defined; that is, they are unmixed and unconfused with anything of a different nature.
Purity (*suddhatā*). Non-excess, being that as the ultimate, and the absence of distinction. "Entirely" (*kevalakappaṃ*): the meaning is "having made it entirely firm.
"Entirely" (*kevalaṃ*) refers to *nibbāna*, because of its seclusion from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).
One who has attained that is "entire" (*kevalī*), one who has realized cessation and whose taints are exhausted (*khīṇāsava*).
Furthermore, this word *kappa*—whether with a prefix (*sa-upasagga*) or without a prefix (*anupasagga*)—is intended to indicate the mere term *kappaniya* as it occurs in the compound *okappaniya*;
otherwise, in the enumeration of the meanings of the word *kappa*, the term *okappaniya* would remain unindicated.
"By means of the conventions of recluses" (*samaṇakappehi*) refers to the designations of recluses established by the sequence of the Vinaya. "Always" (*niccakappaṃ*).
"At all times. "Paññatti" is a designation for that venerable one, namely, "Kappa.

"With hair and beard trimmed" means with hair and beard cut by a razor. "The two-finger-breadth rule" (dvaṅgulakappa) refers to the allowance of a two-finger-breadth [growth] once the time of midday has passed.
"Leso" is a pretext. Even the partial pervasion of a radiance capable of pervading everything without remainder occurs due to some specific cause.
To show that this [light] pervades everything entirely, the word *kappa* is taken here in the sense of "all around"; thus he said, "without remainder, on all sides.

Since the bodily radiance of the deities extends for a distance of twelve *yojanas*, and the light arising from their garments, ornaments, and so forth remains even beyond that, it was said: "like the moon, like the sun."
"And having made a single radiance, a single light. Why did these great kings sit down in the presence of the Blessed One?
Is it not true that for the most part, when deities approach the Blessed One, they speak while standing and then depart?
This is indeed true; however, there is a specific reason for sitting here, and to show that, the passage beginning with "of the deities" was spoken.
Thinking, “This so-called *paritta* is venerable as it is connected with seven Buddhas; therefore, we should not stand while receiving it,” they sat down out of reverence for the *paritta*.
Why, however, did Vessavaṇa alone speak here, and not any of the others? To show the reason for this:
The passage beginning with “kiñcāpi” has been stated. One is “trustworthy” (vissāsika) by frequent visiting. “Skilled” (byatta) means confident;
and because that proficiency of his arises from having trained well, he says “well-trained” (susikkhita).
For just as among humans, so too among devas, someone may be well-trained due to familiarity in a previous birth; and even there, only someone [specific] [attains] the intended meaning...
He is capable of speaking, endowed with speech that is polished, complete in both words and syllables.
The explanatory gloss for "of great influence" (*mahesakkha*) is "possessed of majesty" (*ānubhāvasampanna*); alternatively, "of great influence" means "having a large retinue.
By seeing the danger in the taking of life itself, the benefit of abstaining from it becomes evident through its opposite; thus, [he speaks of] the danger...
Having thus shown [the dwelling], it is said: "In those lodgings. Regarding "in those lodgings":

these are the forest abodes (*araññāyatana*) described by such phrases as "wilderness forests" (*araññavanappatthāni*), which serve as the places of residence for monks; they are designated as "lodgings" (*senāsana*) because monks must lie down and sit within them.
"Dwelling permanently" refers to those who reside constantly in celestial palaces (*vimāna*) associated with trees or mountains.
“Those who dwell permanently. “Because they are bound” means because they are strung together and connected by way of verses.

With the intention that Vessavaṇa, desiring to have the Blessed One learn the protective chant (paritta) being spoken by himself, said, “Venerable sir, may the Blessed One learn it,” the challenger asked:
“But is there such a thing as a Dhamma not directly perceived by the Blessed One?”

"Codesi. The Teacher, demonstrating that for the Blessed One—whose range of knowledge is unimpeded in all respects—there is nothing that is not directly perceived, said "There is none," and then spoke the words beginning with "for the purpose of making way," thereby clarifying the intention of Vessavaṇa who was saying, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One learn it.
For just as Pañcasikha, the Gandhabba-devaputta, [acted] for the sake of the gods...

Just as [Sakka] approached the Blessed One and proclaimed the Dhamma exactly as he had heard it in the presence of the Thirty-three gods and the Brahmā Sanankumāra, so too this Great King, together with the others,
requested an opportunity to proclaim to the Blessed One the protective chant (paritta) composed in verse at Āṭānāṭā city, saying: "May the Blessed One, venerable sir, learn it."
He said this not in order to urge him to master it thoroughly. Therefore, "let him learn" means:
let him take it up for protection so that this *paritta*, having been merely proclaimed by me, may bring benefit to the four assemblies for a long time;
let him accept it—this is the meaning. "When told by the Teacher" means when it was announced to the Teacher, to the four...
The meaning is: "in the discourse of the Teacher to the assemblies. "For a happy dwelling" means for a dwelling in happiness obtained through non-harming by yakkhas and others.
277. All seven Buddhas are "possessors of vision" because there is no difference in their state of possessing vision across the five kinds of vision.
Therefore, just as they possess the state of being visionaries, all other qualities—such as compassion for all beings—are likewise present in all seven Buddhas.

They are common; therefore, since the names of the Buddhas are based solely on their qualities (*guṇa-nimittaka*), and not derived from gender, physical characteristics, or arbitrary whim, these seven names for each Buddha—spoken as "of the Visionary One" (*Cakkhumanta*) and so forth—are intended to illustrate their specific qualities.
To show that the commonality of these names should be applied according to their meaning:
“Sabbepi” and so forth is what was said. “Compassionate toward all beings” means those who have compassion for all sentient beings through a great compassion that is not shared by others.
“One who has washed away the defilements” means one who has completely washed away the stain of defilements from their own and others’ mental continua with the water of the Noble Eightfold Path.
“One who has crushed the armies of Māra” means those who have crushed even the five Māras along with their retinues. “One who has lived [the holy life]” means...
They have lived the holy life of the path and the tenfold noble abiding. Because they have lived [this life], their state of having warded off evil is expressed;
thus, the word "of the brahmin" (*brāhmaṇassa*) is not explicitly mentioned.
"Liberated" means liberated without remainder by way of the five liberations that are not shared with others. "From a limb" means from a limb of the body, or from a limb of knowledge.

Furthermore, there are the rays issuing from the body in the form of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), the eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*), the radiance at the time of his Great Departure (*nikkhamanappabhā*), the fathom-wide aura (*byāmappabhā*), and the radiance of the *ketumālā* and *uṇhīsa*;
and there are the rays issuing from the factor of knowledge (*ñāṇaṅga*) in the form of the radiance arising during the Twin Miracle (*yamakamahāpāṭihāriya*) and other such events.
These alone are not what is meant by the expression "one who possesses eyes" (*cakkhumā*) and so forth.
There are seven names, yet there are indeed many other immeasurable names as well. To explain how this is so, it is said:
"Innumerable are the names by which the Great Sage is called according to his qualities. By whom was this said? By the General of the Dhamma (Sāriputta).
If that is so, why did Vessavaṇa take only these? It is said: "By way of the names familiar to himself. [This refers to] those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsava).
"Janā" means those intended [by the Teacher]. For although they are born from the defilements of karma (*kamma-kilesa*), they will not be born again in this way;
thus, in this sense, they are "janā. As it is said: "And he who has become a consumer of time"—this is merely the heading of the teaching, meaning it is merely an illustration.
Alternatively, this is a designation of the whole by means of a part. Furthermore, when malicious speech (*pisuṇavācā*) is abandoned, harsh speech (*pharusavācā*) is necessarily abandoned as well.
Since even lying is [absent], they are called "even (api) gentle (suṇā). "Great" (mahattā) means those whose self (attā)—that is, their intrinsic nature—is great;
thus he said, "having attained greatness. Alternatively, "great" (mahantā) means having great ends (mahā antā); it is said that their conclusion is final Nibbāna.
Or, they are endowed with great virtues such as moral discipline (sīla). This, first of all, is according to the method found in the Commentary.

This is the meaning. According to the opinion of others, however, *nibbāna* is called *mahaṃ* because it is to be honored (*mahanīya*) and worshipped (*pūjanīya*) by the Noble Ones, such as the Buddhas;
those who possess this *mahaṃ* are *mahantā*, meaning they have vision of *nibbāna*. *Nissāradā* means free from timidity; the meaning is "fearless.
Therefore he said, "with their hair standing on end gone" (*vigatalomahaṃsā*).

*Hitanti* means with a mind intent on welfare; the sense is that he seeks the benefit of sentient beings. *Yathābhūtaṃ vipassinsūti*: they saw the five aggregates of clinging, as they truly are, through their arising and so forth, in various ways.

Regarding the phrase *“Ye cāpi”*—which was previously stated in the indefinite plural form of the first person (*paccattabahuvacana*), meaning "those [of us] also"—it is here specified by means of the dative plural (*sampadānabahuvacana*) as “to them also,” followed by the words *“namatthu.”*
And having brought over the word *ca*, one connects it because of the non-deviant relationship between the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ*.
Alternatively, the construction is: "They saw [him] while paying homage. "Of the first verse" refers to the verse stated thus: "And those who have attained Nibbāna in the world.
"Of the second verse" refers to the verse immediately following that. In this context, "merely the opening of the teaching" refers to [the teaching concerning] the other Buddhas as well.
When it comes to the mention of names, the mention of the name of this very Blessed One is merely the opening of the teaching;
therefore, the intention is that those [other names] are also already included by way of their meaning. Thus he said, "This too," and so forth.

In that context, "this" refers to this verse. In the previous interpretation, because there was no need for the word "of him" (*tassa*) as a qualification, it was stated that "the word *yaṃ* is merely a particle."
Furthermore, here, because the connection is intended in the sense of "may it be for him," he said, "whom they revere, O Gotama," showing that "yaṃ" is a noun in the singular accusative case.
(278) Why was the passage beginning with "From whence the sun rises" commenced? [It is] those yakkhas and others who [acknowledge] the Teacher’s authority over the Dhamma...
Not accepting the king’s command, and wishing to issue a proclamation saying, “We shall impose such-and-such a punishment upon them,” they [sought] their own sons—
who were subject to their authority throughout the four great continents surrounded by two thousand minor islands—
as well as the twenty-eight generals of the *yakṣas* and others, for the sake of instilling faith, reverence, and great respect toward the Teacher.

Having announced this, it was undertaken for the purpose of rebuking those who deserve censure. In that context, regarding the passage beginning with "from where it rises," it is said, "from whichever place it emerges.
But from which place does it emerge? First, for the inhabitants of Pubbavideha, it is said to rise when it stands at the meridian;
however, for the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, it is said to rise [when it stands at the meridian] for them, and for those of Uttarakuru—
