By this method, the manner in which the sun rises and sets in the remaining islands should also be understood.
This matter has already been explained below in the commentary on the Aggañña Sutta. He is called "the son of Aditi" according to worldly convention;
for worldly people say that the gods are the sons of Aditi and the asuras are the sons of Atithi. Because of his kindling...
But the meaning is that the sun (Ādicca) blazes forth by means of the manifestation of light simultaneously across the three continents.
Regarding the term *maṇḍalī*, the vowel *ī* has the sense of "abundance"; thus he says, "one who possesses a great *maṇḍala* is a *maṇḍalī*.
For his celestial palace (*vimāna*) is a vast *maṇḍala*, measuring fifty yojanas in length and breadth. By the phrase "even Saṃvarī ceases," it follows that the day also [ceases].
It should be understood that the meaning "it is born" has also been stated. "The night disappears" means because of the vanishing of the darkness characterized by the shadow of Sineru.
"A body of water" means the ocean. "In that place" refers to the upper portion of the eastern ocean relative to the sun.
This was said with reference to its movement. For to those standing in Jambudīpa, it appears as if the sun is rising from the eastern ocean. Therefore he said, "From where the sun rises.

It is called the ocean (samudda) in the sense of being well-shaken (sammā-uddana) within itself, and in the sense of being completely agitated (sabba-so-undana) and disturbed (kiledana). For the ocean has the sense of being disturbed.
A lake. "With flowing water" (*saritodaka*) means having water extending for many thousands of *yojanas*; or, it is "with flowing water" because rivers flow into its water.

Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, stands in the center of the world-system (*cakkavāḷa*); with the intention that it should be spoken of by making that [mountain] the primary point of reference, he said, "from here, from Sineru.
However, since the determination of directions is not fixed, he said, "from their place of sitting..."
"Or" is what was said. "Of them" refers to the four Great Kings. Their place of sitting is the city of Āṭānāṭa;
for while sitting there, they recited this protective charm (paritta). Or, it means from their place of sitting in the presence of the Teacher.
In either case, the eastern direction is that which is called the place where the sun rises.
In this context, they praise only the eastern quarter. Therefore it is said: "From here, that is the eastern direction.
However, the sun, the moon, the constellations, and so forth, revolve keeping Mount Sineru to their right and the Cakkavāḷa mountain range to their left.
Wherever their rising is perceived is the eastern direction; wherever their setting is perceived—
That is the western direction. On the right side [of Sineru] is the northern direction, and on the left side is the southern direction;
thus, for the inhabitants of each of the four great continents, Sineru is indeed the northern direction. Therefore, because the determination of directions is not fixed, it is said:
"Thus people describe it. "Which direction" means the eastern direction. "Glorious" (yasassī) means having a great retinue. Its measure is one hundred thousand koṭis.

For the deities constantly attend upon him. Because they are the lords of the Cātumahārājika gods—who have acquired the name "Gandhabbas" because they are the limit of fragrant medicinal herbs, grasses, and forest trees such as sandalwood and *nāga*-trees, and because they attain a state of brilliance through them—and because [he is their master], it is said:
"Me sutaṃ. Here, "me" is merely a particle. "Sutaṃ" means "renowned" (vissuta). This is the meaning here.
The interpretation: That Great King Dhatarattha also had many sons. How many? Eighty, ten, and one.
They were of one name. How so? They were named Indra. And it is heard and renowned in the world that they were "of great fruit.
Adicca was of the Gotama clan; the Blessed One was also of the Gotama clan. Because of this shared clan with Adicca, Adicca is his kinsman.
"Of him, the Kinsman of the Sun": he is the Kinsman of the Sun (*Ādiccabandhu*) because he is the kinsman of the Sun; [the phrase] "of that Kinsman of the Sun.

"By the blameless" means by the divine abode (*brahmavihāra*), which is the opposite of what is blameworthy. "You behold specifically and generally" means you look upon them by way of pervading them and by way of understanding the distinctions among their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*), latent dispositions (*anusaya*), conduct (*cariyā*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*). Having spoken thus, they pay homage: "To the World..."
Having praised [him] as "compassionate," they pay homage. Regarding the phrase *sutaṃ naneti*, the particle *nu* has the sense of "surely" (*nanu*) in this context.
However, in the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), with the intention that it means "not [by others]," the meaning "by us" (*amhehi*) is stated.
"This" (*etaṃ*) refers to this act of paying homage by non-human beings, the deities, after they have thus praised him. They say this, the sons of the Great King Dhatarattha.
279. Regarding the phrase "by which they are called *petas*," one should understand the meaning through ellipsis (*vacana-sesa*), and not according to the literal sense alone.
Showing this, he said: "By whichever direction they are told to be led out. The words "let them burn" and so forth refer to the *petas*.
"Let their hands, feet, and so on be cut off" refers to those who are malicious backbiters. "Let those who commit the destruction of life be slain," and so forth.
“They are called *pavuccantī*,” or they are gathered together; the meaning is that they are collected with the thought, “Enough of these.
For in this way, the meaning is established even without an explicit remainder of words (*vacanasesa*). He speaks of the “secret seed” (*rahas-saṅga*) with reference to the seed.
280. Regarding the phrase “in whichever direction the sun goes to its setting,” the meaning should be understood according to the method explained in the passage, “from whichever place it rises.”
281. In whichever direction the delightful Uttarakuru is situated, from here that is the northern direction—this is the construction [of the sentence].
"Mahāmeru" means a great mountain, a mountain worthy of veneration, designated as Meru. Therefore he said, "Mahāsineru, the king of mountains. It is made of silver;
for indeed, by its radiance, the ocean water in that direction appears like milk.
"Made of jewels" means made of sapphire (*indanīla*). For in that way, the water of the ocean in the southern direction is mostly perceived as blue in color, and so too is the sky.
Humans are born there. How are they born? The construction is: "without 'mine-ness' (amama) and without possessions (apariggaha).
The intended meaning is that they are devoid of the sense of ownership (*mamatta*), being free from the thought "this is mine, this is mine."
Anticipating the objection that "if they have no sense of possession such as 'this is my wife,' then there would be no boundaries here either— such as 'this is my mother' or 'this is my sister'—
due to their lack of recognition of the status of mother and so forth," he says,
"or his mother," and so on. Regarding the phrase "lustful passion does not arise," it is because of the power of virtue established by the very nature of things (*dhammatā-siddha*).
Some say: "As soon as the son is seen, milk flows from the mother's breast;
by that sign, the mother's recognition of the son as 'son' and the son's recognition of the mother as 'mother' are established.
He said, "and ploughs," because it was stated with a change of grammatical gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*). "Uncultivated" means not ploughed, where the work of tilling has not been performed.
“Rice grains” means that, by the power of the merit of beings, the fruit of that rice plant consists of nothing but rice grains due to the absence of husks and so forth;
it is caused by the influence of their merit. “A frying pan” is said to be the name for a cooking vessel, as indicated by the word *ukkhalī*.
“Having poured in” means having placed the rice grains inside. “With smokeless embers” means with fire alone, devoid of both smoke and glowing coals.
When fire arises from the Jotika stone, how could there be any smoke or embers?
Since "food" here is intended specifically as boiled rice, he uses the restrictive phrase "only food" and, showing what is thereby excluded, says: "there is no other curry or sauce.
If that is so, does it mean their food lacks any variety of flavor? No; showing this, he says: [text continues].
He said: “As they eat... [and so on] ...there is flavor.
There is no mind of stinginess because of the power of virtue established by the very nature of things (*dhammatā*). For they dwell entirely without possessiveness or sense of ownership anywhere.
Furthermore, this specific distinction should also be understood there as being established by the power of the merit of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru: therein—
It is said that in various regions there are delightful trees, their branches and twigs covered with dense, thick foliage, resembling gabled houses;
these fulfill the function of dwellings for those people, where they live happily.

Furthermore, other well-grown trees stand there with flowering tops at all times, and the water reservoirs are likewise covered with blossoming lotuses, blue water-lilies, white lotuses, fragrant lilies, and so forth.

They remain at all times exhaling a supreme fragrance from every side. Their bodies, too, being free from the defect of excessive height and endowed with perfect proportions, do not succumb to old age;

thus, they remain for the full span of their lifespan, free from wrinkles, grey hair, and other such defects, their speed, strength, prowess, and beauty remaining entirely unimpaired. Because they subsist on the fruit of non-action...

Furthermore, they have no suffering arising from agriculture, trade, and so forth, nor from the search for food; consequently, they have no possession of male or female slaves, laborers, and the like, nor do they face dangers such as cold, heat, gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, creeping reptiles, or thorns.
Just as it is at the time of dawn during the last month of summer when the temperature is perfectly balanced between cold and heat, even so it is at all times.
The temperature becomes exactly temperate, neither too cold nor too hot, and no harm or affliction arises for them.

For those who consume only uncultivated, naturally grown rice—free of red powder and husk, fragrant, and consisting of whole grains—no disease whatsoever arises, such as leprosy, boils, eczema, consumption, cough, asthma, epilepsy, or old age. They... [do not suffer].
They are hunchbacked or dwarfish, one-eyed, with withered arms, lame, paralyzed on one side, deformed, or deficient in their faculties.
Even the women there are neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair;
they possess forms of supreme beauty. Indeed, they have long fingers, copper-colored nails, pendulous breasts, slender waists, and faces like the full moon.
With large eyes, soft limbs, joined thighs, white teeth, deep navels, slender calves, long, dark, curling hair, broad and beautiful hips,
neither too hairy nor hairless, they are fortunate, pleasant to touch according to the season, delicate, gentle in speech,
and adorned with various ornaments as they wander about. For they always appear as if sixteen years old, while the men appear as if twenty-five years old.
They do not become attached to their sons or wives; this is the natural law there.
Furthermore, men and women there dwell in the enjoyment of sensual pleasures for exactly seven days, after which, freed from passion, they depart each to their own place.
There, as here, there is no basis for conception in the womb, no basis for the maintenance of a pregnancy, and no basis for childbirth.
Or it may be painful. Just as a golden image emerges from its red mold, so too do infants emerge from the mother’s womb unhindered by phlegm and other such substances, quite easily;
this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) in that regard.
However, after giving birth to a son or a daughter, the mother places them in a place for them to move about and becomes indifferent.
They go according to their pleasure. When men or women see them lying there, they place their fingers [near the infants];
by the power of their karma, milk flows forth from those [fingers], and by that the children are sustained.
Growing in this manner, after only a few days, they have acquired strength and approach young women.
The children [take] the men. And from the wish-fulfilling tree itself, garments and ornaments are produced for them here and there.
Indeed, delicate garments of various colors and variegated hues, soft and pleasant to the touch, are seen hanging here and there upon the wish-fulfilling trees.
They are interlaced with various colored gems, blazing with networks of diverse rays of light.
From the *kappa* tree hang various kinds of garland-work, creeper-work, and wall-paintings, as well as golden ornaments for the head, neck, hands, waist, and feet.

Likewise, musical instruments such as the *vīṇā*, *mudiṅga*, *paṇava*, *saṃmatāḷa*, conch, flute, *vetāḷa*, *parivāṇi*, and *vallakī* hang here and there from it. And there, many fruit trees bear fruits the size of jars.
They bear fruits of sweet flavor, by partaking of which those beings are not afflicted by hunger or thirst even for seven days.
There, too, rivers flow with perfectly pure water, possessing beautiful landing-stairs, delightful, free from mud, with beds of sand,
neither too cold nor too hot, covered with fragrant water-born flowers, and wafting a sweet scent at all times.
There are no thorns, weeds, rough bushes, or creepers there; they are entirely free of thorns and abound with flowers and fruits.
Sandalwood and agarwood trees exude their resin of their own accord.

And those wishing to bathe place their clothes and ornaments together at the river’s landing-place, descend into the river, and having bathed, as each one emerges, they take the uppermost garment and ornament.
They take [them], yet it does not occur to them, "This is mine; this is another's.
For that very reason, there is no quarrel or dispute among them. Their play for sensual pleasure lasts only seven days, after which they wander about as if free from passion (*vītarāga*).
And wherever they wish to sleep upon a tree, right there they find a bed. When they have died...
Furthermore, seeing beings [in such a state], they do not weep or grieve; having adorned them, they lay them down.
At that very moment, birds of such a kind approach and carry the dead to another continent. Therefore, there is neither a cemetery nor a place of impurity there.
Nor do the dead from that place arise in hell, in the animal realm, or in the sphere of hungry ghosts.
“They are reborn in the world of the gods through the power of the five precepts, which are established by the very nature of things (dhammatāsiddha),” they say.
Furthermore, their lifespan is always exactly one thousand years. All of this should be understood as being established by the very nature of things for them, just like those five precepts.
*Tattha* means in that island of Uttarakuru.
"Having made it single-hoofed" means having made even one with many hooves as if it had only one hoof; the sense is "having made it like a horse.
Since, after saying "cow," he further says "cattle," he states "except for the cow" to show that here all other four-footed animals besides the cow are intended by the term "cattle."
"Of her" means of the pregnant woman. "The back is able to bend" means that due to the heavy burden of the womb, when those [objects] are placed upon it, the back bends;
she is able to endure their sitting down, as if she were seated cross-legged on a couch. "Possessing right view" means possessing right view through the path of action (kamma-patha).
"Therein" means in Jambudīpa; for it is there that the conventional usage of "country" (janapada) occurs.
Not in Uttarakuru; for it is said, "among those dwelling in border regions and among non-Aryans.
"Of that king" refers to the Great King Vessavaṇa. Thus he speaks of himself as if he were another.

This same method applies to the subsequent passages as well. Various celestial vehicles, such as chariots and the like—adorned with many kinds of diverse jewels and having various shapes—are indeed present.
They possess well-tamed mounts to which they are yoked; there is no need for them to exert themselves in the preparation of such vehicles.
"These" refers to the elephant-vehicles and so forth. "Of them" refers to the female attendants of Vessavaṇa. These are the vehicles that become ready and stand up for them to mount.
Even while lying down or sitting, they travel about within their respective celestial mansions like the sun and moon.

He said, "The word *nagarā* is stated with a change of gender (*liṅgavipallāsa*); the meaning is 'there were cities'. *Āṭānāṭā* by name was a city that had received its name according to the feminine gender.

"Standing in that" means standing in that region in the city named Parakusitanāṭā. "From there, straight toward the northern direction. "Of this" refers to the city of Kasivanta. "In the later part" means in the subsequent section; the sense is "further on.
*Kuvera* is his name acquired from his previous birth; by that very context, [it refers to] he by whom this prosperity was attained.
In order to explain his past karma, the passage beginning with “It is said that this one... was spoken. *Ucchuvappaṃ* means a field of sugarcane.
*Avasesasālāhi* means by means of the remaining *yaṃta*-sal trees; this is an ablative expression. *Tattheva* means in that very same sal tree given for the sake of merit.
*Paṭiesanto* means seeking or investigating each individual object (*paṭi paṭi atthe*). Not only did they investigate, but furthermore—
He said, "establishing him in that matter," meaning "examining and instructing him in each respective point.
"Yakkha-raṭṭhika" refers to the lords of the yakkha-kingdoms. And those appointed at the gate of King Vessavaṇa’s residence are the "yakkha-gatekeepers";
it is of these yakkha-gatekeepers [that he speaks].

Because the ancient water, protected by the earth-basin, emerges from below after having been rained down, it is therefore said that "having taken the water from the lotus-pool, the clouds rain," as if it were poured forth by the clouds after being drawn from there.
*Yato* means from that earth-basin. *Sabhā* refers to the assembly hall where the *yakkhas* wait upon [the deities].
"In that place" means in the forest where the *yakkhas* dwell on the bank of that lotus pond. "Always bearing fruit" means having produced fruit at all times.
"Always in bloom" means having flowers produced at all times. "Filled with flocks of various birds" means joined by various kinds of bird-flocks;
indeed, by those throngs of birds flying hither and thither and wheeling about.
Because that lotus pond was as if crowded, it is said: “thronged with flocks of various birds.
“By *koñca* birds” means by *sārasa* waterfowl.
By the phrase “crying out thus,” it is shown that because they cry out in such a manner, their conventional designation is “*jīvañjīvaka*.”
[The text] shows this. Regarding the phrase "with uplifted hearts," the same method applies here as well. Therefore, he said, "raining down in this way.
As for the *Pokkharasātaka* [trees], they received the name *Pokkharasātaka* because of their lotus-like shape.
It "shines at all times" means it shines during all seasons; there is no cessation of its splendor due to winter or any other season.
And thus it shines constantly, being adorned with ever-blooming water and land flowers, surrounded by trees heavily laden with fruit, and possessing water endowed with the eight qualities. 282.
"Preparation" (parikamma) means preliminary service. "Having purified" means, in the presence of the teacher, by way of not failing even in a single syllable.

"Having purified everything": "well-mastered" means that it has been correctly mastered with speech that is well-rounded in its words and phrases, polished, distinct, flawless, and capable of making the meaning known. For it is said: "having thoroughly purified both the meaning and the phrasing.
Indeed, it is only for one who knows the meaning that the phrasing becomes pure, not for one who does not know it.
"Words and phrasing" means without omitting either the words (*pada*) or the phrasing (*byañjana*). For it is in this way that it is called "complete.
"Having misrepresented" means having altered it otherwise. It does not possess majesty because it lacks radiance and because its meaning is not marvelous.
"In all respects" means without exception, from the beginning, the middle, and the end. It possesses majesty because it does not violate the natural linguistic usage.
Because it is accomplished through the state of being well-recited.

Thus, having shown that when there is perfection of application after abandoning failure of application, the protective chant (paritta) accomplishes its purpose, he now says "for the sake of gain," etc., in order to show that when there is perfection of intention after abandoning failure of intention, it accomplishes its purpose.
This recitation of the protective chant is for the sake of warding off harm for sentient beings.

His prior cultivation of knowledge and compassion constitutes the side of renunciation. “Having made loving-kindness the precursor” means having placed before oneself the pervading of beings with thoughts of welfare through the mental application of *mettā*.
“Or the site,” and so forth, is the Blessed One’s announcement of the accomplishment previously performed in the midst of the four assemblies. “The site of the house” (gharavatthu).
"Vasanagehaṃ" means a dwelling place. Even if one dwells in another's house, one should not obtain residence there as a permanent resident (*nevāsika*);
rather, the intention is that staying for a time without the great kings or the yakṣa generals even knowing of it is what is intended by "not measured.
"Samitiṃ" refers to a gathering of yakṣas and others. Although in the Pāḷi it appears as "na me so," [this applies] to the others as well.
However, because the Great Kings shared a single intention, Vessavaṇa spoke thus, keeping their intention in mind as well.
"Anāvayha" means unfit to be married off (anu-anu vahituṃ), that is, unfit to be obtained as a bride at all times;
the meaning is that he is one who cannot be led away [as a bride]. Therefore he said, "not fit for marriage. "Avivayha" means not to be led away [from the family]; [it refers to] a maiden.
The meaning is that it is improper to take [it]. Therefore he said, "not fit for marriage.
That in which the conceit of "I" (ahaṃmāna) is placed is the self (attā), that is, personal existence (attabhāva). Those things which have the self as their object are called *attā*;

these are insults (*paribhāsā*). By means of those [insults], they are made complete through speech. Just as *yakkhas* are to be reviled, so the insults that occur in such a manner are called *yakkha-akkosa*.
Namely, those such as "Kaḷārakkhi," "Kaḷāradantā," and "Kāḷavaṇṇā. "Opposed" (*viruddhā*) means obstructing or being in conflict with others.
"Impetuous" (*rabhasā*) means full of aggression; this is the intended meaning. Therefore he said, "by means of superior action" (*karaṇuttariyā*).
Alternatively, "impetuous" (*rabhasā*) means reckless. "Obedient to the mind of the master" means *manassā*, that is, servants.

Those who, saying "What shall I do, venerable sir?", remain under the control of their master are spoken of in this way. Therefore it was said: "Of those who are the mind-servants of the yakkha generals.
Those who are restrained by command are called "restrained" (avaruddha); however, since they are adversaries to the one who gives the command, it is said:
"enemies and foes" (paccāmittā verino). "Should be censured" (ujjhāpetabbaṃ) refers to what follows below.
Having reflected thus, one should consider it; for that "informing" (*ujjhāpana*) is the making known of their lowly deed, hence he said, "they should be made to know.
Commentary on the Discussion of the Preparatory Rite for the *Paritta*:
The preparatory rite for the *paritta* must be explained; thus, the preparatory rite for the *Āṭānāṭiya-paritta* consists of the preliminary service (*pubbupacāra*).
The *Mettasutta* and other such discourses should be recited; for in this way, having become well-practiced, they become powerful. Therefore he said, "First indeed," and so forth.
In the phrase "either flour or meat," the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of non-restriction; by it, fish, ghee, soup, and so on, are included.
They find an opportunity [to enter] by way of food that is dear to oneself and by way of a place that is dear to oneself.
By the words, “The *paritta*... should be sat down,” it is shown that even the purity of the monk reciting the *paritta* must be desired.
The passage, “The reciter of the *paritta*...
surrounded on all sides,” refers to the provision of external protection during the recitation of the *paritta*.
“‘A mind of loving-kindness... should be practiced’—this is the internal protection and the arrangement of protection on both sides.
For in this way, non-human beings are unable to create obstacles for the performance of the protective recitation (paritta).

The discourse on auspiciousness (maṅgala) should be recited by way of preliminary service. ‘The assembly of all’ means the gathering of all the bhikkhus in that monastery or within the precincts of that village.”

It should be announced: "Everyone must assemble in the courtyard of the cetiya. It is not permissible for anyone not to come, whether due to fear of non-human beings (*amanussa*) or fear of the king's command.
Since it is a non-human being who has been questioned under the pretext of having been seized, it is said: "The one seized by a non-human being should be asked, 'What is your name?
This refers to when [the requisites] such as garlands and perfumes are being assigned for the purpose of worship.
“*Patti*” means the gift of merit to you. “*Patti in alms-food*” means the gift of merit when alms-food is being given.

“*To the deities*” refers to the generals of the *yakkhas*. “*The protective chant (*paritta*) should be recited*” — here too, everything such as “having preceded with a mind of loving-kindness,” “the discourse on auspiciousness (*maṅgalakathā*) should be spoken,” and “in the grove of the monastery,” applies to the performance of protective chants for laypeople.
The preliminary work (parikamma) already described must indeed be performed.
"He resolves upon the body" means that, as if entering the body, he takes possession of it;
he resolves and remains fixed by means of his own power alone, so that it no longer functions according to the will of the one who grasped it [in life]. Therefore, he said:
“‘It enters’ is a synonym for that very [state]. It clings means it remains attached and adheres right there. Therefore he said, “it does not depart.
“Increasing the disease” means increasing the disease that has arisen due to the inability of the elements to function in equilibrium.
And by the occurrence of disharmony among the elements and the lack of appetite for food, that which has been grasped...

The blood in the body dries up and the flesh withers; however, because the *yakkha* acts as if causing this through the agitation of the elements (*dhātu*), it is said, "making [the body] scant in flesh and blood.
(283) Their names are so called because they are designated by such names as Indra and others. "From that" means after that announcement. "Them" refers to...
"Yakkha generals": "There will be no opportunity" means there will be no chance to harass monks, nuns, laymen, or laywomen, because they have been properly provided with protection.
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Hidden Meaning) on the commentary to the *Āṭānāṭiya-sutta*.
10. Commentary on the Saṅgītisutta 296.
"In ten thousand world-systems" means in world-systems numbering ten thousand that constitute the Buddha-field (*buddhakhetta*).
For in this [central] world-system, only gods and humans have performed their duties; in the others, the gods partake of excellence. Therefore...

It is said: "having spread the net of knowledge over the ten-thousandfold world-system. This "spreading of the net of knowledge" is simply the operation of knowledge by way of discerning the underlying tendencies (*āsaya*) and other traits of various beings. Therefore, he said:

"surveying the world," meaning surveying the world of beings (*sattaloka*), seeing it by specifically penetrating their underlying tendencies (*āsaya*), latent dispositions (*anusaya*), temperament (*carita*), and inclinations (*adhimutti*).

The meaning is this: they will cause blessings to be recited [with the thought], "May that become for them a ground of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*) for the attainment of distinction in the future, and may it lead to their welfare and happiness for a long time.

"Having comprehended by means of the three Piṭakas" means having comprehended—that is, having investigated—by way of grouping together those things to be grouped from the three Piṭakas according to single items, pairs, and so forth. "Questions" are the matters desired to be known.
However, he says, "having adorned it with one thousand and fourteen questions," because in this sutta they appear by way of the single [question] and so forth,
totaling one thousand and fourteen. Thus, having presented the questions here in summary, he will later, at the conclusion of the sutta,
demonstrate them himself by counting them through analysis, beginning with, "two questions were stated by way of the single [question]," and so on.
297. Description of the Ubbhataka New Assembly Hall:
Because it was established on high, that assembly hall appeared as if lifted up from the ground; thus it received the name “Ubbhataka.
Therefore he said: “It is called such because of its height. “Assembly hall” (*sandhāgāra*) refers to a single large hall used for purposes such as preparing for military expeditions.
For kings, having stood there, sit down and settle matters by saying things such as, "Let so many go forward, let so many stay behind," and they establish boundaries;

therefore, that place is called a *sandhāgāra*. Furthermore, from the time they arrive at the site of departure until they reach home and attend to the cleaning of the floor with cow-dung and so forth, for one or two [muhūrtas], it is so designated.
It is called a *sandhāgāra* because kings assemble there during the day; it is also called a *sandhāgāra* because it is the hall where those kings consult together on matters of state.

Alternatively, because they gather there and coordinate the duties of household life—such as saying, "It is appropriate to plow at this time, and to sow at this time"—it is therefore called a *sandhāgāra*, meaning a house that holds together the domestic life in its every detail.
In this context, it is called a *sandhāgāra* because they gather (*sandharanti*) there; that very hall is thus a *sandhāgārasālā*.
"Deities" refers to the household deities. Because it was not inhabited by them as a dwelling place, it is said, "or by any human being.
However, humans did indeed perform activities such as sitting there for the purpose of carrying out work. But [the thought occurred]: "The Teacher’s coming here himself—this is for us..."
Showing that they thought correctly in this way—being joyful and delighted, thinking, "It is solely by virtue of our merit; oh, how meritorious we are!"—the text says, "By us," and so forth.
(298) *Aṭṭakā* refers to the platforms constructed for the purpose of painting. *Muttamattā* means that at that very moment the new work on the assembly hall was completed;
by this, it clarifies the meaning already expressed by the phrase "not long since built," and so on.
Those for whom the forest (*arañña*) and the monastery (*ārāma*)—that is, the place to be delighted in—are their [dwelling] are "forest-dwellers" (*araññārāmā*).

"Sabbasanthari" means that which spreads out (*santharaṇa*), or where everything (*sabba*)—meaning the whole—is spread out; this is a designation in the neuter abstract form (*bhāvanapuṃsaka*). Therefore he said:
"Just as it is entirely spread out."
299. *Samantapāsādika* means that which brings forth confidence from every side, in every respect, due to its elegance.
The statement, “It occupies a space of eighty cubits,” is said because the bodily radiance of the Buddhas naturally pervades a space of eighty cubits.

However, by means of the power of supernormal success (*iddhi*), it shines even over an infinite and immeasurable space. This is according to the [six] colors: blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, and translucent.
"Six-colored. "All the quarters of space": this is said because of the abundance of the radiance from his body.

A void obscured by clouds, mist, and the like does not shine; however, the sky when filled with stars shines forth, resplendent on all sides with their radiance. Thus he said: "like the vault of heaven with its stars risen."

“Sabbapāliphulla” means blooming from the roots up to the tips of the branches. The phrase beginning with “paṭipāṭiyāṭhapitānaṃ” (of those placed in succession) and so forth is a simile based on a supposition;
for that reason, the word “viya” (as if) is employed. “Overpowering their own glory with its glory” means that by means of its own splendor, it surpasses their splendor.
The statement “all the bhikkhus as well” refers to them [the trees] as being “of few desires,” and so forth.
This should be applied by way of the mundane qualities among the qualities mentioned. For not all of them are attainers of the ten bases of discourse (*dasakathāvatthu*).
Therefore it was said: “Having reflected upon the Suttanta... they will reach Arahantship. Consequently, those among them who are noble ones (*ariya*) are indicated by way of all the terms;
however, those who are worldlings (*puthujjana*) [are indicated] by those terms that illustrate mundane qualities.
Regarding the phrase "padehi" (with his feet), it was not stated below as "the eighty great elders," and so forth; for previously, those destined for *arahantship* were included.

The "Buddha-appearance" (*buddhaveso*) consists precisely in the physical body being adorned with the eighty minor marks, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man, and the variegated splendor of the bodily radiance, the halo, and the garland of light.
[This applies] to the body of the Blessed One as he emits the six-colored rays of a Buddha during his looking forward, looking around, and so on.
It is the supreme excellence, the unique quality of a Buddha, the ultimate tranquility, and the grace of a Buddha. "Therein" means in that [assembly].

"Connected with the Discourse on the Delight in the Council Hall" refers to that which is associated with the virtues of the council hall—beginning with the phrase "it wards off cold and heat"—and which pertains to the benefits of the merit arising from the construction of the council hall.
"Miscellaneous discourse" refers to those discourses not included in the formal recitations (*saṅgīti*), which are for the benefit of those who listen.
The detailed exposition is adorned with various and extensive similes and reasons according to their respective inclinations, and is variegated by manifold methods.

Therefore, he said, "Then indeed," and so forth. This is because, like bringing down the Ganges from the sky, it allays the fever of body and mind for those who hear it through its meaning, which is perfectly pure due to being free from defilement and immeasurable due to its vast and noble nature.
Like one pulling earth from a field, it is because the meaning is extremely difficult for others to grasp or because of its great essence.

Like one holding a great rose-apple tree by its top and shaking it, it is because of connecting what precedes with what follows by way of the conditions for such movement. Like one who, while traveling a league...
[etc. ...is nursing a child, it is because of casting the teaching into the end of the Four Noble Truths, resulting only in the knowledge of the meaning and the knowledge of the Dhamma.
Because it brings about the attainment [of the goal] by providing the nectar of the Dhamma, which is pleasant and sweet. "Honey-clump" (*madhugaṇḍa*) means a mass of honey.
Regarding the phrase "to each one who was silent," this repetition (*āmeḍita-vacana*) is stated to show that it expresses a desire for a response;
thus, the words "whichever... whichever" and so forth were spoken. In the word *anuviloketvā*, the prefix *anu* has the same meaning as *pari*.
In this context, it should be understood that the Teacher’s surveying was performed with both of his two eyes.
Having stated it briefly as, “having looked here and there with the fleshly eye...,” the passage beginning with “With the fleshly eye... is spoken in order to demonstrate that matter in detail.
“Hand-fidgeting” (*hatthakukkucca*) refers to what is done with the hand in a fidgety manner; it is called “fidgeting” because it is simply a state of being ill-composed. Thus...
One should understand this as "foot-fidgeting. They sat motionless due to their own well-disciplined nature and out of reverence for the Buddha.
The phrase beginning with “But having increased the light,” etc., is stated with the intention that the Blessed One sometimes acts in this manner as well;
for this knowledge is not something to be accomplished through such an effort on the part of the Teacher’s disciples. It [perceives] even what is hidden or situated at a great distance.
Since the occurrence of the fleshly eye regarding visible forms is desired, this must be investigated. "The state of Arahantship, the basis for Arahantship":

having placed the sign upon the surfaces of their eyes—meaning, by virtue of their success in the application of meditation, the sign consisting of the aspect of tranquil faculties and the absence of sloth and torpor found on the surfaces of the eyes of all those bhikkhus—[he placed it] upon his own.
"Having placed [it] in the heart and observed it. The intention of the objector is: "Why does he feel weary?

Because he is bearing the strength of a hundred thousand million elephant-kings. The Master [replies]: "This is the very nature of conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), namely, impermanence (*aniccatā*).

But those things which are impermanent are, by their very nature, suffering (*dukkha*) precisely because they are oppressed by arising and passing away. Among those things whose nature is suffering..."
Among those, in order to show that this was the condition for the arising of suffering in the Teacher’s body, it was said, "To the Blessed One," and so forth.
Back-wind arose, and that indeed was due to the condition of karma performed in the past.
This matter should be understood according to the method presented in the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the *Udāna*.
Commentary on the Story of the Split Nigaṇṭhas: 301.
This has already been stated below in the commentary on the *Pāsādika Sutta*.
302. "Desirous of teaching the well-expounded Dhamma" means desirous of speaking the Dhamma after having made it well-expounded by the Teacher.

Or, wishing himself to explain the well-proclaimed Dhamma to the bhikkhus, he does so; for indeed, it is by taking up precisely the Dhamma taught by the Teacher from here and there that disciples explain it to their fellow celibates.
(Commentary on the Single Stanza)
303. "It should be spoken by those who are in harmony" means that it should be spoken by those who have become harmonious with one another;

the sense is that it should both be recited (*sajjhāyitabba*) and praised (*vaṇṇetabba*). To show how the communal chanting (*saṅgāyana*) takes place among those in harmony, the phrase beginning with "with single voices" (*ekavacanehi*) was stated.
"With single voices" means with identical voices due to the absence of contradiction. Therefore he said: "with non-contradictory voices," and so forth.

"Desiring to show the flavor of concord" means that, through skill in teaching, he wishes to demonstrate in many ways—by way of single instances, pairs, triads, and so forth—the experience of the flavor of concord within that Dhamma recitation for which it is desired.
"All beings" refers to beings without exception; showing them by briefly dividing them according to the different types of existence (*bhava*).

He said, “In the sense-sphere existence and so forth,” and so on. A compound with an external meaning (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) occurs even between words in different grammatical cases, as in the example “hair-on-the-chest” (*urasiloma*);
thus he said, “Their subsistence is by means of nutriment, hence they are ‘subsisting by nutriment’ (*āhāraṭṭhitikā*).

Alternatively, the analysis of the compound here should be understood as: “That by which one stands is ‘subsistence’ (*ṭhiti*); their subsistence is nutriment, hence they are ‘subsisting by nutriment. “Subsisting by nutriment” means subsisting by way of conditions.

The meaning is: "existing in dependence on conditions. Here, the word *āhāra* (nutriment) has the sense of "condition," as in such passages as: "This nutriment leads to the arising of unarisen sensual desire," and so forth.
For in this way, by the phrase "all beings," even non-percipient beings (*asaññasatta*) are included.
Furthermore, this state of being sustained by nutriment is, in the ultimate sense, a conditioned phenomenon (*saṅkhāradhamma*), not a phenomenon pertaining to a "being" (*sattadhamma*).
For this very reason, the commentators of the Aṭṭhakathā say: "In the passage where it is stated, 'All beings subsist by nutriment,' the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka) is to be understood.
If that is so, how is it that [the text] says, "All beings"? This is not a fault, for this teaching is based on individuals (puggalādhiṭṭhānā).
As the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu becomes completely disenchanted with one thing, completely dispassionate toward it, and completely liberated from it..."
“Seeing the limit rightly and having fully realized rightness, one makes an end of suffering in this very life.
What is that one thing? ‘All beings subsist by nutriment’—this is the one thing.

Thus, regarding the statement “all beings subsist by nutriment,” it is said that in discourse which is expressed in terms of persons (*puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhārā*) exist in dependence upon conditions, by way of the category of nutriment.

The condition-dhamma has been stated in general; this single dhamma is called nutriment (*āhāra*). "Having known it as it truly is" means having fully awakened to its intrinsic nature (*yathāsabhāvato*).
"Well-expounded" means taught correctly in the very manner in which it was fully awakened to.
One who is critical, failing to practice even what has been spoken as it truly is, [misinterprets] a sutta passage of interpretable meaning (*neyyattha*) as being of definitive meaning (*nītattha*).
Burning [with anger], he stands on the mere words "all beings" and challenges [the author] with the words beginning "But surely...
The Teacher, proclaiming therein the intended meaning without error, says "It is not contradictory," and then states: "For their nutriment is jhāna.
"Jhāna" here refers to the fourth fine-material-sphere (rūpāvacara) jhāna, which brings about existence in the single-aggregate realm (ekavokāra-bhava) by way of fading away from perception (saññā).

In the Pāḷi, however, the statement “without nutriment” (*anāhārā*) is said with reference to the absence of the four kinds of nutriment in the non-percipient realm (*asañña-bhava*), not because of the absence of nutriment as a condition (*paccaya-āhāra*).

Regarding the phrase “even though this is so,” if only those things in which the word “nutriment” is specifically conventionalized within the Teaching were taken here in the expression “subsisting by nutriment” (*āhāraṭṭhitikā*), then the fault of being too narrow (*abyāpitadosa*) would follow. Now, if...
It was begun in order to show that [the statement] "all conditioned phenomena (paccaya-dhamma) are intended as nutriment" would fall into contradiction with this passage on nutriment (*āhāra-pāḷi*).
To explain the intention with which it was said, "it is not contradictory," he said, "For in this sutta... and so forth.

The status of being nutriment in the primary sense (*nippariyāya*) belongs to edible food and the others because they bring about the eightfold materiality consisting of nutritive essence (*oja*). For just as edible food...

By taking in the material form consisting of the eightfold nutritive essence (*ojas*), it supports the material body; likewise, contact and the other [mental factors] support the mental body by taking in feeling and the rest.

Therefore, although they possess the quality of being producers, the specific state of supporting found in the nutritive essence and so forth is predominant and constitutes their primary function as nutriment.
Thus, those very phenomena characterized by the nature of nutriment have been described in this way. Herein:
In this *Saṅgītisutta*, nutriment (*āhāra*) is called a condition (*paccaya*) by way of a figurative expression (*pariyāya*).
Every conditioned phenomenon (*dhamma*) that is a condition receives this designation because it brings about its own fruit. Therefore, he said: "For of all phenomena," and so forth.
Therein, "of all phenomena" means of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhata-dhamma*). Now, in order to support the aforementioned point with a sutta:
“By that very [means],” and so forth, is what was stated.
“This” refers to nutriment as condition (*paccayāhāra*). Even the figurative nutriment (*nippariyāyāhāra*) is included;

for insofar as it too produces and supports [the result] by way of being a condition, it receives the designation [of nutriment]. Therein, there is both figurative nutriment and non-figurative nutriment.

Regarding the two kinds of nutriment: although in the non-percipient realm (*asaññabhava*) the literal nutriment (*nippariyāyāhāra*) is not found, the conditional nutriment (*paccayāhāra*), which possesses the characteristic of figurative nutriment (*pariyāyāhāra*), is indeed found.
Now, in order to demonstrate this very point in detail, it was said: "For when a Buddha has not arisen," and so forth.
Because the cultivation of jhāna is not possible for those who rely on the doctrines of other teachers once a Buddha has arisen, [the text specifies] "when a Buddha has not arisen."
It is said, "in the Buddha's [dispensation]. Since those belonging to the Dispensation do not produce such a jhāna, it is said, "those who have gone forth in a sectarian order.

For the sectarians (titthiyas), perceiving liberation in a specific mode of rebirth, or seeing the danger in the absence of knowledge and dispassion and the benefit in their presence, produce the attainment of non-percipient beings and are reborn in a plane where there is no opportunity for progress; but those belonging to the Dispensation do not. Regarding the wind-kasiṇa:

"Having performed the preliminary work" means: having produced the first three jhānas in the air kasiṇa, and having mastered the third jhāna, one emerges from it and performs the preliminary work for the attainment of the fourth jhāna. Therefore he said, "having produced the fourth jhāna.
Why, however, is the preliminary work mentioned here specifically in relation to the air kasiṇa? Whatever is to be said on this point—
This has already been explained in detail in the *Brahmajāla-ṭīkā*. *Dhī* is a particle used in the sense of loathing;
therefore, *dhī cittaṃ* means "I loathe the mind. *Dhibbatetaṃ cittaṃ* means "May this mind of mine indeed become loathed.
*Vata* expresses esteem (*sambhāvane*); thus, he speaks while esteeming that loathing. *Nāma* also expresses esteem.
In this way, he conceives of the non-existence of the mind. To show the danger and the benefit regarding the existence and non-existence of the mind, it is said: "For the mind...

and so forth. "Having generated patience and preference" means having generated this patient contemplation of views (*diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti*)—namely, that "the non-existence of the mind alone is good and excellent"—and having developed a liking for that.

Because one who has developed jhāna reaches the state of being "partaking of stability" (ṭhitibhāgiya) and thus possesses undiminished jhāna, such development of jhāna occurs only for one who has gone forth in a dispensation (titthāyatana);
therefore, he said, "in the human world. "Was established" means it was placed [in the mind] at the time near death.
If it were to arise through a mode such as standing and so forth, it would persist until the breaking up of the body by the power of kamma.
"He might remain in that very same posture" refers to the passage beginning with "by means of that posture.
"Even of such things as these" means even of such things as are insentient. By the word "even," he shows that it is all the more so for those things that are sentient.
Anticipating the objection, "But how can nutriment be beneficial to these insentient things? he provides an illustration in that regard.
Demonstrating this, he said, "Just as," and so forth.

Those who spend the day solely through exertion and diligence, and having obtained some mere trifling result as its overflow, maintain their livelihood, are those who subsist on the fruit of exertion. But those who subsist solely on the fruit of their own merit—
They are those who subsist on the fruit of merit. However, for those in the hells, there is neither the making of a livelihood through initiative and effort, nor even a trace of the fruit of merit;
thus it is said: "But as for those hell-beings... they are not said to subsist on the fruit of merit.
It is called "nutriment consisting of mental volition" by way of providing sustenance for the rebirth-linking consciousness, and not for anyone else whatsoever.
With the intention of [refuting] the "fruit," he challenges [the opponent] by asking, "Are there five nutriments?

The teacher says, "'Five' or 'not five'—this should not be said," in order to show that while your challenge might find its place if the nutriment intended were the non-figurative (nippariyāya) one, that challenge has no place here; and then, showing that it is indeed the figurative (pariyāya) nutriment that is intended here:
“Is it not said that ‘a condition is nutriment’? he asked. “Therefore” means because any condition whatsoever is intended by the term “nutriment.
Now, in order to support the very point just stated with the canonical text (pāḷi), he said, “With reference to which...,” and so forth.
Furthermore, in order to show that even by way of primary nutriment the inhabitants of hell are sustained by nutriment, he said, “Edible nutriment...,” and so forth.
"...it accomplishes [its function]," it is said. If this is so, do those in the hell realms also experience pleasure? No; in order to show this, "even saliva," and so forth, was stated.
"Three" refers to the three immaterial nutriments, because of the absence of physical nutriment (kabaḷīkārāhāra).

"Of the remainder" means of those remaining after excluding the non-percipient beings (asaññasatta). For nutriment as a condition for beings born in the sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava) and so on belongs to all of them.
"Common" (*sādhāraṇa*). "This question": this refers to the question thus posed, "What is the one single state? "Having explained" means having answered.

By the passage, "In this and that [instance]... suffering arises," just as here the first question was concluded and the second was not extracted, so too, with this same intention, regarding the subsequent questions concerning the "threefold pairs" (*dukatika*) and so forth—
This shows that in those various places, the extraction (*uddharaṇa*) and the handing over (*niyyātanā*) were performed only at the beginning and the end, but not for the remaining sections.
"Condition" (*paccaya*) means that from this [cause] the fruit proceeds; it is the cause. Because it itself conditions its own fruit, it is called "volitional formation" (*saṅkhāra*);
thus he says: "In this [context] as well... it is called 'volitional formation'. "Nutriment-condition" (*āhārapaccaya*) is a condition distinguished by the sense of nourishing (*āharaṇa*).
In this context, bringing forth (*āharaṇa*) has the primary function of producing, while consolidating (*saṅkharana*) has the primary function of supporting;
this is the distinction between them. Therefore it was said: "This is the distinction here from the preceding [section].
When the literal sense of nutriment is taken, even if one says "all beings," non-percipient beings would not be included; thus, the word "all" has a limited scope, just as...
In such passages as “All tremble at the rod,” etc., there is no inclusion of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) and so forth.
For it would have been evident [that they were excluded], since questions pertain to both the specific and the general. Yet the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā did not include them.

The intention is that there is no such thing as a conditioned phenomenon (dhamma) that is unconditioned (asaṅkhata). Here, in the second question, the connection is that “volitional formation” (saṅkhāra) is spoken of specifically as a condition.

When he had attained full enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), at that very moment all that is to be known (sabbaññeyya) became realized; thus he said, "having sat upon the great seat of enlightenment (mahābodhimaṇḍa).
"Sāyaṃ" means by himself alone. "Addhaniyaṃ" means capable of enduring a journey, persisting for a long time by way of succession.

Therefore he said, "by one [person]," and so forth. "By the rule of successive narration" (paramparakathāniyamenā) means by the rule of narrating in succession—that is, by the sequence of meaning and phrasing as they have been determined.
The meaning is "by way of the discourse. "By way of the single [questions]" means: that which has a single [question] as its measure is "single" (*ekaka*); it refers to the question.
"By way of that single [question]"—the intention is that the answer for the single [question] is completed.
The commentary on the single [questions] is finished.
Commentary on the Suffering (Dukkha): 304.
Having first stated that the four aggregates possess the nature of "name" (*nāma*) by way of their being designated, he speaks next with the intention of describing the same for Nibbāna;
for he will later explain how even that possesses such a nature of being named, in the sense that "it names" or "it causes to bend."
Regarding this, he says "in the sense of naming" (*nāmanaṭṭhena*) meaning "in the sense of the act of naming" (*nāmakaraṇaṭṭhena*), with the intention that it refers to their own names.
For in this way, this naming of theirs is preeminent. Therefore he said: "They arise while actually making their own names," and so forth.
Now, in order to clarify this matter by way of contrast, he stated: "Just as... and so on.
That name by the mere act of being given which they are called "name" is not a common name (*sāmañña-nāma*), a fame-based name (*kittima-nāma*), or a quality-based name (*guṇa-nāma*);

rather, it is a spontaneously arisen name (*opapātika-nāma*). Having thus shown the three preceding types of names by way of illustration and having rejected them with the words "not so for feeling and the rest," [the author] shows that the other type of name alone is "name" in the sense of "making a name."
He says, “For feeling and so forth,” and so on. As for the statement, “The great earth and so forth,” one might ask:
“Is it not the case that here the earth, water, and so forth are not intended as ‘name’ (nāma), but rather as ‘form’ (rūpa)? This is true;

however, because the earth and so forth share the commonality of being spontaneously arisen names (*opapātika-nāmatā*), they are used as an illustration in the phrase “just like the earth and so forth,” in the same way as contact, feeling, and the rest.
It is so called because, unlike immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), material phenomena (*rūpadhamma*) do not possess the intrinsic nature of "name" (*nāma*).

For immaterial phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and feeling (*vedanā*) always have the name "contact," etc., and because they never undergo a change of name—unlike earth and so forth, which might pass from being called "hair" to "the frontal globe of an elephant"—they are always designated by their own names.
Thus, the four aggregates and Nibbāna are "name" in the sense of being the makers of names (*nāmakaraṇattha*). Now...

Just as the contact of designation (*adhivacana-saṃphassa*) does not come to be grasped by those who have not accumulated the necessary requisites without the name of designation, those [phenomena] whose grasping is dependent on the name are called "name" (*nāma*).
Form (*rūpa*), however, reaches its state of being grasped by means of its own intrinsic nature of being affected (*ruppana-sabhāva*), even without the instrument of a name;
thus it is "form. Therefore he said: "When these have arisen," and so forth. Here too, in the phrases beginning with "just as in the case of the earth," etc., [the same principle applies].
The meaning should be understood in the same manner as previously stated, because it is presented by way of illustration.
By the phrase "In the past, too," and so forth, he shows that the designation "name" (nāma) is established for feeling and the other aggregates, and that this [designation] is beginningless.

Thus, even though feeling and the others possess divisions such as past and so forth, their status as "name" (nāmabhāva) is absolute in the sense of being a maker of names; this is so even when they are devoid of those specific divisions.
However, showing that there is nothing whatsoever to be said regarding nibbāna—which is of a single nature and permanent—he says:

“But nibbāna... is called ‘name’ in the sense of naming. “In the sense of naming” means in the sense of being designated as a name. “They incline” means that because they invariably have an object, they lean toward it;
the meaning is that they do not function without them. “All” refers to the four aggregates and nibbāna. In which...
The aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) occurs only with respect to the object; because they are associated with it, the aggregates of perception (saññākkhandha) and the others also occur therein.
Thus, it is as if that [feeling] leads them there, since they do not occur without it. This same method applies to the aggregates of perception and the rest;
hence it is said, "they lead one another toward the object. "In blameless states" refers to the paths, fruits, and so forth. Although in some...

The status of being an object-dominance condition (ārammaṇādhipati) is indeed found even among material phenomena; however, this is especially prominent in Nibbāna because its nature consists in absolute peace and excellence.
Therefore, it is said that [Nibbāna] "directs itself toward itself" by way of being an object-dominance condition.
For in this way, even when Noble Ones spend an entire day occupied with it as their object, they never reach satiety.
“By way of being afflicted (*ruppanaṭṭhena*): by this he shows that it is called *rūpa* because it is afflicted (*ruppati*).

In this context, *ruppana* is the production of a dissimilar state when there is a convergence of opposing conditions such as cold and so forth. But is it not the case that even non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*) obtain a dissimilar production when there is a meeting of opposing conditions?
True, they do obtain it, but it is not more manifest (*vibhūtatara*). For here, it is this more manifest form of affliction that is intended.
[It is so called] because of being affected by cold and so forth. For this has been said: "Bhikkhus, it is because it is affected (ruppati) that it is called 'form' (rūpa).
By what is it affected? It is affected by cold, and it is affected by heat," and so on. If this is so, how is there the designation "form" in the Brahma-world?
Even there, the designation "form" certainly exists because of not transcending that intrinsic nature (taṃsabhāva). Or [it may be understood] by way of supporting conditions.
The meaning should be understood as "the coming together of dissimilar conditions. Others say:

"That which is the state of being a cause for the arising of something dissimilar within one's own continuity, that is *ruppana* (being affected). In this view, *rūpa* means that which "is affected" (*ruppayati*), i.e., brings about a change.
Some say: "The word *ruppana* is conventionally established in the sense of undergoing change through impact. In this view...

In the case of non-material phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), there is no possibility of applying the designation "matter" (*rūpa*) because of the absence of impingement (*saṅghaṭṭana*). Others say: "Impingement is the state of being struck (*ruppana*).
They explain: "Of that" means "of matter. However, it is more appropriate [to read it] as "of name-and-matter" (*nāmarūpassa*).

For just as there is a detailed exposition for matter, so too for name—by way of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanākkhandha*) and so forth, and by way of the crushing of pride (*madanimmadana*) and so forth—as set forth in the *Visuddhimagga*.
"Thus they have been stated. In this way, this dyad functions by encompassing those phenomena that possess intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) as included within the triad of the wholesome (*kusala*).
Regarding "ignorance" (*avijjā*): it is ignorance because it finds (*vindati*) what should not be found—such as "self," "living being," "woman," "man," and so forth.

It is ignorance because it does not find what should be found—such as "suffering," "the origin [of suffering]," and so forth. Furthermore, the entire collection of phenomena (*dhammajāta*) is ignorance in the sense of making things unknown.
Ignorance (*avijjā*). It is called ignorance because it causes sentient beings to rush headlong into the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) when that cycle has not yet ceased.
As for its essential meaning, it is the delusion that obscures the intrinsic nature of the four truths, beginning with suffering; thus it is said: "ignorance regarding suffering and the rest.

Craving for existence (*bhavapatthanā*) refers to the craving that functions by way of longing for the realms of existence, such as the sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*); hence he says: "that which is the desire for existence among the various states of being," and so forth.
Thus, this dyad is taken for the purpose of showing the manifestation of the root of the round.
“Becoming-view” (bhava-diṭṭhi) means the eternalist view established by grasping the five aggregates as “self and world” and apprehending them with the thought, “It will continue to exist.
Therefore he said, “‘Becoming’ is so called,” and so forth. That which will be is “becoming” (bhava).
“Exists at all times” means that it persists; this is the meaning of *sassata*. “Eternalism” (*sassata*) is the state of being eternal. “Annihilationist view” (*vibhavadiṭṭhi*):
having grasped the very pentad of aggregates as “self” and “the world,” it is the settled view of annihilationism (*ucchedadiṭṭhi*) by way of apprehending that [self/world] as “it will not exist”;

this is the meaning. Therefore he said, “‘Annihilation’ (*vibhava*) is said,” and so forth. It is called “annihilation” (*vibhava*) because it will cease to be, perish, or be cut off; thus it is annihilation (*uccheda*).
"By which one does not feel shame" means: by whichever dhamma the collection of dhammas associated with it, or the person, does not feel shame or embarrassment;
or, having applied a change of gender, the meaning should be understood as "by whichever dhamma.

"That which ought to be felt as shame" is an instrumental case used in the sense of the accusative; it means that one does not feel disgust toward the dhammas such as bodily misconduct that are fit to be felt as shame.

Meaning: Shamelessness (*nillajjatā*) is the lack of disgust toward evil. Regarding the phrase "that which one does not dread," the meaning should be understood here in the same manner as previously stated.
However, in the expression "by that which is to be dreaded" (*ottappitabbena*), the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause; the meaning is:

"by means of bodily misconduct and so forth, which are fit to be dreaded and which serve as the causes for dread. In the expression "by that which is to be felt shamefully" (*hirīyitabbena*), it should be understood in exactly the same way.
The meaning should be understood as follows: "The mode of not being terrified" means the mode of not being struck with fear regarding evil.
The meaning of such phrases as "that which one feels shame for" should be understood according to the method explained in the immediately preceding dyad.

That which has its origination within oneself—namely, birth and so forth—is "internally originated. Because it exists outside of one's own internal self, its origination occurs externally, in the mental continuum of another.

"Of these" means originating externally. "Self-mastery" (*attādhipati*) is the self itself as the dominant factor; because it originates internally, it is called "having the self as its master" (*attādhipateyya*) by virtue of coming from self-mastery.
The same principle applies here to the term "having the world as its master" (*lokādhipateyya*).
"Established in the nature of shame" means established in the form of loathing evil. "Established in the nature of fear" means...

Therefore, it remains in the form of a state of agitation. Furthermore, the fact that moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*) originate internally and so forth is stated because they are manifest in various contexts;
however, this is not because they are ever dissociated from one another.
For there is no shame that is devoid of fear, nor is there a dread of evil that is devoid of shame.

"Dukkha" means hardship, or its meaning is "undesirable. "Vippaṭikūlagāhī" refers to one who grasps [the teaching] in a manner contrary to the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (dhammānudhammapaṭipatti).
"Vipaccanīkasāta" means that which has a disagreeable practice as its pleasant or desirable aspect;

thus, it refers to one who finds pleasure in what is contrary [to the teaching]. One who is thus disposed lacks respect for the Teacher's instruction and for those who give such instruction within the sequence of the Dispensation.
He said, "In the sense of disrespect. "Its action" means the volition proceeding by way of disrespect toward that person who is difficult to speak to;
this is "difficult-to-speak-to-ness" (*dovacassa*). "The state of that" means the state of existence of that aforementioned difficult-to-speak-to-ness;
it is difficult-to-speak-to-ness itself in terms of its actual meaning. For this very reason, he said: "In terms of its meaning, it is the aggregate of mental formations (*saṅkhārakkhandha*)."

For it is because the aggregate of volitional formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) is dominated by volition (cetanā) that this has been stated. "In this manner" means in the manner of grasping what is contrary to the right path.
The passage beginning with "those persons who are faithless" was spoken to show that persons are called "evil" due to their association with evil qualities such as lack of faith and immorality.
That volition by which a person becomes one who is "crooked through evil" is [the volition described here].
Showing that "bad friendship" (*pāpamittatā*)—or alternatively, the four formless aggregates (*arūpino khandhā*) occurring in that mode—is itself bad friendship, he said:
"That too, in its actual meaning, should be regarded as being like 'difficult-to-speak-to-ness' (*dovacassatā*).

[He explained] "one who is easy to speak to" (*subbaco*) and so forth by means of such phrases as: "One in whom speech is pleasant—that person who grasps things in a favorable way, who is compliant, amiable, and respectful."

And because the meaning of the immediately preceding pair is intended [here] as "one who has virtuous friends (kalyāṇamitta) is one whose friends are virtuous persons such as those endowed with faith," he says:
"Being easy to speak to... should be understood by way of the opposites of what was stated. "Both" refers to being easy to speak to and having virtuous friends.
The specific modes of the occurrence of those aggregates are "being easy to speak to" and "having virtuous friends."
And since they are said to be both mundane (*lokiya*) and supramundane (*lokuttara*), it was stated: "They are spoken of as a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.

Because they are divided into many categories according to the distinction of their bases (*vatthu*) and so forth, yet are taken collectively as a heap (*rāsi*) by way of their respective classes, they are indeed "classes of offenses" (*āpattikkhandha*).
Furthermore, when intermediate offenses (*antarāpatti*) are not included, there are five such classes of offenses.
There are offenses; moreover, in their inclusion, there are seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).

The wisdom that knows: "These are the offenses, there are this many offenses, and such is the manner of their commission," is skill in offenses (*āpattikusalatā*). Thus he said, "Of those [offenses]," and so forth. "Of those offenses" means among those offenses.
In that regard, when they stand as if having mixed bases (*vatthu*), their distinctions are difficult to discern.
And the second mention of "offense" is made to show specifically what is called skill in offenses: namely, the determination [of offenses] without confusion regarding them.

"Together with the formal act" (saha kammavācāya) means together with the formal act itself. A "formal act" (kammavācā) is speech that constitutes a formal act because it serves as the procedure for emerging from an offense;
such speech includes both the speech of the proclamation (*anusāvana*) and the speech proceeding thus: "I shall see [the offense]."
Simultaneously with that formal proclamation (kammavācā), the wisdom that thoroughly understands the delimitation of emergence from each respective offense—
knowing that "by this formal proclamation there is emergence from this offense; and while the first or third proclamation is being performed,
or when the word 'I shall restrain myself' has been completed"— is skillfulness regarding the emergence from offenses.

"Emergence" (*vuṭṭhāna*) refers to the bringing about of non-obstruction for an offense as it was incurred; thus, by the inclusion of emergence itself, the inclusion of confession (*desanā*) is also established.
Regarding meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), it is said:
"Prior to this, preliminary work (*parikamma*) occurs; after this, the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*); in between, the attainment. Thus [is the sequence] of attainments.
Wisdom that knows the delimitation of absorption is skillfulness in attainment. Skillfulness in emergence is the state of being skilled in emerging;
it is even more so the knowledge that performs the delimitation of the emergence. Therefore he said, "By means of the very time-limit as delimited," and so forth.
"Capable of emerging" means capable of causing [the mind] to emerge.

Regarding the phrase “skill in the elements” (*dhātukusalatā*): here, the earth element and so forth, the pleasure element and so forth, and the sense-sphere element and so forth are all included within these [eighteen].
Thus, when skill in these is demonstrated, skill in those is also demonstrated.

Therefore, having stated, “The eighteen elements: the eye element... up to ...the mind-consciousness element,” it is said, “[the treatise] which defines the individual nature of the eighteen elements.”

It has been stated. In that context, "definers of intrinsic nature" means those that bring about the realization of the intrinsic nature as it truly is. The word *paññā* (wisdom) should be applied individually in the phrases "wisdom of hearing," "wisdom of retention," and so forth.
The wisdom of hearing and retention regarding the elements (*dhātu*) is wisdom consisting of learning (*sutamaya*);

the others consist of development (*bhāvanāmaya*). Even among those, the wisdom of comprehension (*sammasana-paññā*) is mundane. For that is insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*), while the other is supramundane. [This is] by way of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth.
Attention (*manasikāra*) is the act of attending to [the object] by way of its impermanence and so forth; skill in that regard is "skill in attention.
Showing this divided into three parts—beginning, middle, and end—he said: "the wisdom of comprehension, penetration, and review.
For the wisdom of comprehension is its beginning, the wisdom of penetration is the middle, and the wisdom of review is the end.

The wisdom that knows the classification of those [bases] according to their elements, characteristics, and so forth, by way of learning them both in terms of their verbal expression and their meaning, is the wisdom of knowing through learning (*uggahajānanapaññā*).
The wisdom that knows by way of the methods of comprehension, penetration, and review is the wisdom of knowing through attention (*manasikārajānanapaññā*).
This is because, in terms of their meaning, the bases are indeed elements, and attention occurs by way of learning and so forth.

The method of attention for those very [elements] is as follows; therefore, in order to show the three kinds of proficiency—beginning with proficiency in the elements—as being included within a single portion, it was said, "Moreover," and so forth.
Just like hearing, both grasping and reviewing are performed by one possessing limited knowledge;
thus he said, "Hearing, grasping, and reviewing are mundane. At the moment of the Noble Path, there is the attention of comprehension (*sammasana-manasikāra*).
Regarding "completion" (*nipphatti*) and "conclusion" (*pariniṭṭhāna*), it is stated that they can also be understood in a sense pertaining to the supramundane; thus it is said:

"The attention of comprehension (*sammasanamanasikāra*) is a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane. The "conditioning mode" (*paccayākāra*) is the state of being a condition of the conditioning factors—such as causes (*hetu*) and so forth—toward their own conditionally arisen effects by way of being a root-cause-condition (*hetupaccaya*) and so on.
This, moreover, pertains to the twelve factors of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*), beginning with ignorance (*avijjā*).

It is said to be "twelvefold" by way of the twelve modes of conditionality (*paccayākāra*). "By way of apprehension, etc. means by way of apprehension (*uggaha*), attention (*manasikāra*), hearing (*savana*), comprehension (*sammasana*), penetration (*paṭivedha*), and reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇa*).

It is a "station" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands [there], owing to its being dependent on that; and it is a "cause" (*kāraṇa*) because of its acting as a causal condition (*hetupaccaya*), by way of making and producing.
The connection is: "The meaning of these two dyads should be understood with respect to those ear-consciousnesses, etc. Those...
In the first method, the fact that certain phenomena (*dhammā*) are the "possibility" (*ṭhāna*) for another phenomenon by virtue of being its cause,

and those same phenomena are the "impossibility" (*aṭṭhāna*) for a phenomenon incompatible with them by virtue of not being its cause, illustrates the status of possibility and impossibility for that very phenomenon according to the distinction of its fruit.

In the second method, however, even though the fruit is undifferentiated, their status as possibility and impossibility is shown through the distinction among the conditioning phenomena (*paccayadhamma*).
"Made clear" (dīpita) is the distinction between these two. For never does the noble ones' perfection of view (diṭṭhisampadā) become a cause for grasping at permanence;
however, non-action (akiriyatā) might be its cause.

Straightness (ujju) is the state of being straight (ajjava); it means the absence of crookedness, the absence of curvature, and the absence of deviousness. This meaning is [explained] by way of the negation of non-straightness (anajjava).

To demonstrate this, it was said: “crookedness like a cow’s urine-stream,” and so forth. Since this lack of straightforwardness in monks generally arises from improper search (*an-esanā*) and wandering outside the proper range (*agocara-cāritā*), he said: “For a certain one... wanders.
This is called “crookedness like a cow’s urine-stream” because of the crooked nature of the practice from beginning to end. “Similar to the former” refers to the first [type].
He is like a bhikkhu who has completed his training. "Crookedness in the middle" refers to falling into a state of crookedness in the midst of one's practice.
"Crookedness at the tip of a plough" refers to falling into a state of crookedness at the conclusion. This is called "uprightness" because it is established as being straight in every respect.
"Uprightness" (*ajjavatā*) is a description of its mode; it is a description of that specific mode in which one's uprightness functions.
The meaning is as follows: one who feels shame (*lajjati*) is *lajjī*, that is, possessed of moral dread (*hirimā*); the state of being such is *lajjavaṃ*, which means moral dread (*hirī*).

Alternatively, one who possesses shame is *lajjī*, just as one says "one who wears a garland" (*mālī*) or "one who possesses deceit" (*māyī*); the state of being such is *lajjībhāvo*, which is simply that same shame. Endurance and patience toward offenses and the like is *adhivāsanakhanti*.

Purity of virtue is *soraccaṃ*. For that is a delight in beautiful deeds; or rather, it is the state of having well-restrained oneself from evil, which is abstinence (*viratatā*), called *soraccaṃ*. Therefore he said, "the state of being easy to please" (*suratabhāvo*).
Regarding the passage beginning with “Name and form,” here is another method of interpretation:

“In the sense of making its own name” means that it possesses the intrinsic nature of making its own name independently, without depending on anything else. For that which makes the name of another depends upon that other;
therefore, because it requires something else, it does not possess the intrinsic nature of making its own name. Consequently, for the great multitude...

Relatives, as well as the qualities and those who perform the initial naming, do not fall into the state of being "name" (nāma). Furthermore, for that which has its name conferred by others, there is no inherent nature of performing the act of naming;

thus, it truly lacks the state of being "name.
