However, because feeling and the other aggregates are established by their own intrinsic nature, the state of being "name" is predicated of the names "feeling," etc., due to their having the nature of performing the act of naming. [The same applies to] earth and so forth.
By way of this illustration, he demonstrates only the establishment of the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) of "name" (*nāma*), and not its commonality as a category of name.
However, because the word "name" is conventionally established (*nirulha*) only for immaterial phenomena (*arūpadhamma*), it does not apply to earth and so forth;

thus, those [material things] do not possess the status of being "names. For just as material phenomena are designated by names such as "hair" and so on when they have abandoned the name "earth" and so forth, so too [feeling and the rest] would have to abandon the name "feeling" and so on...
There is a mode of occurrence of immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) that can be designated by another name in the form of a synthesis.

Alternatively, material phenomena (rūpadhamma)—such as the eye and so forth, and visible forms and so forth—are manifest even without a name because of their relationship as the illuminator and the illuminated;
immaterial phenomena are not like this, for they are dependent upon a name for their apprehension, just like the contact of designation (adhivacana-samphassa).
It is called "name" (*nāma*). And because contact through resistance (*paṭigha-saṃphassa*) is not as manifest without a name as the eye and so forth are, it is called "name";

or else, it is included here because, due to its immateriality, it shares the same nature as other "names," or because it shares the same nature as other types of contact. For even the etymological meaning applies here:

that which causes to form is "form" (*rūpa*), and that which causes to bend is "name" (*nāma*); thus both the latter and the former [definitions] are possible in this context. "Causes to form" means...

The meaning is that it makes itself manifest even without a name. "Names" (nāmayati) means that, because it would otherwise remain unmanifest in the absence of a name, it creates a name for itself as its own manifestor;

this is the meaning. Regarding "by way of the object-predominance condition" (ārammaṇādhipatipaccayatāya): although material form (rūpa) may indeed function as an object-predominance condition, it is not a condition with such exceptional influence in the manner of a name as Nibbāna is the supreme consolation; therefore, Nibbāna alone is called "name" (nāma).
“Ignorance and craving for existence”—this dyad is for the purpose of showing the manifestation of the root of the round for beings.
For "manifestation" (*samudācāra*) means that which manifests; thus, the root of the round itself as its manifestation is the "manifestation of the root of the round.
Alternatively, by showing the root of the round, the occurrence of the roots of the round is shown; thus, the manifestation of the roots of the round is the "manifestation of the root of the round."
The meaning is: "for the purpose of showing that.
And in each case, the expression "both self and world" is stated by taking into account the specific modes of grasping as "self" and as "world";
or else, it refers to one who grasps one aggregate as "self" and another aggregate, which serves as the object of its enjoyment, as "the world."
The phrase "both self and world" is said either with reference to one who, having grasped their own self as "self," grasps the self of another as "the world.
"Sahadhamma" means the Dhamma that is to be practiced together; that which exists therein is "sahadhammika," and [the word refers to] that person who is a fellow practitioner of the Dhamma.
By treating the word *āya* as non-different from the term *dovacassa*, it is stated as “*dovacassāyaṃ*”;

alternatively, the course or occurrence (*ayana*) of being difficult to correct is “*dovacassāyaṃ*. Since there is a following after even while practicing, and an associating through one’s underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*), he said:
“*sevanā... pe... bhajanā*. Devotion in every respect is *sambhatti*.

“Simultaneously with the formal act (*kammavācā*)” means together with the formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) or the formal act of settling by covering over as if with grass (*tiṇavatthāraka*), and simultaneously with [the declaration] beginning, “Venerable sirs, I have fallen into such-and-such an offense. For it is simultaneously with the formal act that the emergence from the offense is delimited;
[namely,] for an offense characterized by a rule (*paññatti-lakkhaṇā*), the cause is bodily action or verbal action characterized by transgression.
Or, because the *kammavācā* (formal ritual proclamation) is the cause for emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*), it is stated as "together with the *kammavācā*" by way of knowing the fruit along with its cause.
By this same method, the meaning should also be understood in the phrase "together with the preliminary work" (*saha parikammena*).
All wisdom that has the elements (*dhātu*) as its object is skill in the elements (*dhātukusalatā*); the intention is that skill in attention (*manasikārakusalatā*) is a portion of that.

In the first passage as well, the wisdom of comprehension and penetration was mentioned. However, since—in the ultimate sense—it is precisely the wisdom of insight and so forth that constitutes skill in attention, it was stated [there] as "the wisdom of comprehension, penetration, and reviewing of those very same elements.
Showing that all wisdom having the sense bases (*āyatana*) as its object is skill in the sense bases, he says: "the wisdom of learning, attending to, and knowing the twelve sense bases."

Having said that, he further stated, "Moreover," and so forth. Alternatively, "attention" (*manasikāra*) refers to the mental attention directed toward both sections—the *āyatana-pāḷi* and the *dhātu-pāḷi*—once they have been brought to mind.
Thus, she learns them, attends to them, hears their meaning for that purpose, and retains them both in letter and in sense, [reflecting]:
"This is called the eye-base (*cakkhāyatana*); this is called the eye-element (*cakkhudhātu*)," and so on.
Wisdom that knows the delimitation by way of intrinsic nature and by way of enumeration is called "wisdom of learning" (uggahapaññā) and so forth.

In the section on attention (manasikāra), however, all four kinds of wisdom are termed "learning"; the attention directed toward impermanence and so forth that proceeds from that [wisdom] is called "attention as learning" (uggahamanasikāra).
Its knowing is simply its occurrence; or rather, it is said: "Just as the learning occurs, so too does the attention proceed."
Knowledge of learning is knowledge of the material to be learned. Knowledge that "attention should be directed in this way, and when it is directed thus" is knowledge of attention.
Both of these are called "skill in attention. For even learning deserves the designation "attention" by virtue of its association with attention.
And whatever is to be attended to, as well as whatever is the means for attending, all that is "attention."
It is appropriate to speak [of these]; therein, skill is proficiency in attention (*manasikāra-kusala*). Insight (*paññā*) is comprehension (*sammasana*);
associated with the Path, it accomplishes the function of comprehending impermanence and so forth by abandoning the perception of permanence and so forth. Attention is associated with comprehension;
associated with the Path, it accomplishes the function of attending to impermanence and so forth in that very same context. Thus he said: "Comprehension and attention..."

"Mixed with the mundane and the supramundane. Skill in dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādakusalatā*) is the knowledge of how ignorance and the other factors function as conditions for the formations and so forth that arise from them, in the sense that "by this condition, this comes to be.
Endurance (*adhivāsana*) means forbearance; for it consists in not creating opposition toward the misconduct or harsh speech of others, but rather [bearing it] oneself.
Having brought [the mind] to a state of receptivity, it is called "endurance" (adhivāsana). "Non-harshness" means the absence of anger.
"Absence of weeping" (anassuropo) is the non-production of tears in the eyes of others due to mental distress. "Serenity of mind" (attamanatā) means being well-disposed;
it is the mind’s own state of being uncorrupted, which is serenity of mind. Alternatively, taking the continuum of consciousness as a single unity, it is called "mind."

The state of being pleased (*sakamanatā*) arises within him through a mind accompanied by joy (*pītisahagata*). Alternatively, a person who is pleased is one whose state is "pleased-ness" (*attamanatā*);
to prevent the view that this belongs to a "being" (*satta*), it is stated as "of the mind" (*cittassa*).
Patience (*khanti*) has the characteristic of endurance; it is called "endurance-patience. Gentleness (*soracca*) is the state of having pure virtue; for it is a delight in beautiful deeds.
Gentleness (*soratta*) is the state of being well-restrained from evil and the quality of abstention.
Therefore, it is called "the state of being easy to speak to" (*suratabhāva*). One who is *sakhila* is said to be one of gentle speech; his state is *sākhalya*, which is the quality of gentle speech.
Now, showing the passage that proceeds by way of contrast to clarify that very point, he says: "In this context, what is gentleness? and so forth. Therein:
“*Aṇḍaka*” refers to resinous masses on trees with poisonous sap, or to the protrusions of *ahicchattaka* mushrooms and the like;
these they call “*aṇḍaka*. However, when the sapwood of a tree has been heated, the powder-masses that arise like eggs, or the knots, are also “*aṇḍaka*.
But here, because of its state of being harmful and harsh, or because it is of the nature of a “*aṇḍaka*,” speech is called “*aṇḍaka*.”

It is said. It should be understood as harsh, entering while rubbing against the ear like a lotus stalk. Because it is produced by anger, those things that accompany it are called "adjuncts of anger" (*kodhasāmanta*).
A *porī* is a woman who has grown up in the city; speech that is delicate and soft is called *porī* because it is like such a woman.
Regarding the word "therein" (*tattha*), a construction is also possible where it refers back to the action stated as "it is spoken" (*bhāsitā hoti*).
In this context, "by speech" (vācāya) means: by means of that speech which brings about the volition expressed in such terms as "gentleness of speech" (*saṇhavācatā*).

"Gentleness" (*maddava*) is the state of being soft toward a person who is friendly; thus, it is "friendliness and gentleness. It is "deficient in two ways": deficient in material goods (*āmisa*) when they are not obtained, and likewise deficient in the Dhamma.
Through the non-attainment of both material goods and the Dhamma, [one fails] for oneself and for others...
Indeed, *paṭisanthāra* is the mending, closing, and securing of a gap, a fissure, or a breach that arises in between.
To clarify this both by its essential nature and by way of practice through the lens of the textual tradition, he said, "In the Abhidhamma as well," and so forth.
"Without taking the top" means without taking the top for oneself. "Giving a summary" (*uddesadāna*)...
"Reciting" refers to the recitation of the *pāḷi* (the canonical text) and the *aṭṭhakathā* (the commentary). "Commentary on the *pāḷi*" means the explanation of the meaning of the *pāḷi*.
"Delivering a discourse on the Dhamma" means the teaching of the Dhamma by way of public recitation (*sarabhañña*), chanting (*sarabhaṇana*), and so forth.
"Compassion" refers to the divine abiding of compassion (*karuṇā-brahmavihāra*). "The preliminary stage of compassion" refers to the access concentration (*upacāra-jjhāna*) that precedes it.

He speaks thus. In the canonical text (Pāḷi), however, whatever compassion there is is called simply "compassion" (karuṇā), whereas "liberation of mind through compassion" (karuṇā-cetovimutti) refers specifically to that which has reached absorption (appanā).

The same principle applies to loving-kindness (mettā). Having derived the suffix -yya from the word *suci* in the sense of an abstract state (bhāva), and having substituted the letter *e* for the letter *i*, this is the explanation;
thus he says: "Purity (*soceyya*) means the state of being pure (*sucibhāvo*). Let it be granted that purity is indeed the state of being pure; of that—
But how is it that loving-kindness (mettā) is a preliminary stage? To this he says:

"And this has also been stated," and so forth. One whose mindfulness is lost is "muṭṭhassati"; the state of such a person is "muṭṭhassacca," which is a state opposed to mindfulness, not merely the absence of mindfulness.
Because when there is an opposing factor, by its influence mindfulness is departed from or has wandered away.

Thus it is called "lapse of mindfulness" (*sativippavāsa*). In such terms as "unmindfulness" (*assati*), the vowel *a-* should be understood as denoting the opposite [of mindfulness], not as a simple negation of existence.
That by which the mind stands upon an object as if floating on water—like a gourd in water—without plunging into it, is "floating" (*pilāpanatā*).
That by which even an object already grasped is forgotten and not remembered is "forgetfulness" (*sammussanatā*).

Just as ignorance (*avijjā*) is the opposite of true knowledge (*vijjā*) because it is to be abandoned by knowledge, so too is lack of clear comprehension (*asampajañña*) the opposite of clear comprehension; it is indeed ignorance itself.

"Breaking of the restraint of the faculties" means the destruction of the restraint of the faculties. "Without reflection" means without reviewing and without investigating the dangers and benefits in the consumption of food in an improper manner.
"By non-reflection" is a name for the lack of reviewing regarding what ought to be done. Lack of reflection is ignorance.

The sign (*nimitta*). "Unshakable knowledge" (*akampanañāṇa*) refers to knowledge that cannot be overcome by that [sign]; it consists both of the reviewing knowledge regarding each respective stage and of supramundane knowledge which is the pinnacle of reviewing.
In the direct sense, the development of the path (*maggabhāvanā*) is what is called "development" (*bhāvanā*), as well as whatever is for its sake;
and both of these are to be desired only by one who is currently developing them, not by one who has already completed the development.
It is said: "The power that arises for one who is developing [it]. Therefore he said: "That which is the cultivation, development, and frequent practice of wholesome states.
Granted that stability among associated states is indeed the sense of power, yet being unshakable by opposing factors is the preeminent sense of power;
thus it is said: "by way of being unshakable through non-remembrance" (*assatiyā*). This is because of the subduing of contrary states.
Calm (samatha) is concentration (samādhi). Insight (vipassanā) is wisdom (paññā) because it sees by way of various aspects such as impermanence and so forth.

"Having grasped that aspect" means having grasped the aspect of concentration. Having grasped and observed that aspect by which the mind was previously concentrated—being neither sluggish nor agitated, but middling and having entered the path of development—one [proceeds]. "By way of the sign" means by way of the cause.

“‘The same method applies’—by this, he refers by extension to the meaning that exertion itself, having taken up that mode [of activity], is the ‘sign of exertion’ (paggāhanimitta) by way of being the cause for the renewed occurrence of exertion;
its meaning should be understood according to the method stated under serenity (samatha).
Exertion is energy (vīriya), so called because it exerts the mind by not allowing it to fall into the side of indolence.”
Non-distraction is one-pointedness because it is the opposite of distraction and agitation.

It is called the "power of reflection" regarding supramundane states because it brings about the function of reflective discernment; likewise, the mixture of the two pairs of factors—calm and exertion, and calm and its sign—is stated because of the presence of subsequent activity through the observation of the mode of occurrence that previously arose during the cultivation of calm.

Transgression is the violation that causes the breaking of the virtue one has undertaken. Non-restraint is the destroyer of virtue. "Destroyer of right view" means it corrupts the right view that proceeds by way of such principles as "there is giving.
"Accomplishing virtue" means bringing about its completeness in every respect; thus he said, "by accomplishing and fulfilling," for the word *sampadā* has the sense of fulfillment.
"Mental virtue" refers to the abandoning of covetousness and so forth by means of purifying virtue.
"Knowledge consisting in the fulfillment of view" means knowledge that occurs by way of fulfilling right view, beginning with the view of existence (*atthikadiṭṭhi*).
"Capable of bringing about purification" means capable of becoming a condition for the higher purifications, beginning with purification of mind (*cittavisuddhi*);
for it is only very pure virtue (*sīla*) that serves as its proximate cause (*padaṭṭhāna*). "Vision capable of bringing about purification."

It is the right vision beginning with the knowledge of one's own deeds (kammassakatāñāṇa) that is capable of leading to and bringing about the purification of knowledge and vision, as well as Nibbāna, the ultimate purification.

Therefore he said, "In the Abhidhamma," and so forth. And herein, the knowledge that understands one's own deeds through both positive and negative concomitance—namely, "This unwholesome kamma is not one's own; but this kamma is one's own"—is the knowledge of one's own deeds.
Therefore he said, “And herein,” and so forth. The phrase “even what is done by another” is stated by way of illustration;
just as [an act] done by another is not called one’s own karma, so too what is done by oneself is not called one’s own karma.

Or rather, the meaning should be understood thus: “even what is done by another who has been incited by oneself. For that which is done by means of inciting another— [that too is not one’s own karma].

"Is called 'accompanied by its own action' (sakakamma)"—this is the intended meaning here. "From the destruction of welfare" means from the ruin of all welfare, whether pertaining to this life or otherwise.
"From the generation of welfare" means from the production of welfare in this world, welfare in the next world, and the ultimate welfare (paramattha).

Furthermore, at the time of undertaking [the practice], there is the verbal truth (vacīsacca) occurring as "impermanent, suffering, non-self," as well as the insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that penetrates the characteristics [of phenomena].

It conforms [to the truth] because it penetrates right there. And it does not contradict nor oppose the ultimate truth (paramatthasacca), which is Nibbāna, because it leads exclusively to its attainment.
"Knowledge and vision" (ñāṇadassana) means vision that consists of knowledge; by this he refers to the Path. Energy associated with that [Path] alone is meant.

He spoke of the energy associated with the first path. The phrase beginning with “Furthermore” (*apicā*) was stated to show that all wisdom of the path is indeed purification of view (*diṭṭhivisuddhi*).
And showing that this very method accords with the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, he said the passage beginning with “In the Abhidhamma, however” (*abhidhamme pana*).

Since what is called "spiritual urgency" (*saṃvega*) is knowledge accompanied by moral dread (*ottappa*), therefore, by way of seeing the objects of spiritual urgency as fearful—that is, as things to be dreaded—...

This is knowledge of occurrence. Therefore he said, "the fear of birth," and so forth. It is called *bhaya* (fear) because they fear it; birth itself is the fear, hence "the fear of birth" (*jātibhaya*).
It is "to be stirred by" (*saṃvejanīya*) meaning it should be felt as a shock, feared, and made one to tremble. "Place" (*ṭhāna*) means cause; the sense is "basis.
"Of one who has become stirred" (*saṃvegajāta*) means of one in whom agitation has arisen. "Exertion in means" (*upāyapadhāna*) means energy to be exercised by way of a means.
“Of wholesome states” (*kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ*) means of blameless states such as virtue (*sīla*) and so forth. “By cultivation” (*bhāvanāya*) means by way of their arising and increase.
“Of one who is not content” (*asantuṭṭhassa*) means of one who is not satisfied because of falling into contraction [of mind], thinking, “Enough with this much;

what more can be done with this much? “Desire for more” (*bhiyyokamyatā*) is the wish to produce [wholesome states] further and further. “Relinquishing of desisting” (*vosāna*) means being incapable of contraction. “Contentment” (*tussanaṃ*)...
*Tuṭṭhi* is contentment; *asantuṭṭhi* means there is no contentment for this person, and its state is *asantuṭṭhitā*.
When the flow of energy (*vīriya*) is proceeding, turning back or retreating midway is *paṭivāna*; one who has that is *paṭivānī*, and one who does not have it is *appaṭivānī*;
its state is *appaṭivānitā*. *Sakkaccakiriyatā* refers to [the performance] of wholesome states...
In the act of doing, there is thoroughness in performance and respectful performance. Constant performance means performing at all times.
Uninterrupted performance means performing without stopping in between or leaving it incomplete. Non-slackened conduct means not proceeding with a sluggish state.
Non-abandonment of desire means not casting off the desire for what is wholesome. Non-abandonment of the burden means not casting off the burden of energy in the performance of what is wholesome.
*Āsevanā* means cultivation with diligence. *Bhāvanā* means development and expansion. *Bahulīkammaṃ* means repeated performance.

The three types of clear knowledge (*tisso vijjā*) are: the knowledge of recollecting past lives, the knowledge of the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhaya-ñāṇa*). These are the three types of clear knowledge.
They are "clear" (*vijjā*) in the sense of piercing through opposing factors and in the sense of making known the aggregates and so forth in which one previously dwelt.

"Liberation" (*mutti*) means "emancipation" (*vimutti*). Since this specific distinction must be understood through the departure from opposing factors (*paṭipakkha*) and the departure from their counterparts (*paṭiyogi*), the phrase beginning with "And here...

was stated in order to show both of these. In that context, because the attainments (*samāpatti*) are well-liberated from adverse states by way of that specific distinction, they are free from apprehension and delighted in the object; taking that distinction as the basis, those [attainments] are superior.
Because it is a releasing and because it is a resolute determination upon the object, it is called "resolutions"; thus it is said, "and the resolutions of the mind.
Because it has escaped specifically from all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it is liberation (*vimutti*).

"Knowledge of destruction" (*khaye ñāṇa*): it is called "destruction" (*khaya*) because it exhausts the defilements by way of their total eradication; this refers to the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), which is included therein.

"Knowledge is the knowledge of destruction. "By way of rebirth-linking" means by way of the re-linking of the defilements to be abandoned by each respective path back into the continuity of the aggregates within the arisen path. "In that which has become non-arising" refers to the respective fruit.

"At the conclusion of non-arising" means: non-arising is the path that effects non-arising; at its conclusion, or at the conclusion consisting in the non-occurrence of defilements—this is the meaning of "in the breaking [of the continuity]."
The commentary on the dyads is finished.
Commentary on the triads (305):
To show that there is no agent other than the phenomenon itself, it is defined by way of the instrument of the agent as "greed is so called because it lusts."

It has been stated [thus]. The meaning is also appropriate by way of the instrumental and abstract (bhāva) derivations: "one is corrupted by it" (*lubbhati tena*) and "it is mere corruption" (*lubbhanamattam eva*).

The same method applies here to the terms *dussati* ("is corrupted") and *muyhati* ("is deluded"). It is unwholesome (*akusala*) in the sense of being produced by lack of skill (*akosalla*), because it is exclusively unwholesome in nature;
and it is a root (*mūla*) because it effects the firm establishment of the states associated with itself, not because it effects the state of unwholesomeness itself.
For the unwholesome nature of unwholesome states, and the wholesome nature of wholesome states and so forth, does not exist by way of their roots.

If that were the case, then in the two types of deluded consciousness (*momūha-citta*), the delusion (*moha*) would not be unwholesome. "Of these" refers to greed and the rest. [The terms] such as "non-greed" (*alobha*) are defined by way of their opposites, according to the method of negation: "it does not lust, thus it is non-greed.
They are called "bad conduct" (*duccarita*) because they are not good (*na suṭṭhu*) with respect to their conditions, their associated phenomena, and their mode of occurrence; they are not right.
They have been set in motion. "Ugly" means loathsome in the present and undesirable in the future because of their nature.

"By the body" means by means of the body-door acting as the instrument. "From the body" means from the body-door. The meaning in such phrases as "well-practiced" should be understood as the opposite of what was stated [previously].
That training rule whose transgression results in an offense originating from the body is [to be observed] at the body-door.

The training rule (sikkhāpada) has been laid down. "Non-transgression is bodily good conduct" is said by way of the virtue of restraint (vāritta-sīla), or else by way of the virtue of performance (cāritta-sīla)—that is, that for which there is an offense in its non-performance.
The determination of verbal misconduct and good conduct should also be understood according to the method already stated.
"Laid down in both cases" means laid down in the door of the body and in the door of speech. Of the training rule...
Transgression itself is mental misconduct because there is no training rule (sikkhāpada) prescribed for the door of the mind;
this should be understood by way of an offense originating from non-action in respect of the two doors.
Non-transgression is the non-transgression of the aforementioned offense, which is mental good conduct. "The non-transgression of every training rule is mental good conduct."

Some [say this]. For both of these—namely, the morality of conduct (*cāritta-sīla*) and the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) prescribed specifically for that—are, when not transgressed, either bodily good conduct (*kāya-sucarita*) or verbal good conduct (*vaci-sucarita*).

"Taking life" (*pāṇātipāta*) means that by means of this, a living being (*pāṇa*) is caused to be slain; it is the volition (*cetanā*) proceeding in such a manner. The same applies to taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and the others.
He said: "But the three volitions beginning with killing living beings [constitute bodily misconduct].

Even when they arise at the door of speech, they are called bodily misconduct because the name of the karma arising at one door is not abandoned even when it arises at another door, due to its general mode of occurrence and its frequent occurrence. Therefore, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā said:
"Karmas move through the doors; the doors do not move through the karmas."
"Therefore, actions are established through their respective doors.
One should connect this by bringing in the fact that verbal misconduct arises both at the door of the body and at the door of speech.

"Phenomena associated with volition" refers to those phenomena associated with volition that constitutes mental action; however, those associated with volition that constitutes bodily or verbal action [are also included].

Covetousness and the rest are either included within their respective categories or are not so designated. The same principle applies here to the statement that "states associated with volition are mental good conduct.

Furthermore, the three types of volition and the three types of abstinence—which function by way of the non-performance of the three kinds of misconduct—are also bodily good conduct, because they function by way of the non-performance of bodily transgression; [this is] by means of the body...

However, when undertaking the training rules (*sikkhāpada*), there is nothing at all that need be said regarding the nature of virtue (*sīla*) as good conduct of body. The same method applies to good conduct of speech.

Regarding the phrase "connected with sensual desire" (*kāmapaṭisaṃyutta*): here, there are two kinds of sensual desire (*kāma*), namely, sensual objects (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual-desire (*kilesakāma*).

In that regard, according to the category of sensual objects, a thought connected with sensual desires by way of taking them as its object is "thought of sensual desire" (*kāmavitakka*). But in the category of defilement-sensual-desire...
It should be construed as "associated with sensual desire" by way of association (*sampayoga*).

In such cases as "associated with ill will," the meaning is to be understood precisely by way of association. Even when "associated with ill will" is taken to mean "associated with the basis for ill will," the construction is obtainable in both ways.
The same method applies here to "associated with cruelty": beings are cruelly harmed by means of this [state].
It is called *vihiṃsā* because it is the harming of beings; thus, the meaning of the word should be understood as "connected with that [harming]," hence "connected with cruelty.
The occurrence of ill-will thoughts (*byāpādavitakka*) directed toward disagreeable and unpleasant formations should be illustrated by way of non-place and resentment (*aṭṭhāna-ghāta*).
To show the limit of ill-will thoughts, it is said: "up to destruction" (*yāva vināsanā*). Destruction...
"But is killing living beings [the only thing]?"—why was it said that "there is no such thing as a *saṅkhāra* that can be made to suffer"?
Is it not the case that even those things designated as "sentient beings" who are intended to be "made to suffer" are, in actual fact, nothing other than *saṅkhāras*? This is true;
however, because those bound by the sense-faculties experience suffering due to their possession of consciousness, they are the objects of the thought of violence (*vihiṃsā-vitakka*).
Desirable objects are designated as "beings. However, regarding those things that do not experience suffering because they lack the application of the aforementioned characteristics, it was said:
"The thought of cruelty does not arise with respect to formations (saṅkhāra).
To show where it does arise and how it arises, it was said: "These beings," and so forth.
"Renunciation" (nekkhamma) is called non-greed because it has emerged from greed; it is also the first jhāna because it has emerged from the hindrances;
it is all wholesome states because they have emerged from all unwholesome states; and it is Nibbāna because it has emerged from all conditioned things.
It is "connected with renunciation" by way of decisive support, association, and being made an object.

Connected with renunciation (*nekkhamma*). Right intention (*sammāsaṅkappa*) is the thought of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*). Now, in order to show this by way of its classification according to the planes, the passage beginning with “He... is stated.
“In the preliminary stage of the foul” means in the preliminary stage of the foulness absorption (*asubhajjhāna*).
And here, the mention of the “foul” is made for the purpose of showing the direct opposite of sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*); for the thought of renunciation is the antidote to sensual thought.

And having done so, the jhānas of loving-kindness, compassion, and so forth, together with their preliminary stages, are mentioned by one who intends to show the basis for the two subsequent reflections.
"In the foulness-jhāna" means in the first jhāna having the foul (asubha) as its object;
for he explains by applying the designation of the whole to a part, just as one says, "the branch on the tree. "Making jhāna the foundation" is merely an illustration. That...

For even at the time when the path and fruit have arisen after having reflected upon jhāna, that [jhāna] is supramundane. It is non-ill-will (*abyāpāda*) because it is the opposite of ill-will (*byāpāda*), or because one does not bear ill-will toward anything by means of it;
thus it is loving-kindness (*mettā*). "Associated with non-ill-will" means associated with that [loving-kindness].
"In the loving-kindness jhāna" means in the first jhāna attained by way of the cultivation of loving-kindness. "In the compassion jhāna"—here too, it is exactly the same.
This is the method. *Avihiṃsā* (non-cruelty) is the opposite of cruelty (*vihiṃsā*); or, it is that by which one does not harm living beings, thus it is non-cruelty—namely, compassion (*karuṇā*).

Now, one might object: "Since non-greed (*alobha*) and non-hatred (*adosa*) are mutually exclusive, there can be no clear distinction between these thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhamma-vitakka*) and the others, which arise on their basis, because they would not be mixed with one another?
To show that this is not so, the passage beginning with "When... is commenced.
"Non-greed is the head" means that non-greed is predominant.

When a state of consciousness arises with non-greed as its primary factor and renunciation as its weight, through the modes of being determined, matured, and active, then the thought of renunciation, having found its opportunity, becomes established.
Furthermore, by way of non-ill-will (*avyāpāda*), which has the characteristic of non-hatred and is associated with that [non-greed], whatever...

The state of non-ill-will-thought may arise; and when there is the state of non-ill-will-thought, because of being by nature non-harming toward anyone, the state of non-cruelty-thought may also arise—those being the other two.
"Following upon that" means they are followers of that very renunciation-thought;
since they are not seen as having their own distinct forms, they are to be inferred from it, according to the principle: "When that exists, these exist; when that is absent, these do not exist."
[They] exist. The meaning in the remaining two [categories] should also be understood by this same method.

"By the very method already stated" means that it should be understood by the very method stated in the *Vitakkattika* (the triad on applied thought) as "thought associated with sensual desire is sensual-desire-thought," and so forth, because there is no difference in their meaning.
If this is so, why was it taught again? It is merely a repetition of the teaching, given in accordance with the inclinations of those who would understand through such a presentation.

The mode of arising for these [two types of thought] should be understood as being like that of sensual thought (*kāmavitakka*) and so forth, according to the passage beginning, "Of those two, they arise both in relation to beings and in relation to formations.

Regarding this, he states the reason: "For these are associated only with that [sensual desire]. "In the same way" means that just as the status of sensual-sphere and so forth was stated for thoughts of renunciation (*nekkhammavitakka*) and so on by the passage beginning, "In the preliminary stage of the foul (*asubha*), it belongs to the sensual sphere," in exactly the same way, it is so for those two as well.
The status of the perception of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saññā*) and so forth as belonging to the sense sphere (*kāmadhātu*) and other realms should also be understood accordingly.
"Connected with sensual desire" (*kāmapaṭisaṃyutta*) means connected with sensual desire by way of association (*sampayoga*). "Reasoning" (*takka*) is so called by way of conjecture.

"Applied thought" (*vitakka*) is so called by way of specific conjecture. "Intention" (*saṅkappa*) is so called by way of planning and deliberation. This applies to others as well who are connected with sensual desire.

Among existing phenomena, it should be understood that the term *dhātu* (element) is conventionally established specifically for thoughts (*vitakka*) associated with sensual desire, because such thoughts are preeminent in the occurrence of sensual intention.
This same principle applies to the element of ill will (*byāpādadhātu*) and the others.

Furthermore, all unwholesome phenomena constitute the "sensual-desire element" (*kāmadhātu*), because they are the nature of an element that is desired by those of inferior inclination, and because they possess the essential nature of objects for defiled sensual desire.
Meaning: "He afflicts" means he oppresses. "Therein" refers to that aforementioned triad of the sense-sphere element (*kāmadhātu*).

A discourse that includes all unwholesome states by including the other two within the sense-sphere element—which itself comprises all unwholesome states—is a "comprehensive discourse. A discourse on the three elements without mutual confusion is an "unmixed" one.
Since the other two are already included, the other two elements are thereby taken up.
Because it has been stated, "In this way, all unwholesome states are the sense-sphere element (kāmadhātu)," there is an over-extension of the general definition to its own specific domain.
Therefore, [the Blessed One] excludes [them] from the sense-sphere element which encompasses the other two elements. "Having extracted" means having singled them out.
It is appropriate to say that the Blessed One demonstrates it in this way: he taught the element of ill-will (*byāpādadhātu*)... [and so on]... Why?
First, exceptions (apavāda) take hold, and after that, the general rule (ussagga) proceeds;
or rather, the general rule proceeds while setting aside the domain of the exceptions and avoiding them—this is the method well-established in the world.
"Two kinds of discourse" refers to the two types of discourse mentioned in the immediately preceding triad: "comprehensive" and "unmixed. Therein:

It should be understood by way of bringing [the meaning] forward according to the method already stated. Therefore, the meaning stated there should also be brought here and understood through such passages as:
"When the element of renunciation is grasped, the other two are also grasped," and so forth.

"In the sense of emptiness" means by way of the emptiness of self (*attasuññatā*). Sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) is "sensual desire" (*kāma*), with the latter member of the compound elided; it is a "constituent" (*dhātu*) in the sense of emptiness.
"And so forth" refers to the sense-sphere realm (*kāmadhātu*). "The Brahmā-world" refers to the Brahmā-world designated as the plane of the first jhāna.
"When the term 'realm' (*dhātu*) has been employed," such as in the expression "the sense-sphere realm, the form-sphere realm," and so on—"should be delimited by way of existence":
its meaning should be delimited by way of "existence" (*bhava*), such as "sense-sphere existence, form-sphere existence," and so on, and not by way of any particular realm.

And just as a delimitation by way of existence (*bhava*) must be made where the element (*dhātu*) occurs, so too a delimitation by way of the element must be made where existence occurs, because the element is delimited by way of existence.

It is "cessation" (*nirodha*) because the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) ceases therein; that very [cessation] is the "element of cessation" (*nirodhadhātu*) in the sense of emptiness (*suññatā*), which is Nibbāna. And when the round of defilements has ceased...
The round of the ripening of kamma has indeed ceased.

It is said that the triad of inferior elements (hīnadhātuttika) is to be defined by the triad of the inferior (hīnattika) in the Abhidhamma: "Inferior elements are the twelve unwholesome consciousness-arising states.
For these are "inferior elements" in the sense of being base. They exist in the midst of the inferior and the sublime.
The middle element consists of the remaining phenomena of the three planes. The sublime element, in the sense of being unsurpassed and non-afflicting, consists of the nine supramundane phenomena.

"Possessing the five strands of sensual pleasure" means that sensual lust has these five strands of sensual pleasure as its objects; thus it is called "pertaining to the five strands of sensual pleasure. "In the realms of form and formlessness" means...

"In the realms of existence born of form and formlessness as they have been attained. However, since there is no such thing as "aspiration" (*patthanā*) regarding those not yet attained, it is included by the very phrase "aspiration by way of existence" (*bhavavasena patthanā*).
"Craving for jhāna" (*jhānanikanti*) means craving for the fine-material and immaterial jhānas.
"Aspiration by way of existence" means aspiration for existences. Thus, by all four terms respectively, [the object] is the sublime existence-born realm (*mahaggatūpapattibhava*).

Craving that has as its object the sphere of sublime kamma-existence (*mahaggata-kammabhava*), that is accompanied by the view of existence (*bhava-diṭṭhi*), and that consists in the aspiration for existence, is called "craving for existence" (*bhava-taṇhā*).

By the elision of the final member of the compound, the view of non-existence (*vibhava-diṭṭhi*) is termed "non-existence" (*vibhava*); craving accompanied by this non-existence is "craving for non-existence" (*vibhava-taṇhā*).

Craving that has the five bases such as form as its object within the sphere of sensual desire (*kāma-visaya*), and which consists in powerful lust, is "craving for sensual pleasure" (*kāma-taṇhā*). This is the first method. Furthermore, all [three types of craving]...

Because of the statement, “The phenomena of the three planes are ‘sensual pleasures’ (kāmā) in the sense of being desirable,” all craving (taṇhā) that occurs with reference to them and is dissociated from views is “craving for sensual pleasure” (kāmataṇhā); this is the second method, and this is their distinction.

As for the word “pana” in the phrase “In the Abhidhamma, however,” the word *pana* indicates a specific qualification; by it, [it is shown that] there is something other than attachment to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañcakāmaguṇika-rāga*).
This clarifies the distinction that in the Abhidhamma, greed whose object is a phenomenon belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) is designated as "craving for sense-pleasures" (*kāmataṇhā*).
Although it is the same as the other triads, because it follows immediately after the teaching that proceeds by relying on craving itself, it deserves to be called a "turn";
thus it is said, "by this turn. "By this turn" means "by this method. "In the sense of being an object of passion" (*rajanīyaṭṭhena*).
In the sense of being desirable. "Having encompassed" means having grasped. "From that" means from craving for sensual pleasures (*kāmatanha*).
"Having extracted" means having singled out. This indicates the other two types of craving: craving for form (*rūpatanha*) and craving for the formless (*arūpatanha*).

By this it is shown that "craving for sensual pleasures" is a general term for all greed, whereas "craving for form" and "craving for the formless" are specific terms for it, just as [the terms] "lust for the strands of sensual pleasure" are.
It shows [the craving for] form-attachment and formless-attachment. "Craving for cessation" is craving directed toward the cessation of existence, the total cutting off of existence.

For since the annihilationist view—[thinking] that there is the complete annihilation of one's self while remaining in a human state, a sense-sphere deva state, or a fine-material or immaterial-sphere state—occurs with reference to the cessation of existence, therefore the craving associated with it [also occurs].
Craving proceeds by taking that very [existence] as its object.

"In the round" means in all three types of rounds. For just as they bind the being who possesses them to the round of kamma and result—by way of not allowing escape from it—serving as the condition for their successive rebirths, so too do they bind them in the round of defilements.

"Existing" (*satī*) means existing in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*). "In the division of form and so forth" (*rūpādibhede*) means in the classification of form, feeling, and the rest. "In the body" (*kāye*) means in the aggregate of the aggregates (*khandhasamūhe*).

"Existing" (*vijjamānā*) means existing in the ultimate sense, being apprehended as such. For while a self (*attā*) and so forth imagined by view do not exist in the ultimate sense, this view itself certainly does exist.
"Investigating" (*vicinanto*) means examining the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*). "Is pained" (*kicchatīti*)...

He becomes weary. "Grasping" (parāmasati) means he grasps from another. For one who takes up [the view] that "purification comes through virtue, purification comes through vows" has, in effect, passed beyond the path to purity and is said to grasp from what lies beyond it.

The "twenty-based views" (vīsativatthukā diṭṭhi) refers to [views] regarding phenomena such as form and so forth, treating each of them individually as the basis, or as the support, or as the master [of the self].
There are twenty types of self-view (*attadiṭṭhi*) occurring by way of conceptualization based on twenty bases.
"Doubt" (*vimaṭī*) means that, because there is an absence of right or wrong reflection regarding phenomena, one wavers in the sense of being uncertain; the meaning is non-undertaking [of the path].
"Misapprehension" (*vipariyāsaggāha*) is the perverted apprehension of what is not the path of purity as "the path of purity."
"In the sense of having resided for a long time" means by virtue of having been inhabited for a long duration, that is, by way of its antiquity.

"In the sense of flowing" (*āsavana*) means in the sense of streaming forth; the meaning is "in the sense of proceeding. It "flows" (*savati*) means it proceeds. The vowel *ā* has the sense of a limit (*avadhi*).

Limits are twofold, distinguished as exclusive (*maryādā*) and inclusive (*abhividhi*). Among these, an exclusive limit functions by excluding the action from beyond it, as in: "He has rained up to Pāṭaliputta."

"Devo" [is used here]. This prefix *ā-* functions as an all-pervading action (*abhividhi-kiriyā*), as in the expression: "The fame of the Blessed One has spread up to the peak of existence (*bhavagga*).
This *ā*-sound should be understood as having the sense of pervasion (*abhividhi*).
He says this with reference to the Vinaya Piṭaka, where in some places two taints (*āsava*) are mentioned; for therein it says: "Of the taints pertaining to the present life..."
“For the sake of restraint, for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives”—thus the taints are presented in two ways.
"In some places" refers to the *Āsava Sutta* in the Third Nikāya (*Tikanipāta*), as well as other suttas such as the *Saḷāyatana Sutta*. For even in the *Saḷāyatana Suttas*, only three are mentioned:
"Friends, there are these three taints: the taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance. They lead to hell.

"Leading to hell. Since here wholesome and unwholesome kamma associated with the taints (*āsava*) is taught by way of the term "taint," the taints are included by virtue of their leading to rebirth in the five destinations. Thus, three [types] appear in this *Saṅgīti-sutta*.

Here, although other states such as conceit exist—which occur from the peak of existence down to the stage of change-of-lineage (*gotrabhū*)—they are [excluded] because they involve the grasping of a self or what belongs to a self.

Their similarity to "taints" (āsava) is due to their pervasiveness and their quality of causing intoxication; this applies to these alone and not to others. Therefore, it should be understood that the term *āsava* is conventionally established for these alone.

Nor should one think here that the "taint of views" (*diṭṭhāsava*) has been omitted, because both craving for existence (*bhavataṇhā*) and the view of existence (*bhavadiṭṭhi*) are included by the very inclusion of the "taint of existence" (*bhavāsava*).
The so-called "taint of sensual desire" (*kāmāsava*) is so called in the sense of desiring and in the sense of flowing.
And [it is] indeed already stated, since there is no difference in meaning.

"Sensual seeking" (*kāmesanā*) is so called because one seeks or searches for sensual pleasures by means of it; it is the lust that arises through the mode of longing for sensual pleasures, through the mode of searching for them, or through the mode of enjoying them.
"Becoming-seeking" (*bhavesanā*), however, is the longing for becoming, arising through the mode of delighting in becoming and clinging to becoming.
One whose passion is active. "Of that which is esteemed by those who hold wrong views" means of that which is imagined and honored by followers of other sects.
"Of the holy life" (brahmacariya) means of the practice of asceticism. "Associated with that" means associated with those [states] such as passion and wrong view, being yoked together with them.
"Kamma" means unwholesome kamma; for that too, proceeding by way of the basis for rebirth in the realms of sense-desire and so forth, "seeks" (esati).
It is so called. "Extremist views" is merely an illustration; for any wrong view whatsoever that has asceticism as its cause is indeed a search for the holy life (*brahmacariyesanā*).
Regarding "shape and configuration": it is a particular mode of existence. In what manner? By what way is it configured?
The meaning is "evenly established. Etymologically, however, *vidhā* means "distribution" (*vidahana*), which is "establishment in a distinguished manner" (*visiṭṭhākārena avaṭṭhāna*).

It is called *vidhā* because it is "placed in a dissimilar manner" (*vidhīyati visadisākārena ṭhapīyati*); thus, it is a "portion" (*koṭṭhāsa*). It is called *vidhā* because of its "burning" (*dahana*)—that is, its holding or supporting—in various ways according to the inferior and so forth;
thus, it is "conceit" (*māna*). [The phrase] "by way of superior, equal, and inferior" refers to the states of being superior, equal, and inferior.
[It arises] by way of things as they are and not as they are. Three types of conceit are said to arise in one who is superior; the same method applies to those who are equal and inferior.

Therefore he said, "For this conceit," and so forth. Now, in order to show the ninefold conceit already mentioned according to the classification of its objects (*vatthu*), he said, "Therein," and so forth. Why does it arise in both kings and renunciants? Because they are especially...
“They regard themselves as superior. Now, in order to demonstrate that meaning in detail, he says, beginning with “A king,” and so forth.
In the phrase “Who is there like me? the word *ko* has the sense of negation; the intention is that there is no one else who is equal.
“Of these very ones” refers to kings and those who have gone forth. It arises because it has a superior object. The same method applies to the conceit, “I am inferior.”

This is a demonstration of the three modes of occurrence for the conceits of equality, superiority, and so forth: either thinking, "What other royal official is equal to me?"; or, "What difference is there between me and others?"; or, "I am indeed named 'Minister'... [and so on]... I am named [such-and-such].

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "slaves, etc.," those who live under the dependence of others—such as laborers, servants, and the like—are included. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*)... [the rest of the sentence follows].

Or rather, when [the term] is taken [in its primary sense], he himself shows that even "Pukkusas, Caṇḍālas, and so forth" are included. Now, is it not the case that this thing called conceit (māna) has the essential nature of uplifting (saṃpaggaha-rasa)?

How then can it occur in the context of self-deprecation (omāna)? Even that [conceit] proceeds by way of disparaging others through the basis of its own establishment, functioning precisely as an act of uplifting;
thus, there is no contradiction. For this very reason, he said: "Thinking 'Am I not a slave?', one performs these acts of conceit. Likewise:
His state of conceit regarding what is as-it-is has been described.

Like craving for existence (*bhava-nikanti*) and like the view of self (*attadiṭṭhi*), conceit regarding what is as-it-is is not a great offense; therefore, those [two] do not lead to the states of misery (*apāya*).

For they are conceits regarding what is as-it-is because they are based on things exactly as they have become (*yathābhūta-vatthuka*). And the phrase "to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship" is used because of its abandonment without remainder.
It has been said. Furthermore, by the second and third paths, those [defilements] that are respectively more gross and most gross are abandoned.
For conceit (*māna*), which functions as the thought "I am," is abandoned in the higher paths because it is the direct opposite of right view (*sammādiṭṭhi*).

They are called "conceits not in accordance with reality" (*ayāthāvamānā*) because they take as their objective base what is not truly so; for that very reason, they possess a state of being highly reprehensible.
Those [fetters] to be abandoned by the first path have been stated.
It is called *addhā* because it constantly moves (*atati*), goes, and proceeds; thus he says, "three *addhās* means three times.
"By way of the Suttanta method" means according to the manner presented in such discourses as the *Bhaddekaratta-sutta*. For therein it is said: "And whatever, friend, is the mind..."
"Whatever phenomena [there are], both of these are present.
If consciousness is bound by desire and lust for that which is present, then because consciousness is bound by desire and lust, one delights in it;
delighting in it, one is swept away by present phenomena. This was said with reference to the "present as duration" (*addhā-paccuppanna*). Therefore, he said:
“Prior to rebirth-linking,” and so forth. “The interval between those” refers to the intermediate present period between death and rebirth-linking;

because it lies midway between the past limit and the future limit, it is referred to as the “past and future limits” in such passages as, “He is doubtful about the past and future limits,” and “Ignorance regarding the past and future limits.
This phenomenon of dissolution is included within the past time-period.
He said: "That which is beyond dissolution is called the past time. Likewise, since an unarisen phenomenon is included within the future, he said:
"That which is prior to arising is called the future time. Regarding the "three moments": these are the three moments of arising, subsistence, and dissolution.
For when a phenomenon arises through the concurrence of causes and conditions, and when it passes away—thus in both [of these two moments]...
The "present" is like the moment of duration (*ṭhitikkhaṇa*) among the moments. For phenomena (*dhamma*), arising (*udaya*) is that which is to be reached, conditioned by the state of ripening;

passing away (*vaya*) is conditioned by the state of dissolution; and duration (*ṭhiti*) is the interval between those two. If this is so, does it follow that this "time" (*addhā*) is itself a phenomenon?
It is not a phenomenon, but rather a distinction of states (*avatthābheda*) of a phenomenon; and based upon that, the conventional designation "time" (*kāla-samaññā*) is used in the world.
In order to show this, it was said: "And this so-called distinction of past and so forth," and so on. "Here" means in this world.

"By that very conventional expression" refers to the conventional designation by which a phenomenon (*dhamma*)—depending upon its various specific states—is expressed as "past," "future," or "present.
For although time does not exist in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*), because it is merely the occurrence of phenomena, it belongs to that very phenomenon.
Depending on the specific state of its occurrence, it is expressed by that very same conventional term as "the past period" and so forth.

Since the word *anta* is established in common usage in the sense of "end" (*pariyosāna*) and "limit" (*koṭi*), he says "the end itself is *anta*" to show that meaning; the meaning is "the limit is the end.
"The further portion" means the opposite side. "It goes to the conclusion"—that is, the continuity of existence (*bhavappabandha*) reaches its termination.
"Herein" (*ettha*) means within, the limit (*koṭi*). "The going to the end" (*antaṃ niṭṭhānagamanaṃ*) means the end, the conclusion.

Since it is said, "This indeed is the end of suffering," he says "the further side" (*parabhāgo*), meaning the opposite shore of the ocean of suffering. It is called "end" (*anto*) because it is measured, overcome, or despised; thus it is base.
It is called "end" (*anto*) because it is measured and known by way of portions; thus he says "a portion is the end" (*koṭṭhāso anto*). [Those who are] "peaceful" (*santo*) in the ultimate sense...
A "personality" (*sakkāya*) is a body that exists as a collection of phenomena (*dhamma*); these are the aggregates (*khandhā*).

However, since it is those [aggregates] existing as noble truths that are intended here, it is said: "the five aggregates of clinging. "Former craving" refers to the craving that establishes those [aggregates];
it is craving already established prior to their production. "Becoming non-occurrence" means that both of those do not occur there; thus, it is the state where their non-occurrence takes place.
If the Truth of Suffering and the others are included because they are mutually analyzed by such phrases as "personality-existence is internal," then why is the Path not included?
To this he says, "But the Path," and so forth. Therein, "by way of being a means" (*upāyattā*) means by way of its state as a means; the meaning is:

by way of its being a cause that brings about [the goal]. But if the cause is already included by the inclusion of that which possesses the cause, then would it not follow that by the inclusion of personality-existence (*sakkāya*), its cause—namely, ignorance—is also included?

Is the origin of identity (sakkāyasamudaya) included because it is its cause? If it were included by that inclusion, then this would result in a dyad—just like the dyad of the conditioned (saṅkhata-duka) and the dyad of the conditioned-with-cause (sappaccaya-duka)—and not a triad.

However, just as the origin of identity is included when identity is grasped, so too the means to the cessation of identity (sakkāyanirodhupāya) should be grasped when the cessation of identity is grasped; if that were the case, it would be a tetrad.
This [person] would incur [the offense], not the triad; therefore, by the inclusion of "possessing a cause," the inclusion of "cause" itself need not be considered separately.

However, the following intention (adhippāya) here would be appropriate: here, both the personhood-aggregate (sakkāya) and the origin of that aggregate are beginningless, and they are endless so long as there is no cultivation of the Path due to the non-cessation of conditions; but Nibbāna, because it is without conditions, is eternal in its own right.
"Existing at all times" means it is beginningless and without end. Thus, by this common characteristic, the Great Elder groups these three truths into a triad called "the three ends.

However, since the Noble Path is not like that—being obtained only occasionally and at rare intervals—in order to demonstrate its extremely difficult manifestation, he places it outside the triad; this is my own opinion on the matter.
“Dukkhatā” means the state of suffering (*dukkhabhāva*), or simply suffering itself, just as “devo” (a god) is the same as “devatā” (a deity).

Furthermore, this word *dukkha* is applied even to pleasure (*sukha*) and equanimity (*upekkhā*), which do not have the nature of suffering, by taking into account some particular quality of being undesirable.

Therefore, in order to exclude those [other states], it is distinguished by another word *dukkha* that denotes suffering by its very nature, as in the term “*dukkhadukkhatā*” (the suffering of suffering).
He said: Even when there is an absolute identity of nature, there may still be a suspicion of deviation (vyabhicāra) due to some aspect of similarity with another phenomenon;

therefore, it must be specified, as in the cases of "visible form" (*rūpa-rūpa*) and "sesame oil. "By way of being conditioned" (*saṅkhāra-bhāvena*) means by way of being constructed (*saṅkhata-bhāvena*).
They are called "formations" (*saṅkhārā*) because they are constructed by conditions; [this refers to] neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Because they are being constructed...

For indeed, because of their lack of essence and their state of extreme weakness, conditioned phenomena (saṅkhārā) proceed in such a way that they are afflicted even at the very moment of their acquisition, just as they are at the moments immediately facing dissolution;
thus it is said: "Because they are conditioned, they are oppressed by arising, aging, and dissolution.

"Therefore" means for the reason just stated. "Due to the absence of any other intrinsic nature of suffering" refers to the absence of what is designated as the suffering of suffering (dukkhadukkhatā) and the suffering of change (vipariṇāmadukkhatā).
Because there is no other nature of suffering [than this]. "It changes" (*vipariṇāmeti*) means it undergoes transformation; the meaning is that it vanishes. Therefore, he said in the *Papañcasūdanī*:
"Suffering due to change (*vipariṇāmadukkha*) is the state of non-existence. For those who have not fully understood the basis [of feeling], the cessation of pleasant feeling appears as suffering;
this point can be illustrated by the separation from what is dear. Therefore, he said:

“‘Of pleasure,’ etc. This refers to the method previously stated. However, because that method relies on a specific portion and has as its object merely a particular type of feeling, the second method beginning with “Furthermore” was stated in order to show the suffering inherent in all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāradukkha*) without exception.

But is it not the case that, according to the statement “All conditioned phenomena are suffering,” even pleasant and painful feelings would necessarily fall under the category of the suffering of conditioned phenomena? True, this is so; however, that is a general characterization which is set aside by...
It is excluded by the mention of "other forms of suffering," so there is no contradiction. For this very reason, he said: "except for painful feeling and pleasant feeling.

It has a false nature because it does not exist in the way one hopes it will—"it will bring me benefit and happiness"—and because it occurs as a perversion, such as perceiving the foul and so forth as "beautiful";
thus, its nature is falsehood, which is the meaning. [This applies] to those such as matricides and others.
For even while they are occurring, they proceed only because they desire welfare and happiness; thus, those states are wished for with the thought, "May they bring about my welfare and happiness.

Likewise, due to the strength of the perversion that perceives the beautiful and so forth in what is actually foul, unpleasant, impermanent, and non-self, there occurs an engagement in wrong views that are fixed for immediate retribution;
thus, those states function as the occurrence of perversions such as the beautiful in regard to the foul and so forth. This being so, when there is the giving of a result...
It is "fixed" because it gives its result immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates; and since it is both wrong view and fixed, it is called "fixed in wrongness" (*micchattaniyata*).

Since when many deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) have been committed, that which is strongest among them ripens and not the others, one cannot say that its state of being fixed is due to the production of an inevitable result;
therefore, it is said: "when there is the giving of the result. "Immediately after the breaking up of the aggregates" means immediately after death.

This is the meaning. For in the description of death (*cuti*) as "the breaking up of the aggregates" (*khandhānaṃ bhedo*), by this statement it is said that when the giving of the fruit occurs, the time for these [karmas] to bear fruit is immediately after death and not otherwise;
thus, certainty is expressed through the restriction of the time of fruition, not through a restriction on the act of giving the fruit.

This applies even to other [karmas] whose time of fruition is certain—namely, those to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*) and those to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).

It would follow that [the action] is fixed; therefore, just as those things whose nature is to ripen (vipākadhammadhamma) possess the quality of being subject to ripening by their own intrinsic nature even when they do not ripen due to the deficiency of other conditions,
so too, even when they do not ripen because a powerful *ānantariya* [kamma] has already yielded its result,
the *ānantariya* actions possess a fixed nature regarding the giving of their fruit, and their occurrence possesses the nature of an *ānantariya* by their own intrinsic nature.
Their certainty and their state of being an immediate result (ānantariya) should be understood as being due to the very nature of the giving of the fruit.
And it must be accepted that their occurrence possesses the nature of being certain and the nature of being an immediate result, because— in the absence of another stronger immediate result—
they invariably yield their fruit immediately after death.

[Objection: But in this way, would it not follow that for other [karmas] to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), since they must necessarily yield their fruit immediately after death when no other giver of ripening exists, they would possess the nature of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*) and their occurrence would be of a fixed nature? [Reply:

It does not follow, because their ripening is to be averted by a mental aspiration (*cetopaṇidhi*) of a different kind and by means of an injury; thus, there is an absence of the quality of yielding fruit exclusively in the immediately following existence.
However, there is no intention that turns back the fruit of the immediate (ānantariya) karmas— just as the second jhāna and so forth turn back the first jhāna and so forth—
because all immediate karmas have Avīci as their fruit; nor is an intention capable of turning back the power of an immediate karma,
as the mental aspiration of a virtuous person desiring rebirth in a lower plane is capable of producing rebirth in a higher plane.
There is [a state] that causes one to fall into Avīci even against one’s will, yet there is no karma whatsoever that destroys an ānantariya deed.

Therefore, their very occurrence has the nature of producing an exclusively immediate result. Furthermore, although many ānantariya deeds have been committed, they are determined by their intrinsic nature because they are fixed in their exclusive maturation and because there is no possibility of their ceasing to ripen.
They are indeed fixed. Furthermore, immediately after the cutting off [of the roots], the fruit is called "immediate" (*anantara*);

those [karmas] are connected to that immediate state, they have the habit of performing the immediate act by way of producing that [fruit], and they have that as their purpose; thus, by their very nature, they are indeed "immediate" (*ānantariya*).
Among those of identical nature, when the result has been given by one, the others [no longer have] the duty to be performed by themselves.
Because it has already been performed by that [first action], they do not produce a second or third rebirth-linking;

nor is it because of the destruction of their capacity. Thus, there is no cessation of their fixed state of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*). For a thing of the same nature does not destroy the capacity of another thing of the same nature.
However, it should be understood that for one [action], others may also serve as supporting factors. Regarding "the true nature" (*sammāsabhāve*):

Regarding the true nature of reality (*sacca-sabhāva*): it is "determined" (*niyata*) because it is absolute and gives its fruit immediately; this refers to the determination of rightness (*sammatta-niyama*). "Not determined" (*na niyata*) means it is not determined in either way.

"Of the remaining phenomena" (*avasesānaṃ dhammānaṃ*) refers to phenomena other than those that are defilements, actions with immediate retribution (*ānantariya-kamma*), and factors leading to liberation (*niyyānika-dhamma*).
"That darkness" (*tama-andhakāra*) is the analysis of the compound as *tamo* (darkness) and *andhakāro* (blindness). Ignorance (*avijjā*) is called "darkness" in the sense of obscuring the object.
For this very reason it is said: “Darkness has been dispelled, light has arisen; the mass of darkness has been shattered,” and so forth.
Doubt (*vicikicchā*) is spoken of under the heading of ignorance (*avijjā*), because it is never dissociated from great delusion. “Having approached” means having reached.
“He doubts” means he generates doubt and falls into uncertainty by way of such thoughts as, “Did I exist in the past? and so on. To resolve with conviction...
"He is not able" means he is not able to resolve [the mind] by way of serene confidence and resolute conviction. Therefore, it says, "he does not become confident.
For as long as doubt has not subsided regarding a particular object, so long there is no opportunity for the resolution of faith therein.
Not only does the resolution of faith fail to establish itself there, but even the resolution of certainty does not find a footing at all.
"They need not be guarded" means that there is no duty of guarding anywhere in the sense of "these must be guarded by me," because there is simply nothing further left to be guarded.
"Guarded by mindfulness alone" means that since negligence was eradicated at the foot of the Bodhi tree along with its latent tendencies,
those things which are called "to be guarded by mindfulness" are indeed always guarded.
"There is no bodily misconduct for the Tathāgata" means that for the Tathāgata, what is called bodily misconduct simply does not exist, because the Blessed One’s bodily conduct is perfectly pure.
It is not impure; it is indeed pure because the defilements that are the causes of impurity have been abandoned.
Nevertheless, in the Vinaya, there might appear a slight trace of impurity on their part due to a lack of gratitude.
In order to show that it was not the Blessed One [who spoke these words], the passage beginning with “But not... was stated.

Therein, regarding the phrase “an offense of building a dwelling,” one should connect the word *āpatti* (offense) from the plural form “offenses” (*āpattiyo*) by means of the singular; for gender and number conform to the thing denoted.
This same principle applies to the remaining cases as well. The mention of “at the mind-door” is because that offense originates through non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhānatā*).
It has been stated: "For there is no offense formally designated (paññatta) in the mind-door.
"By way of being subject to reproach" means by way of being censurable, but not by way of an offense characterized as misconduct (*duccarita*), since the Blessed One rejects such [a view].
Just as in the case of the Venerable Mahākappina: "I might go to the Uposatha, or I might not go. I might go..."
He reflected, "I might not attend the formal act of the Saṅgha. Mental misconduct (*manoduccarita*) is unwholesome conduct pertaining to the door of the mind.
It is called "misconduct" because it is disapproved by the Teacher; it is not so by its own intrinsic nature.
For the Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One, acting solely for the welfare and happiness of the world including the devas, [prohibited it] due to his inclination toward absolute seclusion.
Rejecting the mental state of the Dhamma General (Sāriputta), which was contrary to that [of the Blessed One], he said, “Indeed, you should not...
nor should you produce such a thought. Therefore, considering that the Elder’s mental state was not praised by the Blessed One, it became what is called a mental misconduct;
and since the rejection of that [state] constitutes a reproach, he says, “while attributing a reproach for that mental misconduct.”
But for the Blessed One, even this much was not the case; for when he said in the Pavāraṇā Sutta, "Come now, monks, let me invite you;

do not find fault with me regarding anything, whether bodily or verbal," the community of monks replied, "Venerable sir, we do not find fault with the Blessed One regarding anything, whether bodily or verbal. [This shows] the Teacher’s purity of bodily conduct and so forth.

He accepted it with his head. For this absence of misconduct on the part of the Lord of the World had been a constant feature of his conduct even while he was on the stage of a bodhisatta, let alone on the stage of a Buddha; showing this, he said, "And this is not surprising," and so forth.

The qualities and attributes belonging exclusively to Buddhas, and not to others, are called "Buddha-qualities" (*buddhadhammā*). Thus, they are indeed the unique qualities (*āveṇikadhammā*) of the Buddhas.

...are so called. In that context, the statement regarding the absence of misconduct of body, speech, and mind—beginning with “There is no misconduct of the body for the Tathāgata”—is a praise of the qualities attained because bodily actions and the rest follow after knowledge according to their respective functions; it is not intended to show them as distinct, independent factors (āveṇika-dhamma).
For when all bodily actions and the rest follow after knowledge, how could there be any possibility of misconduct of the body and so forth? [Regarding] the Buddha’s...

They say that the three knowledges described by the phrase “unobstructed knowledge,” and so forth, are distinct from omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), just like the knowledges that delimit the four modes of birth and the five destinations.
However, being one and the same, what is called "unobstructed knowledge" across the three times is simply omniscient knowledge itself.
"There is no decline of zeal" means there is no decline in the zeal for the welfare of sentient beings. "There is no decline of energy" means...
There is no decline in energy for one who follows thoughts of security and seclusion.
They say: “No frolic” means there is no activity with the intention of play; “no noise” means there is no impulsive activity.
However, impulsive activity is “frolic,” and doing something else with the thought “I will do something else” is “noise. A “lapse” is a failure, something not reached by knowledge.
"Sahasā" means acting with haste; it is a hurried performance. "Abyāvaṭo mano" refers to a purposeless activity of the mind. By "unwholesome mind," he refers to ignorance and equanimity;
however, this reading appears somewhat confused according to the recension of the Dīgha-bhāṇakas. This reading, on the other hand, is unconfused:
"The Blessed Buddha’s knowledge is unimpeded regarding the past, regarding the future, and regarding the present. By these three..."
For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these six qualities, every bodily action is preceded by knowledge and follows after knowledge;

so too are all verbal actions and all mental actions. For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these six qualities, there is no decline in his zeal, no [decline] in his teaching of the Dhamma, and no [decline] in his energy.

He lacks concentration, he lacks wisdom, and he lacks liberation. For the Buddha, the Blessed One, who is endowed with these twelve qualities, there is no joking, no shouting, no lack of pervasion [of attention],
no hurriedness, no unengaged mind, and no equanimity without discernment.
In this context, "equanimity of non-reflection" is equanimity of ignorance. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
And here, having included the Tathāgata’s purity of livelihood within the purity of conduct of body, speech, and mind, the Elder has taught the triad by way of the three types of conduct.

“Kiñcanā” means trifles (kiñcikkhā). However, these [defilements] such as lust and so forth are called “kiñcanā” because they are like obstacles in the sense of being a hindrance (palibundhanaṭṭhena). Therefore he said: “‘Kiñcanā’ means impediments (palibodhā).

Regarding the phrase “in the sense of burning along,” this means in the sense of burning repeatedly. To dispel the doubt—namely, how immaterial states (arūpadhammā) such as lust, which exist for only a moment, can burn along—he said:
“In this regard, there are instances (vatthūni),” with the words “are to be seen” understood as the remainder of the sentence.

"In that regard" means in the sense of the burning away of lust and the other defilements. "Bases" refers to the causes that have become manifest through direct experience, being well-known both in the Teaching and in the world.

Lust, having arisen, becomes sharp; therefore, the fire element originating from it, by its extreme sharpness, burns the region of the heart together with the co-nascent phenomena, just as the external fire element does.
[It was] with its support (*sanissaya*). Because of that, that bhikkhunī, having been consumed by the fever of disease as if by fire, died. Therefore it is said:

“Having been consumed by that very [fever], she passed away. Since the burning away of the supports of hatred (*dosa*) is already evident, the phrase beginning with “by way of delusion (*moha*)” was stated in order to show the other [support].
“Having transgressed” means having exceeded [the limit].
Granted that the three fires beginning with the fire worthy of offerings (*āhuneyya*) are desired by the brahmins, yet they are merely what those [brahmins] desire;
they do not accomplish such a purpose for living beings. To show those things which do accomplish the welfare of living beings, it was said:
"Āhuna is so called," and so forth. In this context, *āhuna* refers to the offering (*havana*) or worship (*pūjana*) performed with reverence (*ādara*), that is, honor (*sakkāra*).
They are called "those worthy of offerings" because they deserve such offerings. Therefore the Blessed One said:
