"Monks, 'worthy of offerings' is a designation for mother and father.

And to the extent that, due to their great kindness toward their children, right conduct toward them brings benefit and happiness, to that same extent wrong conduct toward them brings harm and suffering; thus he said: "Toward them... [and so forth].
"...are being reborn. This is the meaning: it is the sense of "burning" (anudahanattha) by virtue of being the condition for the burning of children who have acted wrongly toward their parents.

This should be understood through the story of Mittavindaka, which illustrates how a man named Mittavindaka, having acted wrongly toward his mother, experienced the suffering of the states of misery (āpāyika-dukkha) for a very long time because of that very misconduct.
Now, in order to clarify how this matter occurred during the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, the passage beginning with “Mittavindaka indeed” was spoken.
The intention is that [he did so] out of greed for wealth, not out of a desire for the Dhamma. It is called “fearless from all sides” because it cannot be obstructed by anyone.
He prevented [him] with the intention that voyages across the ocean are beset with many obstacles. “Having made an interval” means by way of passing over [the distance].
Having placed [the boat] between two feet,
the ship remained stationary due to the power of his evil karma, because the wind did not blow. One day, experiencing prosperity through the influence of the protected uposatha observance,
just as he had been told by the previous ones, "Do not go further," so too was he told by each subsequent one.
He said: "While being told by them, 'Do not go further and further on! *Khuracakka-dharam* means a man bearing a wheel with edges like the blade of a razor.
He attended upon [her] through the power of his evil karma.
*Catūhi* means by four female spirits (*vimāna-peti*) resembling celestial nymphs (*accharā*); the ellipsis to be supplied is "having experienced prosperity."
"Aṭṭhajjhagama" means she attained eight celestial palaces (*vimāna*) that were even more distinguished than those [previously mentioned] by way of the objects of sensual pleasure, such as forms.
"Atriccha" means desiring this or that object of sensual pleasure because of being possessed by excessive greed, which is termed "atricchā.
"Cakka" refers to a razor-wheel. "Āsada" means it strikes or reaches [the victim] by way of bringing about harm.
"He" refers to the householder, the husband. "In the same manner as before" means by way of being a condition for the non-burning [of the body].

"An unfaithful wife" means one who acts transgressing her husband, that is, an adulteress. "Suffering at night" refers to the suffering of being bitten by a dog manifested through the power of her own evil kamma.
"Having deceived" refers to going to the place of business without having informed him.
It is said. "Paṭapaṭantī" means making a *paṭapaṭa* sound; for this is an onomatopoeic expression. This "fist-technique" (*muṭṭhiyoga*), it is said, was the means by which those dogs disappeared:
namely, spitting a lump of saliva onto the ground and rubbing [the spot] with the foot.
Therefore it is said: "He did so. The dogs disappeared."
“Dakkhiṇā” means that when the four requisites are given, welfare and happiness are seen through them.
One who is worthy of that gift is “dakkhiṇeyya,” namely, the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.
This should be understood according to the method found in the *Revatīvatthu*, the *Vimānavatthu*, the *Petavatthu*, and their respective commentaries.
Regarding the phrase “The inclusion of matter is threefold”: is it not the case that inclusion is of only one kind?
Why, then, is it said to be “fourfold”? Because the word *saṅgaha* (inclusion) is used here as a term whose meaning is not yet determined, rather than being used in its specific sense.
In passages such as “The inclusion of matter is threefold,” the word *saṅgaha* is fourfold according to its own respective meanings; this is what is intended here.

Meaning (*attha*). Alternatively, meaning itself—when its specific distinctions have not yet been determined and it has reached a state where it must be grasped in a general sense—is stated as "compendium" (*saṅgaha*) in such passages as "the threefold compendium of matter" (*tividhena rūpasaṅgaho*);
thus there is no fault. For if the specific distinction were already determined, that [meaning] would possess only a single mode;
it does not do so prior to that. Even when "compilation of classes" (*jātisaṅgaho*) is said, because the word "class" (*jāti*) is a term that requires a complement, [it refers to] one's own class...
The meaning "support" (saṅgaha) is indeed understood here because no other [meaning] suitable for the connection has been stated, just as in the expression “supporting mother and father.
However, in the Commentary, in order to show the intended meaning without leaving it incomplete, it is simply stated as “grouping by birth” (jātisaṅgaha).
It is the grouping of those of the same birth, or the grouping according to a common birth; thus, it is “grouping by birth” (sajātisaṅgaha).
It is called *sañjāti* because things are born (*sañjāyati*) therein; the inclusion by way of birth is *sañjātisaṅgaho*;
the meaning is that there is an inclusion according to the classification of birth. Inclusion by way of such an action is *kiriyāsaṅgaho*.

"The reckoning of the aggregate of form" means that it comes to be reckoned or numbered as "the aggregate of form" because its intrinsic nature is to be affected (by change). This refers to the reckoning of form by way of the three divisions that will be explained hereafter.
The meaning of "the inclusion of material form by way of three parts" is that it is to be enumerated.
It is called "visible" (*nidassana*) because it is seen—that is, it is cognized through direct perception—referring to the visible base (*rūpāyatana*);

or alternatively, it is "visible" because it shows itself, meaning its state of being observable, its state of being the objective domain of eye-consciousness (*cakkhuviññāṇa*), and [its arising] from that visible base.
Even though there is no difference [in the term itself], in order to distinguish the visible form base (*rūpāyatana*) from other phenomena, it is treated as if it were something else;
thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "it is 'with visibility' (*sanidassana*) because it is together with visibility.

For when phenomena have become one through their commonality of intrinsic nature (*dhammasabhāva*), it is appropriate to apply a metaphorical designation (*upacara*) by treating that specific nature which causes differentiation as if it were something else. In this way, the distinction of meaning is realized.
"It exists" means: "capable of striking the eye" because of its capacity to impact the eye. And "striking" should be understood as being like a physical blow.

According to the second alternative meaning, the construction is: "it is called 'non-demonstrable' (anidassana) because it has no demonstration (nidassana), which is to say, it lacks the state of being demonstrable.
And here, among the ten bases (āyatana), [the characteristic] applies to each as appropriate, either by itself or by way of its support.

And the state of being face-to-face with those [objects] that have arrived and those that have not yet arrived, which consists of mutual falling upon one another and striking against one another, is that by means of which, when other conditions for change such as mental effort (*byāpāra*) are present, a change arises in the eye and other faculties regarding their objects.
In this context, "effort" (*byāpāra*) is the reaching out of the eye and other faculties toward their respective objects;
"desirability or undesirability" (*iṭṭhāniṭṭhatā*) refers to the quality of forms and so forth; and "bending of the mind" (*cittassa ābhujana*) is the inclination of the consciousness toward them.

These are included by the word "etcetera. Because they undergo transformation through the operation of other conditions, they are considered "other"; thus, transformation (*vikāra*) consists of assistance and injury.

However, here the decisive support (*upanissaya*) is taken as a subordinate condition. If the instrumental cause of a cause is also accepted as being simply a "cause," then it too might be included therein.
"Of the aforementioned kind" means of the kind described as "consisting of eye-consciousness."
Regarding the phrase "there is no resistance for it," here too the connection is made by supplying the words "of the type already mentioned. The remaining sixteen kinds are subtle matter.

"They construct" means they aggregate. For volition, because its essential function is exertion (*āyūhana*), while it proceeds as if distributing associated states to their respective functions and binding them together, it aggregates them by that very specific function.
Just as [a heap] comes to be, so too, when the collection of conditions is present, one’s own states that are subject to ripening seem to be constructing and accumulating.
Therefore he said: “Co-nascent... they form a heap. *Abhisaṅkharoti* means: having made it distinguished (*abhivisiṭṭhaṃ*), one constructs (*saṅkharoti*).
For the meritorious formation (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*) is far more distinguished than the fruit of the other.

Having distinguished [the factors], one synthesizes them by way of condition, by way of intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*), and by way of the mode of occurrence, because each possesses an intrinsic nature distinct from the others.
This same method applies to the others as well. It is called "meritorious" (*puñña*) because it produces the fruit of a state worthy of honor and because it causes one's own continuum to flourish.
"Of great mental volitions" means of those volitions occurring within great minds, due to their great majesty such as the production of an incalculable lifespan and so forth.
There are exactly eight volitions that are wholesome in the sense-sphere. Why is it said, "thirteen as well," when one might instead say "nine"?
This is said in response to the objection: "Is it not the case that development devoid of knowledge is improper? To this he says, "Just as... and so forth.
"One who performs the preliminary work for the kasiṇas" means one who performs the preliminary work for jhāna regarding the kasiṇas. "Earth, earth," and so forth...

For development (*bhāvanā*) consists in the preliminary work (*parikamma*) on the kasiṇa. Because that preliminary work has been well-mastered, for one who is devoted to it, there may arise a mind devoid of knowledge due to a lack of earnest application toward it.
The same principle applies to the reviewing of jhāna as well. Some even include the drawing of the mandala within "development."

The mental states and mental factors that proceed as giving are "giving" (dāna). Among these, the volition of exertion (*āyūhana-cetanā*), which constitutes the active operation therein, is said to arise with giving as its object and with giving as its basis. The same applies to the others. This is called the "concise teaching";
the meaning is that this is a concise explanation of the meaning regarding the formative action of merit (*puññābhisaṅkhāra*). It is an exposition of the meaning.
The phrase "with a mind of joy" (*somanassacittena*) should be understood as merely showing the occurrence of rejoicing (*anumodanā*).

For one recollects even with a mind accompanied by equanimity (*upekkhā*). Although the constant virtue (*niccasīla*), the Uposatha virtue, and the restricted virtue (*niyamasīla*) are indeed virtue, the statement beginning with "for the sake of fulfilling virtue" (*sīlapūraṇatthāya*) was said in order to show virtue that is complete and endowed with all its factors. This is the demonstration of the method (*nayadassana*).
Or rather, the volition that arises in one who goes to the monastery thinking, "I shall undertake the constant virtue, the Uposatha virtue,
and the restricted virtue," as well as in one who, having undertaken them, reflects upon that undertaken virtue with the thought, "Excellent! Well done!", and while purifying that virtue—
this is how the application of the term "consisting of virtue" (sīlamaya) should be understood here.

Since the method of development by way of serenity was already taken up previously, the passage beginning with "as stated in the *Paṭisambhidā*" is now spoken in order to show that same method by way of comprehension (*sammasana*).
Therein, "as impermanent" means from the state of impermanence. The same method applies here as well for "as suffering" and "as non-self.
In that context, those five aggregates of clinging which were defined by way of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are, because of the doors and objects, [subject to]...
They receive their classification by way of the phenomena that proceed through the doors; therefore, six sets of six are taken according to the six doors and so forth.
However, because among the characteristics the characteristic of non-self (*anattalakkhaṇa*) is difficult to discern, the six elements were taken for its clarification.
Following that, those *kasiṇas* upon which outsiders fixate on a self—those [are now addressed] for these [people].

These [objects] appear merely as the mode of presentation by way of being the objects of the jhānas; however, the ten kasiṇas are taken up for the purpose of showing that "these are indeed those jhānas.
Following that, the thirty-two parts are taken up by way of their repulsive aspect as an accompaniment to the contemplation of suffering.
Previously, these phenomena were taken up briefly by way of the aggregates (khandha); now—
The twelve bases (*āyatana*) and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are included in order to show that mental attention should be practiced in a manner that is neither too concise nor too detailed.
Among these, the faculties (*indriya*) are included to demonstrate the state of non-self (*anatta*);
for although these phenomena are empty, inactive, and devoid of agency, they proceed by way of their own intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*) through the exercise of sovereignty (*ādhipacca*). Thus...

Although these phenomena (dhammas) are divided into many categories, the three elements (dhātus) are included in order to show that they are, in fact, only threefold by virtue of being comprised within the three planes of existence.
Having thus shown the sign (nimitta), nine types of existence (bhava)—beginning with sensual existence (kāmabhava)—are included in order to show the process of occurrence (pavatta).
Through skill in attention occurring toward these specific objects of direct knowledge (abhiññeyya-visesa), [one enters] into the subtle and refined [states].
The jhānas and the immeasurables (appamaññā) are included in order to show that attention should be directed toward the sublime states (mahaggata-dhamma) that have been produced.
Therein, "jhānas" refers to the fine-material-sphere jhānas whose objects are those remaining [from the list] as previously stated.

Furthermore, the factors of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda-aṅga) are included in order to show that these phenomena must be attended to by way of analysis according to the distinction between conditions and the things arisen from conditions.
For attention to the mode of conditions (paccayākāra-manasikāra) easily and more thoroughly clarifies the three characteristics;
therefore, it was taken up last. Thus, these aggregates and so forth, which were taken by way of their being objects for comprehension, are twenty-fivefold when categorized by division;
however, when taken according to their subdivisions such as the past and so on, they number one hundred and ninety-eight. This...

This is the establishment of the text (*pāḷivavatthāna*) here; however, those who desire an investigation of the meaning (*atthavicāra*) should understand it according to the method stated in the *Visuddhimagga-vaṇṇanā* within the *Paramatthamañjūsā*.

"Non-meritorious" (*apuñña*) means not meritorious (*na puñño*). Its meaning should be understood through the opposite of the meaning assigned to the word "merit" (*puñña*). Of the continuum (*santānassa*)...
Because the hindrances and other causes of movement have been thoroughly suppressed, and because there is an absence of movement known as craving for form (*rūpataṇhā*), it is "unmoving" (*aniñja*);

that which is unmoving is called "the imperturbable" (*āneñja*). For indeed, every fourth jhāna, whether having form as its object or the sign of form as its object, is called "the imperturbable" in the primary sense.
It is sevenfold as follows: four who stand on the paths and three who stand in the lower fruits. The "three trainings" refers to the three trainings beginning with higher virtue (*adhisīla*).
One is a "trainee" (*sekkha*) because one is born into them; for a noble person (*ariyapuggala*), being born through noble birth, is born into the trainings, not into a [biological] womb.
Alternatively, a "trainee" is one whose nature is to train. Or, in a discourse focused on the individual (*puggalādhiṭṭhāna*), it refers to the trainee.
The phenomena consisting of the three paths and fruits, which are not shared with others, are spoken of by way of the "trainee" (sekha).

As for the term "adept" (asekha), this is a negation applied wherever there might be a suspicion of being a trainee; thus, it should be understood that the state of being an adept applies to mundane [states] and to Nibbāna.
For the trainings—comprising virtue, concentration, and wisdom—are themselves liberated from their respective opposing defilements.
Because they are completely purified and do not even fall into the state of being objects for the defilements, these are appropriately called "trainings" (sikkhā);

they exist in all eight paths and fruits. Therefore, just as one who possesses the four paths and the three lower fruits is born into those trainings, so too is one who possesses the fruit of arahantship; and thus, for the Arahant who possesses them, [the training] is just as it is for others.

Since one who possesses training (sekha) is called "one in training" (sekkha), and since one for whom training and virtue (sīla) proceed is also called "one in training," the term "non-trainee" (asekkha) is employed to exclude that;

it is a negation of the aforementioned state of being a trainee. For when training proceeds within the fruit of Arhatship (arahatta-phala), because the duties of training have been fully accomplished, those [factors] do not perform the duty of training, but exist solely as the fruit of training.
Because they occur [only occasionally], they do not deserve the designation "training" (*sikkhā*);
nor does one who possesses them deserve the designation "trainee" (*sekkha*), nor the description "one whose nature is training" or "born in the trainings.

However, in the lower fruits, training performs the function of training because it serves as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the insight and so forth of the path of the once-returner; thus, it receives the designation "training."
They are worthy of that title, and those who possess it are worthy of being called "trainers" (*sekkha*)—meaning "those whose nature is to train" and "those born into the trainings.
Furthermore, by the definition "one who trains is a trainer," one whose training is not yet completed is indicated.

Immediately thereafter, having stated "one whose taints are destroyed" and so forth, and then saying "one who does not train is an adept" (*asekkha*), one whose training is completed is indicated; it is not indicated as being devoid of training.
Because he is grasped as the third type of person. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "one who has reached growth in training is an Asekha":
in this sense, since some noble one established in the very qualities of training (sekkhadhamma) attains the state of an Asekha, the qualities of the path of Arahatship are "grown" (vuddhippatta);
and because one possesses those [qualities], being established in the highest path, one is designated a "Sekha" according to the meanings already stated.
"Has he attained the state of one beyond training (asekkha)? No, because that designation is applied to those things similar to it.
For the fruit of arahantship is not distinct from the path of arahantship, except for its performance of functions such as full understanding (pariññā) and its nature as a result (vipāka).

Therefore, it can be said that those very same qualities of one-in-training (sekkha-dhamma) have "attained the state of the qualities of the supreme fruit. And the bliss of the result is more peaceful than the bliss of the wholesome (kusala).
"More sublime" means that those qualities have reached growth; one who possesses them is called "one beyond training" (*asekha*).
"An elder by birth" means one who is older by birth, advanced in years, and has reached the stage of old age.

Because he has for the most part attained stability in the duties pertaining to birth and family through his long-standing seniority, he is called a "birth-elder" (*jātithero*). These are the qualities that constitute an elder.
The qualities that produce stability in the Teaching are those which crush opposing factors. One who has attained stability in the qualities about to be mentioned is called a "Thera" (Elder).

"Virtuous" (*sīlavā*) means endowed with praiseworthy and preeminent virtue; the meaning is "perfected in virtue. By this, he expresses the absence of foolishness, which is characterized by immorality.
"Learned" (*bahussuto*) means one by whom much—such as the discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so forth—has been heard; by this, [he expresses the absence of] the lack of learning...
By the phrase "through the power of reflection," he speaks of the absence of childishness and its establishment through that power.
By the phrase "attainer of the four jhānas," he explains the absence of childishness—consisting of the hindrances and so forth—and its establishment through the power of meditation.

By the phrase "through the destruction of the taints" and so on, he indicates the total absence of childishness, which is synonymous with ignorance, by virtue of being an elder whose taints are exhausted.
And he shows its state of being established. Here, the completion of the sentence does not apply to the whole collection, but rather to each individual term;
showing this, he says: "When these things have been thus spoken," and so forth. Or, one who has the name "Thera" is "the Elder.
Giving (*dāna*) is that by which one's own possession is given to another, either for the sake of assistance or for the sake of honor; it is the volition of relinquishment.

“Giving itself” means consisting of giving. The word *maya* is used merely for the sake of completing the meter. It is “meritorious activity” (*puññakiriyā*) because it is both merit—in the sense already stated—and an action, by virtue of being a kamma-state.
“Of benefits such as being dear and pleasing to others, and being worthy of service”:

[this refers to] “by way of the aforementioned” [types of volition], that is, by way of the volition consisting of giving, the volition consisting of virtue, and the volition consisting of meditation, as stated in the Triplet on Formations (*Saṅkhārattika*).
"These are to be understood" is the connection [of the sentence]. "In this" means among these bases for making merit (*puññakiriyavatthu*).
"One who acts with the body" means one who sets in motion the application of relinquishment by means of one's own body. "For that purpose" means for the sake of giving.
"Uttering the words, 'Give this gift'" refers to one who speaks thus. "Or, having adverted to the perfection of giving" means as follows: "The giving of food and so forth..."

At the time of giving, that becomes a basis for meritorious action consisting of giving; likewise, because one acts with the very head of giving at the time of giving, having adverted to the perfection of giving with the thought, "May this gift consisting of giving be a condition for perfect enlightenment.

"Standing at the head of the practice" means [standing] in the virtue of conduct, thinking: "This so-called gift is my family lineage, my family tradition, my family succession, and my family custom."
Standing firm in the virtue of conduct (*cārittasīla*). Just as the volition of giving (*dānacetanā*), although it proceeds by way of relinquishing the object to be given,

becomes a basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya*) for one who gives while standing at the head of the practice— because it proceeds in such a manner through both the prior formation and the subsequent volition—
so too for one who gives after establishing the contemplation of the object to be given as subject to destruction and decay.

The basis for meritorious action consisting in development (*bhāvanāmaya-puññakiriyavatthu*) pertains to the volition preceding [the act] and the volition following it with respect to the object to be given, because it proceeds in such a manner.

The volition of reverence (*apacīti-cetanā*) is that which is accompanied by reverence; it is so called because one is revered by means of it—just as "delight-and-lust" (*nandīrāga*) is itself "accompanied by delight-and-lust."
"Accompanied by honor" means it arises together with, or concomitant with, the aforementioned forms of honor; it is a basis for meritorious action that proceeds by way of showing respect.
That volition by which one is engaged in the performance of duties toward those who are senior in age and in virtues is "service";
service itself is "accompanied by service. [It is so called] because of what is reckoned as service...
Or, it is "accompanied by service" because it occurs together with the undertaking of duties (*vatta-paṭipatti*) through the very act of instigating them;

such an occurrence is a basis for the performance of merit (*puññakiriyavatthu*). It is "the giving of what has been received" (*pattānuppadāna*) because by means of this, the merit obtained within one's own continuum is handed over to another.
Likewise, it is "the rejoicing in what has been received" (*pattabbhanumodana*) because by means of this, one exults in the merit received from another.
That by which one merely rejoices in what has not been given is "rejoicing" (*abbhanumodana*). That by which one teaches the Dhamma is "teaching" (*desanā*);
teaching itself is "consisting of teaching" (*desanāmaya*). That by which one hears is "hearing" (*savana*); hearing itself is "consisting of hearing" (*savanāmaya*).
The straightening of view—that is, of knowledge—is "rectitude of view" (*diṭṭhijugata*). In all instances, the term "bases for the performance of merit" (*puññakiriyavatthu*) applies.
The neuter gender [of the term] is used because it refers to [the act of] looking after.

*Apacāyana* (reverence) is the performance of respectful service by way of worship; it is honor (*apaciti*). *Veyyāvacca* (service) is the performance of various duties for those who are senior in age or virtue, as well as for those who are ill.
He said "therein," etc., to indicate the distinction between these. The four requisites...
The phrase "having given to all beings" is an expression of excellence by way of partial inclusion;

even if one gives whatever gift is suitable or performs some meritorious deed and dedicates it with the thought, "May the merit belong to only a few, or to just one," that too is indeed the bestowing of what has been attained.
However, that [dedication] is not of great fruit because it is tainted by craving. One teaches others with a gentle mind through the radiation of benevolence.

Having brought [the meaning] together, it should be connected. "Thus" means: having heard this Dhamma in this way, thinking, "Having become learned, I shall assist others by teaching the Dhamma," one listens to the Dhamma with a mind softened by the radiation of benevolence (*hitapharaṇa*).
For in this way, his hearing will be of great fruit, as it becomes a condition for the right practice of both himself and others. "Of all" means: of everyone.
Of the ten bases for the performance of merit. "The characteristic of certainty" means the inherent nature that determines the state of great fruitfulness.

"Precisely by way of straightness of view" means by the very straightness of proceeding through right view—which functions according to the method beginning with "there is giving" and so forth—due to having cast far away the two extremes of "it exists" and "it does not exist. For, among giving and the rest, whatever...
By means of this very right view, it becomes purified, greatly radiant, and vastly expansive.

"By the three preceding ones" refers to those three mentioned in the Pāḷi text. They are included within the basis for meritorious action consisting in virtue (*sīlamaya-puññakiriyavatthu*) because they possess the nature of conduct-virtue (*cāritta-sīla*).
They are included within the basis consisting in giving (*dānamaya*) because they have the intrinsic nature of giving (*dāna-sabhāva*) and because they are the domain of giving (*dāna-visaya*).
Granted, it is appropriate to say that teaching belongs within the category of giving consisting in material gifts (*dānamaya*), by virtue of its nature as a gift of the Dhamma;

however, because it consists in the practice of wholesome states, it is said to belong within the category of development consisting in cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*), as if it were established at the head of the bases of liberation (*vimuttāyatana*) along with hearing.
Some say, "It belongs in development consisting in cultivation because it inclines one toward right view. And indeed, [the teacher] himself [inclines] toward right view.
The recollection of merit performed, the dedication of that merit for the benefit of others,
the praising of virtues, and the rejoicing in meritorious deeds and right practice performed by others—
these various kinds of merit are included within the "straightening of views," because they succeed only through that means.

“Accusation” (*codanā*) is the application for the purpose of purifying another’s conduct; those things upon which it proceeds are the bases for accusation (*codanāvatthu*), namely, what is seen, heard, and suspected.
Therefore, he said, “the causes for accusation. In the phrase “by what is seen,” the instrumental case is used in the sense of a cause;
the meaning is “by means of the cause that is seeing. What, then, is that which is seen? He says: “transgression. And “having seen” means “on account of seeing.”
This is the meaning here, as in the phrase, "having seen with wisdom. The meaning in the cases of "having heard" and so forth should also be understood according to this method.

*Parassa* means from another, or having heard the speech of another. *Diṭṭhaparisaṅkitena* means by what is suspected through following what has been seen, or by a transgression suspected in that manner.
The same method applies to the remaining two phrases as well. He reproaches.
“Either by pointing out the offense, or by refusing communal living, or by refusing respectful conduct.
However, since an overly detailed exposition would result in excessive prolixity regarding this matter, he said, “This is the summary here.
But for those who desire the full detail, showing the means for its attainment, he said, “The detailed explanation, however... should be understood.”

“Arising through sensual pleasures” (*kāmūpapattiyo*) means being reborn by means of sensual pleasures; the meaning is that they are possessed of them. Possession consists both in their indulgence and in their acquisition;

thus he said, “either the indulgence in sensual pleasures or the obtaining of sensual pleasures. “Sensual pleasures present before them” means that, unlike the second and third groups [of beings], these are not created by themselves or by others.
However, because they subsist on the fruit of their own exertion and action, they exist by way of both [those two factors].

Those for whom sensual pleasures are present are "those with present sensual pleasures" (*paccupaṭṭhitakāmā*). Since those pleasures are, for the most part, fixed for them, they are called "those with fixed sensual pleasures" (*nibaddhakāmā*).
"Dwellers in the four divine worlds" refers to the gods from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Tusita heaven.

"Those in the states of misery" (*vinipātikā*) are those belonging to the woeful states. Those for whom sensual pleasures are created by others are "those whose sensual pleasures are created by others" (*paranimmitakāmā*).
“By way of habitual practice” means knowing by inference, not by direct perception. “They exercise mastery” means they attain the state of being drunk according to their own desire.
The phrase “they engage in sexual intercourse,” however, was stated for the purpose of refuting certain [wrong] views.
Therefore he said, “But some,” and so forth. They [hold that] for the Yāma devas it is by mere mutual embracing, and for the Tusita devas...
They say that for the Nimmānarati devas, the purpose of sensual desire is accomplished by a mere touch of the hand; for the Paranimmitavasavatti devas, by a mere smile;
and for the [Tusita] devas, by a mere look. They say it is "by the union of the couple" for the other two [deva realms].
This is because those [lower realms] lack such detachment from sensual pleasures, and because sensual pleasures become progressively more refined, more excellent, and most excellent as one ascends.
However, it should be stated that they lack any [auspicious] outflow (*nissanda*).

"The function of sensual pleasure" (*kāmakicca*) refers to the bliss of contact (*phassasukha*) which brings about the immediate subsiding of feverish distress. "Sensual pleasures" (*kāmā*) refers to the enjoyment of sensual objects. "Just as before" (*pākatikā eva*) means exactly the same as those mentioned below.
"Designated as one" (*ekasaṅkhātaṃ*) means having a single form, a common form; the meaning is either "well-known" (*samaññātaṃ*) or "having a common state" (*samānabhāvaṃ*).
"Attainment of happiness" means the successful acquisition of happiness. "Below" means below the plane of the first jhāna, among humans or among devas.
"The happiness of the first jhāna" refers to the wholesome first jhāna. Furthermore, the distinction between lower and higher is indeed obtainable by way of planes:

having produced the wholesome jhāna among the Brahmakāyika devas, one is reborn among the Brahmapurohita devas; or, having produced the wholesome jhāna among the Brahmapurohita devas... [the text continues].
Or because the experience of the happiness of karmic fruition is obtained among the Mahābrahmās.

And here, since the attainments of the second and third kinds of happiness are being described by way of the planes of the second and third jhānas, the attainment of the happiness of the first jhāna is stated specifically by way of the plane of the first jhāna.
"Tintā" means moistened, both by the happiness of jhāna and by the body touched by the sublime matter produced by that jhāna.
"Excellent wealth" is the meaning. For this very reason he said, "saturated on all sides," and so forth.
Since the bliss of fruition is more excellent and occurs more frequently than the bliss of the wholesome due to its greater tranquility, it was therefore stated:
"This too was said with reference specifically to the bliss of fruition-jhāna. "Of them" refers to the Ābhassara devas. Because the bliss accompanied by rapture is exceedingly sublime...

Because their minds are overwhelmed by that, a great greed for existence arises. "Tranquil indeed" means it is exceedingly peaceful due to the disappearance of the agitation of applied and sustained thought, as well as rapture and elation.
It is called "sublime" precisely because of its state of tranquility, owing to its having been brought to a state of excellence by its own conditions.
Therefore he said, "sublime indeed. By means of that which is insatiable, one reaches the perfection of happiness.
They are called *tusita* because they have passed away (*itā*) into a state associated with happiness and satisfaction (*tuṣā*), which is joy (*pīti*).
Since they do not aspire for anything beyond that, precisely because there is no greater happiness than that, it is said: "Therefore... having become satisfied.
"The bliss of the third jhāna" means the bliss that is the fruition of the third jhāna.
The seven noble wisdoms (*ariyapaññā*) are the respective unique wisdoms of the seven noble ones, beginning from the stage of the eighth person (*aṭṭhamaka*).
With the exception of supramundane wisdom (*lokuttarapaññā*), all remaining wisdom is called "wisdom" (*paññā*).

All wisdom belonging to the three planes (*tebhūmika*) is neither to be called "of one in training" (*sekkhā*) nor "beyond training" (*asekkhā*); it is "neither-of-training-nor-beyond-training," which is the wisdom of the worldling (*puthujjanapaññā*).
"In those prescribed by yoga" means: prescribed by wisdom, transformed by wisdom, and accomplished through skillful means (upāya-paññā).
"In the spheres of action" (kammāyatana): here, action itself is the sphere of action; or, it is called a "sphere of action" because it is both action and a basis for livelihood and so forth.
This same method applies to the spheres of craft as well. And therein, action is twofold: inferior, such as the work of a carpenter, and superior.
Agriculture, trade, and so forth. Craftsmanship (*sippa*) is also twofold: inferior, such as the craft of a reed-worker, and superior, such as arithmetic and accounting.
Knowledge (*vijjā*) is the field of knowledge; it should be understood as being strictly righteous, similar to the *nāga-maṇḍala*, protective charms (*paritta*), *phudhamana*, and mantras.
Now, some wise men, like Bodhisattvas, [provide] the comfortable dwelling for human beings through these.
Those who desire [to learn] do not see others performing [the acts], nor do they learn them once they have been performed.
They do not hear from those who are doing them; rather, they perform them through their own natural inclination and reflection.

Even when performed through one's own natural inclination and reflection by those possessed of wisdom, these become exactly like those performed by others after having learned them from them. This is "kamma as one's own property" (*kammassakata*).
“Knowledge that knows thus: ‘This karma belongs to beings; this does not belong to us’” refers to the knowledge of conformity to the truths (*saccānulomika*).
For it is called “conformity to the truths” because it conforms to the penetration of the truths.
Now, in order to show the manner in which it proceeds, the passage beginning with “‘Form is impermanent,’ or…” was stated. Therein, the word “or” (*vā*) has the sense of non-limitation.
It should be understood that the characteristics of suffering (*dukkha*) and non-self (*anatta*) are also included, because they are not separate from the state of impermanence (*anicca*).
For whatever is impermanent is suffering; and whatever is suffering is non-self [this appears as an additional reading, as it follows from the established fact].
"That which is of such a nature" means that which has the essential nature (sabhāva) described above. "Conformable patience" (*anulomikā khanti*) and so forth are synonyms for wisdom (*paññā*).

For it is "conformable" (*anulomikā*) because it conforms by demonstrating non-contradiction with the five causes previously mentioned—the sense-sphere of action (*kamma-āyatana*), and so forth—and likewise because it conforms to the truth of the path through its conduct for the welfare of beings, and to the ultimate truth, which is Nibbāna.
All these causes are "endurable" (*khama*); that is, it is able to endure them and withstand being seen.

*Khanti* (endurance/acceptance). *Passati* (sees) is *diṭṭhi* (view). *Roceti* (finds pleasing) is *ruci* (inclination). *Munāti* (understands) is *muti* (wisdom). *Pekkhati* (beholds) is *pekkhā* (contemplation).

And these phenomena, such as the spheres of action (*kammāyatana*) and so forth, when being reflected upon, are endured through this reflection; thus it is "acceptance through reflection on the Dhamma" (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*).
"Attains without hearing from another" means that he attains it by reflecting for himself, without hearing the instructional words of another.
"This is called" means that this is what is termed wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmaya-paññā*).

Furthermore, this arises only in those well-known Bodhisattvas. Even among them, the knowledge conforming to the truths (*saccānulomika-ñāṇa*) arises only for two Bodhisattvas who are in their final existence;
the remaining wisdom arises for all those of great wisdom who have fulfilled the perfections (*pāramī*).
"Having heard from another, one acquires" means that all things acquired— whether by seeing others performing the spheres of action (*kammāyatana*) and so forth,
or by seeing them performed by another, or by hearing the words of another speaking, or by learning them in the presence of a teacher—
are to be understood as "acquired having heard from another. "Of one who has attained" means of one who possesses meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
This is merely an illustration. For it is specifically insight-wisdom (*vipassanā-paññā*) and path-wisdom (*magga-paññā*) that are intended here by the term "developmental wisdom" (*bhāvanā-paññā*).
A weapon is something required for the purpose of crushing adversaries;

yet there is no adversary comparable to lust and the other defilements, and the crushing of that [adversary] is the Buddha’s word itself. Thus, having stated, "The heard [word] alone is the weapon," he says that "in meaning, that is the Three Pitakas."

He said, "The word of the Buddha. Now, explaining that meaning, he begins with "For that... and so forth, and supports it with the scriptural passage beginning with "One who has heard as a weapon" (*sutāvudho*).
Therein, "he abandons the unwholesome" means he relinquishes the unwholesome by way of its specific counteractive factor (*tadaṅga*) and so on.
"He develops the wholesome" means he arouses and increases wholesome states such as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*). Pure...

"He preserves himself" means that by means of that abandonment of unwholesome states and through that cultivation of the wholesome, he brings about an individual existence purified from the defilements of lust and so forth.
"Of those whose bodies are secluded" means of those who have withdrawn their bodies from the company of crowds after having abandoned such social association. This, then, is bodily seclusion.
It is not merely being alone; rather, it is the application of renunciation (*nekkhamma-yoga*) such as the first *jhāna* and so forth. Thus he says, "of those who delight in renunciation.
"Seclusion of mind" (*citta-viveka*) is the state of the mind being secluded from the company of defilements (*kilesa-saṅgaṇika*) after having abandoned them.

Since that occurs by way of the *jhānas*, liberations (*vimokkha*), and so on, he says, "of those with purified minds who have attained supreme clarity. "Seclusion from the substrata" (*upadhi-viveka*) is *nibbāna*.

For by the realization of that, a person attains the state of being without acquisitions (*nirupadhitā*). Therefore he said, "of persons who are without acquisitions," meaning those who have reached the cessation of formations (*visaṅkhāra*), those who have attained Nibbāna, and those who possess the attainment of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*).

Since learning (*suta*) is also called a weapon in the sense of providing a refuge, he said, "this too. For it has been stated: "relying on that. And here, although seclusion through learning (*sutapaviveka*) is also [included],...
It is by means of wisdom alone that one achieves the intended state of being armed; however, wisdom can achieve this intended state of being armed even without learning or certain kinds of seclusion.
Therefore, wisdom is mentioned separately as an "arm" in order to demonstrate its specific efficacy.
Thus he said: "He who possesses it [is not afraid] from anywhere," and so forth.
"Unknown and unrecognized Dhamma": in the beginningless cycle of saṃsāra, there was nothing unknown or unrecognized that is the Deathless Dhamma;
rather, it is the faculty that arises through this prior mental application (*pubbābhoga*) of one who has set out in practice with the thought, "I shall know the Dhamma of the Four Truths.
As for what is stated in the *Saṅgaha-vāra* of the Pāḷi—"there are nine faculties"—that refers to a specific mode of manifestation established by that prior mental application.
This was stated for the sake of illustration; however, in actual meaning, it is precisely right view of the path (*magga-sammā-diṭṭhi*). Thus he said:
"This is a designation for the knowledge of the stream-entry path (*sotāpatti-magga-ñāṇa*). "The faculty of higher knowledge" (*aññindriya*) means the faculty of thorough understanding.
What is meant is that it is the faculty of knowing those very same four noble truths already known by that path, without overstepping the boundary of what has been known through the first path.

Therefore he said: "The faculty that has become full knowledge (aññābhūta), that has become understanding (ājānanabhūta). It is called *añña* because it understands (*ājānāti*); it is "become full knowledge" (*aññabhūta*) because it has become the state of one who knows, or because it has become [such] by way of understanding.
"Among those who have fully known" (*aññātāvīsū*) means among those established after having understood the Four Noble Truths which are to be known.

Therefore he said: "Among those who have reached the culmination of the function of knowing," meaning among those who have attained the completion of the function of knowing, which is divided into thorough knowledge (*pariññā*) and so forth.

The "fleshly eye" refers to the eye-sensitivity (*cakkhupasāda*). The fleshly eye consists of fourteen components: the four elements, color, odor, flavor, nutritive essence, origin, shape, vitality, state, body-sensitivity, and eye-sensitivity; such is the lump of flesh with its fourteen constituents.
Because one sees forms there by expanding the light of the kasiṇa, it is said that "the divine eye is knowledge dependent on light."

The meaning that mundane wisdom (lokīyapaññā), when dissociated from the divine eye and the wisdom-eye, constitutes the "wisdom-eye" (paññācakkhu) is established even without being explicitly stated, since the divine eye has been mentioned separately; thus it is said: "The wisdom-eye is mundane and supramundane wisdom.
Higher virtue is "higher training in virtue" (adhisīla). "Because it is to be practiced" means because it is to be cultivated. This is what is called higher virtue.
This is because of the state of being a complete restraint of bodily and verbal actions, and because it serves as the proximate cause (*padatthāna*) for the virtue of the Path (*maggasīla*).

Higher mind (*adhicitta*) is so called because it serves as the foundation for the concentration of the Path (*maggasamādhi*). Higher wisdom (*adhipaññā*) is so called because it serves as the foundation for the wisdom of the Path (*maggapaññā*).
Now, in order to establish their status as higher virtue and so forth through reasoning, it was said: "Even when [the defilements] have not yet arisen," and so on. Therein:
“Unarisen” means not yet having occurred. Higher virtue (*adhisīla*) alone is the condition for the attainment of Nibbāna.
Regarding the phrase “having attained,” the words “by one aspiring for Nibbāna” should be supplied and connected here.
“The doer of good [reaps] good, and the doer of evil, evil;”
"He experiences both, for the doer follows after them.

Thus, they say that the wisdom of "kamma as one's own property"—which serves as a condition for the longing for liberation through the state of spiritual urgency (saṃvega) arising from the observation of the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) in the past and the future—is "higher wisdom" (adhipaññā).
Regarding the status of mundane virtue and so forth as "higher virtue" (adhisīla) and so on:
The phrase "by way of a method" (*pariyāyena*) was stated in order to show that very same point directly (*nippariyāyaṃ*).
"The body pertaining to the five doors" (*pañcadvārikakāyo*) refers to the collection of phenomena such as contact (*phassa*) and so forth within the five sense-doors.

It is called "development of the body" (*kāyabhāvanā*) because it is both the body and a development by virtue of being cultivated. This is because, for those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*), through the attainment of the supreme path, all defilements...

"Abandoned" means that from the moment they were abandoned, because of the total absence of their cultivation, there are no longer any phenomena cognizable by the eye or ear—even those yet to come—let alone the black [defilements].
Therefore, the body of the five doors is indeed well-developed. Thus it is said: "For one whose taints are destroyed...
it is well-developed. It is not weak as it is for others, because the defilements that cause weakness have been entirely abandoned.
Insight (*vipassanā*) is the unsurpassed vision because it correctly perceives conditioned phenomena through the contemplation of impermanence and so forth.
The Path is the unsurpassed practice because there is no practice superior to it. Fruition is the unsurpassed liberation because its state is unshakable.
Alternatively, Fruition is the unsurpassed vision because it proceeds by directly seeing *nibbāna* even for a single day. *Nibbāna*...
The "unsurpassability of liberation" is due to its having emerged from all conditioned things (*saṅkhata*).

Showing that the unsurpassability of the vision of Nibbāna is stated by taking the word *dassana* (vision) in the sense of an object (*kamma-sādhana*), he said: "For there is nothing further beyond that to be seen.

It is "unsurpassable" (*anuttara*) because there is nothing superior to it; and he said "the highest, the foremost" to indicate that the unsurpassable itself is the unsurpassable state (*anuttariya*).
"Concentration" refers to the remaining [factors] categorized according to the fivefold method and the fourfold method;
it should be understood that by this very reference to the threefold concentration, the fivefold method is also included within the Suttantas.
Regarding what ought to be said there, it has already been stated in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*, known as the *Paramatthamañjūsā*; therefore, in that regard—
This should be understood according to the method already stated.

It is called "coming" (*āgamana*) because it comes to this; thus, "from that coming. "From its own quality" (*saguṇato*) means from its own inherent nature. "From the object" (*ārammaṇato*) means from the dhamma that serves as the object.
"Having adhered to non-self" means having established insight (*vipassanā*) with the thought, "All conditioned phenomena are non-self."
"Having seen as non-self" means having first penetrated the characteristic of non-self of formations as "non-self.
"He emerges from [the perception of] non-self" means that through insight leading to emergence, which proceeds by way of the aspect of non-self, he reaches emergence via the Path.

[This occurs] due to the absence of those defilements that create the state of non-emptiness—namely, the defilements associated with views (*diṭṭhekaṭṭhā*) which are conditioned by the adherence to a self.
Insight is called "emptiness" (*suññatā*) because it suppresses [the defilements] and because it grasps the emptiness of self as it truly is. [Objection:

Is it not the case that, in this way, emptiness belongs to insight by virtue of its quality and not by virtue of its source; thus, in the ultimate sense, it does not exist [as a distinct dharma]? [Reply:

This is true regarding the acquisition of the name, but not regarding the conferring of the name—therefore, this is no fault. Alternatively, what is called a discourse on the Suttantas is a figurative discourse (*pariyāya-kathā*), not a discourse on the Abhidhamma.
There is no further fault in [the term] being used in a non-figurative sense (*nippariyāya*).
For when a name is acquired based on its qualities (*saguṇa*) or its object (*ārammaṇa*), there is confusion, because it is possible for a single thing to acquire another name.

However, when a name is acquired based on its origin (*āgamana*), there is no confusion, because there is no possibility of acquiring another name, and because such a thing is impossible. Therefore...

The passage beginning with “another” has been stated. “Due to the absence of defilements that produce signs” means because of the suppression of those defilements which are conditions for grasping at such things as the sign of permanence.
Granted, this insight proceeds by stripping away the sign of permanence and so forth;
however, because it does not relinquish the sign of formations (*saṅkhāra-nimitta*), it does not receive the name “signless” in the absolute sense. This, however, was stated in a figurative sense.
For indeed, because it is a teaching in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*), the name "signless" (*animitta*) for the Path is extracted in the Abhidhamma. And in the Sutta it is said:
"Cultivate the signless and abandon the underlying tendency to conceit;
then, through the full realization of conceit, you shall wander at peace."

The method of the signless (*animitta*) has been presented. It is so called because of the absence of defilements that produce longing, due to the suppression of those defilements such as the longing for pleasure.

It is "empty of lust and the rest" because it is secluded from lust and the rest through their abandonment by way of complete eradication. Lust and the rest themselves are the "signs of lust" and so forth;
for lust and the rest that have arisen previously serve as the cause for the lust and the rest that arise subsequently.

Lust and the other [defilements] are themselves called "lust-aspiration" (rāga-paṇidhi) and so forth because they serve as conditions for such aspiration. Nibbāna, by its very nature of being the unconditioned (asaṅkhāra), is free from all conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra);
thus it should be understood as empty of lust and the rest, and devoid of aspirations directed toward the signs of lust and the rest.

And herein, equanimity regarding formations (saṅkhārupekkhā), together with its conformity [to the path], is insight leading to emergence; that which contemplates emptiness is called "emptiness" (suññatā).
It is called "wishless" (*appaṇihita*) because one perceives it as suffering and because it withers the longing of craving.
Standing in the position of the path of arrival for the attainment of the Path, it gives the name "void," "signless," and "wishless" to the Path.
Once the name is obtained from the perspective of its arrival, its names based on its qualities and its object are established as a matter of course; however, [the name is not established] otherwise.

Since the designation "name" (nāma) is established everywhere because it arrives [from the ultimate level] when there is the acquisition of names through qualities and objects, it is the cause for the establishment of the complete name;

and because it functions to define that "for all [beings], the connection with the three types of names is through qualities and objects, not from arrival," the acquisition of the name in the primary sense is principally from arrival alone and not from the others,
whereas in the secondary sense, the acquisition of the name should be understood as being threefold.
It should be understood that this investigation was conducted in the commentary by means of the passage beginning with “threefold discourse.

Purity (sucibhāva) refers to the state of being pure through the removal of the impurities of the defilements; it is the state of being undefiled. Therefore he said: “It is to be understood by way of the three types of good conduct.

These belong to the Sage (muni), thus they are called *moneyya*. Those qualities by which one becomes known as a Sage because of his sage-like wisdom regarding the welfare of both [self and others] are thus...
He said, "The states that produce the state of a sage (moneyya) are the practices of sagehood (moneyyapaṭipadā).
In this context, because there is the non-doing of what should not be done with the body and the doing of what should be done,

and because there is the knowing of the object designated as the body— starting with "In this body there are head-hairs"— and because of the arising, the passing away, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding the body.
The thorough understanding [of the body] as it truly is, the path of insight that proceeds by way of such thorough understanding,
the abandoning of desire and lust for the body by means of that, and the attainment to be reached after the cessation of bodily formations—
all these factors of the practice of moneyya (noble silence) that proceed by way of the body are called "bodily moneyya. Therefore, regarding that meaning:
To demonstrate this, the Pāḷi has come down as: “The abandoning of the threefold bodily misconduct,” and so forth. The same method applies to the other two [types of misconduct] as well.
In that context, wisdom that proceeds by taking both suggestive speech and literal speech as its object is knowledge with speech as its object.

Thoroughly understanding that speech in terms of its origin and so forth is the full understanding of speech. Knowledge that proceeds by taking the eighty-one types of mundane consciousness as its object is...
Knowledge regarding mental objects is *manoviññāṇa*. The thorough understanding (*parijānana*) of its origin and so forth is "full understanding of the mind" (*manopariññā*);
this alone is the distinction. "Āya" means that prosperity comes from this; it is the growth of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), thus he said, "Āya is growth.
"Apāya" means that prosperities depart by means of this; it is the decline of wholesome states, thus he said, "Apāya is non-growth."
"Of this and that" refers to gain (*āya*) and loss (*apāya*). One "approaches" or "resorts to" a cause or means (*kāraṇa-upāya*) by which there is gain and loss.
In this context, increase is twofold: from the removal of what is harmful and from the arising of what is beneficial; likewise, non-increase is twofold:

from the persistence of what is harmful and from the failure to arise of what is beneficial. "The understanding of these" refers to the comprehension of those things designated as gain and loss, according to the aforementioned classifications.
The thorough understanding of increase and decrease as they truly are is skill, proficiency, and subtlety. To demonstrate both of these by means of the canonical text itself, it is said:
"For this has been stated," and so forth.
Therein, "this is said" refers to that [understanding] regarding the non-arising and cessation of these unwholesome states, and of wholesome states...
Wisdom regarding the non-arising and cessation of these wholesome states, and the arising and increasing of unwholesome states—this is called skill in acquisition (*āyakosalla*).
Now, in order to show skill in avoidance (*apāyakosalla*) by means of the canonical text itself, it is said: "In this regard, what is...
and so forth. Therein, "this is called" refers to that which pertains to the non-arising and cessation of these wholesome states, and the arising and increasing of unwholesome states.
“Wisdom—this is what is called skill in decline. Here it may be asked: “Let skill in progress be wisdom;
but how does skill in decline become wisdom? One might think thus: “The capacity to produce decline is what is called skill in decline”;
however, that is merely his own opinion. For only one who possesses wisdom, when reflecting thus, [realizes]: “For me, while attending to this, unarisen wholesome states...”
He understands: “Unarisen phenomena do not arise; arisen phenomena cease. Unarisen unwholesome phenomena arise; arisen [unwholesome phenomena] increase.
Having understood this, he does not give rise to unarisen unwholesome phenomena and abandons those that have arisen.
He gives rise to unarisen wholesome phenomena and brings those that have arisen to full development through cultivation. Thus...
Skill in decline is also wisdom. "All" means both that which belongs to the side of skill in acquisition and that which belongs to the side of skill in decline.
"Means appropriate to each" means being the means for whatever task is to be done in each respective case.
"For the purpose of treating that" means by way of knowing the cause for acting immediately in order to avoid urgent business or danger.
"Arising on the spot" (*ṭhānuppattika*) means that its arising occurs at that very moment; it refers to the cause that arises from the situation itself, by way of knowing that [cause].
"Occurring in a manner of intoxication" means by way of the state of reaching intoxication due to the intoxicating nature of one's own object.
The elevations that are occurring. "Free from illness" (*niroga*) means healthy. "Acting with pride" (*mānakaraṇa*) means the production of conceit.
"Standing in youth" means being established in youth; the meaning is "relying upon youth. The life of all beings is indeed fragile through death and followed by suffering;
yet, without regarding either of these two, and relying instead on the ease [of existence] due to the conditions for its continuous persistence—
To show that pride regarding one's longevity is a form of conceit that arises, it was said, "I have lived long," and so forth.
*Adhipati* means the foremost or the lord; that which comes from such a lord is *ādhipateyya*.
What is that? It is the non-doing of evil. Thus he said, "I am thus much," and so on. In this context, virtue and the other qualities should be understood as purely mundane.
"From that liberation" means from mundane liberation (*lokiya-vimutti*). "The eldest" means the lord, the venerable one; this is the meaning.
And herein, the non-doing of evil by taking oneself and the Dhamma as the governing principle should be understood by way of moral shame (*hirī*);
the non-doing [of evil] by taking the world as the governing principle is by way of moral dread (*ottappa*).
“Points of Controversy” (*kathāvatthūni*) means the bases for the occurrence of discussion. Since discussion does not proceed without them, they are called “causes of discussion.
The meaning of the word *addhāna* has already been stated above;

in its essential sense, however, it is merely the occurrence of phenomena (*dhamma*). And here, “phenomena” refers specifically to the aggregates (*khandha*), for there is no movement of these [aggregates] apart from them.
He said: "The meaning is 'past phenomena,' 'past aggregates. Furthermore, this so-called "time" (addhā)—like the directions and so forth—is a mere designation based on the occurrence of phenomena;
it is neither a primary constituent (upādā) nor an actual phenomenon (bhūta-dhamma). To demonstrate this point, the passage beginning with "Moreover" (apicā) was stated.
In order to explain in detail the meaning briefly stated as "in the sense of piercing the darkness and in the sense of making known," the passage beginning with "past lives" (pubbenivāsa) was spoken.
"Past lives" refers to the aggregates (khandha) in which one previously dwelt. "Darkness" (tama) means the darkness of delusion (moha). "Pierces" (vijjhati) means it strikes down;
the meaning is that it abandons. And by that very piercing of the obscuring darkness, past lives become known—that is, made manifest.
It is called "knowledge" (*vijjā*) because it makes known. "That" refers to death and rebirth.

It is called a "divine abiding" (*dibbo vihāro*) because it is an abiding that brings about the state of being a distinguished deva at the time of rebirth. [Objection: But would this not result in other [mental states] also having the status of divine abidings?
[Response: No, because those [other states] lack the specific distinction of occurring by way of bestowing benefit upon sentient beings and so forth.

It is designated as a "divine abode" (brahmavihāra) because it is established by way of being faultless and supreme. It is "noble" (ariya) because it is utterly pure, because it is free from conflict through the eradication of its opposites, and because it is to be attained;

or alternatively, it is noble because it follows immediately upon the attainment of the state of a noble one (ariya). Or else, it is a noble abode because the noble ones resort to it (ariyānam ayanti).
The remainder is exactly as explained below.
The commentary on the triads is finished.
The commentary on the tetrads.
306. "Previously" refers to the commentary on the Great Foundations of Mindfulness (*mahāsatipaṭṭhāna*) below.
"That which is desire" (*yo chando*) means the desire that exists by way of desiring. "State of desiring" (*chandikatā*) is the condition of desire, or the mode of producing desire.

"Wish to act" (*kattukamyatā*) is the desire to do. "Skilled" (*kusalo*) means clever or produced through skill. "Desire for the Dhamma" (*dhammacchando*) is desire for the intrinsic nature (*sabhāva*).
For this so-called "zeal" (chanda) is of many kinds: zeal of craving (taṇhā-chanda), zeal of views (diṭṭhi-chanda), zeal of energy (vīriya-chanda), and zeal for the Dhamma (dhamma-chanda).
Here, it is the zeal for wholesome states consisting in the desire to act that is intended. "He generates zeal" means he arouses that zeal;
for when one sets it in motion, one is said to generate it. "He exerts effort" means he applies exertion and strives. Energy...
"He exerts" means he arouses physical and mental energy (*vīriya*). "He steadies the mind" means he uplifts the mind by means of that very co-nascent energy.
"He strives" means he performs the effort (*padhāna*) of energy.
Furthermore, these terms should be connected respectively with arousing, cultivation, development, frequent practice, constancy, and performance. Avoiding prolixity:
“This is the summary here,” he said.
Regarding the phrase “dependent on desire”: concentration that occurs by depending on desire—thinking, “For one who has desire, there is mental concentration;
it is so for me”—having made desire the primary, the chief, and the precursor, is called *chandasamādhi* (concentration through desire).

"Consisting of striving" (*padhānabhūtā*) means born of striving, or having attained the state of striving. "Formations" (*saṅkhārā*) refers to the right effort (*sammappadhāna*) that accomplishes the four functions.
"Endowed with those qualities" means possessed of and associated with the aforementioned concentration and energy.
"Basis of success" (*iddhipāda*): by way of the term for accomplishment, in the sense of succeeding; by means of this, beings succeed, they prosper and grow.

By this method, it is said that they have "reached the pinnacle. For those factors associated with wholesome consciousness such as access-concentration (upacāra-jjhāna) and so forth—which have attained the designation of "success" (iddhi)—the zeal-concentration (chanda-samādhi) and the formations of striving (padhāna-saṅkhāra) serve as the "feet" in the sense of being their foundation (adhiṭṭhāna).
Since the preceding success serves as the foot, the basis, and the proximate cause for the succeeding success, it is therefore stated: "or the foot which has become success."

The rest is as in the case of the second basis for psychic power (*iddhipāda*) and so forth. Although an investigation into the bases for psychic power also appears in the *Janavasabha Sutta*, that too is presented only in brief;
therefore he says: "But the detailed exposition... is shown [in the Paṭisambhidāmagga].
(307) "Visible state" (*diṭṭhadhamma*) refers to the personal existence (*attabhāva*) that has become directly manifest; thus he says: "In this very personal existence."
"For the sake of dwelling in happiness" means for the sake of dwelling in non-material happiness through the state of being free from defilements.

"The meditative attainments of fruition" refers to all four meditative attainments of fruition. "At a later time" means at a time subsequent to the attainment of the destruction of the taints (*āsava*). "The meditative absorptions that have been produced" refers to the attained meditative absorptions of the fine-material and immaterial realms.

Regarding "the sun, moon, lamps, gems, and so forth": by the mention of "lamp," he refers to the oil lamp. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of meteors, lightning, and the like.

"He brings to mind the light" means that he brings to mind—that is, he establishes in his mind—the light of the sun, moon, and so forth, as it was perceived during the day and at night, precisely according to how it was perceived.
He brings it to mind in such a way that for him, who has well-developed the light-kasina (*ālokakasiṇa*), [the light appears]...
Like the light of a *kasiṇa*, it is available as desired and for as long as desired.
That light remains present during the night, by means of which one establishes the perception of day there and becomes free from sloth and torpor as if it were daytime. Therefore he said:
"As by day, so by night. Just as the light was seen at night—meaning just as the light of the moon and so forth was seen and obtained during the night—in the very same way...
"He attends to it by day" means that he attends to that light by day in the same manner as when it was seen at night; he places it in his mind.

"By what is not covered" means by that which is not covered by the veil of sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). "Unconcealed" means not shrouded. "With its radiance" means with the radiance of clear knowledge (*ñāṇobhāsa*).
Whether it be the light for dispelling sloth and torpor, the light of the *kasiṇa*, or the light of preliminary work (*parikamma*), it is the same.
Or, like the light of the defilements, this entire light originates from knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
"For the sake of attaining knowledge and vision" means for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
For here, the knowledge of the divine eye—both that which sees celestial forms and that which sees others—is intended by the term "knowledge and vision. "He attends to the perception of light" means:

The "light" mentioned here is the light for dispelling sloth and torpor (*thinamiddha*). The "preliminary light" (*parikamma-āloka*) is the light set in motion by way of performing the preliminary exercises for the knowledge of the divine eye (*dibbacakkhu-ñāṇa*).
In that context, it is stated with the qualification "of one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsava*) by way of the former [type of light];
for in his case, sloth and torpor are thoroughly abandoned, whereas this is not so for others. By way of the second [type of light], it is said: "Even when he has arrived," and so forth.
It has been stated. Therein, "in that" refers to the knowledge of the divine eye. "Even when present" means even when it has been acquired;

"even when not yet present" means even when it has not yet been acquired. Since the preliminary light arises by virtue of such a foundational jhāna alone—because that [jhāna] is endowed with specific qualities such as purity and clarity—it is therefore said: "He develops... pe ...the foundational... and so forth.
“Of one possessing the seven bases” means of one who possesses the seven bases as described in the passage beginning, “He acts with clear comprehension in going forward and in returning.
Although trainees (sekkhā) also possess thorough knowledge (*pariññā*), it is said that only Arahants are those for whom the objects of thorough knowledge have been definitively known;

thus it is stated, “For one whose taints are destroyed, the basis is known,” and so forth. “By the state of having known the basis and the object” refers to the basis (*vatthu*) and the object (*ārammaṇa*).
And it is by virtue of having known [the object] as it truly is. For just as when one wandering in search of a snake has discovered its lair,
the snake itself is also considered discovered— since it is easy to capture with the power of spells and antidotes— so too,
when the basis and the object that serve as the locus for feeling are known, even for a beginner, feeling is indeed known according to its specific characteristic.

This is because it is easy to grasp that [characteristic] by way of its general characteristic (*sāmaññalakkhaṇa*), much more so for one who has exhausted the taints (*khīṇāsava*) and has fully understood the basis (*pariññātavatthu*).
For him, feeling (*vedanā*) is known and manifest even at the moment of arising, the moment of presence, and the moment of dissolution.
Therefore he said, "In this way feelings arise," and so forth. Furthermore, the mention of feeling, perception, and thought in the Pāḷi is merely illustrative.
Demonstrating this, he says, “Not only...,” by which he shows that all remaining phenomena are likewise known through their arising and so forth.
Now, in order to show that feelings and the rest are known not only from the perspective of moments, but also from the perspective of conditions;
and not only by way of those whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava), but also by way of certain trainees (sekkha)—he says, “Moreover...,” and so forth.
It has been stated. In that context, "from the origination of ignorance" (*avijjāsamudayā*) means from the arising of ignorance; the sense is "due to its existence.
For arising, which is the opposite of cessation, is also a term for existence. Therefore, the meaning is:

when ignorance established in a previous existence exists, there is the arising of feeling in this present existence. By means of ignorance and so forth—which belong to the past time and so on—their co-operative causes [are indicated].
It should be understood that arising and the other characteristics are also included. Among the conditions for the occurrence of feeling, contact (phassa) is particularly powerful;

therefore, it alone is mentioned as "from the arising of contact. However, when that is included, the physical basis (vatthu), the object (ārammaṇa), and so forth are also necessarily included by virtue of their common nature as conditions for occurrence.
Thus, the demonstration of the arising of the entire feeling, without exception, from its conditions has been clarified.
It should be seen. By the phrase "the characteristic of production" and so forth, he speaks of the seeing of arising by way of moments (*khaṇa*).

It is called "arising" (*uppāda*) because it arises from this; thus, "arising" refers to both the characteristic of condition (*paccayalakkhaṇa*) and the characteristic of moment, taking them together as one when he says, "In this way, the arising of feeling is known."

“He attends to it as impermanent” means: this thing called feeling, because it is not eternal, has a beginning and an end, is delimited by arising and passing away, is fragile in every moment, and is merely temporary;
therefore, he attends to it as impermanent, thinking, “It is impermanent.
For him, its appearance as destruction and vanishing becomes known and manifest. “He attends to it as painful” means: precisely because of its impermanence...

For one who attends to feeling as "suffering" because it is oppressed by arising and passing away, because it is itself suffering, and because it is the basis for suffering, its appearance as something to be feared and something to be dreaded becomes known and manifest.

Likewise, because of its impermanence and its very nature as suffering, feeling is devoid of self, coreless, substanceless, not subject to one's will, and empty; thus one attends to feeling as non-self.
When one attends to it, its manifestation as empty, void, and ownerless becomes known and clear.

The phrase beginning with “as destruction” is a conclusion of the very meaning already stated. Therefore, the transformation of the case ending should be understood according to the sense as: “one knows feeling as destruction, as terror, and as empty.
Thus, “with the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of feeling” means that through the non-arising cessation of ignorance by means of the supreme path (aggamagga).
The non-arising and cessation of feeling occurs due to the absence of its conditions. The remainder should be understood according to the method explained in the section on origination (*samudaya*).
Here, "development of concentration" refers to the development of insight-concentration that has reached its culmination among the Noble Ones;
the meditative attainment (*jhānasamāpatti*) should be understood as its foundation.
It is exactly as stated in the *Mahāpadāna*.

"Without taking a measure" means without taking a specific location, as in the case of the meditation on the foul (*asubha-bhāvanā*). By not taking a measure even with respect to a single being, one pervades them without exception.
They are called "immeasurables" (*appamāṇā*) because there is no measure to be grasped for them; and being immeasurable, they are thus "immeasurables" (*appamaññā*).
In the sense of being a support, they are "supports" (*apassenāni*); here, this is a designation for those very things by relying upon which a bhikkhu is capable of training in the three trainings.
These, moreover, consist of: forbearance as endurance when reflecting on conditions;
avoidance of what is to be avoided; and the removal of what is to be removed. Therefore he said: "Reflecting, one endures one thing," and so forth.
In this context, it is called *saṅkhā* because it appears, presents itself, and manifests correctly; thus he says, "by *saṅkhā*, that is, by knowledge.
That which is called "cultivated after having discerned" (*saṅkhāya sevitā*) is the cultivation of that which, when cultivated, causes unwholesome states to diminish and wholesome states to increase;
thus he says, "he cultivates only that which is fit to be cultivated. This same method applies to patience (*adhivāsanā*) and the others as well.
"To enter within" means he does not allow [the mind] to proceed within his own internal consciousness.
Commentary on the Four Noble Lineages (Ariyavaṃsacatukka): 309.
The word *vaṃsa* appears in such passages as "he sits having passed beyond the backbone," where it refers to the beam that must be placed at the junction of two rafters.
Just as one who is entangled in a wide-spreading bamboo thicket,
so too is the attachment to children and wives;
like a shoot breaking free from the bamboo, one should remain unattached.
In such passages as “One should wander alone like the horn of a rhinoceros,” it refers to a single individual.
In such passages as “the sound of kettledrums, the sound of tabors, the sound of flutes, the sound of gongs and cymbals,” it refers to a particular musical instrument, which is also called a “flute.
In such passages as “an elephant that has died with its backbone unbroken,” it refers to the backbone of elephants and the like.
