In the phrase "in the middle part of the back," it refers to the middle of the spine. In expressions such as "I shall establish the family lineage" (*kulavaṃsa*), it refers to a family line.

In expressions such as "a protector of the lineage, a guardian of the tradition" (*vaṃsānurakkhako paveṇīpālako*), it refers to the succession of qualities, that is, the continuous occurrence of a sequence of virtues.

Here, however, it should be understood as referring to the continuity of the virtues consisting in contentment with the four requisites and delight in meditation. Furthermore, regarding that lineage, there are both the lineage of family and the lineage of qualities, which serve as examples.
To demonstrate this, the passage beginning with “yathā hi” was stated. Therein, “khattiyavaṃsa” means the lineage of the khattiya clan.
The same method applies to the remaining terms as well. “Samaṇavaṃsa,” however, means the stream of recluses, the succession of recluses.

Regarding the phrase “mūlagandhādīnaṃ,” by the word “ādi,” just as there is an inclusion of things such as heartwood scents, so too here an inclusion of things such as cow’s milk should be understood. By the second...
Furthermore, by the word "etc. (ādi), [the inclusion of] Kāsika cloth, cream of ghee, and so forth is intended.

The term "noble" (ariya) applies both to humans who are not non-Aryans and to those whose dwelling place is called "the noble sphere" (ariyaṃ āyatanaṃ). As it is said: "To whatever extent, Ānanda, there is the noble sphere...
It also applies to worldly virtuous people, as in: "Those who are noble, whose bodily actions are purified... and so forth.

In such passages as "I am one among them," however, in order to show that those who have penetrated the Noble Truths—whose etymological derivation is obtained by the phrase "far from the defilements" (ārakā kilesehi), and so forth—are intended here, the question "But who are those Nobles?
was asked, and the reply beginning with "The Nobles are called... was stated.
Therein, having first shown in their own forms those Perfectly Enlightened Ones (Sammāsambuddhas) who appeared during the interval from the beginning of this aeon (*kappa*) until now,

the text says “Furthermore,” and so forth, in order to show the Noble Ones (*ariya*) without exception by including other Perfectly Enlightened Ones, Private Buddhas (*paccekabuddha*), and disciples of the Buddhas. Therein, as long as the Dispensation (*sāsana*) has not...
"As long as he remains invisible, the Teacher indeed still exists"—this refers specifically to this Blessed One and those who are currently disciples of the Buddha;

thus, the term "present" (*paccuppanna*) is used. If, however, one were to claim that those individuals existing at various times are "present," then there would be no need to mention the past and the future.
Now, just as the Blessed One said: "Bhikkhus, the Dhamma... [and so forth].
“I shall teach the holy life that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and the right phrasing;
I shall reveal it—entirely complete and pure—in its sixfold sets. Thus he praised the teaching on the Six Sets with eight phrases.
Likewise, regarding the Noble Lineages in the Great Discourse on the Noble Lineages, he spoke of the lineages of the noble ones: “Bhikkhus, there are these four...”
"The noble lineages are foremost, ancient, traditional, old, unadulterated, never before adulterated, they are not being adulterated, nor will they be adulterated;

they are uncensured by wise recluses and brahmins. Having brought forward those nine phrases with which he spoke in praise, and extolling them by way of eulogy, he said, "But these indeed... and so forth. "Foremost" (aggā): [as above].
They should be known as "lineages" (*vaṃsa*) because they possess the quality of excellence and because they accomplish that state of excellence.
They should be known as "ancient" (*rattaññū*) by those who know antiquity, because they have been practiced in such a manner by the Buddhas and others for a long time.
They should be known as "lineages" in the sense of being the lineages of the Noble Ones, beginning with the Buddhas. "Ancient" (*porāṇa*) means old; it does not mean recently arisen.
*Asaṃkiṇṇā* means not scattered, not discarded. Therefore he said, "not removed. *Na apanītapubbā* means not previously discarded;
because they constitute the means for fulfilling the three trainings, they have never been abandoned. For that very reason, they are not being removed now, nor will they be removed in the future.
Those wise ones who, through the very knowledge of the true nature of phenomena (*dhammasabhāva*), are recluses who have stilled their evil.
And there are those who are brahmins with evil removed; they are neither reviled nor rejected by them.
For those who are not to be reviled are not to be censured or disparaged. Because they are not to be abandoned, they are not to be rejected.
Regarding the phrase "contented," here, showing precisely the kind of contentment intended, [the author] says: "contented by way of contentment with requisites."
It has been stated. Here, a bhikkhu’s contentment exists by way of jhāna, vipassanā, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase *itarītarena*: it means "by this or that. This word *itara* expresses indefiniteness;

when stated twice, it becomes synonymous with the expression "whatever" (*yena kenaci*). Thus it is said, "by whatever [means]. And because it expresses indefiniteness, just as in the case of "coarse" (*thūla*) and so on—
It is a term denoting "one of several"; likewise, terms such as *yathāladdha* (as-obtained) and so forth are also terms denoting "one of several.

In this context, showing that it is specifically the second alternative (*pakkha*) that is intended here, he says, "Then indeed," and so forth. [Objection: But are not *yathāladdha* and the others also merely "excessive" (*thūla*) and so forth?
[Response: This is true; nevertheless, there is a distinction. For that contentment which exists with respect to the excessive things obtained as they were found—this...
It is contentment with whatever is obtained, and nothing else. For this is not intended to be based merely on the requisites themselves;

rather, it must also be based on what is appropriate for one’s own physical strength. Furthermore, it should be understood that all three types—thūla-duka and so forth—are obtainable in regard to robes;
the middle type is common to all four requisites, while the last is obtainable in regard to both robes and lodgings.
"These three contentments" is stated by way of a comprehensive inclusion. For those who, including even the requisite for the sick within almsfood itself,
speak of fifty kinds of contentment— twenty regarding robes, fifteen regarding almsfood,
and fifteen regarding lodgings— all of these are included, as appropriate, within these very three contentments.
"They go to the assembly.
"The robe should be known" means that the robe should be known by its kind, such as: "This particular robe is allowable.
"The field for robes" is the source from which a robe arises. "Rags from the dust-heap" refers to a rag-robe that has attained the characteristics of a rag-robe.
The meaning is that the robe is to be understood. "Contentment with robes" means that all contentment obtainable regarding robes is to be understood.
The ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*) connected with robes are to be understood, by being content with which one is truly satisfied through contentment with robes.
*Khoma*, *kappāsika*, *koseyya*, *kambala*, *sāṇa*, and *bhaṅga* are the *khoma*-robes and so forth. Among these, *khoma*...
“Khoma” refers to a robe made from linen thread; the same applies to the remaining types.
“Sāṇa” is a robe made from hemp (sāṇa) fibers. “Bhaṅga,” however, is a robe made by mixing some of all these materials, such as linen thread and so forth.
Some say, “Bhaṅga is also made only of wool. “Six” is a limitation of the number. If this is so, what other class of cloth is there besides these?

Is it not the case that [these materials] do not exist? It is not that they do not exist; however, in order to show that they are suitable for these [other materials], the phrase beginning with “dukūla and so forth” was stated.
By the word “and so forth” (ādi), there is an inclusion of *paṭṭuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭṭa*, *cīnapaṭṭa*, *iddhija*, and *devadatta*.
Among those, *dukūla* is a suitable counterpart to *sāṇa* because it is made of flax (*vāka*). *Paṭṭuṇṇa* is cloth produced in the region of Paṭṭuṇṇa.
For it is stated in the *Amarakośa*: “*Paṭṭuṇṇa* is a specific kind of silk (*koseyya*). Fabrics produced in the country of Soma and the country of Cīna are called *somāra-paṭṭa* and *cīna-paṭṭa*.
The three types beginning with *paṭṭuṇṇa* are variations of silk, because they consist of thread made by insects.

That which is “born of psychic power” (*iddhija*) refers to the robe produced through the merit-power (*puññiddhi*) of those who have come as monks (*ehibhikkhus*); that is one of the [five] starting with linen (*khoma*).
And it is also of the same kind as those [other robes]. "Devadinnan" means a robe given by deities;
that is produced on the wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*), similar to the cloth given to the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī.
That too is of the same kind as linen and so forth, because it possesses the nature of one among them. "These" is a word expressing inclusion and restriction, meaning "these alone."
The meaning [of the term *kappiya*] is as follows: robes that are allowable because they are suitable for the use of the Buddha and others.
Now, in order to show by way of illustration those things excluded by the restrictive definition (*avadhāraṇa*), it is said:
“grass-cloth,” and so forth. Therein, *kusacīra* is cloth made from *kusa* grass or other similar grasses; or [cloth made from] fibers such as *potakī*, *vāka*, and so on.
*Katacīvara* is a garment made of bark. *Phalakacīvara* is a garment made from wooden planks, whether four-cornered or three-cornered.
*Kesakambala* is a blanket made from the hair of humans. *Vālakambala* is a woolen blanket made from the tails of yaks, horse-tails, and so forth.
*Potthaka* is cloth woven from the threads of *makaci* (hemp). *Camma* refers to any kind of hide, such as the hide of deer and so on. [The phrase] "with owl feathers" refers to...
"Garment made by sewing" refers to an owl-wing robe. "Tree-cloth" means cloth made from the skin of animals such as snakes, or cloth made from *tirīṭaka* trees;
this is the meaning. "Creeper-cloth" (*latādussa*) is woven from very fine creeper fibers. "Eraka-grass cloth" (*erakadussa*) is made from *eraka* grass fibers.
Likewise for "plantain cloth" (*kadalidussa*). "Bamboo-cloth" (*veḷudussa*) is made from fine bamboo fibers. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), bark cloth and other such materials are included.
"Unsuitable robes" because they bear the banner of the heretics.

"And by way of the eight matrices" means by way of the eight matrices for the arising of robes that have come down in such passages as, "he gives within the boundary," "he gives according to an agreement," and so forth.
For it was for the purpose of showing the fields for the acquisition of robes that the Blessed One [taught this].
“Bhikkhus, there are these eight headings,” and so forth, by which the headings (mātikā) were established. For “headings” (mātikā) means mothers, as they give rise to the arising of robes.
“Cemetery cloth” (sosānika) is that which has fallen in a cemetery. “Shop cloth” (pāpaṇika) is that which has fallen at the door of a shop.
“Street cloth” (rathiya) is a rag discarded on a street through a window by those seeking merit. “Rubbish-heap cloth” (saṅkārakūṭaka) is a rag discarded in a place for refuse.
*Sināna* means a bathing cloth; that which spirit-doctors discard after washing the head, saying, "This is the cloth of a black-eared one," and then depart.
*Tittha* refers to a bathing-cloth, a rag discarded at a bathing place. *Aggidaḍḍha* means a place burnt by fire; for people discard such a spot.
*Gokhāyitaka* and so forth are well known; for people also discard those.
"Having hoisted the banner" means that by those boarding a ship or entering into battle, the banner-staff has been raised; the intention is that the robe wrapped thereon was discarded by them.
"By a monk who approves" means by a monk who consents to a householder's robe. "For about one month" means for a period of about one month, known as the "robe-month.
It is permissible to think [of it] during that time, but not beyond that—this is the intention. For this is for the purpose of restraining craving in its entirety.
"Practice in the Dispensation": the rag-robe wearer accomplishes this in half a month because his acquisition is not dependent on others;
for the other, however, because it is dependent on others, only a full month is permitted. Thus, "half a month"... [and so on]...
"contentment with thoughts" because thinking is limited in duration.
Although he wished for the Mahāthera to be his companion there, out of profound respect he said at the village gate, "Venerable sir, I shall go.
The Mahāthera, knowing his intention, said, "Friend, I shall go.
Entering the village, he asked a question in order to prevent that monk from having an opportunity for such a thought: "Obstructed by excrement..."

He was oppressed by the urge to defecate. At that time, because the defilements were suppressed by the power of the surge of joy and gladness that had arisen toward the Tathāgata through the recollection of the Blessed One’s austerities, he attained the three fruits right then and there...
[as before] ...The thought, "Where shall I obtain it? is preceded by a desire for gain; therefore, it is said, "without thinking thus," "it is good."
What need is there even to mention thoughts such as, "I shall obtain [something]," or "I shall obtain something pleasing"? How, then, should it be said?
He says: "Going with the meditation subject as the primary concern. By this, he shows that one should not think about anything at all on account of the robe.
Furthermore, since even an unattractive search might become a condition for [distraction], he says, "taking along a pleasant bhikkhu."
"Being brought" means that a person, having learned that "these monks are wandering in search of rag-robes," brings from places such as a charnel ground a cloth that has fallen there.
"Even for one who accepts what is obtained in this way" means even for one who accepts what has been obtained without violating the contentment with what is acquired.
"Only by the measure sufficient for oneself" means for the purpose of making a single-layered or double-layered robe from whatever rag-robes have been obtained.
By the phrase "only by the measure sufficient for oneself," the restriction excludes any expectation of more.

Walking from door to door in sequence, like one who wanders for alms in a village while practicing *sapadāna-cāra*, is called "avoiding greediness" because it keeps greed for robes at a great distance.
"To maintain" means to sustain the physical body.
"By means of washing" means by way of cleansing. "Leaves" refers to leaves such as those of the mango (*amba*) or rose-apple (*jambu*).

"Without disturbing" means without disturbing one's contentment. "Only in a sufficient manner" means that whatever one wishes to make—such as an inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) or others—one takes the material obtained, whether coarse or fine, according to the measure required for it, and then makes it.

"Merely for the purpose of covering the three circles" means that its making is solely for the purpose of covering the three circles, as stated: "If the lower robe [nivāsana] does not cover the navel-circle, it must cover the knee-circle; if the other [upper robe], the throat-circle;
[and the outer robe], the knee-circle. In terms of actual substance, however, its size is exactly the minimum measurement prescribed for the three robes.
"Without having examined" means without having investigated.
"At the time of sewing the cloth" means at the time of joining the circles and stitching. "In seven turns" means in seven rounds of stitching.
"Contentment with what is allowable" is the absence of making any alteration by way of designating a permissible mark (*kappabindu*).

Since the warding off of cold and so forth is established by implication, the phrase "merely for the purpose of concealing the private parts" is stated to show the primary purpose for the use of the robe.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Merely for the purpose of concealing the private parts.
It is permissible; yet, satisfaction is not attained merely by that much, because of the lack of requisites and the failure to obtain [offerings] from those worthy of gifts.
"Standing in the qualities conducive to harmony" means standing in the common use [of requisites] together with virtuous bhikkhus.
By the words "Thus," etc., [the author], while demonstrating that the first noble lineage consists of the ascetic practices of wearing rag-robes and using only three robes,
as well as their being the conditions for those [other qualities], shows that these qualities are mutually productive and supportive of one another.
He illuminates [this]. This same method applies from here onwards as well.
Regarding the statement, “He is contented and speaks in praise [of contentment],” four logical alternatives (catukkoṭika) are possible;

therein, only the fourth alternative is praised and extolled by the Teacher, and thus the Great Elder (Mahāthera) gave his teaching in that manner. One is contented, but [does not speak] of contentment...
One does not speak in praise of contentment, just as the elder Nālaka [is described at length in the *Nālaka Sutta* of the *Sutta Nipāta*].
One is not contented oneself but speaks in praise of contentment, just as Upananda the Sakyan-son.
One is neither contented oneself nor speaks in praise of contentment, just as the elder Lāḷudāyī. One is contented...
And he is one who speaks in praise of contentment, just like the Elder Mahākassapa.
"Improper search" (*anesanā*) means an unsuitable search. Therefore he said "unbecoming" (*appatirūpa*); it is not fitting, not appropriate, and unsuitable for those established in the Teaching.
"Acting with hypocrisy" (*kohaññaṃ karonto*) means acting deceitfully and deluding others for the sake of obtaining robes.
“Trembling” (*uttasati*) means he trembles repeatedly due to the agitation of craving (*taṇhā*). “Being terrified” (*paritasati*) means he is terrified on all sides.
Just as all applications of body and speech arise solely for that purpose, so too he trembles in every respect. “Greed” (*gadhita*) is said to mean a “clinging” (*gaddha*);
here, it is intended in the sense of the characteristic of covetousness (*abhijjhā*). One who has no such greed is “unattached” (*agadhita*); thus he says: “Unattached... [etc.]”
"Greedy with lust": they become deluded through the influence of craving, or they have attained that accumulation [of suffering].
"Uninvolved" means not having approached it. "Unsubmerged" means not overwhelmed. "Unenveloped" means not covered by the veil of craving.
"Seeing the danger" means seeing the fault both pertaining to the present life and to future lives. He escapes from indulgence characterized by attachment.
"By this" means by way of escape; "this is the purpose"—one who understands that is "one of wisdom regarding escape. Therefore it was said: "Understanding... [as far as] ...pajānanto.

"He does not exalt himself" means he does not praise himself, does not lift himself up, does not regard himself as superior. The passage beginning with "I am" is a demonstration of the manner of such exaltation.
"He does not disparage" means he does not revile, nor does he regard others as inferior. Regarding that contentment with robes:

Regarding that twentyfold contentment with robes as already described: although, by the inclusion of the aforementioned types of contentment, even the absence of improper search for robes and so forth is indeed included—since those exist when this [contentment] exists and are absent when it is not—the praising of one's own virtues, self-exaltation, and disparaging others are not explicitly included here;
therefore, [the text says]: "In the case of praising one's own virtues and so forth..."

The word “or” (*vā*) expresses an alternative option. Here, the phrase beginning with “skilled” (*dakkho*) shows by means of which qualities his aforementioned contentment and so forth are accomplished.
In that regard, by the term “skilled,” he shows the wisdom that originates those [qualities];
by “diligent” (*analaso*), the energy of exertion; by “clearly comprehending” (*sampajāno*), the wisdom of manifestation; and by “mindful” (*paṭissato*)—
By this, he demonstrates the practice of non-confusion therein.
"Almsfood should be understood" means almsfood should be understood according to its classifications. "The field for almsfood" is the place where almsfood arises.
"Contentment with almsfood should be understood" means contentment with almsfood should be understood according to its classifications.
In this context, medicine also falls under the category of almsfood (*piṇḍapāta*). For it is included among items such as clarified butter (*sappi*) because they must be brought [for consumption].
The "field of alms" (*piṇḍapātakkhetta*) is the place where alms arise; it is called a "field" because it is like a field.
It is a "place of arising" (*uppattiṭṭhāna*) because [alms] arise therein or by means of it. Indeed, a monk’s almsfood arises from the Saṅgha by way of formal assignment (*uddesa*) and so forth.
Alternatively: there, food to be given to the entire Saṅgha is *saṅghabhatta*.
Food to be given by specifying a certain number of bhikkhus is *uddesabhatta*. Food to be given after having invited [the recipients] is *nimantana*.
Food to be given by means of distributing lots (*salākā*) is *salākabhatta*. Food to be given on one day during one fortnight is...
Food given on the [fortnightly] half-month is *pakkhika*. Food to be given on the Uposatha day is *uposathika*.
Food to be given on the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipada*) is *pāṭipadika*. Food to be given to newcomers is *āgantukabhatta*.
Food to be given specifically at the main residence is *dhurabhatta*. Food to be given for the sake of a particular hut is *kuṭibhatta*.
“Vārabhatta” is a meal that must be given in turn by village-dwellers and others. “Vihārabhatta” is a meal that must be given for the sake of a monastery.
The remaining terms are self-evident.
He reflects: “Where indeed shall I go for alms today? or “Where shall we go for alms?”
When the Elder said, “In such-and-such a village, Bhante,” that was indeed a fitting reply;

however, referring to the specific state of mind by which one says “having thought,” he said, “having thought this much. “From that time on” means from the moment of standing at the pavilion of applied thought (*vitakkamāḷaka*) and engaging in reflection.
“If one reflects further than that, one has fallen away from the Noble Lineage”—this applies to all three [types of noble lineages].
This should be understood by way of those belonging to the Noble Lineage (ariyavaṃsika), not by way of the solitary wanderer alone.
For every member of the Noble Lineage is permitted to apply thought only once, and not beyond that. "Excluded" means being outside the state of belonging to the Noble Lineage.
This very contentment with thought is not disturbed by attention to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) and is purified by it. The same applies to the following cases as well.
This is the method. For this very reason it was said: "One should go by way of the meditation subject.
The word *eva* is used here in the sense of exclusion (*aṭṭhāna*). It should be construed as: "Only that which is sufficient for maintenance should be taken.
"In this" means in this receiving of almsfood. "Little" means even less than the measure required for one's own maintenance. It should be taken [in such a manner].
For the purpose of pleasing the donor’s mind. “Only by measure” means that one should take only as much as is necessary for one’s own maintenance.
To show the reason for the statement “it should be taken by measure,” it is said: “For, in the matter of receiving,” and so forth. “Smeared over” means to destroy or remove.
“Cast down” means to ruin by misapplying it to an improper place. “The Teaching” means the Teacher’s instruction.
Instruction. He does not do it; he does not practice it.
Just as those who go on alms-round walk from door to door in regular succession, [the Buddha] said, "One should go from door to door," meaning contentment through the avoidance of greed.
"Having had [anything extra] removed" means having had what is superfluous taken away.

It is called "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because by means of it one escapes from craving for food. Regarding the statement, "The talk is for the purpose of dispelling hunger," the other purposes—such as the maintenance of the body—are understood through implication; thus he says, "It is called contentment with regard to hunger... The intention is that one should not store food and consume it on a later day.

As for the other case (eating stored food), it is already prohibited by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Standing in the qualities conducive to harmony" (*sāraṇīyadhamma*) means standing in the state of sharing enjoyments with virtuous monks.
“By lodging” means by bed and by seat. For wherever one lies on a couch or the like, or in a dwelling or the like, that is a *sena* (bed).
Wherever one sits on a chair or the like, that is an *āsana* (seat). Having combined both together, it is called “lodging” (*senāsana*). Therefore he said, “a couch,” and so forth.
Therein, a “couch” is one made of cane and so on; likewise for a “chair. A “couch-cushion” and a “chair-cushion” [are also included].
The bedding (bhisi) is of two kinds. A vihāra is an entire dwelling enclosed by a wall;
some say it is a "long-faced palace" (dīghamukhapāsāda). An *aḍḍhayoga* is a long palace; some say it is a "dwelling with a roof covering only one side.
A *pāsāda* is a square palace; some say it is a "long, square palace. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof. A *guhā* is simply a mountain cave.
*Leṇaṃ* is a shelter with its door closed. *Aṭṭo* is a house with thick walls, which has a roof made of bricks alone without using rafters;
some also say it is built in the shape of a watchtower (*aṭṭālaka*). *Māḷo* is a particular type of dwelling comprised of a single peak with many corners;
some call it "a lodging constructed in the shape of a circle."

“In the same manner as described for almsfood” means it should be understood according to the appropriate method stated for almsfood, beginning with: “The alms-collecting bhikkhu thinks: ‘Where shall I dwell today? and so on, up to:
“Thinking beyond that, he has fallen from and is excluded from the noble lineage.
Furthermore, even when seeking a resting place, one should not think, “Where will I find it? but rather proceed with the meditation subject as the primary focus.
"‘One must go,’ and so forth—all this is according to the previous method.
But why did the Great Elder, while demonstrating contentment with requisites here, not include contentment with the medicinal requisite for the sick?
To show that this should not be viewed in such a way, he said: ‘The medicinal requisite for the sick, however, is included within almsfood itself.’"

He says: the intention is that they share the common characteristic of being things to be brought forth. If this is so, then in that case, just as with alms-food (piṇḍapāta), the fifteen kinds of contentment—such as contentment with thought (vitakka-santosa) and the rest—should also be intended there? Showing that this is not so, he says "therein," etc.

But is it not the case that here only twelve ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) have found their application, while the one practice of sitting constantly (nesajjikaṅga) is not applied anywhere? To this he says:
“He practices the noble lineage that delights in development (bhāvanārāma-ariyavaṃsa) by means of the ‘always-sitting’ factor (nesajjikaṅga).
Showing that this meaning is indeed recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā*, he said, “And this has also been stated,” and so forth.
The passage beginning with “As if spreading out the earth” and so on is a demonstration of the extreme difficulty of the teaching on the noble lineages because of its vast scope.

Regarding that teaching: because a teaching, when expounded in detail for the sake of attaining the Noble Path, is adorned with a thousand methods—as was the case in the *Cittuppādakaṇḍa*—and this discourse on the Noble Lineage Delighting in Meditation is likewise expounded in detail for the sake of attaining the Noble Path, it is said: “Adorned with a thousand methods…” and so forth.
He began the teaching. Because it delights by being directed toward the destruction of opposing factors, it is called "delight" (*āramaṇa*) or "pleasure-grove" (*ārāma*);

thus he says, "the meaning is 'delight' (*abhirati*). A compound with an external referent (*bāhiratthasamāsa*) occurs even through words in different grammatical cases, as in "hair on the chest" (*urasiloma*) or "black on the neck" (*kaṇṭhekāḷo*);
thus he says, "one whose pleasure-grove is in abandoning is 'one who delights in abandoning' (*pahānārāmo*). In the sense of that which is to be delighted in...
Alternatively, the compound should be understood here as follows: "abandoning is his delight" (*pahānaṃ ārāmo assa*) thus it is "one whose delight is abandoning" (*pahānārāmo*).
By the phrase "he delights while abandoning," [the author] shows that the words "abandoning" and "delight" function as the agent (*kattusādhana*) and that they form a *kammadhāraya* compound.
Because it was stated, "he delights while developing," the same method applies here for the term "one whose delight is development" (*bhāvanārāmo*).

Granted that it is said, “He cultivates the noble lineage of delighting in development (bhāvanārāma-ariyavaṃsa) by means of the ‘always-sitting’ factor (nesajjikaṅga),” because such practice is suitable for the application of development;
nevertheless, by virtue of the always-sitting factor, there is a state of non-offense for certain offenses for a monk who always sits.
Including this as well, [the author] says, “of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅga),” and states, “Having reached the Vinaya, one must stand firm regarding the heavy [offenses].”
Because practice by way of not abandoning effacement is for one who stands within the Vinaya, it is said: "For the thirteen...
it is thus explained. Granted that discourses on virtue (*sīla*) have indeed appeared here and there even in the Sutta and Abhidhamma Piṭakas;
however, when those qualities by which the purification of virtue occurs are explained, there is an abundance of discourse on virtue.

The Vinaya Piṭaka has been explained; likewise, the Suttanta Piṭaka consists largely of discourses on meditation (bhāvanā), and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka is indeed explained by means of the fourth noble lineage (ariyavaṃsa). Thus it is said:
"By one who delights in meditation, the remaining two Piṭakas have been explained. Starting with the phrase "He delights in cultivating renunciation" (*nekkhamma*), therein—

Because it proceeds as a teaching, or because all the phenomena of serenity, insight, and the path—being designated as "renunciation" (nekkhamma) by way of their departure from their respective opposites—are included therein, that text is called the "Renunciation Text" (nekkhammapāḷī);
thus he said, "It should be recited by means of the Renunciation Text. Therefore, it is said in the Commentary: "All wholesome states are renunciation."
...so it is said. By way of the *Dasuttara-suttanta* means by the teaching of the *Dasuttara-suttanta*, or rather, by the method presented in the *Dasuttara-suttanta*;
the same principle applies to the other two [sections] as well.
“He” refers to the bhikkhu devoted to wakefulness. “Renunciation” (*nekkhamma*) is so called because of its state of having emerged from sensual desires.

The preliminary stage of the first jhāna. That which is described by the passage beginning, “Having abandoned covetousness for the world,” is the preliminary development (pubbabhāga-bhāvanā) of the first jhāna intended here;
therefore, the meaning should be understood in exactly the same way for the terms “non-ill will” and so forth.

Whatever else needs to be said regarding this should be understood according to the method explained in the *Brahmajāla-ṭīkā*. For [this excludes] the eight attainments that are accompanied by exertion (*saupāyāsā*).
Here, the teaching proceeds by way of the eighteen great insights and the four noble paths.
Furthermore, the statement, "One delights in developing one state, one delights in abandoning one state," is not spoken according to the method found in the *Dasuttara Sutta*;
for there it says, "One state is to be developed; one state is to be abandoned."

and the teaching has come down [in this way]. Nevertheless, since there is no difference in meaning, it is stated in the *Nekkhamma* discourse of the *Paṭisambhidāmagga* according to the sequence found there:
"Delighting in developing one quality, he delights in abandoning one quality.
This same method applies to the remaining sections as well. And because this is called the Teacher’s teaching on the Noble Lineages (*ariyavaṃsa*),...
For the Venerable Dhammasenāpati Sāriputta Thera brought here, by way of recitation, the teaching as taught by the Teacher himself;
therefore, in the *Mahāariyavaṃsa Sutta*, showing the conclusion according to the Teacher’s own mode of instruction, he said:

"In this way, monks, a bhikkhu is one who delights in development. This same method applies to the subsequent modes of exposition concerning the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhāna*) and the Abhidhamma presentation.
Although here the application has been made by way of a summary through the method of contemplation of the body alone,

the application should be understood in detail by way of the twenty-one bases. As for what ought to be said regarding the terms "as impermanent," and so forth, that should be understood according to the method stated in the commentaries on the *Visuddhimagga*.
310. They are called "strivings" (*padhānāni*) because one strives here by means of accomplishing restraint and so forth, and because they are the means (*padehi*) for that striving.
They are "supreme efforts" (*uttamavīriyāni*), meaning the best efforts, because they accomplish a distinguished goal.

"The effort arisen in one who is restraining" refers to the diligence of one who, through mindfulness, establishes [the mind] and closes off the eyes and other senses so that covetousness and the like do not arise.
"Arisen energy. "Of one who abandons" means of one who dispels. "Arisen energy" refers to the energy that functions as the means for accomplishing that very abandonment.
The same principle applies here to the phrase "arisen energy of one who develops.
"The sign of concentration" is concentration itself; for the concentration previously arisen is the cause for the seclusion of the concentration arising subsequently.
It is called the "sign of concentration" because it arises [as such].
"Due to seclusion from the acquisitions" means due to being secluded from, or escaped from, the acquisitions such as the aggregates (*skandha*).

"Having come to that" means having attained that *nibbāna* by means of the Path. It is "dispassion" (*virāga*) because passion and the like fade away (*virajjanti*) therein, or by means of it. Thus...
Cessation should also be seen. Since the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) are intended here in their mixed form, it is therefore said:
"either by way of the object or by way of what is to be attained. In that context, "by way of what is to be attained" means by way of being inclined toward that [cessation].

"Resolving upon relinquishment" (vossaggapariṇāmī) means having its transformation directed toward relinquishing; it is of a nature to transform through both the act of giving up and the act of leaping forward [into cessation].
Therefore he said, "Two kinds of relinquishment," and so forth. The "relinquishing of the aggregates" occurs by way of the abandoning of the defilements bound to them;
thus, in the very same manner that insight abandons the defilements, it likewise merits being said to "abandon" the aggregates which have those as their cause.
Because insight possesses the quality of leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminibhāva*), [he said: "Insight... relinquishes... and so on.
Because it flows toward, inclines toward, and tends toward *nibbāna*, reaching it by way of its downward slope, it receives the designation "launching into" (*pakkhandati*).
And the Path abandons the defilements and the aggregates by way of their total eradication;
therefore, launching, abandoning, and relinquishing should be understood respectively according to insight and the Path. "For the sake of relinquishing" (*vossaggatthāya*):
It is for the purpose of relinquishment through renunciation and for the purpose of relinquishment through leaping forward. "Matures" means it ripens.
That maturation is desired because of its attainment of the state of leading to emergence and its attainment of the state of the Noble Path;
thus he said, "it reaches the state of insight and the state of the path. Regarding the remaining phrases: "the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena..."

In passages such as “he develops,” this refers to the remaining sections of the factors of enlightenment (*bojjhaṅga*). It is called “auspicious” (*bhaddaka*) because it is auspicious, beautiful, and exceedingly rare;

for no other object of concentration (*samādhinimitta*) is so difficult to find, since it is exclusively beneficial by way of suppressing unwholesome states such as the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and dispelling lust (*rāga*).
And there is that which is diametrically opposed [to concentration]. Regarding the phrase "he guards":

here, "guarding" refers to the practice by which no decline occurs from the concentration already attained; and since that [practice] occurs through the destruction of its opposites, he says "concentration," and so forth.
"The perception of the skeleton, etc. means the jhāna of the skeleton, etc.; for he speaks of jhāna by way of its primary characteristic, which is perception (*saññā*).

"Knowledge regarding the Dhamma of the Four Truths by way of a single penetration" means knowledge that proceeds by way of a single clear realization (*ekābhisamaya*) regarding the four Noble Truths; the meaning is "path-knowledge" (*magga-ñāṇa*). Because it is included within the Four Truths, it is knowledge regarding Nibbāna, the state of cessation, which is within the Four Truths;
by this, he speaks of "fruit-knowledge" (*phala-ñāṇa*). Since the fruit that follows immediately after the path conforms to the path...
Since it proceeds by way of the subsiding and abandoning of those states belonging to the side of origination,

therefore, even regarding the truth of cessation, the "knowledge of the state" (dhamme ñāṇatā) is said only of the knowledge of the fruit— that is, the proceeding in accordance with that realization of the path through its actualization—
and not of any knowledge whatsoever that has Nibbāna as its object. Hence it was said, "As it has been stated," and so forth.
And here, while it may be granted that path-wisdom is called "knowledge of the Dhamma" because it penetrates the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths, how is it that fruition-wisdom is so called?
This objection is resolved by the fact that it proceeds with reference to the Dhamma of cessation (nirodha).
For both types of wisdom, through their own direct realization independent of others, [comprehend] the Dhamma of the Noble Truths by way of their function.

Because it occurs with respect to its object, it should be understood as "knowledge of phenomena" (*dhammeñāṇa*). For this word "phenomenon" (*dhamma*) refers to the Noble Truths because they possess an unerring intrinsic nature;
or else, it refers to the supreme conditioned phenomenon, which is the Noble Path, and to the phenomenon that is its fruit.
In that context, the wisdom associated with them is "knowledge of phenomena."
"Knowledge by way of consequence" (*anvayeñāṇa*) means knowledge of following along. "Having seen directly" means having penetrated the four truths directly through path-knowledge.

"Just as now" means that just as the five aggregates of clinging are the truth of suffering at present, so too were the five aggregates of clinging the truth of suffering in the past and will be in the future; this is stated by way of similarity.

This same method applies to the truth of the origin and the truth of the path. The word *ayameva* (this very) is used for emphasis. However, in the case of the truth of cessation, there is no similarity because it is eternal and possesses a single intrinsic nature.

Thus, "knowledge in the conformity of that knowledge" means that in the conformity—that is, the following along—of that knowledge of phenomena (*dhammañāṇa*) by way of the sequence beginning with "so also in the past," there is the knowledge of conformity (*anvaya-ñāṇa*). This is [the knowledge] of conformity.
“Knowledge” (*ñāṇa*) is the connection [to the context]. With the words “Therefore he said,” etc., he clarifies the aforementioned meaning by means of the Pāḷi.

“He” refers to the bhikkhu who stands having attained knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhamma-ñāṇa*). “By this Dhamma”: because it has the Dhamma as its domain, it is called “Dhamma” by way of the designation for its domain—that is, by the knowledge of the Path (*magga-ñāṇa*);
or else, the instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative, meaning “by this Dhamma known,” that is, by the knowledge of this Dhamma of the Four Truths.
The meaning is: by means of the knowledge of the path established through knowing. "By what is seen" means by seeing the Dhamma of the Truths through vision and being established therein.
"By what is attained" means by having attained the Truths and being established therein. "By what is known" means by having understood the Truths and being established therein.
"By what is fathomed" means by having fathomed the Dhamma of the Four Truths and being established therein. Such, then, is the meaning here according to the *Abhidhamma-ṭīkā*.
It has been stated. Furthermore, both types of knowledge regarding the path and its fruition (*maggaphala-ñāṇa*) constitute knowledge of the Dhamma (*dhamme-ñāṇa*).

Since it is the root and the cause for the "leading of the leading" (*nayanayana*) through review (*paccavekkhaṇā*), it is not incorrect to say that by means of those two kinds [of knowledge] there is "the Dhamma.

Likewise, because the Dhamma of the Four Noble Truths has been known, or because the Dhamma—consisting of the path and fruition—has attained association with the penetration of the truths, there is the "leading of the leading."
The meaning "it is known by this state (dhamma) as an object of knowledge, or through association with knowledge" is not untenable.
"It leads the method regarding the past and the future" means that it leads, carries, and directs the method toward the past and the future.
However, this is not the function of path-knowledge (*magga-ñāṇa*); it is the function of reviewing-knowledge (*paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa*). But the Teacher [assigned] path-knowledge...
Regarding the past and the future, it is called "leading" (*nayana*) because it is like leading [someone] along a path, since it is rooted in the path.

For one who has developed the path, there occurs what is called "reviewing" (*paccavekkhaṇā*). This is not the production of some other knowledge as a "leading," but rather a specific mode of the activity of that very knowledge.
"Leading around" (*pariyo*) is the leading around—that is, the delimitation—of the minds of others; it is in that "leading around" (*pariye*). Therefore he said: "Of others..."

"In the delimitation of consciousness. The remainder is called "conventional knowledge" (*sammutiñāṇa*) because it is conventionally recognized as "knowledge. As for the etymological meaning: it is "knowledge regarding the conventional," thus "conventional knowledge.
For, unlike the knowledge of the Dhamma and so forth, it lacks the specific function of penetration;
rather, by virtue of the commonality of knowing—which consists in the illumination of the object—it is included among those things conventionally recognized as "knowledge. This is the meaning.
Alternatively, conventional knowledge is so called because it occurs by way of convention and grasps its object through the door of convention.

Or else, the remaining knowledge— which is dissimilar to the other three types of knowledge— is termed "conventional knowledge" because it is included within conventional knowledge due to its commonality with that which is dissimilar to them.

Granted that the knowledge of the path of stream-entry and so forth are themselves the knowledge of suffering and so forth; however, he speaks thus—"having reached arahantship"—by way of an exalted description.
It is called "emerging" (niggamana) because one emerges from the round (vaṭṭa) by means of it; this refers to the meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths.

The first two truths constitute the round, because they are the state of occurrence and the cause of occurrence. The other two, however, constitute the non-round (vivaṭṭa), because they are the state of cessation and the cause of cessation.
“Insistence” (abhinivesa) refers to the insistence of insight (vipassanā), because mundane knowledge has reached a state that is contrary [to the ultimate].

“Not turning away” (no vivaṭṭe) means there is no insistence regarding turning away, because it is not its object. “The textual tradition” (pariyatti) refers to the lineage of meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna).

“Having mastered” (uggahetvā) means having made it thoroughly familiar through recitation. Or, “having mastered” means by way of hearing, memorizing, questioning, mental scrutiny, and so forth, as appropriate, according to the text and the meaning.

"Having grasped [the object] higher and higher with the mind. "He performs the work" means he performs the work of yoga by way of the sequence beginning with the discernment of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

If the application of insight (*vipassanābhinivesa*) and the learning and so forth were restricted only to the first two truths, one might ask: "How then is this meditation subject of the Four Noble Truths produced?
To this he says, "In the two," and so on. Granted that the latter two truths are also to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*), yet they are to be fully understood (*pariññeyya*).

However, since that [object] is not present there, there is no activity of insight (vipassanā). Rather, remaining at the mere level of hearsay, one directs attention [to it] as "lovely" because of its state of absolute excellence;
as "dear" because it generates a fervent, non-sensual joy; and as "agreeable" because it increases the mind by producing a progressive delight.
Therefore he said, "It is called the truth of cessation," and so forth. In the two...

"Regarding the truths" means regarding the two truths that have become its objects; for the Path, proceeding by way of penetration through non-delusion directed toward them, is said to proceed "directed toward" them.
The three [truths] are the truths of suffering, origin, and the path. "By way of function" means by way of non-delusion.
"One" refers to the truth of cessation. "By way of object" means also by way of making it an object.
In that regard, penetration is indeed obtainable by way of the function of non-delusion. "Two truths" refers to the truths of suffering and its origin.
"Difficult to see" means because they are impossible to perceive. For suffering and its origin are coarse;
suffering is evident even among animals, as is their craving for food and so forth. Also, by way of oppression and so on, and accumulation and so on, [it is said]: "This is suffering, this is..."
They are "profound" because they cannot be fathomed by knowledge according to their true nature. "Two" refers to the two truths of cessation and the path.

Because of their subtle and delicate state, and because they are difficult to penetrate with knowledge according to their true nature due to their inherent profundity, they are said to be "hard to see.
*Commentary on the Tetrad of Factors of Stream-entry, etc.*
311. *Sota* means the noble stream (*ariyasota*), by the elision of the first word [of the compound]. Its initial, very first attainment is *sotāpatti*, which is the acquisition of the first path.
The factors (*aṅga*) of that [attainment] are the causes consisting of the means for its realization; these are the "factors of stream-entry" (*sotāpattiyaṅga*).

Therefore he said: "The meaning of *sotā... pe ... attha*. Because of possessing peaceful bodily action and so forth, because of being endowed with peaceful qualities, and because of proclaiming peaceful qualities.

And those who are good are "true persons" (*sappurisa*). In this context, pointing out specifically those by whose means one obtains the hearing of the true Dhamma (*saddhamma*) which brings about the penetration of the Four Noble Truths, he says:
"of the true persons, beginning with the Buddha. The true Dhamma is the Dhamma of the good or of the virtuous.
For that [Dhamma], when practiced according to the instructions, prevents one from falling into the suffering of the states of woe (*apāya*) and the suffering of *saṃsāra*.

“Saddhamma” (the True Dhamma) refers to the Dhamma that is good because it possesses such excellent qualities as being upheld (*dhāreti*) and so forth; or it is the Dhamma that is real, existing, praised, or beautiful;
or it is the Dhamma of the *sata*, meaning the Noble Ones (*ariya*); or it is the Dhamma that establishes them in that state.

It also refers to the scriptural learning (*pariyatti*) described in passages such as, “Here, a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma. However, because its scope is vast, not all of it [is suitable] for everyone.
Showing that which is appropriate for each specific case, he says: "Hearing the Dhamma of the Three Piṭakas that is conducive.
*Yoniso-manasikāra* (appropriate attention) has already been explained above. "By way of the preliminary practice" means by way of the application of insight (*vipassanā*).
"By means of confirmed confidence" means by means of the confidence arisen after knowing the qualities of the Buddha and the others through the penetration of the Truths.
Furthermore, that confidence is called "unshakable" because it cannot be moved by anyone among the gods and others; thus he said, "with unshakable confidence.
"In this" means in these four tetrads, specifically in the tetrad of food.
"By way of coarse and refined objects" means by way of objects such as boiled rice, gruel, and so forth, which are both coarse and refined. This, moreover, is the grossness and subtlety of food.
“Taking the food of crocodiles as a comparison, the food of peacocks is subtle,” and so forth; this has been explained in detail in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā).
“By way of the stationing of the object” means by way of the stationing-condition for occurrence, which is designated as the object. It is called *ṭhiti* because it stands (*tiṭṭhati*) therein;
the object itself is the stationing, hence “stationing of the object. For this very reason he said, “the visible-form object,” and so forth. This is the meaning of “object” (*ārammaṇa*).
And here, the meaning of "support" (upatthambhana) is to be understood, not merely the characteristic of an object.
It is called *rūpūpāya* because it approaches matter that has become a support. Therefore he said: "having approached matter," and so forth.

It stands depending on the aggregate of matter (*rūpakkhandha*), because it does not function in its absence. "That" refers to its standing and functioning in dependence upon the aggregate of matter. "This" refers to the term "*rūpūpāya*."
This is the statement. "Having the aggregate of form as its range" means that the aggregate of form is its range, its sphere of activity, its basis, and its condition.

"Supported by form" means that form is its foundation by way of being a concomitant cause (*sahakārīkāraṇa*). Thus, by these three terms, it is precisely the state of the aggregate of form being a concomitant cause for the volitional consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇa*) that is stated here. It is "moistened," as it were, by moisture.
Just as rice mixed and moistened with condiments becomes palatable and fit for digestion, so too, kamma-consciousness mixed and moistened by delight (*nandi*) becomes desirable and fit for fruition.

"The other" refers to unwholesome states such as those accompanied by hatred, as well as wholesome states; the construction is that these become moistened by way of decisive support (*upanissaya*). Thus...
"Proceeding" means proceeding by way of teaching as such a means for form. It attains growth through its nature as a state of fruition (*vipākadhammatā*).
In that regard, there is "growth" by way of the production of the fruit in the direct sense (*nippariyāya*); "increase" by way of the production of the fruit in the indirect sense (*pariyāya*);
and "abundance" by way of the production of the outflow fruit (*nissandaphala*). [This occurs] through the production of the fruit to be experienced in the present life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*).

The construction is as follows: it attains "growth" by way of increasing, "increase" by way of producing fruit to be experienced upon rebirth (*upapajjavedanīya*), and "abundance" by way of producing fruit in subsequent lives (*aparāpariyāya*).
He says, "But by these," and so forth, because attainment (*patti*) occurs exclusively in the formless realm (*arūpabhava*) by way of feeling (*vedanā*), means (*upāya*), and so on.
And by doing so, the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) in the Pāḷi is justified.

It exists. By the phrase "approaching form" (*rūpūpāya*) and so forth, just as form and the other [bases] which serve as the decisive support (*upanissaya*) for the volitionally conditioned consciousness (*abhisaṅkhāra-viññāṇa*) are included, so too are those [bases] by which it is to be produced included;
this is the intended meaning when he says, "it was not stated by way of tetrads...".
For even a resultant phenomenon (*vipāka-dhamma*) is said to have "approached" the consciousness that is itself of a resultant nature, because it has been moistened by delight (*nandi*).
Therefore he said, "with the sprinkling of delight" (*nandūpasecanam*). These [terms] have already been explained in detail in the *Siṅgāla-sutta*.
By means of this, one comes to health; thus it is *bhava*, the condition for illness. When existence (*bhava*) has increased, it is *abhava*.
For here the prefix *a-* has the sense of increase, as in the cases of *saṃvarāsaṃvara* and *phalāphalam*. By the word "etc. in "oil, honey, molasses, etc.,"...
The mention of ghee and fresh butter, as well as the mention of oil and so forth, is merely illustrative; it should be understood as including all requisites for the sick.
Alternatively, "existence after existence" (*bhavābhava*) should be understood as both minor and major rebirth-existence (*upapattibhava*).
This being the case, the statement beginning with "But of these... is justified. For [the following] is for the purpose of abandoning rebirth-existence:
Specifically, it refers to the fourth noble lineage (*ariyavaṃsa*). "Of the arising of craving" (*taṇhuppādānaṃ*) means of the occurrences of craving;

the meaning is: of the cravings that arise for the sake of robes and so forth. "At the time of performing the exertion" (*padhānakaraṇakāle*) means at the moment of application to meditation (*bhāvanānuyoga*).

"Cold and so forth are not endured" is said with reference to the period prior to the actual practice of meditation. "Is endured" (*khamati*) means it bears up or overcomes [the discomfort]. "The stilling of thought" (*vitakkasamanaṃ*) is merely an illustration.
It is the practice that proceeds by way of the complete subduing of all defilements.

It is called a *dhammapada* because the state (*dhamma*) consisting of the distinctions of concentration, jhāna, and so forth, is reached (*pajjati*) or practiced (*paṭipajjīyati*) by means of it. Non-covetousness itself is the *dhammapada*;
thus, it is "the *dhammapada* of non-covetousness. This, first of all, is the method regarding the side of non-greed; however, regarding the other side:
The section on phenomena beginning with non-covetousness is the factor of non-covetousness. "Non-anger" means non-hatred; the meaning is loving-kindness (*mettā*).
"Well-established mindfulness" means mindfulness properly established with respect to the body and so forth. "By way of mindfulness as the head" means by way of mindfulness as the primary basis.

Because meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) have concentration as their primary basis, it is said, "or attainment. Granted that the development of absorption occurs even regarding the impurities of beings endowed with consciousness.
It is dominated by non-greed because it proceeds by way of disgust for the body and by way of grasping at the aspect of repulsiveness;
however, its occurrence by way of the sevenfold skill in comprehension and so forth is dominated by mindfulness.

Desiring to include this [meditation] within the third category of the "Dhammapada" (the path of dhammas), he said, "or by way of the ten kinds of foulness. This is because it proceeds by way of bringing about welfare and so forth.
The cultivation of the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) is opposed to ill-will and has non-ill-will as its primary quality; thus it is said: "The four divine abodes...
[the] verse on the Dhamma. Therein, the construction is: "the jhānas and so forth have been attained.

The perception of the repulsiveness of food from the time of its ingestion onwards occurs precisely through the stability of perception, because that perception has stability as its proximate cause (padatthāna); thus, the perception of repulsiveness in food [is also included].

These are included within the third Dhammapada itself. Since the development of the kasiṇas serves as the foundation for formless attainments (*ārūppasamādhi*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), and since the first development of mindfulness of breathing among the sevenfold types of mindfulness of breathing is specifically the primary factor for concentration—being the cause for the fulfillment of the seven factors of enlightenment, true knowledge (*vijjā*), and liberation—it is included within the fourth Dhammapada.
This also includes those [attainments] acquired by means of the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*).
These [other practices] should indeed have been included here; however, they are not included because wisdom (*paññā*) is the primary factor.

Among the "undertakings of dhamma" (*dhammasamādāna*), the first—the practice of the naked ascetics (*acelaka*)—is painful both at present and in the future, as it brings about the suffering of the lower realms (*apāya*) and the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭa*).

Furthermore, the term "practice of the naked ascetics" should be regarded as merely illustrative, since it shows that even the practice of the clothed wanderers (*channa-paribbājaka*) brings about both kinds of suffering.

The second [member]... pe ...the practice of the holy life (brahmacariya) is for the sake of bringing future happiness even though there is suffering at present. "Drinking of sensual pleasures" is the enjoyment of sensual pleasures according to one's desire.
By the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even for one who does not obtain them," it is shown that what need is there to speak of one who does obtain them?
The meaning of "aggregate" (*khandha*) is the propping up or the supporting of evil states such as immorality; and that, moreover, consists of virtue and the rest.
He said: "The meaning of 'aggregate' (khandha) is the meaning of 'quality' (guṇa). Because the word *khandha* has quality as its object, it should be understood that it carries the sense of "quality.

In the phrase "aggregate of liberation" (*vimuttikkhandha*), what is intended are the qualities of dhamma that are perfectly liberated from their opposites; they are not those that are unliberated, nor those currently being liberated.
Since the aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth, which are included in the teaching along with those [qualities], are also threefold, he said: "the fruit-virtue..."

And by this very [statement], it should be understood that in all four instances, only the fruit is mentioned; thus, here the "aggregate of liberation" (vimuttikkhandha) is intended to mean right intention, right effort, and right mindfulness as included within the fruit.
This is because, in the sense of providing support, the associated states proceed therein with stability. By this very [reasoning]...
The status of shamelessness (*ahirika*) and lack of moral dread (*anottappa*) as powers within their own domain should also be understood as established.

For their immovability by way of their opposites is not absolute. Indeed, the immovability of shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) is preeminent because wholesome states possess great strength while unwholesome states are weak.
Therefore the Blessed One said: "Weaknesses overcome him; dangers crush him."
This teaching is by way of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakkhiyadhamma*); thus it is said, "by way of serenity (*samatha*), insight (*vipassanā*), and the path (*magga*).
*Adhi* is merely a prefix; it does not carry the sense of "superior" or "additional" as it does in terms such as *adhicitta*.

Demonstrating the meaning of the word *adhiṭṭhāna* according to its function as an instrument (*karaṇa*), a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), or an abstract state (*bhāva*), he says, "or by that," and so forth. They stand by means of that foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
Persons who possess superior qualities in their own right practice stand firm in that very foundation of right attainment;
the construction of the sentence is: "the standing, the foundation, and the right practice. By the first foundation. "Wisdom of the highest fruit" is a designation for the most excellent state.
"The subsiding of defilements" means the absolute cessation of defilements. These are the foundations according to the first method.
Since these have been taken only partially and not in their entirety, the phrase beginning with "And by the first" is stated in order to show them in their full extent (*nipparisesato*).
By the expression "beginning with," both the wisdom of the jhānas and higher knowledges (*jhānābhiññā-paññā*) as well as the wisdom of the path (*magga-paññā*) are included.
By the word "beginning with" in the phrase "beginning with the truth of speech," the truth of abstinence (*virati-sacca*) is included. By the third "beginning with," [the cessation of] defilements...
It includes the abandonment of transgressions, the abandonment of obsessions, and the abandonment of underlying tendencies by means of the lower paths.
By the phrase "defilements suppressed," having stated the subsiding of defilements through their suppression by means of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*),
the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to the subsiding of those same defilements through their total eradication (*samuccheda*) by means of the lower paths.

He embraces [them]. The wisdom of the fruit of arhatship (*arahattaphala-paññā*) has been described according to the highest exposition; otherwise, there would also be the inclusion of the truth of speech and so forth.
And Nibbāna, by virtue of its quality of being non-forgetful, deserves to be specifically designated as "truth" in the sense of being supreme;

by virtue of being the cause for the relinquishing of all defilements, it is "renunciation" (*cāga*); and because of the state of the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*), it is "peace" (*upasama*). Thus it is said of the Elder.
The intention is as follows: wisdom (*paññā*) is so called because its fruit is the knowledge of what is preeminent;

and relinquishment (*cāga*) and tranquility (*upasama*) are so called because they arise when the defilements have been entirely abandoned and stilled. Thus, specifically, the knowledge of the fruit of Arahantship is called "peace. Therefore, the Elder said:
"By the remaining [terms], the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship is explained."
Commentary on the Tetrad beginning with the Answering of Questions (Pañhabyākaraṇādicatukka-vaṇṇanā) 312.

"Black" (*kāḷaka*) means soiled; the meaning is that it causes the mind to lose its luminosity. However, in this context, only that which has reached the level of a course of action (*kammapatha*) is intended;
thus he says, "the action of the ten unwholesome courses of action. Alternatively, it is black because it is the cause for a dark rebirth. Therefore he said:
“Black ripening”: rebirth in the states of misery (apāya) and wretchedness among humans is the black ripening.
This is said to be its dark nature. “From producing”: from causing to be produced. “White”: bright; the meaning is that it makes the mind radiant.
Or, it is white because it is the cause for a fair birth. Therefore he says, “white ripening. Rebirth in the heavenly realms and [prosperity] among humans...

Beauty and bright kamma-result—this is said to be its luminosity. According to the exalted description, however, it is said to be “because of being reborn in heaven,” the meaning being “because of causing rebirth.
“Mixed kamma” is kamma performed by way of mixture, such that at one time it is black and at another time it is bright.
Having stated, “it has both pleasant and painful results,” therein, regarding pleasure and pain:
In order to show the mode of occurrence, it was said, "For mixed karma," and so forth.

The designation "black" and "white" for karma is due to its being the cause of black and white rebirths; however, because it leads to diminution (*apacayagāmitā*), the application of the term "white" is not intended here for the karma that destroys both—that is, the karma that effects the exhaustion of karma.
Thus he said: "Both... this is the meaning here. In that context, "of both results" means:

Of that which has been realized as having both types of fruition. For here, the fruition included within the state of prosperity (*sampattibhava*) is intended by the term "bright fruition" (*sukkavipāka*), not the utterly pure fruition of the noble fruits (*ariyaphala*).
Previous births and the passing away and rebirth of beings are to be realized by means of direct perception; the others are to be realized by means of attainment.
It is to be realized by means of direct experience through penetration without confusion. But is it not the case that even here, reflective contemplation (*paccavekkhaṇā*) proceeds directly?

True, it proceeds directly in the sense of seeing its own form; however, it does not proceed by way of making it an object of direct experience, because it turns its back on those who have already made it an object of direct experience.
Therefore he said, "by the body," and so forth.
“They strike down” (*ohananti*) means they strike and submerge from below. And being thus situated, they sink downwards; hence it is said, “they cause to sink” (*osīdāpenti*).

It is called the flood of sensual pleasures (*kāmogha*) because it is sensual pleasure (*kāma*) in the sense of being desired, and it is a flood (*ogha*) in the sense already stated—or alternatively, the flood of sensual pleasures is the flood within sensual pleasures.

To show that the flood of existence (*bhavogha*) is indeed craving for existence (*bhavarāga*), it was said, “in the realms of form and formlessness,” and so forth. Among those, the first [flood] pertains to the realms of rebirth.
Lust is the first; the second pertains to kamma-existence; the third is accompanied by views regarding existence.
Just as it is "lust" (*rāga*) in the sense of coloring (*rañjana*), so too it is called a "flood" (*ogha*) in the sense of overwhelming (*ohana*).

They "yoke" means that they yoke—i.e., join together through impact—the suffering beings in one existence with kamma and its result, and from one state of existence to another; thus they are "yokes" (*yoga*). In their essential meaning, the yokes of sensuality and so forth are to be understood as being like floods, because of their nature as yokes.
"Disjoining" means they disjoin the person who has entered upon the path from the yoke of sensual desire and so forth. "Yoking" (*yojana*) is the act of defiling;
"tying" (*gantha*) is the act of binding, or the state of being fettered like chains and shackles—this is the distinction between them. "To obstruct" (*palibundhati*)...
It "obstructs" by not releasing through the non-granting of escape. "This very [is it]" refers to one's own established views, such as eternalism and so forth.
"Truth" means what is real.
They are called "clinging" (*upādāna*) because by means of them a basis is firmly and strongly grasped. Furthermore, that which is their mode of grasping in that way—
Since that too, in its actual meaning, is simply grasping, he said: "Graspings (upādānāni) means modes of grasping. "In the sense of grasping" means in the sense of grasping firmly by way of desire.
"Again, in the sense of grasping" means in the sense of grasping firmly by way of false adherence. "By this" refers to this [practice] such as virtue and observances.
"Purity" means purity from the cycle of existence (saṃsāra). "By this" refers to this holding of views. "'Self'..."
While describing them, one both speaks and, by way of dogmatic adherence, clings to them.
As many as there are [categories] where beings, though not actually mixed, appear as if mixed due to their belonging to the same class, these are "wombs" (*yoni*).

In terms of their actual meaning, however, they are specific modes of the partial manifestation of the aggregates (*khandha*) distinguished by the place of origin, such as from an egg and so forth; thus he said, "Wombs."
"Divisions. "On a bed" means on a bed such as one spread with flowers and so forth.
Or, they are born having lain there; thus it is called a "bed. This should be understood by way of humans and the deities of the earth.

Maggots are produced in putrid fish and the like. "As if fallen by way of rebirth" (upapajjavasena) means as if fallen by way of spontaneous birth (*upapatti*). Because of their independence from external conditions...
Or those who perform meritorious deeds at the time of falling [from a higher realm] are "spontaneously born" (*opapātika*); it is these very ones who are referred to here as "spontaneously born.
Regarding the phrase "among gods and humans," he says "among the earth-dwelling gods" (*bhummadevesu*) to show those whom he intends by the mention of "gods.

Because they die through the application of nutriment due to their own loss of mindfulness, it is said: "The first [type of non-percipient beings] is by way of the 'corrupted by play' (*khiḍḍāpadosika*)."
Because they die due to mental corruption directed toward themselves and others, it is said: "The third is by way of mental corruption.
Because they do not die through their own volition nor through the volition of another, but solely through the exhaustion of merit, the fourth...
[and so on] ...should be understood.
Commentary on the Tetrad on the Purity of the Gift (Dakkhiṇāvisuddhādicatukka), §313:
The "gift" (dakkhiṇā) refers to the act of giving, not to the object to be given. "Purification" means great radiance; however, that should be understood as being due to its great fruit.

Thus he said, "they become of great fruit. "To the ignoble" (anariyānaṃ) means to those who are not good. Since they are of base conduct, he said, "to the lowly" (lāmakānaṃ). "Transactions" (vohārā) refers to all dealings or expressions; in terms of meaning, it is the volition (cetanā) proceeding in such a manner. Therefore he said, "And here," and so forth.

Commentary on the Fourfold Set Beginning with "One Who Torments Himself" (Attantapa-ādicatukka): 314. Among those, "one who is naked" (acelaka) is mentioned merely as an illustration, since it applies even to covered wanderers (channa-paribbājaka) who are devoted to self-mortification.
"Not endowed with virtue and so forth" means one who is incomplete in such qualities as virtue (sīla).

"Tamobhūto" means having become darkness due to the state of being devoid of light. Therefore he said, "become like darkness," meaning he has become or been born like darkness due to the state of being devoid of light;
or the meaning is that he has reached the state of darkness. "Tamameva" refers to the very darkness characterized as previously stated.
"Paraṃ parato ayanaṃ gati niṭṭhā" means going, movement, or destination beyond, further on. By the phrase "having been reborn in a low... [etc.]," his state of darkness is indicated.
By the phrase "he fulfills the three types of misconduct," he shows his state of having darkness as his destination (*tamaparāyana*), because he has fallen into a state of non-illumination.

Having become such [a person]—that is, having been reborn in a low... [state]—by the phrase "he fulfills the three types of good conduct," he shows his state of having light as his destination (*jotiparāyana*), because he has attained a state of illumination.
The meaning of the other two cases should be understood according to the method explained above.

The syllable *ma* is merely for the purpose of joining words (*padasandhimatta*), as in the case of the word “*aññamañña*” and others. “By the four winds” means by the winds arising from the four directions.
“By the doctrines of others” means by the doctrines of other proponents of wrong views. Having stated “unshakable,” he provides the reason for that:
“by immovable faith,” meaning by the faith that has come through the Path. Regarding the phrase “because it has become attenuated”: here—
The slightness of his defilements should be understood by two reasons: by their infrequency of arising and by the weakness of their obsession.
For in the case of a once-returner, the defilements do not arise frequently as they do in the case of the common worldling who follows the round of existence; rather, they arise only occasionally.
And when they do arise, they do not arise as crushing or overwhelming forces, as they do in the case of the common worldling who follows the round of existence; for [they arise] in two ways...
However, because they have been abandoned by the paths, they arise only as very weak and attenuated forms.

Thus, due to the attenuation of the defilements, the splendor of his qualities, and the gentleness of his virtues, he is called a "once-returner" (*sakadāgāmī*), a lotus among ascetics. "Due to the absence of lust and hatred" means due to the total absence of lust and hatred, which are the obstructions to the blossoming of his qualities.
"He will soon blossom" means that through the blossoming of the supreme path, he will do so before long.
It will blossom with the fulfillment of the splendor of all qualities without exception; therefore, he is called the Non-returner, the Lotus of the Recluses (*samaṇapuṇḍarīka*).
For "lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*) refers to the red lotus; it is said that this blossoms quickly. "Water-lily" (*paduma*) refers to the white lotus;
they say that this blossoms after a long time. [The phrase] "of the knots and defilements" refers to those things that bind the mind.

Because of the total absence of the higher-fettering defilements (*uddhambhāgiyakilesa*), he is called "the delicate ascetic" (*samaṇasukhumāla*) due to having attained a state of supreme delicacy through his status as an ascetic.
The commentary on the tetrad is finished.
And the commentary on the first section for recitation is completed.

Commentary on the Five [Aggregates] (Pañcaka-vaṇṇanā) 315. Just as the Noble Truths are included within the Truths, so too are the aggregates of clinging included within the aggregates. Having thus shown the division among the aggregates by way of the mundane and the supramundane, he says, "The aggregates of clinging are mundane," because those other [aggregates] lack that quality.
"To be gone to" means to be reborn. For just as, in the case of kamma-existence (*kammabhava*), although there is no ultimate agent, [rebirth occurs] through the completeness of conditions...
The established [term] is conventionally expressed as "made by a being characterized by a continuity that possesses that [action].

Likewise, although in the ultimate sense there is no goer, the destinies characterized by the state of rebirth are conventionally expressed as "to be gone to" by those [beings] who, through their respective kamma, are said to have "done" those kamma-actions.
That for which [rebirth] arises arises only as something increasing.

“Ayo” means suffering (*sukha*). Since there is no “*ayo*” (iron/suffering) here, it is called *niraya*. For that very reason, because there is nothing here to be relished, he said it is “without relish” (*nirassāda*).
He said, “The aggregates are spoken of together with their location,” because the term *niraya* is conventionally established even for locations such as the Avīci hell.

He said, “In the fourth [case], the location is also [included],” because in the world the term “deity” (*deva*) is conventionally established even for specific locations such as the sun’s celestial mansion.
"Āvāse" (in the dwelling) is the locative case used for the sphere of activity. One is reborn as a ghost or a python due to a clinging mind and a low disposition.
Having demonstrated the danger through various reasons, one acts in such a way that others do not obtain [the food], because of one's own dependence on what is uneven and dependence on the powerful.
Through envy of beauty, one praises only one's own beauty.
Regarding the praise of others, one speaks of various faults, asking, "What kind of character does he have?
The Dhamma of penetration belongs only to the Noble Ones (ariyas), and since they do not harbor stinginess because it has been entirely abandoned, its non-existence [in them] is certain;
thus he says, "In the Dhamma of the scriptures," and so forth. "Having learned this Dhamma, he has distorted the meaning by turning it around otherwise..."
“It will be lost”—thus one does not give out of concern for the Dhamma.
“Having mastered this Dhamma, this person will become conceited, arrogant, and unpeaceful in mind, and will produce demerit”—thus one does not give out of concern for the individual.
This non-giving is not stinginess, because the defining characteristic of stinginess is simply absent.

“They obstruct the mind” means they prevent wholesome consciousness from arising by way of the jhānas and so forth; they do not allow it to arise in that manner. “Reached the state of an hindrance” (nīvaraṇappatta) means being in the condition of an hindrance.
