By the phrase “to be abandoned by the path of Arahatship,” he acknowledges that even the underlying tendency to lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya) possesses the nature of an hindrance; this must be investigated. What is there to investigate here? [The question is: “In the formless realm, is there the hindrance of sensual desire? [The answer is: No. Why? Because sensual desire has matter as its object. Since matter does not exist in the formless realm, sensual desire cannot exist there. However, the underlying tendency to lust for existence exists in the formless realm because it takes the five aggregates as its object. Therefore, it is acknowledged that the underlying tendency to lust for existence is an hindrance. But why is it not called an “actual hindrance” (nīvaraṇa)? It is not called an actual hindrance because it is not manifestly active (paccuppanna); rather, it is called an “underlying tendency” (anusaya). Furthermore, the underlying tendency to lust for existence is not included among the five hindrances because it is not a factor that obstructs the mind in the way the other hindrances do. Thus, it is established that the underlying tendency to lust for existence is indeed an hindrance. This concludes the investigation. Now, the meaning of the text should be explained. “They obstruct the mind”: they suppress the wholesome consciousness arising through the jhānas and so forth, and they do not permit it to arise in that way. “Reached the state of an hindrance”: being in the condition of an hindrance. Because of such statements as, "dependent on [the hindrance of] sloth and torpor," it cannot be said that this was spoken "by way of a figurative expression" (pariyāyena).

This is because all phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence possess the nature of sensual desire (*kāma*) in the sense of being desirable, and because even craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) is intended to be included within the state of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*).

Therefore, by saying "sensual desire has reached the state of a hindrance," he refers to the underlying tendency toward craving for existence (*bhavarāgānusaya*), for that is what is to be abandoned by the path of Arahatship.
“Stiffness (thīna) is the sickness of the mind,” according to the statement beginning with “that which at that time is the unwellness of the mind.
Likewise, “torpor (middha) is the sickness of the three aggregates,” according to the statement beginning with “that which at that time [is the unwellness] of the aggregate of feeling.

And here, by the sickness of the mind, there is unwellness of the mind alone; but by the sickness of the three aggregates, there is unwellness of the material body as well due to stiffness and torpor.
Because it is the cause of sleep. Likewise, by the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he indicates that restlessness (*uddhacca*) is to be abandoned by the path of Arahantship;

he does not indicate both [sleep and restlessness], for such duality does not exist in the case of the latter. As for what some say—that [restlessness] "occurs in the continuum of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*) and occurs in the continuum of one in training (*sekkha*)"—that is irrelevant here, because only that which occurs in the continuum of one in training is intended in this context.

“By those” means by the fetters (*saṃyojana*). The general extraction of the term “fetters,” without specifying the distinction between “lower-tier” and “upper-tier” ones, is made here for the sake of its suitability for the fourfold sets that are about to be explained.
Since no defilement whatsoever has been suppressed, one is not exempt from falling into the states of loss;
furthermore, sensual existence (*kāmabhava*) serves as a specific condition for the apprehension of the internal.

For these beings, "internal" (*anto*) is used in the sense of being within; "external" (*bahi*) is used in the opposite sense, referring to existence in the fine-material and immaterial realms (*rūpārūpabhava*).

For it is said that one who has not abandoned the lower fetters (*orambhāgiyasaṃyojana*) is "one with internal fetters," while one who has abandoned them is "one with external fetters. Therefore, "internal" refers to the state of having bonds unsevered, and "external" [refers to their severance].

And because the continuity of the active life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) is bound within [the round of existence], it is said to be "lying outside. For the designation "lying" is used by way of the uninterrupted flow of the life-continuum.
Granted that their external bonds are also not severed, this is stated thus specifically because of the grossness of the internal bond.
Therefore he said: "For them, there is a bond in the sensual realm of existence (*kāmabhava*). By this same method, [it should be understood] for the remaining two [realms] as well.

The meaning should be understood as follows: when the lower fetters (*orambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) that provide the conditions [for rebirth] have not been severed, the higher fetters (*uddhambhāgiya-saṃyojana*) remain beyond calculation.
Because this tetrad is presented here specifically from the perspective of the Noble Ones (*ariya*), ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*), even though they are included, are not mentioned.

“Section of training” (*sikkhākoṭṭhāsa*) means a portion of that which is to be trained in. It is called a “training precept” (*sikkhāpada*) because one trains by means of it; it is thus a means for attaining training. [The meaning] is already established [in the texts], therefore the intention is that it should be understood according to the method presented therein.

316. They are not unwholesome (*akusala*) because their intrinsic nature is undefiled (*asaṃkiliṭṭha-sabhāva*). Nor are they subject to the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*) because they are non-existent phenomena (*abhāva-dhamma*). As for the other [category], however—
The unwholesome is the opposite of what has been stated, and it is struck by the three characteristics.
"Perfection" (*sampadā*) refers to the state of being fully endowed with qualities.
"Pointing out the basis" (*vatthusandassanā*) is the demonstration, in its specific form, of the basis upon which an offense occurs. "Pointing out the offense" (*āpattisandassanā*)...

317. *Padahati* means "he strives"; one who is devoted to meditation is a *yogī*, and his state of being is *bhāvanānuyoga*, the state of striving.
One who possesses *padhāna* (striving) is *padhānika*; by changing the letter *ka* to *ya*, it is stated as "*padhāniyo*.
Because it is said, "Because it has come down from the time of the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*)," this applies to both *paccekabodhisattas* and *sāvakabodhisattas*.
Faith that has "come" from the time of the initial aspiration onwards is simply faith as arrival (*āgamanasaddhā*);
however, it is described in its most exalted sense as belonging to "all omniscient Bodhisattvas. Faith as attainment (*adhigamanasaddhā*) is so called because it has arisen through realization;

it is associated with the highest path and fruit, and is stated to be a constituent factor for one who has entered the stream (*sotāpanna*). It is "immovable" because it cannot be overcome by opposing factors.

By way of being unshakable. *Okappanā* means having entered and leaped into [the object], it is the act of resolving. The arising of confidence (*pasāduppatti*) is simply the state of being confident toward an inspiring object.

*Suppaṭividdhaṃ* means well-penetrated; it was penetrated in such a way that, through that penetration, the knowledge of omniscience came into the hands [of the Buddha]. It is the faith in whose case there is the perfect enlightenment of a Buddha.
It is impossible and out of the question that one’s faith would not be likewise firm and unshakable because of the Dhamma’s being well-expounded and the Saṅgha’s being well-practiced;
for this reason, the Blessed One said: “Bhikkhus, he who has confidence in the Buddha has confidence in the Dhamma, and he has confidence in the Saṅgha,” and so forth.
The energy of exertion succeeds: “Surely, by means of this practice...”
“By striving diligently with the thought, ‘I shall be liberated from old age and death,’ [one attains health].
He says “free from disease” because the word *appa* has the sense of non-existence, as in such passages as “the word *appa*... indeed.
“Samavepākiniyā” means having the nature of digesting food exactly as it was eaten in a balanced manner; for the stomach (*gahaṇī*) is so called because it digests firmly by way of its intense power.
It produces disease by way of bile-disorders and so forth; or, having become lax, it digests with sluggishness by way of wind-disorders and so forth.

Therefore he said, "neither too cold nor too hot. He said, "one who has indigestion from excessive cold," and so forth, because beings possess cold and heat respectively according to the dullness or sharpness of their digestive fire (*gahaṇī-teja*).
The confession of transgression as it truly is is the disclosure of oneself.
Regarding the word *nāma*, he said: "one who reveals one's own lack of virtue as it truly is. Regarding the phrase *udayatthagāminiya*, he said:

"of those that penetrate the arising and passing away of formations (*saṅkhārā*); this is the meaning here," and so forth with the words "arising" and so on. *Parisuddhāya* means "free from defilements.
*Nibbijjhituṃ samatthāya* means "capable of abandoning the remainder by way of substitution of opposites (*tadaṅga-vasena*)."

"Leading to the destruction of each respective suffering": this refers to that suffering which would occur as long as this knowledge has not been attained, but which no longer occurs once it has been attained.
For it is because of this that the practitioner of yoga is called a "lesser stream-enterer.
*Commentary on the Five [Abodes], beginning with the Pure Abodes (Suddhāvāsa)*.
318. By the phrase “They dwell pure,” etc., he shows that the designation “Pure Abodes” (Suddhāvāsa) applies to them throughout all three periods [of time] without exception.

By saying they are “free from the stains of defilements,” while speaking of the purity of the mental body (nāmakāya), he simultaneously indicates by implication the purity of the physical body (rūpakāya).
Therefore, he says: “Non-returners whose taints are exhausted.”
“In the middle of life” means that wherever one is born—whether in the Aviha heaven or elsewhere—one does not exceed the middle of that particular lifespan.
“In the interval” (*antarā*) means right within that interval, midway. “Having reached the middle” (*upahacca*) means having passed the middle of the lifespan. Therefore he said, “having exceeded.
“Without exertion” (*appayogena*) means without strenuous effort. “Not wearying” (*akilamanto*) means being untiring. “With ease” (*sukhena*) means without difficulty.
He is an "upstreamer" (*uddhaṃsota*) because his stream of craving and the stream of the round of existence flow upwards due to their upward-moving nature;

or, he is an "upstreamer" because his stream of the Path is directed upwards, as it is to be attained by going upwards. He is "one who goes to the Akaniṭṭha realm" (*akaniṭṭhagāmī*) because he goes to the Akaniṭṭha.
Regarding "purifying": it is said that as he is reborn here and there, he is as if purifying those various celestial worlds; thus, "four... [is stated].

"Having purified [the defilements] in the world of the gods. Having been reborn here and there, by virtue of no longer being subject to rebirth even from those realms, he departs from that place as well, having purified and suppressed the stain of craving for existence (*bhavarāga*) within his own world of aggregates (*khandhaloka*), which is designated as "existence born among the gods.
For he, while dwelling for a thousand eons in the Aviha heaven, being unable to attain *arahantship*, proceeds to the Atappa heaven.
Even there, dwelling for two thousand eons, being unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to Sudassa;
even there, dwelling for four thousand eons, being unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to Sudassi;
even there, dwelling for eight thousand eons, being unable to attain *arahantship*, he goes to Akaniṭṭha.
Dwelling there, one attains the supreme path.
319. As for the "five mental barrennesses" (*cetokhila*):
in terms of their actual meaning, they are doubt and anger; however, those [mental states] arise within whichever continuum (*santāna*).
Its quality of hardness and rigidity manifests even more so in the consciousness associated with itself;

thus he said, "the stiffened state of consciousness. Just as when the perfection of the primary characteristics is grasped, the entire splendor of the Teacher’s physical body is indeed grasped, so too, when omniscience is grasped, the entire splendor of the Dhamma-body is indeed grasped.
Showing doubt regarding both of those bases, he said, “one who doubts the body,” and so forth. It heats up the defilements (*kilesa*), thus it is *ātappa*; it is right effort (*sammāvāyāma*).
Therefore he said, “for the sake of *ātappa* means for the sake of exerting energy. “For repeated application” (*punappunaṃ yogāya*) means for the repeated engagement in cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
“For constant action” (*satatakiriyāya*) means for the uninterrupted application of cultivation. Regarding the “dhamma of penetration” (*paṭivedhadhamme*)...
Regarding the phrase "one who is doubting": how does doubt arise with respect to supramundane states (*lokuttaradhamma*)? It is not by way of making them an object of consciousness;
rather, showing that doubt arises toward a conceptualized form obtained through hearsay or modes of discursive thought, he says:
"Insight... they say; one doubts whether that exists or does not exist. And here, "training" (*sikkhā*) refers to the preliminary training (*pubbabhāgasikkhā*).

[This] should be understood. Some say: "In this context, although anger toward fellow celibates (*sabrahmacārī*) is specifically mentioned as its object because it arises frequently due to the production of specific [faults], the gravity of the offense, and the friction caused by signs of living together, nevertheless, anger toward others cannot be understood as 'not a mental barrenness' (*na cetokhilo*).
If that were so, then this [definition] would also apply to doubt (*vicikicchā*).
...a logical inconsistency arises; therefore, it must be understood according to the literal meaning alone.
**Commentary on the Five Mental Barriers (Cetaso-vinibandha), etc.:
320.** They are called "mental barriers" (*cetaso-vinibandhā*) because they bind wholesome consciousness by way of preventing its occurrence. That...
But because they are binding [the mind], as if grasping it with a fist, he said, "having bound the mind," and so forth.

A person greedy for sensual pleasures relishes and delights in both object-sensual-pleasures (*vatthukāma*) and defilement-sensual-pleasures (*kilesakāma*); thus it was said, "in object-sensual-pleasures as well as in defilement-sensual-pleasures.
"In one's own body" means in one's own physical body (*karajakāya*) or in one's personal existence (*attabhāva*). "External form" refers to those of others.
[It refers] to the body and to matter not bound by faculties. "Udarāvadehakaṃ" means that which swells, accumulates, and fills the belly.
"Seyyasukhaṃ" is the pleasure arising from the state of lying down on a bed. "Saṃparivattakaṃ" means having turned over repeatedly.
"Paṇidhāya" means having directed [the mind] by way of craving. Thus, it should be understood that these five kinds of specific greed are indeed called "bonds of the mind" (cetovinibandha).

Only mundane states are spoken of, because only the material form and the faculties are mentioned. The first, second, and fourth [bases] are mundane because they belong to the limited plane (*parittabhūmaka*).

The third and fifth are mundane and supramundane because they belong to the peak of the sense-sphere and the fine-material sphere respectively, and because they belong to the peaks of the sense-sphere, the fine-material sphere, and the immaterial sphere.
The construction [of the sentence] is to be supplied as: "they are spoken of as mundane and supramundane. "By way of serenity, insight, path, and fruit" means:
It should be stated. It is said: "By way of the paths of serenity and insight.
Regarding the commentary on the five factors leading to escape (nissaraṇīya-pañcaka):
321. "They escape" (*nissaranti*); thus, although it should be called *nissaraṇīyā*, the designation is made with the short vowel. This suffix *-anīya* is used here in the sense of the agent.
Just as they are said to be "leading out" (*niyyānika*), so he says they are "escaped" (*nissaṭa*). From what, however, have they escaped? From their respective opposites.

In the sense of being devoid of a living soul (*nijjīva*), he says they are "of a nature empty of self. In terms of meaning, however, they are specific instances of the dhamma-element and the mind-consciousness-element.
For such a bhikkhu, there is no attention directed toward sense pleasures by way of defilements; thus he says, "for the purpose of investigation."
The meaning is: for one who is investigating, thinking, “My mind is now dependent on renunciation; could even a thought of sensual desire arise?
“Entering” means plunging in, but since that does not occur there, he says, “it does not enter.
“Favorable inclination” means a state of settled preference, and “liberation” means resolute conviction; including all of these, [the text says it does not enter].
He says, "He does not attain confidence," and so forth. To the question, "How does his mind remain there when it has become thus?
he says, "But just as... and so forth. "That" refers to the first jhāna. "His" refers to the bhikkhu.

He says "the mind leaps forward" by taking the jhāna-consciousness together with the preliminary-work consciousness (parikamma-citta) as a single unit in terms of its unified function. In its objective sphere...

"Having gone" (*gatatta*) means because it occurs only upon its own object. "Partaking of non-decline" (*ahānabhāgiyatā*) means partaking of stability (*ṭhitibhāgiya*) or partaking of distinction (*visesabhāgiya*).
"Well-liberated" (*suṭṭhu vimutta*) means perfectly liberated by way of suppression-liberation (*vikkhambhanavimutti*).

"Affliction" (*vighāta*) is suffering (*dukkha*) because it afflicts both mind and body. "Fever" (*pariḷāha*) is the distress of sensual desire (*kāmadaratha*) because it burns all around. "It does not feel" (*na vedayati*) because [the affliction] does not arise.

It is called "escape" (*nissaraṇa*) because they escape from it. What escapes? Sensual desires (*kāma*). And by taking it thus, the genitive case in the word *kāmānaṃ* (of sensual desires) is very appropriately used in the sense of the agent.
To the same extent that sensual desires are said to have "escaped from" (*nissaṭā*) that [state], to that same extent the jhāna also receives the designation of having "escaped from" sensual desires;
hence it is said, "because of having escaped from sensual desires. Thus, by way of suppression...
Having spoken of the escape from sensual desire, the passage beginning with "But he who... is stated in order to show the absolute escape by way of complete eradication.

"In the remaining sections" means in the remaining portions. However, this distinction—by stating that the phrase "making that jhāna the basis" and so forth constitutes the non-distinction—is entirely untouched in the second and third sections; it is [only] in the fourth section...
However, in order to show that this too is a distinction, it is said: "And here, the fruit of arahantship should be connected with absolute escape.
This is because the mind of one who has made an immaterial jhāna the basis, attained the highest path, and established himself in arahantship, is said to have escaped from all forms entirely.
For when he emerges from the attainment of the fruit and turns his attention toward form for the sake of investigation, [his mind does not enter into it].

The four preceding sections were explained by way of those for whom serenity is the vehicle (*samathayānika*)—for one who directs the mind [with the thought], "This has been declared"—but this [section] is by way of the dry-insight practitioner (*sukkhavipassaka*).
Therefore, he said, "In pure formations," and so forth. Furthermore, "the arising of 'there is no more identity'":
this arises in one who investigates, "Now there is no further continuity of my identity."
Commentary on the Five Bases of Liberation (Vimuttāyatanapañcakavaṇṇanā) 322.
Regarding the phrase "bases of liberation" (*vimuttāyatanāni*): they are the bases, or causes, for liberation from the suffering of the round of existence; thus he says, "the causes of liberation.
"For one who knows the meaning of the text" means: "here virtue has come forth, here concentration..."

“Herein, wisdom,” and so forth, refers to one who knows the meaning of various passages exactly as they are. “One who knows the passage” means one who examines the passage that illuminates that meaning exactly as it is.
“Taruṇapīti” (nascent rapture) refers to a soft rapture that has just arisen. How does it arise?
As one examines the Dhamma as it was taught, one’s own conduct of body, speech, and mind becomes entirely concordant with it.
In one who is grasping [the object] and has attained joy, *pāmojja* (rapture) arises, characterized by gladness.
"Strong rapture" refers to a state of extreme satisfaction resulting from the repeated practice of the previously arisen rapture;
it is capable of becoming a condition for *passaddhi* (tranquility), which is able to allay the disturbances of body and mind and has reached a state of power.
Rapture arises. Because when the mental body has become tranquil, the physical body also becomes tranquil, it is therefore said: "The mental body subsides.

"He attains happiness" means he attains and finds the non-material, mental happiness capable of serving as the condition for the concentration of mind that is about to be described. "He becomes concentrated."

Here, it is not just any concentration that is intended; rather, showing that it is the unsurpassed concentration, he says, "one becomes concentrated by means of the concentration of the fruit of arahantship.
The phrase beginning with "For this" and so forth is an elucidation of how such a person possesses the causal basis for attaining the aforementioned concentration.
Its state as a "basis for liberation" (vimuttāyatana) is due to its being "withdrawn" (osakkituṃ).

To lead [the mind]. "Concentration itself is the sign of concentration" means that concentration, as it appears in the textual tradition of the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna-pāḷi*), is the "sign of concentration" because it serves as the cause for the further arising of the concentration of meditative development (*bhāvanā-samādhi*). Therefore he said, "In the presence of the teacher," and so forth.
"Liberation" refers to Arahantship, considering it to be liberation through the complete subsiding of all defilements. "They bring to maturity" means...

They accomplish and produce. The meaning is that the perception arisen when the knowledge of the contemplation of impermanence (*aniccānupassanā-ñāṇa*) serves as its support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*) is accompanied by that knowledge.
The same method applies to the others as well. Whatever else needs to be said here should be understood according to the method explained in the *Visuddhimagga-saṃvaṇṇanā*.

Commentary on the hexad: 323.
*Attānam adhi* means "internal" (*ajjhattā*). In the context of a compound, the word *adhi* carries the sense of "predominance" (*adhikāra*) and the sense of "occurrence" (*pavatti*).

"Having taken [them], they proceed": those that proceed with reference to or directed toward the self are "internal" (*ajjhatta*). Those that exist within the internal are "internal-adjuncts" (*ajjhattika*);
thus, even among one's own internal things, the eye and so forth are called "internal-adjuncts" because they are contained within.
Now, making clear the sense of that specific internal state by which they are called "internal-adjuncts," he says: "the internal-adjuncts."
He said: But according to the meaning of the words (*saddatthato*), those which are internal and internal (*ajjhattajjhattāni*) alone are "internal-and-internal" (*ajjhattajjhattikāni*);
this is to be understood just as in the case of the term "Vinayika. From that, "from the internal" means from those internal-and-internal ones, which are what were called "internal" (*ajjhattikāni*).
For the counterparts to the internal are the external, just as external phenomena are the counterparts to internal phenomena. "Internal" (*ajjhattikāni*)—
For it is the eye and so forth belonging to one's own and others' continuums that are called "internal," and likewise form and so forth are called "external.
However, only those eye-objects and so forth that belong to one's own continuum are internal; anything other than those is external.

Regarding the phrase "collections of consciousness," although there is no simultaneous convergence (*samodhāna*) of those consciousnesses because they occur at different times, they are nevertheless grouped together by the mind as a single unit.
It is said to be "aggregated" by way of being massed together, as in the expression "the aggregate of feeling" (*vedanākkhandho*).

"Dependent on eye-sensitivity" means that the wholesome, unwholesome, and resultant consciousness which has arisen having obtained its condition by depending on eye-sensitivity is spoken of here as a single unit by virtue of the commonality of being "eye-consciousness.
Contact dependent on the eye is not "belonging to the eye-door. These are the ten types of contact.
These [ten] are set aside as contact-resultants based on confidence. "By this same method" means by the very method stated regarding contact.
Although craving that occurs directed toward craving within the hexad of craving is also to be understood as "craving for phenomena" (*dhamma-taṇhā*).
"Without reliance" (*appaṭissayo*) means "without approval" (*appaṭissavo*); the description is made by changing the letter *va* to *ya*. When something has been said by a teacher...
*Paṭissava* is the act of assenting out of reverence; it is that which constitutes assent, as well as any kind of reverence similar to it.
That in which such assent does not exist is *appaṭissava*, meaning devoid of reverence. Therefore he said, "one who does not live in a lowly manner.
And just as what is done for the sake of a shrine is equivalent to what is done for the Teacher, so too is what is done in front of a shrine equivalent to what is done in front of the Teacher.

"It is exactly like a mat," he said, and so forth, beginning with "But when [the Teacher] has attained final Nibbāna. "He does not go with respect" means that he does not approach having generated reverence and esteem.

Just as when even a single part of the training is violated and disrespect is shown, the entire training becomes corrupted and disrespect is effectively shown toward everything—so too, from the perspective of the whole, the undertaking of restraint is violated through its individual parts.
"Division" means: even in the case of a single bhikkhu... [as before] ...disrespect indeed occurs. Even by mere lack of reverence, there is indeed non-fulfillment of the training;
thus he said, "One who does not fulfill the training is indeed called disrespectful. Right practice is the characteristic of heedfulness.
"Two-fold" means two-fold by way of the Dhamma and material gifts.

"Discursive thoughts accompanied by joy" (*somanassūpavicārā*) refers to discursive thoughts associated with joy; he says "discursive thoughts conjoined with joy" because the prefix *upa-* is merely a particle.
For in the Abhidhamma, the definition is given as: "wandering, discursive thought... [and so on]... discursive investigation.
"That which has become a cause for joy" means that it is a cause for the arising of joy both by its own nature and by way of intention (*saṅkappa*).

[It is] a condition. Granted that the applied thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) of the limited plane (parittabhūmaka) are inseparable from one another, nevertheless, due to their functional distinction, the activity of applied thought is predominant because of its initial application [to the object]. Subsequently, it is the function of sustained thought;
with reference to this, having stated the prior action as "having applied thought" (vitakketvā), it is said, "he delimits [the object] by means of sustained thought."
The activity of sustained thought (*vicāra*) for one who has previously cultivated it is like wisdom (*paññā*). For it is said in the *Peṭaka*: “Sustained thought is the antidote to doubt.

Regarding the phrase “one who has attained similarity of view,” the right view of the first path—by means of which a person is said to have attained similarity of view—is intended here; thus he says, “in the *Kosambaka Sutta*...”

"The first path has been explained. Here (*idha*) means in this sutta. Since right view (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) is included among all four paths by the mention of "view" (*diṭṭhi*), he said, "All four paths have been explained.

325. *Kodhana* means one whose nature is to be angry. Because he does not become one who is "free from anger" due to his failure to abandon anger, it is said that he "is possessed of anger.

It is stated that when a dispute arises, it generally first arises between two people; thus, it says "between two."

Within the inner assembly means within the circle of the assembly.
Even one who acts to smear over the virtues of others is first struck by his own deed, just as the excrement [strikes] the man who strikes another with excrement.

He who has that is *palāsī*. For a person who is *palāsī* does not give way to a second;
he stands having stretched himself out evenly. Therefore it was said: "endowed with *palāsa*, which is characterized by grasping like a yoke."
The meaning of the words beginning with “issukī” is easily understood because it follows the method already explained below.

326. "Having neglected" (hāpetvā) means having allowed a wholesome state of mind to lapse, by way of failing to provide it with the opportunity to arise.

He utters a false declaration, proclaiming a description of qualities not actually existing in himself, such as: "Indeed, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness has been developed by me," and so forth.

Having understood that "now for me there is no ill will (vyāpāda), it does not exist at all," he says, "signless" (animittā).
Then, in order to show by the absence of which signs the attainment of the fruit of Arahantship is signless, he says, "For that...
and so forth. In this context, it refers either to the sign of lust, or lust itself as the sign.
The sign of lust (*rāga-nimitta*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the signs of hatred (*dosa*) and so forth should be understood.
The signs of form, feeling, and other formations are the "sign of form" and so on. Their appearance as permanent and so forth is the "sign of permanence" and so on.
Since this sign does not exist at all in the fruit of Arahantship, it is therefore said: "For that... is called signless (*animittā*)."
"It pursues the sign" means it follows that sign; it proceeds by taking that as its object.
"The conceit 'I am'" (asmimāna) is the conceit directed toward the self that functions as "I am. [It is the thought]:
"I am this very one," characterized by form, or "this very self, I am," characterized by any one among feeling and so forth. Thus, the conceit "I am" is eradicated.

"By this" refers to the eradication of the conceit "I am," which is the path of Arahantship. By stating, "There is no further conceit 'I am,'" he proclaims its state of non-arising and thereby clarifies its very nature as an eradication.
*Commentary on the Sixfold Set of Incomparables* (Anuttariya-chaḷaka-vaṇṇanā)

327. They are called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) because there are no others superior or more distinguished than them; they are "unsurpassables" (*anuttariya*) simply because they are unsurpassed, just as that which is infinite is called "infinitude" (*ānantariya*).
Thus he says: "The 'unsurpassables' are the unsurpassed. "The unsurpassable vision" (*dassanānuttariya*) is so named because it brings about the distinction of the unsurpassed fruit.
This same method applies to the remaining [unsurpassables] as well. "The attainment of the sevenfold noble wealth" refers to the attainment of the sevenfold supramundane wealth beginning with faith.

The fulfillment of the three trainings (*sikkhattayapūraṇa*) is the complete perfection of the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*). Therein, fulfillment should be understood in its ultimate sense (*nippariyāyato*) by way of the Arahants.

For it is from the stage of the "wholesome worldling" (*kalyāṇaputhujjana*) onward that the seven types of trainees (*sekkha*) are said to fulfill the three trainings; however, the Arahant is one whose training is fully perfected. Thus, these...
The unsurpassed states, both mundane and supramundane, have been explained.
Since the recollections (*anussati*) are the causes for welfare and happiness in this present life and in future lives, they are called "bases of recollection" (*anussatiṭṭhāna*).
Thus, "recalling" means that just as the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānussati*) is a basis for the attainment of distinction, so too [is it said]: "In such a way..."

"For one who recollects the Buddha’s qualities" and so forth. "Access meditation subject" (*upacārakammaṭṭhāna*) means a meditation subject that brings access concentration (*upacārajjhāna*) directly;
but by way of succession, it brings mundane and supramundane distinctions all the way up to Arahantship.
Commentary on the Six Constant Abidings:

328. "Constant abidings" means abidings that occur at all times. For, setting aside the moments of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) and the moments of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*), those whose taints are destroyed (*khīṇāsava*) abide at all times precisely through this abiding in the sixfold equanimity. "Having seen a form with the eye" is stated by way of a metaphorical designation for its support (*nissaya-vohāra*).
For this is a discourse concerning the constituent parts (*sasambhāra-kathā*), as in the expression, "he pierces with a bow. Therefore, it is by way of the head of the support...
"One who is dependent must be seen as grasping," thus he said, "having seen with eye-consciousness.

"Not being enamored by what is desirable" means not producing lust for a desirable object because it has been eradicated by the Path. "Neither glad" means not [glad] even by way of affection based on the household life.
"Nor dejected" means not [dejected] even by way of a change in one's serenity. "Without looking on" means [without looking on] toward what is desirable, what is undesirable, or what is neutral.
"In the grasping of an object that is not even, not right, and improper": this refers to the delusion that arises in those whose taints (āsava) are not yet exhausted;
he dwells equanimous and neutral by preventing its arising, because it has been eradicated by the Path itself. He dwells equanimous specifically by means of knowledge and equanimity (ñāṇupekkhā).
And because this is the attainment of the fullness of his practice and the fullness of his wisdom, he says "by mindfulness," and so forth.

"Equanimity with regard to the sixfold base" (*chaḷaṅgupekkhā*) refers to equanimity with six factors occurring at the six sense doors by way of mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*).
Cognitions associated with knowledge (*ñāṇasampayutta-citta*) are obtained, because without them, clear comprehension is impossible.

"Great cognitions" (*mahācittāni*) means that all eight great functional (*kiriya*) cognitions are obtained. "Constant abidings" (*satatavihārā*) refers to even at times when conditions for the arising of knowledge are absent.

"Because their occurrence is distinct. "Ten types of consciousness" means that ten types of consciousness are obtained by adding the eight great functional (*kiriya*) consciousnesses together with the smile-producing and the body-consciousness. Their occurrence is common to them as well, by way of being neither elated nor depressed.
Because of the statement, "He dwells equanimous," these constant dwellings—which have come down through the sixfold equanimity—are [associated with] "joy."
Having challenged [the opponent] by asking, "How is it obtained?", he himself resolves the matter by saying, "It is obtained through repeated practice.
For although one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) dwells frequently with equanimity toward both desirable and undesirable objects—

just as if they were neutral— because he does not abandon his own state of natural purity, nevertheless, at times when there is an absence of such mental volitional formations (cetobhisaṅkhāra), that which is [the feeling] by its very nature...
Regarding a desirable object, even there the mind of an Arahant proceeds accompanied by joy by way of grasping its true nature;
however, this occurs solely through the force of past habituation. Therefore he said: "It is obtained through habituation.
(Commentary on the Sixfold Set of Noble Births)

329. Regarding the term “births” (*abhijātiyo*), the prefix *abhi-* here is merely a grammatical particle and does not indicate a specific meaning; thus he says “births” (*jātiyo*). The same principle applies to the word “is born” (*abhijāyati*).
Furthermore, the word “is born” (*jāyati*) contains an implied sense of its cause; the meaning is “he produces.
As for what ought to be said concerning birth and the kamma that produces it, in terms of their classification as dark and bright: [the text continues...]
This has already been explained above. It is called *nibbāna* because it extinguishes the defilements by means of their subsiding.
If it were black (*kaṇha*), it would be like the tenfold unwholesome action of misconduct; if it were white (*sukka*), it would be like wholesome actions such as giving and virtue.
What is intended here is the fruit of Arahantship, because of the expression "he is born to the higher states" (*abhijāyati*). That—

Because it is born at the end of the extinction of defilements, it is "nibbāna"; because it is born at the end of the destruction of lust and so forth, it is the "destruction of lust," the "destruction of hatred," and the "destruction of delusion.
Commentary on the Sixfold Set Pertaining to Penetration:
"Penetration" (nibbedha) is said to be nibbāna, in the sense of that which is to be penetrated or pierced through by means of the knowledge of the Path.
The meaning is as follows: "In the knowledge of contemplation of cessation" means perception arisen in the knowledge of contemplation of cessation acting as its support-condition (*nissaya-paccaya*);
the meaning is that it is accompanied by that.
The commentary on the hexad is finished.

330. "In the sense of obtaining success" means: in the sense of causing the attainment of successes beginning with the perfection of virtue (*sīlasampatti*) and ending with perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*);
or, the obtaining of successes is "success-attainment" (*sampattipaṭilābha*), and the cause of that is the "sense of success-attainment."
In the sense of the attainment of success. For this very reason, it is said: "Because it is the cause for the attainment of successes.

Faith itself is called the "wealth of faith" (saddhādhana) in the sense that it is to be cherished as wealth by those who desire the welfare of both worlds. "Among these" means among these various kinds of wealth.

It is the most excellent because it is the cause for attaining all [other forms of wealth], and because, by purifying their defilements, it brings about a state of great radiance and great expansion in them.

Therefore he said, "By means of wisdom," and so forth. In this context, "standing by means of wisdom" means that having established themselves in the wisdom of being the owners of their own actions (*kammassakatā-paññā*) and having fulfilled good conduct and the rest, they go to the heavenly realms. Furthermore, standing both in those [perfections] and in wisdom, they penetrate the knowledges of the disciple-perfections (*sāvakapāramiñāṇa*) and so on.

They are called "requisites for concentration" (*samādhiparikkhārā*) because they surround and prepare the concentration; they are right view and the other factors that serve as the equipment for concentration. However, since it is the cooperative causes that are intended here, he said, "the retinue of concentration" (*samādhiparivārā*).

The qualities of the non-existent and the unwholesome are so called because they establish the state of being unwholesome. "Non-existent" means unattractive and censurable; therefore he said, "inferior.

Having stated, "It was spoken for one who possesses insight (vipassaka) alone," the passage beginning with "In those [qualities] too... was said in order to demonstrate the arising of insight for such a person.
For path-wisdom is pre-eminently called "insight" because it sees the four truths with distinction.
It should be said: "The noble one who possesses that [insight] is a practitioner of insight.

"The teachings of true persons" means the teachings belonging only to true persons, not to those who are not true persons. For it is only through practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*dhammānudhammapaṭipatti*) that one attains the state of being a knower of the Dhamma and so forth, not merely by the recitation of the canonical texts.
"Of what has been spoken" refers to what has been spoken in the form of discourses (*sutta*), verses (*geyya*), and so on.
And [it refers] to both that [term] and other terms that clarify one's own welfare and the welfare of others.
One who knows the meaning through skill in the meaning is "one who knows the meaning" (*atthaññū*). "One who knows oneself" means one knows oneself by way of knowing one’s own measure as it truly is.
By means of moderation in receiving and using, moderation in seeking and giving are also implied.
“Regarding receiving and using,” thus it is said; for in this way they become blameless. “For the attainment of yoga” means for one who is devoted to meditation (*bhāvanā*).
“Too narrow” means too small, because it is impossible for one of sharp wisdom to complete [the training] within that much time.
“The eightfold assembly” refers to the eightfold assembly beginning with the assembly of kṣatriyas.

Others say it is eightfold, taking the fourfold assemblies beginning with the assembly of bhikkhus and the fourfold assemblies beginning with the assembly of khattiyas—these being the human assemblies themselves.
"One should associate with that person by associating with whom unwholesome states diminish and wholesome states increase; conversely, one should not associate with the other."

Thus, one who knows the person to be associated with or not associated with is called "one who knows persons" (*puggalaññū*). In this way, he is said to know whether the awakening of those persons is superior or inferior. 331.
Regarding the phrase "bases for the ten-fold [count]": he says "bases for the ten-fold and so forth" because this designation is formed by the elision of the word "etc. (*ādi*).
“Niddaso” means one who no longer has ten [years remaining]; it is a question concerning a matter desired to be known.
The inclusion of the word “kira” (it is said) is to show that the opinion of those [who hold such a view]—namely, that he is not yet ten years old—is merely a mere thought.

Furthermore, the term “niddaso” is used as a mere designation, because, just as his status as a “nibbīsa” (one who has no more [years]) and so forth is intended, his status as a “ninna-vādi” (one who speaks falsely) is also intended.
“Not only this,” and so forth, is what was said. “Wandering in the village” means wandering in the village for alms.
This is not a designation for the followers of other sects (*tīrthika*), because that characteristic is absent among them.

Nor is it a designation even for one in training (*sekha*) within the Dispensation, much less for an ordinary person (*puthujjana*). As for whom it is a designation, and by whom [it is used]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.*

To demonstrate the reason for this, the passage beginning with "of one whose taints are destroyed" (khīṇāsavassa etaṃ) was stated. For the state of being without rebirth-linking is the direct cause for him;
the others, which appear in the Pāḷi, are causes by way of succession.
The "undertaking of the training" (sikkhāsamādāna) is the correct undertaking of the training; and that should be understood as its fulfillment—thus he said.
“Regarding ‘the fulfillment of the three trainings’ (*sikkhattayapūraṇe*): The undertaking of the training (*sikkhāsamādāna*) is the proper guarding of the training from its very beginning;
and this, in terms of meaning, is delimited by fulfillment, because it is entirely absent when there is no guarding, and because it is fully complete when there is guarding.
“Strong desire” (*bahalacchando*) means firm desire. “The future” (*āyati*) refers to the time consisting of the days and so forth that follow immediately.
He said, "not in a future existence," meaning "furthermore, not on future days and so forth.

For one who fulfills the training, the state of being established therein and the absence of departing affection is the thorough contemplation of phenomena according to their impermanence and other characteristics;

thus he said, "this is a designation for insight (vipassanā). Regarding the phrase "in the removal of craving," this is established through the power of the knowledge of insight such as the contemplation of dispassion (virāga-anupassanā).
In the suppression of craving; in the state of seclusion established by the departure from the company of crowds and the company of defilements, which is the state of being alone;

in the exertion of energy, that is, in the uplifting of the energy of the right strivings—which is the complete cultivation of all energy—as it is said: "in the fulfillment of bodily and mental energy"; and in mindfulness as well as in proficiency.
By means of acting with mindfulness and acting with clear comprehension. It is precisely through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension that the arousal of energy succeeds.
"Penetration by view" refers to the penetration of right view. Therefore, he said, "in the seeing of the path.
For when the full penetration of the truths succeeds, the right view of the path is indeed established.
"Knowledge of contemplation of the foul" refers to the knowledge that proceeds by way of contemplating the tenfold or even the elevenfold foul.

This is the knowledge of proficiency in the contemplation of suffering. "Knowledge of contemplation of danger" refers to the knowledge that proceeds by way of contemplating the danger indicated by the impermanence, suffering, and changeability of formations (*saṅkhāra*). "In the sense of not having been abandoned" means...
By virtue of not being severed by the Path. They "lie latent" (anusenti) because they lie down repeatedly within the continuum (santāna).

For when the necessary conditions are obtained, the defilements that are ready to arise become, as it were, lying down repeatedly within the continuum; therefore, they are called "latent dispositions" (anusaya) in that state.
"Firmly established" (thāmagata) means having reached strength. And this reaching of strength is unique to sensual lust and the other [defilements], not shared with others.
The unique intrinsic nature (sabhāva) should be understood [in this way]. For it is stated in the Abhidhamma: "He abandons the latent tendency that has become firmly established.

Thus, sensual lust itself is the latent tendency; it is "the latent tendency of sensual lust" (*kāmarāgānusayo*). As for those who say, "The latent tendency *of* sensual lust is the latent tendency of sensual lust," that is merely their own opinion.
For there is no such thing as a latent tendency of sensual lust that exists apart from sensual lust itself.
If they were to say, "It is its seed," even that is not found in the ultimate sense apart from it.
This same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
[End of] the commentary on the sevenfold summary for settling legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*).

They are called *adhikaraṇāni* because things are brought forward (*adhikarīyanti*) therein. What is it that is brought forward? The means of settlement (*samatha*). How are they brought forward? By way of settling (*samanavasena*).
Therefore, he said, "they settle the legal issues" (*adhikaraṇāni samenti*), and so forth, meaning that they proceed by way of settling those [issues].
"Of those arisen, of those arisen" means of those that have occurred, of those that have emerged. "For the purpose of settling" (*samathatthaṃ*) means for the purpose of pacifying (*samanatthaṃ*).
“By eighteen grounds” is a statement of definition, just as one might say, “If they should give me these diseases, this medicine must be given.
Therefore, those who dispute on account of any one or another of these are said to be “disputing on eighteen grounds.
*Upavadanā* means abuse; *codanā* means formal accusation.
It is called *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence) because it is a settling [of a dispute] right in the presence of the legal assembly (*adhikaraṇa*).
*Yebhuyyasikā* (decision by majority) is the performance of a formal act (*kamma*) by a majority among those who speak according to the Dhamma within an assembled assembly.
Thus, these four aforementioned types of "presence" (*sammukhatā*) are what is known as *sammukhāvinaya*.
“Presence” (*sammukhībhāva*) is by way of the concord of the Saṅgha, not merely the physical presence of the individuals who act as the performers. “Reality” (*bhūtatā*) means suchness.
For here the word *dhamma* is a synonym for truth, as in expressions such as “one who speaks according to the Dhamma” (*dhammavādī*).
It is called *vinaya* because one is disciplined (*vineti*) by it; it refers to the procedure taught by the Blessed One for the settling of various legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), and of that *vinaya*.
“Presence” refers to presence in the Vinaya. Therefore he said, “As it is... presence. “By whom” means by which person.
“Adversaries regarding the matter” refers to those who are opponents concerning the point defined as the basis for dispute.
“Presence in the Saṅgha” is excluded because the settlement is carried out by persons specifically authorized [for that purpose].
Next is the legal issue of dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). It is endowed with five factors as stated in the passage beginning, “He does not act out of favoritism.
Among these, a secret ballot (*guḷhaka-salākaggāha*) should be conducted when the assembly is full of those lacking shame; an open ballot (*vivaṭaka*) when it is full of those possessing shame;
and a whispering in the ear (*sakaṇṇajappaka*) when it is full of fools. That action for which the majority speaks according to the Dhamma is called the decision by majority (*yebhuyyasikā*).
He said: “By the majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma,” and so forth.
“It is settled by means of the four methods of settling” is stated here as a comprehensive summary;

however, in that context, it should be understood that the pacification occurs specifically by means of two [methods] at a time. “Thus it has been adjudicated”: if there is no offense, both parties should ask for forgiveness.

Now, having pointed out the offense, it has been determined by way of its formal announcement. As for the counteraction (*paṭikamma*), however, that will follow later in the section on the settlement of legal issues concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa-samatha*).

"Unbecoming of a recluse" (*assāmaṇaka*) means not in accordance with the conduct of a recluse; it is something not to be done by recluses. "When there is transgression" (*ajjhācāre vītikkame sati*) means when there is an overstepping of proper conduct.
"Concealing" (*paṭicarato*) means to one who is hiding it. "Worse" (*pāpiyo*) refers to a person due to the abundance of evil; [this refers to] the formal act (*kamma*) to be performed against him.

This is a case for a *pāpiyasika* (formal act of censure). There is no settlement by means of *sammukhāvinaya* (settlement in the presence of the accused) because it cannot be settled without a confession or without forbearance.

"In this context" refers to the confession of an offense. *Paṭiññātakaraṇa* is the performance or action of what has been confessed—namely, the verbal act consisting of the words "you should restrain yourself in the future," as well as the proceeding by way of granting probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth. This is called *paṭiññātakaraṇa*.
“According to what is appropriate” means according to the method stated as: “by two kinds of serenity, by four, by three, or by one.
“In this” refers either to this sutta or to this investigation of serenity (*samatha*). “The method of exposition” means merely the framework for exposition.

Therefore he said, “But the detailed account,” and so forth; it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the commentary on the Vinaya, and therefore [it should be understood] precisely according to the method stated there.
"It should be understood"—this is the intended meaning.
The commentary on the section of seven is finished.
And the commentary on the second recitation-section is completed.

**Commentary on the Eights, 333.** *Ayāthāva* means "not according to reality" (*na yāthāvā*). Because it does not lead to liberation, its intrinsic nature is false; because it functions perversely, it is not according to reality. Because it leads to liberation, its intrinsic nature is correct and its functioning is non-perverse.
**334.** *Kusīta* means "one who sinks into what is contemptible"; this is formed by changing the letter *da* to *ta*. By virtue of which phenomenon...
A person is called "lazy" (*kusīta*); here, that state of laziness is expressed by the word *kusīta*.

For even without a word explicitly indicating an abstract state (*bhāva*), the meaning of the state is understood—as in the expression "the whiteness of the cloth. Therefore, the meaning is "the bases for the state of laziness.
Hence he said: "The meaning is 'causes of indolence' (*kosajja*). He spoke thus because such things as these are indeed the work appropriate for a recluse (*samaṇa*).
“Cīvaravicāraṇādī” means “such as the spreading out of robes. “Vīriyaṃ” refers to the energy of striving;
however, because it is performed by way of walking meditation (caṅkama), it may also be described as “bodily,” which is why he said “both kinds. “Pattiyā” means for the purpose of reaching.

“Osīdanaṃ” is shrinking back from the application of cultivation (bhāvanā). “Māsācitaṃ” means accumulated or heaped up over months; he thinks of it as such. Because the months have become distinct through their maturation...
They become heavy; therefore, it was said, "Just as a ripe māsaka bean," and so forth. The intention is that he has emerged from the state of illness.
335. "Of these" refers to the bases for exertion (*ārambhavatthu*). "By this very method" means by the same method stated regarding the bases for laziness (*kusītavatthu*), such as:
"He exerts two kinds of energy," and so on, up to: "This is the first; come now, I shall exert energy."
The meaning should be understood through such passages as: "Thus, the exertion in cultivation is the first basis for undertaking.
For the exertion that occurs first, in whatever manner, becomes the cause for the subsequent undertaking of energy.
Indeed, the eight bases for undertaking should be understood as either the acts of exertion accompanied by appropriate reflection, or the reflections rooted in those acts of exertion.
336. *Āsajja* means that one gives to someone for the sake of their delight, as a sign of meeting them.
Therefore he said: "In this context, *āsādana* (enticement) is indeed the cause for giving. Regarding *bhaya* (fear), it means for the sake of fear. One might ask:

"Is not fear—like lust and other such states—a defiler of volition (*cetanā*) due to the desire to obtain [something]? Why, then, is it included here? It is not of that same nature as the fear of thieves and so forth.

The phrase beginning with “therein” was stated to show that it was spoken with a specific intention (*sandhāya*). “He gave to me” refers to that which is given after reflecting upon a past favor rendered.
“He will give to me” refers to that which is given out of a desire for a reciprocal favor.
“Giving is good” means that giving is a practice established by the wise, and thus it is a virtuous conduct.
He gives while standing. "For the sake of adornment" means for the sake of beautification. "For the sake of equipment" means for the sake of requisites.
For when one has given a gift and reflects upon it, joy, rapture, gladness, and so forth arise, while greed, hatred, envy, stinginess, and so forth are kept at a distance.
Now, by means of giving, there is the nourishment of favorable states and the removal of adverse states.
And because it serves both as an adornment and as an accessory for the mind of cultivation (*bhāvanācitta*), it is said:
"He gives for the sake of adornment and for the sake of retinue. Therefore he said: "For giving makes the mind supple," and so forth.

Having received [a gift], one becomes supple-minded, thinking, "This person has shown me favor," and the giver likewise [becomes so] toward the recipient. Hence it is said: "It makes the minds of both supple."
"Subduing the unsubdued": through giving, those who are unsubdued and disobedient become subdued and obedient, and they come under one's control. "Non-giving is the destroyer of the subdued":
moreover, non-giving corrupts the mind by producing distress even for those who were previously subdued and obedient.
"The givers rise up," and those who speak kindly [rise up] because they are objects of respect and honor for others. "The recipients bow down."
Those who gather others through generosity and pleasant speech are the gatherers.
The gift of the adornment of the mind alone is supreme because it is undefiled, perfectly pure, and a condition for the excellence of virtues.
337. "By reason of giving" means by way of the cause of giving; the meaning is: because merit consisting of giving has been performed and accumulated. "Rebirths" means...
"Rebirths among humans and devas. "He establishes" means that without arising even once more, he establishes it so that it proceeds in that very same manner higher and higher.
And since that itself is his resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), he says, "it is a synonym for that.
"He increases" means he causes it to grow; he does not diminish it. "Liberated" means intent upon it; the meaning is that it is inclined toward, slanting toward, and leaning toward it.

"Released" (*vimutta*) means "distinguished" (*visiṭṭha*). In the non-figurative sense, "higher" (*uttari*) means "excellent" (*paṇīta*), because even in the middle [of the scale], there is the possibility of distinguishing between the inferior and the middling;
thus it is said: "not developed further" means "not developed beyond that for the sake of the higher paths and fruits.
The mind consisting of giving, directed in such a way, leads [to that result]. As for what is stated in the text beginning with "But that," etc.:

This should be understood as being primarily intended to show the absence of misconduct that acts as an obstacle to rebirth there, and not as being solely intended to show that merit consisting of giving alone leads to such a rebirth.
"Of one whose lust is utterly eradicated" means one whose sensual lust (*kāmarāga*) has been completely cut off; for it is possible for such a person to be reborn in the Brahma-world, but not...

For one whose passion for existence has been utterly severed. And here, by the term "free from passion" (vītarāga), what is intended is freedom from passion regarding sense-pleasures—that state by which rebirth in the Brahma-world may occur.
Therefore he said, "By giving alone," and so forth. If this is so, one might ask: what is the purpose of giving there?

To this he replied, "But as for giving," and so forth. "With a mind softened by giving" means that even toward a hostile person with whom one harbors resentment, one's mind becomes softened by the acceptance of one's gift.
A *parisā* is so called because it sits around (*parisīdati*) and gathers from here and there; it is a multitude.
"Worldly phenomena" (*lokadhammā*) are those phenomena that necessarily occur for the world of beings (*sattaloka*). Therefore he said: "There is no one who is free from these," and so forth.
Because those worldly phenomena sometimes pursue the world and sometimes the world pursues them, respectively, therefore [the text] says here:

Demonstrating this meaning, he cited the sutta passage: "These eight. "Gain" (*lābha*) is the acquisition of food, clothing, and so forth, or those very things themselves because they are to be acquired.
The absence of that is "loss" (*alābha*). Here, by the mention of gain, attachment (*anurodha*) directed toward its objects is included;
by the mention of loss, aversion (*virodha*) is included. For when there is blood, as with pus, there is attachment due to the injury caused by it.
When there is a contradiction, it has already found its opportunity; therefore it was said: "When gain has arrived, loss has also arrived.
This same principle applies to fame and the rest as well.
The commentary on the eight [qualities] is finished.
Commentary on the Ninefold [List] 340.
That in which a fruit dwells, because it proceeds by having that as its cause, is called the "basis" (*vatthu*), meaning the "cause" (*kāraṇa*).
Therefore he said: "The bases of resentment (*āghātavatthūni*) are the causes of resentment. This anger arises in relation to a certain basis.
It does not arise there only once, but rather arises again and again; thus it is said, "it binds.

Alternatively, regarding that resentment which, arising through a particular condition, does not disappear from its own object as if bound, but would surely arise yet again—it is with reference to this that he says, "he binds resentment. Furthermore, by way of its conditions...
"Arising" (nibbattana) is simply "producing" (uppādana); thus it is said, "he does, he produces. Regarding the phrase "How could that be found here?":
here, *taṃ* is a reference to the action (*kiriyā*), and the meaning should be understood through the elision of words (*padajjhāhārena*).
Showing this, he says, "Let that practice of doing harm not be," and so forth. For what reason is it to be obtained? Because of its being purposeless (*niratthaka-bhāvato*).
For beings are masters of their own karma; by whose will, then, would they become afflicted with suffering or happy?

Therefore, the intention is that it is merely my own anger toward him. Alternatively, how could such a cause for anger be found in this person from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramattha*), since there is an absence of both one who should be angered and one who is angry? For this is merely a conditioned formation (*saṅkhāra*).
That is to say, this pentad of aggregates. That which is called a "being" consists of these formations (*saṅkhārā*) that are of short duration and momentary;
the meaning is: who can be angry with whom? What indeed could be gains, apart from non-attainment? 341.

Beings dwell within these, thus they are "abodes of beings" (*sattāvāsā*). The "diverse bodies and diverse perceptions" refers to the various classes of beings distinguished by such categories as the first [of the four meditative attainments].

Because those various classes of beings deserve to be described as the support for the beings included within them—precisely by virtue of being so included—just as a branch is described as the support for its parts because it is the support for the whole (e.g., "the branch on the tree"), therefore it is said: "They are the abodes of beings;
the meaning is 'places of dwelling. Even the Pure Abodes (*suddhāvāsa*) are indeed an abode of beings; [it is not that]...
“Monks, such an abode of beings is easily found, which has not been previously inhabited by me during this long period of time, except for the Suddhāvāsa devas”—because of this statement.
If one asks, "If that is so, why is it not included here?", the reason is stated as "because it does not exist at all times," and so forth.
It should be understood, however, that the Vehapphala realm belongs exclusively to the fourth abode of beings.

342. *Upasamika* means that which brings about the subsiding of the suffering of the round (*vaṭṭadukkha*). That suffering of the round, moreover, subsides when the defilements (*kilesa*) have subsided, and not otherwise;
therefore it is said to be "the maker of the subsiding of the defilements. It leads to full enlightenment (*sambodha*), thus it is "leading to enlightenment" (*sambodhagāmī*).

Regarding the phrase "or the state of non-perception or the formless state": he says this because among those classes of gods where the teaching of the Dhamma is not applicable—due to the very absence of hearing—the "long-lived class of gods" is intended in the Canon.

343. "To be dwelt in successive order" means successive dwellings (*anupubbavihārā*). "In successive sequence" means by way of gradual progression. "Dwellings to be attained" means those dwellings which, having been attained, one should dwell in while being possessed of them.
344. "Successive cessations" means cessations to be brought about gradually and by way of sequence. Therefore he said: "cessations in successive sequence.
The commentary on the section on the new is finished.
345. Regarding the commentary on the *Dasaka*:

Those virtues such as morality (*sīla*) etc., endowed with which a bhikkhu—by virtue of taking refuge in the Dhamma—is called a "protector" (*nātha*) because he protects, rules, and overcomes by means of the Dhamma alone;
those qualities that produce his state of being a protector are thus called "the qualities that constitute a protector" (*nāthakaraṇā*).

He said: “The states that provide a protector... [and so on] ...are the states that provide a foundation. Therein, “providing a foundation for oneself” means they establish one’s own foundation for that which makes them a protector.
One who lacks a foundation is without a protector; one who possesses a foundation has a protector. Thus, the meaning of “protector” (*nātha*) is the meaning of “foundation” (*patiṭṭha*).

Showing that they are “excellent” because of their association with beautiful qualities, he said: “endowed with the qualities of virtue and so forth. Their characteristic is to be free from defilement (*mijjana*).

"One who has friends (*mitta*) is a *mitta*; since he possesses what is called 'noble' (*kalyāṇa*) in the manner already described, the mere fact of his possessing that is expressed by the term 'good friend' (*kalyāṇamitta*).
To show that he dwells with them at all times without ever being separated from them, it was said "having noble companions" (*kalyāṇasahāya*); thus he says, "Those very ones for him," and so forth.
"Those very ones for him" means those very good friends of this bhikkhu. "Because of going together" (*saha-ayanato*).
Because he conducts himself together with others. When there is no meeting of minds, he is compliant; but when there is a meeting of minds, he is compliant both in mind and in body.

One whose speech is pleasant toward a person who is receptive, conformable, and possessed of respect and reverence is "easily spoken to" (*suvaco*). Therefore, it is said: "he can be addressed with ease," and so forth.
"Patient" (*khamo*) means one who endures; in order to demonstrate that very quality of his patience, it is said: "even by harsh [words]," and so forth.
"Vāmato" means wrongly or improperly; "gaṇhāti" means he grasps. "Paṭippharati" means he stands as an obstacle.
"Padakkhiṇaṃ gaṇhāti" means he grasps rightly or properly.
"Uccāvacāni" means large and small. "Tatrupagamanīyā" means leading to this or that, whether large or small.
The meaning is: "approaching by means of the performance of various actions," that is, being capable of accomplishing each respective action.
Alternatively, *tatrupāyāya* means "being the means for the accomplishment of this or that action.

Regarding the term *dhammakāmo*, it is formed as a *bahubbīhi* compound with an external referent (*bāhirattha*), on the principle that a compound may have an external referent even when its members are in different grammatical cases (e.g., *dharme asya kāmaḥ* = "one whose desire is for the Dhamma").
It has been said. Or, because it is to be desired (*kāmetabba*) or loved (*piyāyitabba*), it is *kāma*; [the word] *dhamma* [is added]. Thus, one for whom *dhamma* is *kāma* is a *dhammakāma*.
Since by "dhamma" the *pariyatti-dhamma* (the doctrine as scripture) is intended, he says: "The meaning is that he loves the Buddha-word consisting of the Three Piṭakas.
*Samudāharaṇa* means speaking or utterance (*samudāhāra*). One for whom utterance is dear is a *piyasamudāhāra*. And "himself" (*sayañca*)...
And here, by the word "ca" (and), the term "sakkaccaṃ" (carefully) is drawn forward; thus the construction is: "he himself desires to teach carefully.

It is called *Abhidhamma* because it is the *pariyatti-dhamma* (the Dhamma as formal teaching) that is superior (*adhika*) and more distinguished (*abhivisiṭṭha*) than the seven treatises (*sattappakaraṇa*).
It is called *Vinaya* because the two *Vibhaṅgas* discipline (*vinayana*) both body and speech. *Abhivinaya* refers to the *Khandhaka* and *Parivāra*.

Specifically, this is because of the praise of the qualities of higher conduct (*ābhisamācārika-dhamma*). Indeed, through the fulfillment of the qualities of higher conduct alone, there is the fulfillment of the qualities pertaining to the beginning of the holy life (*ādibrahmacariyaka-dhamma*). "Dhamma" refers to both Piṭakas because they constitute the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyatti-dhamma*). The Path and Fruition are "Abhidhamma," considering that they are directed toward (*abhimukha*) the Dhamma of Nibbāna.
The three trainings belonging to the prior stage, which are the causes for the subsiding of the defilements, are, in brief, dependent on turning away (*vivaṭṭa-nissita*).
“Calm and insight. “Abundant gladness” means powerful gladness. “In the sense of a cause” means in the sense of a sign;
for the exertion of energy has the wholesome states as its sign. Therefore he said, “for the sake of attaining them.
Alternatively, “in regard to wholesome states” is a locative used in the sense of what is to be accomplished, just as in the expression “for the non-tranquility of the mind.”
“Having its proximate cause in improper attention.
(346) “In the sense of being complete” means in the sense of being without remainder; here, the sense of completeness should be understood by way of pervading everything without exception.
The meaning is that it should be grasped in its entirety, not remaining in only one part, as is the case with the sign of foulness and so forth. Of those things having that as their object...
"Of states" means of those states that arise taking that kasiṇa as their object.
"In the sense of a field" means in the sense of a place of origin. "In the sense of a basis" means by way of being a place of occurrence.

Just as a field is the place of origin and the place of growth for crops, so too this jhāna is the cause for the states associated with it, or for the specific types of happiness for the practitioner.
“Having delimited”: this should also be connected with the words “above and below.
For it is only after delimiting that the kasiṇa should be expanded in every direction. “By this or that reason”: by this or that reason for expanding the kasiṇa above and so forth.
To the question “How? he says: “Just as one desiring to see forms [would look] at light. Just as, with the divine eye, one [sees] a form above...

If one wishes to see above, one extends the light upwards; if downwards, one extends it downwards; and if one wishes to see forms all around, one extends the light all around. This is the meaning of "this [is] the kasiṇa.

"Of each" means of each one among the earth-kasiṇa and the others. "For the purpose of not reaching the state of being something else" means for the purpose of demonstrating that it does not reach the state of being another kasiṇa.

Or rather, it is for the purpose of showing that they do not attain the state of being another *kasiṇa*; for a *kasiṇa* extended by one person does not attain the state of being a *kasiṇa* extended by another.
In this way, too, their lack of confusion with other *kasiṇas* should be understood.

It is not "another," such as earth and so forth; for in a place situated in water, there is no earth together with its constituent parts (*sasambhāra-pathavī*). This is what is meant by "confusion with another *kasiṇa*."
There is a confusion with the water-kasiṇa and others. "In all places" means in all the remaining kasiṇas.

It is called "immeasurable" because it does not remain in one place but pervades everything without remainder, due to the non-grasping of a limit. For that very reason they have the designation "kasiṇa. Thus he said, "For that," and so forth.
"Pervading with the mind" means making the object of the mind through the mind of meditation (*bhāvanā-citta*). For the mind of meditation makes the kasiṇa its limited object.
Or he brings it to mind either extensively or as a whole, not just a single part.
The consciousness that occurs in the space cleared by the kasiṇa is called the "consciousness-kasiṇa" by way of its pervasiveness and immeasurability.
For it is likewise called "consciousness-only" (viññāṇañcāyatana). "By way of the kasiṇa" means by way of the kasiṇa as it has been removed.
The upward, downward, and horizontal extent [of the space] should be understood as that which is revealed by the removal of the kasiṇa.
For whatever area the kasiṇa was spread over becomes space through the practice of developing space;
thus, because consciousness proceeds by way of its arrival, pervading the entire extent of that area which has appeared as space, the same applies to the consciousness-kasiṇa.

Because [the directions] above, below, and across have been mentioned, he said: "The state of being above, below, and across should be understood with respect to the consciousness occurring therein by way of the space resulting from the removal of the kasiṇa.
347. Commentary on the Tenfold Unwholesome Course of Action:

Because they are the means for its occurrence and because they constitute the path, it is said "because they are the path. Regarding "in sexual misconduct": this refers to both contentment with one's own wife and going to the wives of others.
Regarding the two kinds of sexual misconduct: these too are called "sensual pleasures" (kāmā) because they are objects of desire.
"In the bases for sexual intercourse" means among those beings who are the bases for sexual intercourse. "Sexual misconduct" (micchācāra) is reprehensible conduct;

and its being reprehensible is due precisely to its absolute baseness, which is why he says, "it is a contemptible and base form of conduct. "With the intention of unrighteousness" (asaddhamma) means with the intention of indulging in what is not the true Dhamma.
"Protected by her family" means protected by her clan. "Protected by those of the same Dhamma" means protected by fellow practitioners of the Dhamma. "Having a husband" means she has protection.
"Subject to punishment" refers to one for whose sexual intercourse the king has established a penalty.

"Bought with wealth" means purchased with money for the sake of being a wife. "Living by her own will" means living according to her own desire. "Living for the sake of wealth" means living for the sake of enjoyments. "For the sake of a garment" [means...].

A woman living [with her family] is a *paṭavāsinī*. One who has been taken after touching the water-bowl is an *odapattakinī*. One who has been taken after removing the head-covering is an *obhatacumbaṭā*.
One brought as a captive is a *dhajāhaṭā*. One for a moment is a *taṅkhaṇikā*. Sexual misconduct committed by overcoming [the other's resistance] is a great offense;
it is not so [grave] when there is a common desire between the two. "In the case of overcoming [the other's resistance]..."

They say that even though one endures the practice of what is not the path while on the path, there is no wrong conduct for one who is being overcome, because of the absence of the prior arising of the intention and application for indulgence.

However, when the mind of indulgence is present, the absence of application is no criterion, since for the most part a woman lacks the application for indulgence. When that [application] is absent, even if the mind of indulgence had been established previously...
In that case, there would be no sexual misconduct; likewise for a man, because of the absence of the actual application of service.
Therefore, with reference to that which occurs by one’s own inclination, there are three [types], and with reference to that which occurs by force, there are three;
thus, including all of them by taking what has not yet been mentioned, it is said: "the four constituent factors."
Root-words (*dhātu*) express specific meanings by means of prefixes (*upasagga*); thus, for the word "abhijjhāyati," the meaning is stated as "directed toward another's goods," and so forth.
In this context, the intended sense should be understood as "the state of being inclined" (*ninnatā*) toward that other's goods by way of coveting them.
Alternatively, the root *jhā*, preceded by the prefix *abhi*, should be regarded as conventionally established (*nirūḷha*) in the sense of coveting. This is by means of the prefix.
Root-words (*dhātu-sadda*) indeed express specific meanings. Since the slight or great blameworthiness of taking what is not given has been explained in the *Brahmajāla-vannaṇā*, he says:
“Like taking what is not given, [theft] is slightly blameworthy or greatly blameworthy. Therefore, [it is said]:
“It is slightly blameworthy when one covets the property of one who possesses few virtues, and greatly blameworthy when [one covets the property of] one who possesses great virtues,” and so forth.
The distinction between what is slightly blameworthy and what is greatly blameworthy should be understood. It should be understood that one’s own dedication [of merit] occurs through the mind alone.

"He destroys welfare and happiness" means that whoever gives rise to such a thought, toward whomever he directs it, he destroys the welfare and happiness of each and every person when they are assembled together.
Regarding the slight and great blameworthiness of harsh speech, this is explained in the *Brahmajāla-vannanā*.
