It is said, “vibhāvitā,” meaning “by harsh speech,” and so forth. Therefore, the distinction between these two should be understood as follows:
“When one harbors ill will toward someone, it is less blameworthy if that person has few virtues, and more blameworthy if they have great virtues,” and so on.
By the phrase “aho vata,” he illustrates the thought of another’s utter destruction; for it is through such a cruel manifestation that the course of action (kamma-patha) comes to be.
"By way of the absence of apprehension according to reality" means by way of the absence of apprehension as it truly is;
that is, by apprehending the intrinsic nature of impermanence and so forth as permanent and so on. "Views falsely" means one sees what is untrue.

By the phrase "like frivolous chatter," he shows that when the habituation is weak, the fault is slight, whereas when it is great, the fault is grave. "The state of being contrary to the mode apprehended."
The state of being contrary to the mode apprehended by wrong view. "Of the object" refers to its nature as it is not actually.
"By way of that state" means precisely by the mode apprehended, which is the contrary mode. Its manifestation to that proponent of a view, or to that object, is thus:
"This is exactly so; it is not otherwise than this."

“By way of nature” means by way of intrinsic essence (*sabhāva*). “By way of factors” means those which are factors among the constituent parts of consciousness, such as the group beginning with contact as the fifth; that is the meaning. “Having volition as their nature” means having the intrinsic nature of volition.
Regarding the phrase “seven in succession,” one might ask:
is it not the case that volition is not mentioned in the Abhidhamma among the courses of kamma? [The answer is: It is indeed mentioned in the sequence.
Is it not the case that the status of these seven as courses of action (*kamma-patha*) is illogical? No; for their non-inclusion is due to other causes.
It is not because volition (*cetanā*) therein fails to reach the state of a course of action that they are not mentioned in the category of courses of action.

Rather, they are not mentioned because the status of being a course of action is indeterminate—meaning that while at times it is a course of action, it is not so at all times. However, when it does become a course of action...
In that case, the inclusion of the category of kamma-paths would not be precluded.

Here it is asked: if the status of being a kamma-path is indeterminate because volition (cetanā) is not always present as a kamma-path, and thus its status as a kamma-path is not fixed, then surely covetousness (abhijjhā) and the rest would also not be mentioned in the category of kamma-paths, since they exist even when they have not attained the status of a kamma-path.
Does it not follow that because their status as courses of action (*kammapatha*) is indeterminate, they too should not be mentioned in the collection of courses of action? It does not follow;
for they are included there because they share the same nature as being courses of action. If this is so, should volition (*cetanā*) also be mentioned there?
This is true; however, since volition consists of killing and so forth, its status as a course of action is already evident, and thus it is not [explicitly] stated.

It might be said as follows: For the status of volition as "kamma" is evident from such statements as, "Bhikkhus, I say that volition is kamma; bhikkhus, the threefold bodily volition is unwholesome bodily kamma.

And it is evident that kamma itself, proceeding as the path for both happy and miserable destinations, as well as for the pleasure and pain arising therein, is called a "course of action" (kammapatha).
Its status as a course of action (*kammappatha*) is not as evident in that way;

however, covetousness and the rest possess the nature of good and bad conduct by virtue of being the striving of volition (*cetanā*), and they possess the status of being paths for the arising of happy and miserable rebirths, and of happiness and suffering, by virtue of being produced by volition (or rather, by virtue of their connection to what is produced by volition).
Therefore, in order to show them by means of that very intrinsic nature, [the text says]: *...* (The remainder of the passage follows).
In the Abhidhamma, volition (*cetanā*) is not stated to be a course of action (*kamma-patha*);

or rather, it should be understood that volition is not mentioned alongside them because it does not belong to that same class. "Having reached the root" means having reached the teaching on the roots; the sense is: when the phenomena whose intrinsic nature is that of roots are being taught.
The statement "taking what is not given has sentient beings as its object" is [found] in this passage from the *Pañhapucchaka-pāḷi*: "The five training rules have only limited objects."
It is not contradictory. For that which is the object of unwholesome conduct such as the destruction of life is itself the object of the abstinence from it;
for abstinence (*virati*) is defined precisely by way of the thing to be transgressed. Alternatively, "having beings as its object" means having the formations known as "beings" as its object;
since this is stated with reference to those very formations, there is no contradiction whatsoever. Thus it is said in the *Sammohavinodanī*: "Those..."

Regarding the training rules (sikkhāpada) stated here as "having beings as their object" (sattārammaṇa): because they take as their object only those formations (saṅkhāra) that are designated by the term "being" (satta), this is the method [to be applied] to the subsequent ones as well.
Some say they have beings as their object because the dissimilar object (visabhāgavatthu)—namely, "woman" or "man"—is to be apprehended.
[The training rule against] idle chatter (samphappalāpa) is so called because of the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing expressed in such phrases as "one was seen, two were heard," and so forth.
In the phrase "covetousness for such [things]," the word *tathā* (such) connects back to all three—seen, heard, and cognized by mind—as well as what is known;
it does not refer merely to the state of having sentient beings as its object, because covetousness occurs by way of seeing and so forth.

Furthermore, even when the wrong view "there are no spontaneously born beings" arises, its object is still phenomena belonging to the three planes of existence; this is the intended meaning regarding its having formations (*saṅkhāra*) as its object.
...have been stated. But how is it that all phenomena of the three planes (*tribhūmaka-dhammā*) become the object (*ārammaṇa*) of wrong view (*micchā-diṭṭhi*)? By way of commonality.
When [the view] occurs as "There is no fruit or result of well-done or ill-done deeds," by its actual meaning, even the phenomena of the fine-material and immaterial spheres are indeed included.
Because of their abundance of pleasure, kings say "Kill him! even while laughing; yet for them, this laughter is directed toward another object, such as the pacification of their own self.
It is said: “He is one who brings [the matter] to a conclusion... [etc.]”. There is no neutral feeling (*majjhatta-vedanā*);

only pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is possible here. False speech arising from greed may be accompanied by either pleasant or neutral feeling, while that arising from hatred is accompanied by painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*);
thus, false speech is associated with three types of feeling. By this method, the classification of feelings in the remaining cases should also be understood as appropriate.
The phrase "by way of two roots" is stated with reference specifically to the associated root [of greed] by way of hatred and delusion;

for it is in the sense of being a root that it possesses the quality of being an assistant. However, if the "root as cause" (nidānamūla) were intended, one would have to say "also by way of greed and delusion.

For people kill living beings even for the sake of material gain or a trifle. Thus he said: "Greed is the cause for the arising of kamma," and so forth. The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
Commentary on the Tenfold Path of Wholesome Action:
From “the taking of life” ... [as far as] they should be understood. Herein, the wholesome paths of action are taught by way of a mixture of the mundane and the supramundane.
Because it is the cause of enmity, the evil state consisting of the taking of life and so forth is designated as “enmity. [The text says: “While standing here, I [ward off] that enmity...”
"Veramaṇī" means she drives him away as if reproaching him, saying, "How can you come?

Or, although it should be called "viramaṇī" in the sense that one desists by means of it, it is stated as "veramaṇī" according to the rules of philology (*nirutti*). Abstinence arising through formal undertaking is "abstinence by undertaking.
Abstinence from transgressing an object as it has presented itself, for one who has not undertaken the precepts but has attained them, is "abstinence by attainment."
Abandonment-by-cutting-off (*samuccheda-virati*) is the abstinence associated with the Path that operates by way of the total eradication of the defilements (*kilesa*).
Although in this context only abstinence is mentioned in the Canon, in the analysis of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-vibhaṅga*), volition (*cetanā*) is also brought forward and shown;

therefore, taking both of these together, he said: "Both volitions and abstentions occur. For non-covetousness, having reached its root, [is included] in the section on the courses of action (*kammapatha*).
Regarding the phrase "non-covetousness" (*anabhijjhā*), the meaning here should be understood as follows: the state described is, by its root, the wholesome root of non-greed (*alobha*).
The same method applies to the other two terms as well.

[Objection: How can those [wholesome states] which have misconduct (*dussīlya*) as their object, or have that [misconduct] as their object, or have the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) and so forth as their object, abandon misconduct? To this [it is said]:...

To show this, the passage beginning with "But how" was stated. It should be understood that they "abandon" [the defilements] because they proceed precisely by way of abstaining from killing living beings and so forth.
Now, if it were to have those [defilements] as its object, it would not abandon them;
for it is not possible to abandon something by taking that very thing as its object, since it is not dissociated from it.

“Non-covetousness” … “of one who abstains”: the meaning is, of one who abandons covetousness. For there is no separate abstention from mental misconduct, since its abandonment is accomplished by non-covetousness and the other factors themselves.
348. Commentary on the Ten Noble Abodes (*ariyavāsadasaka*):
“Abodes only of the noble ones” means they are the *ariyavāsā*; for such [abodes] are impossible for those who are not noble. And here, “noble ones” (*ariya*) refers to—
By way of an inclusive description, those whose taints are exhausted (khīṇāsavā) are included; and since they dwell there at all times without ever being separated from it, it is said:
"The Noble Ones (ariyā) alone have dwelt, do dwell, and will dwell [there]. In that context, "have dwelt" means they dwelt in dependence upon it.

For the Noble Ones' supports consist in such qualities as the abandoning of the five factors and so forth. Among these, there are the abandoning of the five factors, the removal of individual truths, the relinquishing of quests, and the casting off of acquisitions.

Regarding the "modes of non-perception" mentioned as "having scrutinized, one pursues, endures, avoids, or dispels," both the dispelling and the others are accomplished by the path alone; the dispelling is indeed the function of the path.

"Knowledge and so forth" refers to both knowledge itself and the states associated with it. Therefore he said, "When 'knowledge' is stated," and so on. What should be said regarding this has already been stated below.

He accomplishes the duty of protection because he has attained fullness of mindfulness. By the words "while walking," etc., he shows constant undertaking; that should be understood as being due to the absence of distraction.
"Those who have gone forth" refers to anyone who has entered the life of a wanderer, not necessarily those whose evil is stilled (*samitapāpa*).

"Those who address others as 'bho'" refers to brahmins by birth alone. "Separate truths" means those things individually grasped by various proponents of views, each thinking, "This alone is the truth."
The views and truths, etc., are firmly adhered to. For even the "positions of view" (*diṭṭhigata*) are designated as "truths" by virtue of being grasped with the thought, "This alone is the truth.
Therefore he said, "This alone," and so forth. "Extracted" means they have been drawn out from one's own continuum and removed.
"Of the grasping already held" refers to the adherence to views held prior to the attainment of the Noble Path.
"Synonyms for the state of being relinquished" means they are designations for the state of total abandonment by means of the Noble Path.

Because there is no deficiency (*vekaḷya*) in their passing away (*vaya*), they are called "unfailing" (*anūnā*); the meaning is "without remainder. "Searches" refers to the search for sensual pleasures and so forth mentioned below.
The accomplishment of the function of the Path is stated because it demonstrates the state of having abandoned lust and the other defilements.
"The fruit is spoken of by way of reviewing" means that the noble fruit is spoken of by way of its reviewing.
For when the supreme fruit has been attained, one understands the state of the absolute non-arising of lust and the other defilements; and that understanding is the knowledge of reviewing.
*Commentary on the Set of Ten Factors of the Asekha*
"Phalasampayuttadhammā" means both the fruit and the states associated with it; the meaning is "states associated with the noble fruit.
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as "the fruit-dhammas themselves and the states associated with them.
In both instances, it is wisdom (paññā) that is spoken of, in the sense of right seeing (*sammā dassana*). It is called "right view" (*sammā-diṭṭhi*) because it is right seeing.
And it is called "right knowledge" in the sense of knowing correctly. For there is indeed a distinction in the mode of occurrence within their respective domains between seeing and knowing;

this has already been shown above. "Phala-samāpatti-dhammā" means the states (dhammas) in the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti); the meaning is "states accompanied by the attainment of fruition.
Indeed, even the states associated with the noble fruits (ariyaphala) are termed "liberation" (vimutti) because they are entirely liberated from their opposites.
They deserve to be so designated. However, just as the wisdom of the fruit of the Asekhas is called "right view" with reference to its function of seeing,
and is also called "right knowledge" with reference to its function of knowing,
so too the noble fruition-concentration is called "right concentration" with reference to its sense of being undertaken, and "right liberation" with reference to its sense of liberation.
Thus it has been said. And by doing so, the inclusion of the second liberation as "the taintless liberation of mind" (anāsavaṃ cetovimutti) is also justified.
The commentary on the Tenfold Set is finished.
The commentary on the Compendium of Questions.
"Should be brought together" means they should be collected. "Conviction" (okappanā) is strong faith.

"Chanting together" (saṅgīti) is the communal recitation of the meanings taught by the Blessed One here and there for the sake of ensuring that there will be no disputes among the bhikkhus in the future;
and the reason for this is that this teaching of the Sutta proceeded in such a manner.

It is said: "The method of the Saṅgīti is the cause of concord. The Teacher was pleased, saying, "Let it occur to you, Sāriputta, to give a Dhamma talk to the bhikkhus," and he listened from the beginning to the end, having encouraged him;
however, the Blessed One’s approval there was made manifest by his expression of appreciation, "Excellent, excellent!"
It is said: "He gave his approval by means of rejoicing. Thus it became what is called 'spoken by the Victor' (jinabhāsita), not 'spoken by a disciple' (sāvakabhāsita).

For just as a document written by royal officials does not attain the designation 'royal edict' until it has been stamped with the royal seal, but once it has been so stamped it is indeed called a royal edict; even so, "Excellent, excellent... [is the case].
Because this discourse has been marked with the seal of the Conqueror’s word— consisting of the approval (*samanuññā*) signaled by the words of appreciation beginning with “Sāriputta”—
it is known as ‘spoken by the Conqueror’ (*jinabhāsita*) and is a direct utterance (*āhacca-vacana*).
As for that which is not analyzed here according to its meaning, it is indeed easy to understand.
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning of the *Saṅgītisutta-vaṇṇanā*.
11. The Commentary on the *Dasuttarasutta*. 350.
"Friend, O monks"—this is a mode of address used for calling out to disciples; it is a conventional form of address employed for the purpose of addressing disciples.
It is not merely "O bhikkhus"; rather, that is an address to the Buddhas. Therefore he said, "For the Buddhas," and so forth.

By way of the Teacher’s customary mode of address, this very lack of formal address here constitutes placing him in a position of high honor. Because they have arrived at that moment, they have no fixed residence anywhere;
thus they are "those of unsettled residence" (anibaddhavāsā), namely, the resident pupils (antevāsikā). Having taken up their meditation subjects, they are seeking out suitable lodgings.
"Those that go to whatever direction" means *disāgamanīyā*. Now, in order to demonstrate this matter in detail, the passage beginning with "At the time of a Buddha" was stated.
"The meditation subject of foulness" refers to the elevenfold meditation subject of foulness (*asubhakammaṭṭhāna*).

Even therein, having understood the differences between individuals, he gives only what is suitable for each person. Although the meditation subject of mindfulness of breathing (*ānāpānassatikammaṭṭhāna*) is indeed [suitable] for one of deluded temperament (*mohacarita*),...

However, in order to make one a fit vessel for the development of the meditation subject and to remove delusion, one should first be engaged in recitation, interrogation, listening to the Dhamma, and discussion of the Dhamma; thus it is said: "For one of deluded temperament... he explains...
For one of faithful temperament, the first six recollections are especially suitable; of these, however—
In order to show that "practicing" refers to the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipatti*), it was said: "in the inspiring discourses (*pasādanīya-suttanta*)," and so forth.

For one of intellectual temperament (*ñāṇacarita*), that is, one of intellectual character (*buddhicarita*), mindfulness of death (*maraṇassati*), mindfulness of peace (*upasamānussati*), the analysis of the four elements (*catudhātuvavatthāna*), and the perception of the repulsiveness of food (*āhāre paṭikūlasaññā*) are especially suitable;
and in order to demonstrate the qualities that assist these, [it says]: "impermanence, etc.…pe…"
"It speaks," it is said. "Right there" means in the very presence of the Teacher. "The practice to be completed in three months" refers to the path that is to be finalized within three months.
"These monks" refers to the monks who were the fit vessels for this teaching of the Dhamma. "Having come in this manner, they depart..."

However, the phrase "but the bhikkhus" refers to those bhikkhus mentioned by way of designation in the passage beginning with "at the time of the Buddha," and not to the bhikkhus mentioned immediately following as "these bhikkhus.
Therefore, he said, "he sends. "Apaloketha" means "ask for permission.
"The wise," and so forth, are statements giving the reasons for their service and devotion. "He leads them to the fruit of stream-entry," and so forth.

This was stated by way of the majority. For the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, having generally led the bhikkhus to the fruit of stream-entry, would dismiss them, saying, "Thus these are fixed with enlightenment as their destination.
But the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, thinking, "Every rebirth in existence is to be loathed," generally leads the bhikkhus to the supreme goal itself.

“Those who are to be disciplined by disciples” (*sāvakaveneyyā*) means those who can be disciplined by disciples; he says “those who are to be disciplined by disciples,” etc., to show that they are not to be disciplined by disciples alone.

Having established the matrix (*mātikā*) tenfold—meaning having established the matrix ten times each, starting from the single unit up to the ten-unit set—it is called the *Dasuttara* (The Tenfold Increase). It is also called *Dasuttara* because it has reached the state of being tenfold.
It is called *dasuttara* because it proceeds by increasing by ten, starting from the single unit up to the decade.
"In each section" (*ekakasmiṃ pabbe*) means in each of the ten sections, starting from the single unit up to the decade.
"Ten questions each" refers to ten questions each, beginning with: "Which state is most helpful? Vigilance regarding wholesome states," and so forth.
"Questions": "Distinguished" means answered. "I shall proclaim the Dasuttara" is a formal undertaking (*paṭijānāti*) by way of naming the teaching being taught, for the purpose of praising it.
"I shall proclaim" means I shall speak in various ways (*pakārehi*).
For herein, the teaching proceeds by way of five hundred and fifty questions. "Dhamma": here the word *dhamma* is a synonym for the *pariyatti* (the scriptures).
“In such passages as ‘here a bhikkhu masters the Dhamma,’ this Dhamma is characterized by the suttas; therefore he says, ‘Dhamma means a sutta.
This Dhamma brings about Nibbāna for one who practices according to the instruction.
For that very reason, it leads to the cutting off of the suffering of the round of existence (vaṭṭadukkha). And this is its power: [the cessation] of all the aggregates...”
Showing that it is the means for liberation, he said, “for the attainment of Nibbāna,” and so forth. By this, it is stated: “for the attainment of Nibbāna,” etc.
“Making high” means making it exalted, sublime, and excellent, showing it; the meaning is “exerting.
“Generating affection” means producing devotion. And this exertion in teaching is indeed the established custom even of the Buddhas.
Showing this, he said, "The sole way," and so forth.
Regarding the commentary on the single dhamma:

(Ka) The word *kāra* expresses the sense of "assistance" even without the prefix *upa*, as in such passages as, "Bhikkhus, parents are of great assistance (*bahukārā*) to their children. Therefore, he said, "'Of great assistance' means of much assistance (*bahūpakāro*)."

(Kha) When "increasing" (*vaḍḍhana*) is mentioned, the production (*uppādana*) of that which is not subject to immediate retribution is already implied; thus it is said, "it should be developed (*bhāvetabbo*)" means "it should be increased.
For increase is preceded by production. But is it not the case that production is also separately grasped here in the statement, "one dharma is to be produced"?
There is no contradiction, because that [production] has a different scope. For instance: "One dharma... [and so forth].

Having stated that [the object] is "to be fully understood" (*pariññeyya*) by means of all three kinds of full understanding (*pariññā*), it is further stated that "one thing is to be abandoned" (*pahātabba*). (Ga) "By the three kinds of full understanding" refers to the full understanding of knowing (*ñāta-pariññā*), the full understanding of scrutinizing (*tīraṇa-pariññā*), and the full understanding of abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*).

(Gha) "By the contemplation of abandoning" (*pahānānupassanāya*) refers to the contemplation that proceeds by way of abandoning; and this mention of "contemplation" (*anupassanā*) should be understood as referring to them in combination.
(Ṅa) It brings about the decline of the perfection of virtue and so forth; it conduces to falling away.
(Ca) It leads to specific distinctions such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), thus it is "leading to distinction" (*visesagāmī*).
(Cha) It is difficult to realize directly (*duppaccakkhakaro*); it cannot be made manifest by those who have not accumulated the equipment of knowledge (*ñāṇasambhāra*).
"Should be recognized" means it should be known directly by means of knowledge.
"In all cases in the Matrices" means in all the matrices (mātikā) stated by way of dyads and so forth.
And here, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, having directed those bhikkhus toward meditation and desiring to establish them in the supreme goal, first [addressed] meditation...
Showing the quality of being helpful by way of enumeration, he said, "One thing is very helpful.
Then, showing what ought to be accomplished by that which is helpful, he said, "One thing is to be developed.

And since this development is intended by way of insight (vipassanā), he said, "One thing is to be fully understood. Furthermore, full understanding is for the sole purpose of abandoning that which is to be abandoned.

He said: "One thing is to be abandoned. And since one who abandons must first eliminate that which leads to decline (*hānabhāgiya*) and then remain established in that which leads to distinction (*visesabhāgiya*), he said: "One thing leads to decline; one thing leads to distinction.

Furthermore, remaining established in that which leads to distinction occurs through the penetration of what is difficult to penetrate; and if the penetration of what is difficult to penetrate succeeds, the accomplishment of what is to be accomplished is achieved.
"It is indeed already accomplished," he said: "One thing is difficult to penetrate; one thing is to be produced.
Since this dyad occurs through the knowledge of what is to be directly known (*abhiññeyya*) and so forth, he said: "One thing is to be directly known.
And when that which is to be directly known has been directly known, that which is to be realized has indeed been realized. To this extent, one's task is finished; there is nothing further for him.
"Something to be done"—thus, first of all, the Great Elder, pointing out the method of practice for those bhikkhus individually, recited these ten terms in this sequence.
(Ka) Having thus recited the teachings without specific restriction, he now shows them by defining their specific nature, beginning with: "What is the one thing? and so forth.
He began the teaching. Therefore it was said: “Thus the Venerable Sāriputta,” and so forth. This same method applies to the pairs (dukas) and so on. “Veḷukāra” means a bamboo-worker;
for he is called a “veḷukāra” because he works with bamboo products such as making mats and the like.
Having made them “niggaṇṭhi” by removing all internal and external knots. “In each single section” means in each one of the ten sections, beginning with the ones (ekakas).
“Beneficial in all respects” (*sabbatthaka*) means being truly helpful for right practice in every situation.
Now, in order to demonstrate this meaning in detail, the passage beginning with “For this... is stated.

“Causing it to take conception in insight” (*vipassanā-gabbhaṃ gaṇhāpana*) refers to the development of preliminary insight in such a way that, becoming sharp and clear, the subsequent insight matures and joins with the Path.
"In the analytical knowledges of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), etc. means in those things to be accomplished, such as the analytical knowledge of meaning;

the sense is "the gathering of their requisites. This same method applies to the subsequent cases as well. "In the right and wrong places" means in what is to be known as the right place (*ṭhāna*) and the wrong place (*aṭṭhāna*).

"In the great abiding and attainment" means in the great attainment of the abidings such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). "In insight-knowledge (*vipassanāñāṇa*), etc."—by the word "etc.," mind-made psychic power (*manomayiddhi*) is included.
It includes the first [verses]. "In the eight branches of knowledge" (*vijjā*) means according to the method presented in the Ambaṭṭha Sutta, regarding the eight branches of knowledge.
The construction is: "For that very reason, the Blessed One praises. "That" refers to heedfulness (*appamāda*).
"By one endowed with fortitude" means by one possessed of the power of wisdom (*ñāṇabala*). "Having illustrated" means: "In this way too, heedfulness [is the root] of wholesome states..."

Having declared, "He is of great assistance in the accomplishment [of this task]," the phrase "whatever" and so forth was stated to show that it is appropriate to speak by including whatever matter belongs to the side of the blameless within heedfulness (*appamāda*).
(Kha) *Kāyagatāsati* is a designation without shortening [the vowel]; or rather, this compound word should be understood according to its grammatical analysis (*niddesa*).
“Bones heaped together, three years old... [and so on] ...putrid, reduced to powder”—attention occurring in this way is called “attention to powder.
Others, however, say: “Attention occurring in the various postures (iriyāpatha) as if they were powdered.
Here, “with mindfulness arisen” means with mindfulness arisen in regard to these twenty-nine aforementioned bases.

“Associated with pleasure” means, in the direct sense (*nippariyāyato*), associated with pleasure; but in the figurative sense (*pariyāyato*), even equanimity (*upekkhā*) in the fourth jhāna receives the designation “pleasure” because its intrinsic nature is peaceful.
(Ga) The object, such as the visible form and so forth, which serves as a condition, also drips defilements (*āsava*) through its state as an object, just like a sore.

Thus, even in the absence of an actual conjunction, it is "with taints" (*sāsava*) because it exists together with the taints (*āsava*). Likewise, it is "subject to clinging" (*upādāniya*) because it leads to clinging (*upādāna*).
Otherwise, however, the positive and negative formulations are by way of its being a condition.
(Gha) "The conceit 'I am'" (*asmimāna*) means the conceit that occurs as "I am."
(Ca) "By way of reversal" means the initial application of attention that proceeds according to the method beginning with "the impermanent as impermanent.
(Cha) Here, however, the path immediately following insight is intended by the term "immediate mental concentration" (*ānantariko cetosamādhi*). Why?
Because it follows immediately after insight, or because it yields its fruit immediately after its own occurrence. [This is] from the standpoint of the literal meaning of the words.
But "immediate" (*ānantarika*) means: the fruit is immediate; it is connected to that which is immediate, or it deserves that [immediacy], or its function is immediate—thus it is "immediate.
(Ja) "Fruit" (*phala*) refers to the wisdom of fruition (*phalapaññā*); the wisdom of reviewing (*paccavekkhaṇapaññā*) is intended here because its object is unshakable (*akuppārammaṇatāya*).
(Jha) It brings its own fruit, thus it is a "nutriment" (*āhāra*); it is a condition (*paccaya*), as he said: "subsisting through nutriment means subsisting through conditions."
"This one dhamma": he speaks by treating as "one" that which is designated as a condition, using the conventional term "conditionality.
"By means of direct knowledge consisting in full understanding through knowledge": by means of the direct knowledge known as *ñātapariññā*. "Unshakable deliverance of mind":

this refers to the deliverance of the fruit of Arahatship, because it has reached the pinnacle through its unshakable nature. Otherwise, all attainments of fruition (*phalasamāpatti*) are indeed unshakable, because they cannot be disturbed by opposing factors.
"By direct knowledge" (*abhiññāya*) means by one who has obtained direct knowledge (*abhiññeyya*). "By full understanding" (*pariññāya*): here too the method is the same.
"By what is to be abandoned and what is to be realized" (*pahātabba-sacchikātabbehi*): this refers to the words "what is to be abandoned" and "what is to be realized.

Only full understanding (*pariññā*) is mentioned because abandoning and realization function together with full understanding, as they constitute a single occasion. "To be realized" (*sacchikātabbo*) is used specifically [in this context].
The fruit has been explained. It is obtained at the very seventh step alone.

However, the fruit is also obtained at many steps, because it is obtained at the first, eighth, ninth, and tenth. Since that [fruit] is obtained at the tenth alone in the direct sense (*nippariyāyato*), while in the other cases it is obtained only in the indirect sense (*pariyāyato*), he speaks with reservation, saying, "it is indeed obtained."

"Existing by way of intrinsic nature" (*sabhāvato vijjamānā*) means that they are apprehended in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*) by way of that very intrinsic nature—such as being "of great benefit"—by which they were taught.
"According to reality" (*yāthāva*) means non-erroneous. "Of such an intrinsic nature" (*tathāsabhāvā*) means having that same intrinsic nature.

"They do not exist otherwise than thus" means that because they are not false (*avitathattā*), they exist exactly as they are. For this very reason, "they do not exist differently from the manner described," is expressed by all five terms.
He speaks of those phenomena exactly as they truly are, according to the method of "it is so. Furthermore, whatever is known is necessarily endowed with cause and endowed with reason;
thus he says, "by way of cause and reason. He generated conviction—that is, he produced deep confidence—by means of the fact that these are the words of the Conqueror.
The commentary on the single dhamma is finished.
Commentary on the two dhammas: 352.
(Ka) The term "in all places" (*sabbattha*) should be connected with the phrase "in the fulfillment of virtue and so forth. [Regarding the phrase] "In the fulfillment of virtue and so forth..."

By the statement, "They are helpful everywhere, just like heedfulness," it is shown that mindfulness (*sati*) and clear comprehension (*sampajañña*) are helpful in all instances, just like heedfulness (*appamāda*), because they are not significantly different from it in meaning.
For heedfulness is non-separation from mindfulness; and in meaning, that is simply mindfulness never abandoned in any situation, provided it is associated with knowledge (*ñāṇa*).
They are to be seen [as such], because the other [type] lacks such capacity.
(Kha) They are called "preliminary" because they were taught by way of the preliminary practice (*pubbabhāga-paṭipatti*) of those approximately five hundred bhikkhus.
(Cha) Unwise attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*) functions as the cause (*hetu*) in its capacity as the root cause of defilement; in its capacity as that which causes growth...
The condition is that which has come into play. The same method applies to wise attention (*yonisomanasikāra*) as well.

Just as unwise attention and wise attention—which serve as conditions for the defilement and purification of beings respectively—were brought forward and stated in the passage, "These two things are difficult to penetrate," so too, showing that these [other] states should be brought forward and stated in the same way, he said "In the same manner" and so forth.
In this context, the four meditations on the foul and so forth are called "disconnections" because they are the opposites of the yoke of sensual desire and the other yokes.
By the phrase "thus divided," one should understand that it includes such categories as "states belonging to ignorance, states belonging to true knowledge, dark states, and bright states."

(Jha) Because they are made by coming together and combining through conditions, the five aggregates are the conditioned element (*saṅkhata-dhātu*). Because it is not constructed by anything whatsoever, Nibbāna is the unconditioned element (*asaṅkhata-dhātu*).

(Ña) The three knowledges (*tisso vijjā*) are "knowledge" (*vijjā*) in the sense of seeing and in the sense of making known. "Liberation" (*vimutti*) refers to the fruit of Arhatship, because it is liberated in every respect from its opposites. "Higher knowledge, etc. (*abhiññādīni*) refers to higher knowledge, wisdom, and so forth.
These should be explained by way of analysis, as they are similar to the single [factors] in the previous section.
Regarding the phrase "the path has been explained," one should not take the meaning to be "only the path has been explained," but rather "the path has indeed been explained.
This is because the fruit is already included by the expression "knowledge of non-arising" (*anuppāde ñāṇaṃ*).

Similarly, regarding the statement "the fruit has been explained in the section on what is to be realized," one should not take it to mean "only the fruit has been explained," but rather "the fruit has indeed been explained."
The meaning should be understood by means of the mention of "knowledge" (vijjā), since other [factors] are included therein. This same method applies to subsequent instances of this kind as well.
The commentary on the two factors is finished.
The commentary on the three factors.

353. (Cha) *Sotī* refers to the path of non-returning (*anāgāmimagga*). It is so called because it completely transcends the sense-sphere desires (*kāma*) by abandoning them through total eradication.

The path of Arahantship in the formless realm (*arūpa*) is the supreme path that arises having taken a formless jhāna as its basis. "Because of preventing further rebirth" means because it entirely prevents the arising of [rebirth in] the form realms.
It is "cessation" (*nirodha*) because conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*) cease by means of it; thus, it is the supreme path.
Therefore, when the round of defilements (*kilesavaṭṭa*) has been ceased, the other two rounds are also necessarily ceased.
Because that cessation is the ultimate end, the fruit of Arhatship (*aggaphala*) receives the designation "cessation" (*nirodha*); thus he said, "The fruit of Arhatship is intended by 'cessation'.
For, "when Nibbāna is seen through the fruit of Arhatship"—this refers to [seeing it] by means of the path of Arhatship.

This was said because it is the production of the vision of Nibbāna. And by taking it thus, this statement as well—“because it is a condition for cessation, which is designated as Arahatta”—is justified.
(Ja) "The past has an object" means that knowledge has the past section as its object; [namely,] the past aggregates, bases, and elements.
The meaning is "knowledge that proceeds by taking [the path] as its object. The phrase "the path has been declared" should be understood as a definitive statement;
likewise, "the fruit has indeed been declared as that which is to be realized.

(Ña) Furthermore, "knowledge of the destruction of the taints" (āsavānaṃ khaye ñāṇaṃ) intends "knowledge at the moment of the destruction of the taints"; otherwise, it would be the path that had been declared.
The commentary on the three things is finished. Commentary on the four things: 354.

(Ka) A wheel made of wood is a "wooden wheel" (*dārucakka*); likewise for a "jewel wheel" (*ratanacakka*). In the sense of being an authoritative command, the Dhamma itself is the "Dhamma-wheel" (*dhammacakka*). Because of the successive progression from one posture to another, it is the "posture wheel" (*iriyāpathacakka*); likewise, it should be understood as the "wheel of success" (*sampatticakka*).
"In a suitable place" means in a location appropriate for performing meritorious deeds and consistent with right practice. "Attendance" means approaching from time to time.

"Frequenting" means honoring with devotion. "Establishing oneself rightly" refers to the wise establishment of one's own mental continuum by settling it in faith and the other [wholesome qualities]; thus he says, "If," and so forth. This alone is the point here.

“Measure” (*pamāṇa*) refers here to this very wheel of success (*sampatticakka*), which consists of merit performed in the past; among these wheels of success, it is the measure because it serves as the cause for the others.
Therefore he said, “By which,” and so forth. And that same person who has performed merit establishes himself rightly, because one who has not performed merit lacks that quality.
The first is merely mundane (*lokiya*), and even there, it belongs specifically to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*).
"Herein" means in this *Dasuttara Sutta*. "Worldly in the prior stage" means they are indeed worldly, occurring in the stage prior to the Path.
The reason for this has already been stated.

Furthermore, they should be understood by way of the paths of non-returning and so forth: disjunction from the yoke of sensual desire is the path of non-returning; disjunction from the yoke of views is the path of stream-entry; and the other two are the path of Arahantship.
(Cha) "One who has attained the first jhāna" refers to one who has acquired the first jhāna that is not yet fully mastered.

"Perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire assail him" means that as soon as he has emerged from it, perceptions and mental applications associated with sensual desire assail and torment him by way of their object.
For him, there are perceptions and mental applications that leap toward sensual desires.
By means of that [state], the concentration of the first jhāna declines and falls away; therefore, it is called "concentration partaking of decline" (*hānabhāgiyo samādhi*).
"Conformity with that" (*tadanudhammatā*) means having a nature corresponding to that. The statement "mindfulness becomes established" is said with reference to wrong mindfulness (*micchāsati*).
For one whose nature conforms to the first jhāna, having seen the first jhāna as peaceful and sublime...
While relishing, looking forward to, and delighting in it, attachment arises. By way of that attachment, that first jhāna concentration neither decreases nor increases;
it becomes a factor of stability. Therefore it is said: "concentration partaking of stability.
"Accompanied by non-thinking" means that for one who attends to the second jhāna, which is without thinking, as peaceful and sublime, [the concentration] occurs by way of its object.
Perceptions and acts of attention accompanied by non-thinking. "Occur" means they urge and incite one who has emerged from the familiar first jhāna for the sake of attaining the second jhāna;

by way of those perceptions and acts of attention that leap into the second jhāna above it, that concentration of the first jhāna serves as the proximate cause for the arising of the second jhāna, which is its specific excellence.

It is called "concentration partaking of distinction. "Accompanied by disenchantment" means that it is accompanied by insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which is termed "disenchantment," in one who has emerged from that very first jhāna after attaining it.
For insight-knowledge becomes disenchanted and weary when the factors of jhāna appear in their various distinctions; therefore, it is called "disenchantment. "Occurring" means...
They urge and incite for the purpose of realizing Nibbāna. "Associated with dispassion" means associated with Nibbāna, which is designated as "dispassion.
For insight-knowledge is called "associated with dispassion" because it proceeds with the thought, "Nibbāna, which is dispassion, can be realized by means of this path";
the perception and attention concomitant with that [knowledge] are also associated with dispassion.

Indeed, it is so. By way of those perceptions and acts of attention, that first-jhāna concentration is called "concentration partaking of penetration" (*nibbedhabhāgiyo samādhi*) because it serves as the proximate cause for the penetration of the Noble Path. "All attainments" refers to all the attainments beginning with the second jhāna.
"The meaning should be understood": first of all, the meaning of those [categories] such as "partaking of decline" (*hānabhāgiya*) and so forth should be understood in detail.
The Path has been explained because of the extraction of the four Noble Truths. The Fruit has been explained in its own form.
The commentary on the four dhammas is finished.
The commentary on the five dhammas.
355. (Kha) In the phrase “five-factored right concentration,” wisdom is indicated by way of being a factor of concentration;
for he analyzes that very same [wisdom] through the statement regarding the pervasion of rapture (*pīti*) and so forth. Therefore, he says: “It arises pervading rapture,” and so on.

The pervasion of rapture and bliss should be understood according to the method beginning with: “He drenches this very body with the rapture and bliss born of seclusion. This is by way of showing the distinction between states with lust and states free from lust, and so forth.
"Pervading the minds of others. Regarding "pervasion by light": when there is the pervasion of the light of the *kasiṇa*, it refers to the region pervaded by that very light.
Because that concentration is a condition for the seeing of forms, the knowledge of reviewing is the "reviewing-sign" (*paccavekkhaṇa-nimitta*).
"Pervasion by rapture" and "pervasion by happiness" are called "feet" because they arise from the production of the fourth jhāna while remaining established upon the object.
Thus it is said. The pervasion of the mind and the pervasion of light are said to be "like the hands" because they accomplish their respective functions.
The jhāna that is the basis for direct knowledge (abhiññā) is said to be "like the middle body" because it constitutes the very substance of concentration.
The sign of review (paccavekkhaṇa-nimitta) is said to be "like the head" because it is the supreme limb.
Because of the complete disappearance of the burning distress of the defilements, the happiness of worldly concentration is said here to be preeminent;
thus it is stated: "It is pleasant in the present because it is pleasant at every moment of absorption.
By means of each preceding stage, each succeeding one attains a state that is more peaceful and more sublime through the power of prior cultivation.
He said: “Each preceding one... [etc. ...has a pleasant result.

Regarding “due to the subsiding of the defilements”: because it is obtained through the subsiding (*paṭippassambhana*) of the defilements. Regarding “the state of the subsiding of the defilements”: the state of the subsiding of the defilements.
Because it is obtained, because it is attained, because it has reached that state. [This refers to] mundane concentration (*lokiya-samādhi*).
Adverse factors such as the hindrances and attachment to the first jhāna must be suppressed, or other defilements must be restrained;
however, because all defilements have been stilled in this concentration of arahantship, there is nothing to be suppressed or restrained.

Furthermore, because it is attained without effort immediately after the path and at the moment of attainment, and because it has been established so that there is no falling away, [it remains stable].
Or, because it has been established, it is not like a dammed-up water that restrains conditioned formations (*saṅkhāra*).
By the phrase "because of having attained fullness of mindfulness," he shows that even when mindfulness is not currently active, one is still called "mindful" due to the abundance of mindfulness.

By the phrase "by way of the time delimited," he shows that one is mindful by means of the mindfulness that delimits [the object]. Regarding the remaining factors of knowledge (*ñāṇaṅga*): "one possessing five knowledges" is stated here by way of the concentration (*samādhi*) mentioned therein.
The five kinds of knowledge have been both indicated and explained.

The Path has been described under the heading of the faculties, because right effort and the others are included therein. The Fruit has been described, because the aggregates of virtue and so forth pertaining to those beyond training (asekkha) have been explained.
The commentary on the five factors is concluded.
Commentary on the Sixfold Dhamma: 356.
Regarding the statement "the Path has been explained," what is to be said here has already been stated above.
Commentary on the Sevenfold Dhamma.

357. (Ña) By way of cause (*hetunā*): by such reasons as "because it has a beginning and an end," "because it is not ultimate," "because it is temporary," and "because it is the negation of permanence.

By way of method (*nayena*): "Just as these formations are now, so too in the past and in the future they are impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to destruction, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, and subject to cessation"—thus [one contemplates] regarding the past and the future.
By means of the guidance of the eye. Granted that for one whose taints are destroyed, the impermanence and other characteristics of all formations have been well seen and well penetrated;

however, [the author] says, "they are well seen by insight-knowledge," showing that this occurs through the function of non-delusion, whereas in the case of insight, it occurs by way of making them the object.
The fever that arises by way of the defilements has its basis in sensual objects (*vatthukāma*).
And it is said, "The support for sensual objects," and thus: "Both are like a pit of glowing embers in the sense that they are accompanied by feverish distress.
"Of one who is inclined" (*ninnasseva*) means "of the state of being inclined. "Internal" (*anto*) is said in the sense of being base; it refers to craving.

"Byantībhūtaṃ" means "that which has become free from its end" (*vigatantaṃ bhūtaṃ*); thus he says, "become free from excess" (*niratibhūtaṃ*), [or according to the commentary, "become fixed" (*niyatibhūtaṃ*)].
"Free from craving" is the meaning. Here, in this group of seven, the path is described because the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga) have been mentioned.
The commentary on the first recitation section is finished.
Commentary on the Eight Qualities 358.

(Ka) *Ādibrahmacariyikāya*: that which is the very beginning of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) is "pertaining to the beginning of the holy life" (*ādibrahmacariyikā*), just as "the discipline itself is disciplinary" (*venayika*).
Of that pertaining to the beginning of the holy life. But what is it? He says: "by means of wisdom. Of that which is comprised within the three trainings.
[This refers to] that which is comprised within the three trainings, beginning with the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).

"Accompanied by access concentration" means that it is precisely the wisdom of tender serenity (*samatha*) that, proceeding by way of the contemplation of rise and fall, becomes the wisdom of tender insight (*vipassanā*);

[thus, it is called] "the wisdom of tender serenity and insight" [in the Commentary]. "Being the first" means being the initial constituent part; this is stated from the perspective of the teaching (*desanā*). At the time of its arising...
However, there is no beginning, middle, or end to the factors of the path because they are comprised within a single moment of consciousness and arise all at once.

"Affection" (*pema*) means firm devotion; since that which occurs by way of endearment is similar to what is based on household life, it is called "affection based on household life" (*gehasita-pema*).
Because it functions through the mode of honoring, it is said: "that to which the mind is weighty."
"Respectful mind" (*garucitta*); its state is "the state of a respectful mind" (*garucittabhāva*), which means showing reverence toward those who are venerable.
Having stated that "defilements do not arise," he provides the reason for this by saying, "one receives instruction and admonition.

For indeed, when one receives instruction and admonition in the presence of teachers and practices according to what has been taught, defilements do not arise. Therefore, he says "therefore," and so forth.
(Cha) "Petas" refers to those with great psychic power (*mahiddhika*). "Asuras" refers to the gods and asuras (*devāsura*).

Since the petas and asuras are indeed just petas, their inclusion among the petas is established even without being explicitly stated. By saying "they go to the invitation," he shows the reason for including the asuras among the petas through the medium of shared enjoyment and association.

"Of one with few desires" means of one who is without desire. Here, the word *appa* has the sense of "absence," as in expressions such as *appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapā* ("free from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and so forth").

One who has few desires regarding requisites (*paccaya-appiccha*) is one who is devoid of longing for the requisites of robes and the like. One who has few desires regarding attainment (*adhigama-appiccha*) is one who is devoid of longing for the manifestation of attainments such as the jhānas.
One who has few desires regarding learning (*pariyatti-appiccha*) is [one who is devoid of longing] for the manifestation of great erudition within the scriptures.

"Free from desire. "One who has few desires regarding the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga)" means one who has few desires among the ascetic practices, being free from longing through the discernment of those practices.

"By concealing existing virtues" means by the hiding or covering up of the qualities found within oneself, such as the qualities of meditative absorption (jhāna) and so forth, as well as the quality of great learning and the quality of the ascetic practices. "Is accomplished" means it is brought about, perfected, or achieved. No.

"Of one with great desire" means of one endowed with a great longing; or, for one whose desire is great, success does not come about because they do not even desire the practice in accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhamma*).
"Secluded" means secluded in various ways. Therefore he said: "secluded by way of the seclusion of body, mind, and requisites."

By the phrase “by way of the eight bases for exertion,” it is shown that here “physical seclusion” (kāyaviveka) is intended in the sense of being unified through application to meditation, and not merely the absence of social company. “Kamma” means the work of yoga.
“Saṅgaṇikā” is the gathering together or association with beings and defilements; that which has this as its resort (ārāma) in the sense of being something to be resorted to is [saṅgaṇikārāma].
He delights in company; therefore he said, "and by means of socializing with groups," and so forth.

"Of one who has aroused energy" means of one whose energy is exerted, and that specifically by way of being inclined toward seclusion from the substrates (upadhiviveka), as expressed by the words "this is the Dhamma. This same method applies to what follows as well.

For here, concentration (samādhāna) is intended precisely as that which is dependent on turning away (vivaṭṭa); the same is true for wisdom (paññā). By means of the wisdom of self-agency (kammassakatā-paññā)...

Indeed, one who understands that "through the power of karma there is manifold harm in various states of existence" while not yet established [in the path], aspires for the knowledge that brings about the destruction of karma and exerts effort toward that end.
As for the term *papañca*, it is said that pride and the other [defilements] are called *papañca* because they cause the continuum of beings to proliferate (*papañcenti*) and expand within saṃsāra;
thus he says, "of one free from *papañca* means of one who is devoid of the *papañcas* of pride, craving, and views."
The path has been explained according to its own nature. 359.
(Kha) "Purification" (*visuddhi*) refers to purification of knowledge and vision (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*), or indeed absolute purification. "Fourfold purification of virtue" (*catupārisuddhisīla*)...
Virtue possesses fourfold purity because it is untainted by such things as the restraint of the *pātimokkha*.

The "factor of striving for purity" (*pārisuddhipadhāniyaṅga*) is a factor that constitutes the primary effort for the individual's purification; thus he said, "the primary factor for the state of purity.
The state of purification of serenity (*samatha*) is its cleansing (*vodāna*), which is delimited by its proficiency; therefore he said, "the eight attainments of proficiency."
For that which is free from defilements deserves to be called "proficient," whereas that which possesses defilements does not, because it falls into states such as those conducive to decline.

Purification of view is the discernment of name-and-form through the purification from the stains of the seven views. Purification by overcoming doubt is the discernment of conditions through the destruction of the stain of doubt regarding the three periods of time.
Since name-and-form is indeed possessed of conditions, therefore, by one who discerns it...
Since its state of being conditioned is also grasped by way of its meaning, it is said: "Purification of view is the seeing of mentality-materiality together with its conditions.

However, because for one who grasps the condition of mentality-materiality, this occurs precisely through the penetration of the stain of doubt regarding the three periods of time by means of the realization of the mode of conditions, it is called "knowledge of the mode of conditions," and so forth.
As it was stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī-Visuddhi*: "It is called 'knowledge of the stability of phenomena' (*dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa*).
"Knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path" refers to the knowledge established after having discerned what is the path and what is not the path.

Here, "knowledge" refers to nascent insight (*taruṇavipassanā*), spoken of as "purification by knowledge and vision" (*ñāṇadassanavisuddhi*) according to the inclination of those bhikkhus, because it is being described as the insight leading to emergence (*vuṭṭhānagāminī vipassanā*).
If "purification by knowledge and vision" is intended to mean insight leading to emergence, and "wisdom" refers to the wisdom of the fruit of Arahantship, then how is the path included?
The path is included by the mention of "dispassion" in the phrase "of great benefit. For it will be said:
"Here, the path is explained in the phrase 'of great benefit.'"
(Cha) "The diversity of the elements such as the eye" means based on the differentiation of the elements such as the eye, visible forms, and eye-consciousness.
"The diversity of eye-contact and so forth" refers to the classification of contacts such as eye-contact, ear-contact, and nose-contact.

Regarding "the diversity of perception," here the diversity of perceptions such as the perception of visible forms is indeed included; however, that is already covered by the mention of "perceptions of sensual desire" and so forth.
It is grasped. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "perceptions of sensual desire, etc.," there is the inclusion of perceptions of ill-will and so forth.

Because conceptual proliferation (*papañca*) has perception as its source, it is said: "In dependence on the diversity of perceptions, there is the diversity of intentions" (*saṅkappa*). And because of the statement, "Whatever one intends, that one proliferates," it is said:
"In dependence on the diversity of intentions, there is the diversity of desires" (*chanda*). And as for "the diversity of desires":
The diversity of craving and desire (*taṇhāchanda*). "Fever for forms" (*rūpapariḷāha*) refers to the fever of defilement that arises by way of longing for forms, having form as its object.
"Fever for sounds" (*saddapariḷāha*): here too the same principle applies.
For when a defilement arises, even though the object has not yet been reached, it arises as a fever as if it had already been reached. And by way of such a feverish desire for defilements—
"There is a quest for form and so forth," he said; thus, "due to the diversity of the feverish burning, there arises a diversity of quests for form and so forth.
For one who quests in such a manner, if that form and so forth should be obtained, with reference to that he said:
"due to the diversity of the quest and so forth, there arises a diversity of the acquisition of form and so forth."
"Knowledge of contemplation of death" (*maraṇānupassanāñāṇa*) means knowledge that occurs by way of contemplating death; the meaning is "wisdom accompanied by the recollection of death.
"Of one who comprehends nutriment" means of one who comprehends nutriment as repulsive by way of its departure and so forth.
"Of one who becomes weary" means of one who is disenchanted and does not cling to anything whatsoever.
Commentary on the Ten Dhammas 360.
(Jha) "Causes of wearing away" (*nijjarakāraṇāni*) means causes of abandoning. Since the Path is being discussed in this section on direct knowledge (*abhiññāpada*), it is stated:
"This [Path] was mentioned below... and is taken up again. For he will say: "In this section on direct knowledge..."
Although it was stated that "wrong view has been worn away," this should be connected by supplying the word "also. Just as wrong view, even though worn away by insight,
is not yet eradicated, and is therefore mentioned again for the purpose of showing its abandonment through eradication (*samucchedappahāna*),
so too wrong intention and the rest, although abandoned by insight, are mentioned here again because they have not yet been eradicated.
This meaning is to be applied to all terms such as "wrong intention" (*micchā-saṅkappo*); this is shown by the phrase, "In this way, the method is to be extended to all terms.

And here, [the phrase] "and through right liberation, numerous wholesome states reach fulfillment by development" (*sammā-vimutti-paccayā ca aneke kusalā dhammā bhāvanā-pāripūriṃ gacchantī*) [is included].
In this scriptural passage, "right liberation" (sammāvimutti) refers to the complete liberation from opposing states by way of their total eradication and by way of their subsiding.
Furthermore, because of that [liberation], the eight faculties reach full development within the paths and fruits;
thus, even the faculties such as faith and the rest associated with the path are mentioned here. For it is by way of the path that—
"In the fruits, development is called fulfillment. "In the sense of rejoicing" means in the sense of extreme affection;
for this faculty of mental joy (somanassindriya), having the nature of supreme pleasure, proceeds as if moistening and soaking the associated states.
"In the sense of predominance over the continuity of occurrence" means by way of its sovereignty in sustaining the stream of resultant consciousness.
“‘Evaṃ’ and so forth is the conclusion of the very meaning already stated.
‘Six hundred questions together with the [final] addition’ means five hundred and fifty questions.
And here, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati, having established himself in the ten qualities that make one a protector, [contemplated] the ten kasiṇa bases...”
“Developing [the mind] by way of the ten bases (*āyatana*), having established full understanding (*pariññā*), and fully comprehending the phenomena to be understood,

one abandons the ten wrong views and the ten unwholesome courses of action; being established in the ten wholesome courses of action, desiring to dwell in the ten noble abodes (*ariyāvāsa*), and arousing the ten perceptions,
one realizes the ten grounds for the wearing away of taints (*nijjaravatthu*) through direct knowledge and attains the ten qualities of one beyond training (*asekkhadhamma*).”
He brought the instruction for those bhikkhus to its conclusion and finished the teaching.
He said, "Accepting with joy is 'rejoicing,'" as in the passage: "Rejoicing, saying 'Excellent! Excellent!', they received it with their heads [bowed].

"By that state of being uplifted" means by that state of a joyful mind arising from the teaching as it was delivered; therein, "by the knowledge of the meaning and the knowledge of the Dhamma as they were obtained."

The meaning is as follows: “Reflecting upon this very sutta” means attending to the various phenomena—such as those to be directly known—that appear here and there in this sutta, by way of direct knowledge and so forth.

“…Together with the analytical knowledges... they were established” means that, due to their own possession of the necessary supporting conditions (*upanissaya*) and through the power of the Elder’s teaching, they applied themselves to insight meditation (*vipassanā*) as it had been commenced.
Having exerted themselves, they established themselves in the direct knowledge (abhiññā) that accompanies the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).
This concludes the *Līnatthappakāsanā* (Exposition of the Obscure Meaning) on the commentary to the *Dasuttara-sutta* within the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, the commentary on the *Dīgha-nikāya*.
The Elucidation of the Obscure Meaning in the Commentary on the Pāṭhika Chapter is completed.
The Sub-commentary (Ṭīkā) on the Pāṭhika Chapter is finished.
Explanation of the Concluding Discourse.

"Theravaṃsānvaya" means that which has the lineage (*vaṃsa*), tradition (*paveṇī*), and succession (*anvaya*) of the Elders (*thera*), such as Mahākassapa and others; thus, it refers to the Elder school (*theriya*) among the four great schools (*catumahānikāya*).
"Dasabalaguṇagaṇaparidīpanassa" means because it elucidates the multitude of qualities of the Ten-Powered One, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha.
For this Āgama is found specifically in various places, such as the *Brahmajāla*, the *Mahāpadāna*, and the *Sampasādanīya* suttas.
It proceeds by way of elucidating the qualities of the Buddha. For it was said at the beginning:
"of the quality that brings forth faith. "The essence of the Great Commentary" refers to the essential meaning within the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* of the *Dīgha Nikāya*.
The term "only fifty-nine" includes the word "mere" (*matta*) because it is slightly less than sixty.
The phrase "the essence of the root commentary" (*mūlaṭṭhakathāsāra*) refers once again, by way of conclusion, to that very essence of the *Dīghanikāya-mahā-aṭṭhakathā* which was stated previously.
Alternatively, "the essence of the root commentary" means the essential meaning within the ancient commentaries; by this, he shows:
"Having taken the essential meaning from the *Dīghanikāya-mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, while composing this *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, [I have also drawn upon] the other great Nikāyas..."
"In the root commentaries (*mūla-aṭṭhakathā*), he composed this work precisely by taking the essential meaning that is suitable for application here.
Furthermore, the phrase "of the Mahāvihāravāsins" (meaning "residing in the Great Monastery") should be connected with both the preceding and following words:
"proclaiming the system of the Mahāvihāravāsins," and "of the Mahāvihāravāsins..."

"Having taken the essence of the root commentaries. By that merit: "May the whole world be happy"—this means he dedicates his own merit for the attainment of ultimate happiness by the world including the devas, thinking:
"May every division of the world of beings, from the sense-sphere realm upwards, be made happy through the attainment of the three types of enlightenment as appropriate to each.
Thus, he dedicates his merit so that the entire world may achieve supreme bliss.

In terms of extent, the ninety recitation sections, exceeding twenty-five thousand [units], are completed. The commentary on the *Dīghanikāya* was composed by the Master Dhammapāla with a text of approximately twenty-five thousand units in length.

"For the sake of guarding the accumulation of the wealth of virtue and so forth from the thieves of wrong view and the like, it has been carefully fashioned like a casket. (The text up to this point was written later.)
The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning (*Līnatthappakāsanā*) for the Commentary on the *Dīghanikāya*, titled the *Sumaṅgalavilāsinī*, is completed.
The Sub-commentary (*Ṭīkā*) on the *Dīghanikāya* is finished.
